nodes.name: Thurston's geometrization conjecture (geometrization theorem)
nodes.statement: Every closed, orientable 3-dimensional manifold can be cut along spheres and then along tori, in an essentially unique way, into pieces each of which carries one of eight standard geometric structures.
nodes.by: Grigori Perelman, 2002–2003 (conjectured by William Thurston, 1982)
nodes.note: Perelman's proof uses Ricci flow with surgery, completing a program started by Richard Hamilton. It is the three-dimensional analogue of the uniformization theorem for surfaces.

nodes.name: Thurston's elliptization conjecture
nodes.statement: Every closed 3-dimensional manifold with finite fundamental group is spherical: it carries a metric of constant positive curvature, so it is the 3-sphere divided by a finite group of rotations acting without fixed points.
nodes.by: Grigori Perelman, 2002–2003 (conjectured by William Thurston, 1980)
nodes.note: A special case of geometrization, but Perelman's finite-extinction argument proves it without full geometrization, so it is linked here as related and not as resting on it. It is logically equivalent to the Poincaré conjecture together with the spherical space form conjecture.

nodes.name: Poincaré conjecture
nodes.statement: Every closed, connected 3-dimensional manifold in which every loop can be shrunk to a point is homeomorphic to the 3-sphere.
nodes.by: Grigori Perelman, 2002 and 2003 (posed by Henri Poincaré, 1904)
nodes.note: It is the case of elliptization with trivial fundamental group. Perelman proved it directly, by showing that Ricci flow with surgery dies out in finite time, without needing full geometrization. It is the only Millennium Prize Problem the Clay Institute has declared solved. Perelman declined the prize in 2010.

nodes.name: h-cobordism theorem
nodes.statement: Let W be a smooth, simply connected compact manifold of dimension at least 6 whose boundary is two simply connected pieces M and N, each of which W can be continuously shrunk onto. Then W is diffeomorphic to the cylinder M × [0, 1].
nodes.by: Stephen Smale, 1962
nodes.note: When M and N are 4-dimensional (so W is 5-dimensional), Michael Freedman proved the topological version, and Simon Donaldson showed that the smooth version fails.

nodes.name: Generalized Poincaré conjecture in dimensions 5 and higher
nodes.statement: For every n ≥ 5, a closed smooth n-dimensional manifold that is homotopy equivalent to the n-sphere is homeomorphic to the n-sphere.
nodes.by: Stephen Smale, 1960–61 (first n ≥ 7, then n ≥ 5); independently John Stallings (n ≥ 7, 1960) and Christopher Zeeman (n = 5, 6, 1962)
nodes.note: The standard textbook proof removes a small ball and applies the h-cobordism theorem, which covers n ≥ 6. The case n = 5 uses Kervaire and Milnor's work on exotic spheres. Smale's original 1961 proof used handle decompositions directly. Homeomorphic does not mean diffeomorphic: Milnor's exotic 7-spheres show the smooth version fails in general.

nodes.name: Topological Poincaré conjecture in dimension 4
nodes.statement: Every closed topological 4-dimensional manifold that is homotopy equivalent to the 4-sphere is homeomorphic to the 4-sphere.
nodes.by: Michael Freedman, 1982
nodes.note: Freedman also proved the topological h-cobordism theorem for 5-dimensional h-cobordisms between simply connected 4-manifolds. He received the Fields Medal in 1986.

nodes.name: Smooth 4-dimensional Poincaré conjecture
nodes.statement: Every smooth 4-dimensional manifold homeomorphic to the 4-sphere is also diffeomorphic to it; in other words, the 4-sphere has only one smooth structure.
nodes.by: The case of the generalized Poincaré conjecture left open after Freedman's topological proof, 1982
nodes.note: It is the last open case of the Poincaré conjectures. Most experts expect it to be false, but no counterexample is known.

nodes.name: Uniformization theorem
nodes.statement: Every simply connected Riemann surface is conformally equivalent to one of three: the open unit disk, the complex plane, or the Riemann sphere.
nodes.by: Paul Koebe and Henri Poincaré, 1907
nodes.note: Through universal covers it gives every Riemann surface a metric of constant curvature 1, 0 or −1. Geometrization is its analogue for 3-manifolds.

nodes.name: Carleson's theorem
nodes.statement: The Fourier series of every square-integrable function on the circle converges to the function at almost every point.
nodes.by: Lennart Carleson, 1966
nodes.note: This settled Luzin's conjecture. Kolmogorov had shown in 1923 that it fails for merely integrable functions.

nodes.name: Carleson–Hunt theorem
nodes.statement: For every p > 1, the Fourier series of every function f on the circle with |f|ᵖ integrable converges to f at almost every point.
nodes.by: Richard Hunt, 1968
nodes.note: Carleson had called the extension to p > 1 rather obvious; Hunt carried it out. Kolmogorov's counterexample shows that p = 1 is not allowed.

nodes.name: Atiyah–Singer index theorem
nodes.statement: For an elliptic differential operator on a compact manifold, the analytical index (the number of independent solutions minus the number of independent constraints) equals a topological index computed from characteristic classes.
nodes.by: Michael Atiyah and Isadore Singer, announced 1963, proof published 1968
nodes.note: It contains the Chern–Gauss–Bonnet theorem, the Hirzebruch–Riemann–Roch theorem and the Hirzebruch signature theorem as special cases.

nodes.name: Chern–Gauss–Bonnet theorem
nodes.statement: For a closed, oriented, even-dimensional Riemannian manifold, the Euler characteristic equals the integral of a polynomial in the curvature.
nodes.by: Carl Allendoerfer and André Weil, 1943 (general case, proof using embeddings); intrinsic proof by Shiing-Shen Chern, 1944
nodes.note: It came first and was proved independently. The Atiyah–Singer theorem recovers it from the index of one particular operator.

nodes.name: Sogge's local smoothing conjecture
nodes.statement: For the wave equation in n ≥ 2 space dimensions and every p with 2n/(n−1) ≤ p < ∞, averaging a solution over a time interval makes it smoother in the Lᵖ sense, by any amount less than 1/p of a derivative, than at a single time.
nodes.by: Christopher Sogge, 1991
nodes.note: Larry Guth, Hong Wang and Ruixiang Zhang proved it for n = 2 in 2019.
nodes.claim: OpenAI posted a claimed proof for all n ≥ 2 on 26 October 2026, with a Lean formalization, after a claimed n = 3 case in September 2026. If correct, it would also prove the Bochner–Riesz, restriction and Kakeya conjectures. As of November 2026 OpenAI names no outside reviewer and the claim has not been through peer review.

nodes.name: Bochner–Riesz conjecture
nodes.statement: In ℝⁿ, the Bochner–Riesz means of order δ, a smoothed way of summing a Fourier integral, are bounded on Lᵖ whenever δ > max(n|1/p − 1/2| − 1/2, 0).
nodes.by: Means introduced by Salomon Bochner, 1936; proved in the plane by Lennart Carleson and Per Sjölin, 1972
nodes.note: The condition on δ is known to be necessary for p ≠ 2. Sogge observed that his local smoothing conjecture implies it (Proposition 3.2 of the linked survey).

nodes.name: Stein's restriction conjecture (sphere)
nodes.statement: If g is a bounded function on the unit sphere in ℝⁿ, then the Fourier transform of g times the surface measure lies in Lᵖ(ℝⁿ) for every p > 2n/(n−1).
nodes.by: Elias Stein, 1967; proved in the plane by Charles Fefferman, 1970 (sharpened by Antoni Zygmund, 1974)
nodes.note: Terence Tao proved in 1999 that the Bochner–Riesz conjecture implies it. This is the dual form; Stein's original form bounds the restriction of a function's Fourier transform to the sphere.

nodes.name: Kakeya set conjecture
nodes.statement: Every compact set in ℝⁿ that contains a unit line segment in every direction has Hausdorff dimension n.
nodes.by: Proved for n = 2 by Roy Davies, 1971; for n = 3 by Hong Wang and Joshua Zahl, 2025; open for n ≥ 4
nodes.note: Open in dimension 4 and higher.
nodes.claim: OpenAI posted claimed proofs for n = 4 (24 September 2026, without a Lean proof) and, through local smoothing, for all n (26 October 2026). Neither has been peer reviewed.

nodes.name: Kakeya set conjecture in three dimensions
nodes.statement: Every compact set in ℝ³ that contains a unit line segment in every direction has Hausdorff and Minkowski dimension 3.
nodes.by: Hong Wang and Joshua Zahl, 2025
nodes.note: The proof shows that a union of tubes pointing in many directions must have almost maximal volume. The paper is not yet journal-published but is widely accepted. Hong Wang received the Fields Medal in July 2026 for it.

nodes.name: Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness (global regularity)
nodes.statement: For every smooth, divergence-free starting velocity on ℝ³ that decays fast at infinity, and with no external force, the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations have a smooth solution with finite energy for all time.
nodes.by: Clay Millennium Prize Problem, 2000 (official statement by Charles Fefferman)
nodes.note: One of the seven Millennium Prize Problems.
nodes.claim: On 20 November 2026 Levent Alpöge and Tristan Buckmaster posted a paper, with a Lean formalization, claiming smooth compactly supported data on ℝ³ whose solution without force blows up in finite time. This would make the statement false. The proof depends on a numerical certificate that has not been released, and it has not been independently confirmed. OpenAI's September 2026 claim of blowup with a smooth, compactly supported force concerns the forced version of the problem and does not touch this statement.

nodes.name: Leray's existence theorem for weak solutions
nodes.statement: The three-dimensional Navier–Stokes equations have weak solutions for all time for every finite-energy, divergence-free starting velocity: velocity fields that satisfy the equations in an averaged sense, though perhaps not pointwise.
nodes.by: Jean Leray, 1934
nodes.note: Leray also proved that smooth solutions exist for all time when the starting velocity is small enough. Whether weak solutions are always smooth is the open Navier–Stokes problem.

nodes.name: Invariant subspace problem (Hilbert space)
nodes.statement: Every bounded linear operator on a separable infinite-dimensional complex Hilbert space has a closed invariant subspace other than {0} and the whole space.
nodes.by: Open problem in operator theory; Banach-space counterexamples by Per Enflo (1975, published 1987) and Charles Read (1985)
nodes.note: Per Enflo (arXiv, May 2023, expanded April 2024) and Charles W. Neville (arXiv, July 2023) posted claimed proofs. Neither has been published in a journal or accepted by specialists.

nodes.name: Lomonosov's invariant subspace theorem
nodes.statement: If a bounded operator on a complex Banach space commutes with a nonzero compact operator, then it has a nontrivial closed invariant subspace.
nodes.by: Victor Lomonosov, 1973
nodes.note: It goes further than the Aronszajn–Smith theorem of 1954, which covers compact operators. Its short proof uses the Schauder fixed point theorem.

nodes.name: Gauss–Lucas theorem
nodes.statement: If P is a nonconstant polynomial with complex coefficients, then all roots of its derivative lie within the convex hull of the roots of P, that is, the smallest convex polygon containing the roots of P.
nodes.by: Named after Carl Friedrich Gauss and Félix Lucas
nodes.note: It gives a geometric relation between the roots of a polynomial and the roots of its derivative, and is similar in spirit to Rolle's theorem.

nodes.name: Hermite–Hadamard inequality
nodes.statement: If f is a convex function on the closed interval [a, b] with a < b, then f((a+b)/2) ≤ (1/(b−a)) ∫ from a to b of f(x) dx ≤ (f(a) + f(b))/2.
nodes.by: Named after Charles Hermite and Jacques Hadamard
nodes.note: It has been generalized to higher dimensions, for bounded convex domains and positive convex functions.

nodes.name: Identity theorem
nodes.statement: Let f and g be analytic functions on a domain D, that is, an open and connected subset of ℝ or ℂ. If f = g on a subset S of D that has an accumulation point in D, then f = g on all of D.
nodes.note: An analytic function is therefore determined by its values on any small open neighborhood in D, which is not true for infinitely differentiable real functions in general. The connectedness of D is necessary.

nodes.name: Closed graph theorem
nodes.statement: A linear operator T from a Banach space X to a Banach space Y, defined at every point of X, is continuous if and only if its graph is closed. Since for linear operators between normed spaces continuous means the same as bounded, it is bounded if and only if its graph is closed.
nodes.note: It is equivalent to the open mapping theorem. It fails without the completeness assumption.

nodes.name: Jensen's formula
nodes.statement: Let f be analytic in a region of the complex plane containing the closed disk of radius r > 0 about the origin, with f(0) ≠ 0, and let a₁, …, aₙ be the zeros of f in the interior of the disk, each repeated according to its multiplicity. Then log|f(0)| = −∑ₖ₌₁ⁿ log(r/|aₖ|) + (1/2π) ∫₀^{2π} log|f(re^{iθ})| dθ.
nodes.by: Jensen, 1899
nodes.note: It links the moduli of the zeros inside the disk to the average of log|f| on the boundary circle and can be seen as a generalisation of the mean value property of harmonic functions. It is the starting point of Nevanlinna theory.

nodes.name: Theorema Egregium
nodes.statement: The Gaussian curvature of a surface in 3-dimensional Euclidean space can be determined entirely from angles, distances and their rates of change measured on the surface, without reference to how the surface sits in space. So bending a surface without stretching it (a local isometry) leaves its Gaussian curvature at every point unchanged.
nodes.by: Carl Friedrich Gauss, 1827
nodes.note: Gaussian curvature is therefore an intrinsic invariant of a surface. As a corollary, a sphere and a plane are not locally isometric, so no flat map of the Earth can be perfect.

nodes.name: Maximum modulus principle
nodes.statement: Let f be a holomorphic (complex-differentiable) function on a bounded, connected, open set D in the complex plane. If at some point z₀ of D the value |f(z₀)| is at least |f(z)| for every z in some neighborhood of z₀, then f is constant on D.
nodes.note: It can be viewed as a special case of the open mapping theorem, which says that a nonconstant holomorphic function maps open sets to open sets.

nodes.name: Hartogs's theorem on separate holomorphicity
nodes.statement: If a function F from ℂⁿ to ℂ is analytic in each variable z_i separately, with the other variables held constant, then F is continuous. It follows that F is analytic in the n-variable sense.
nodes.by: Friedrich Hartogs
nodes.note: With the extra hypothesis that F is continuous or bounded, the theorem is much easier to prove and is known as Osgood's lemma. There is no analogue for real variables.

nodes.name: Cauchy condensation test
nodes.statement: Let f(n) be a non-increasing sequence of non-negative real numbers. Then the series ∑ f(n) (n from 1) converges if and only if the series ∑ 2ⁿ f(2ⁿ) (n from 0) converges, and if they converge, the sum of the second is at most twice the sum of the first.
nodes.by: Named after Augustin-Louis Cauchy
nodes.note: It follows from the estimate ∑ f(n) ≤ ∑ 2ⁿ f(2ⁿ) ≤ 2 ∑ f(n), whose proof is patterned after Oresme's proof of the divergence of the harmonic series.

nodes.name: Baire category theorem
nodes.statement: In every completely metrizable topological space, and more generally in every complete pseudometric space, the intersection of countably many dense open sets is again dense.
nodes.by: First proved independently by Osgood, 1897, for the real line and by Baire, 1899, for Euclidean space ℝⁿ; the general statement for completely metrizable spaces was first shown by Hausdorff, 1914
nodes.note: A second form says that every locally compact Hausdorff space has the same property. The theorem is used to prove the open mapping theorem, the closed graph theorem and the uniform boundedness principle.

nodes.name: Stolz–Cesàro theorem
nodes.statement: Let (aₙ) and (bₙ) be sequences of real numbers, where (bₙ) is strictly monotonic and divergent, meaning strictly increasing to +∞ or strictly decreasing to −∞. If the limit of (aₙ₊₁ − aₙ)/(bₙ₊₁ − bₙ) exists and equals l (finite or infinite), then the limit of aₙ/bₙ also exists and equals l.
nodes.by: Otto Stolz, 1885, and Ernesto Cesàro, 1888
nodes.note: It can be viewed as a generalization of the Cesàro mean and as a l'Hôpital's rule for sequences.

nodes.name: Darboux's theorem
nodes.statement: Let θ be a differential 1-form on an n-dimensional manifold such that dθ has constant rank p. If θ∧(dθ)^p = 0 everywhere, there are local coordinates (x_1, …, x_{n−p}, y_1, …, y_p) in which θ = x_1 dy_1 + … + x_p dy_p. If θ∧(dθ)^p ≠ 0 everywhere, there are such coordinates in which θ = x_1 dy_1 + … + x_p dy_p + dx_{p+1}.
nodes.by: Jean Gaston Darboux, who established it as the solution of the Pfaff problem
nodes.note: It is a foundational result in symplectic geometry. One consequence is that any two symplectic manifolds of the same dimension are locally symplectomorphic.

nodes.name: Gaussian integral
nodes.statement: The integral of e^(−x²) over the whole real line, from −∞ to ∞, equals √π.
nodes.by: Abraham de Moivre discovered this type of integral in 1733; Carl Friedrich Gauss published the precise integral in 1809, attributing its discovery to Laplace
nodes.note: With a change of variables it gives the normalizing constant of the normal distribution.

nodes.name: Osserman–Xavier–Fujimoto theorem
nodes.statement: If a minimal surface in three-dimensional Euclidean space is immersed and geodesically complete, then the image of its Gauss map is either a single point, in which case the surface is a plane, or contains all of the sphere except for at most four points.
nodes.by: Frederico Xavier and Hirotaka Fujimoto in the 1980s, improving Robert Osserman's 1959 proof of a conjecture of Louis Nirenberg
nodes.note: The bound of four points is optimal: Konrad Voss showed in the 1960s that for every subset of the sphere missing zero to four points there is a complete immersed minimal surface whose Gauss map has exactly that image.

nodes.name: Squeeze theorem
nodes.statement: If (aₙ) and (cₙ) are sequences of real numbers that both converge to ℓ, and a sequence (bₙ) satisfies aₙ ≤ bₙ ≤ cₙ for every n from some index N on, then (bₙ) also converges to ℓ. Likewise, if g(x) ≤ f(x) ≤ h(x) for all x near a point a and both g(x) and h(x) tend to the same limit L as x tends to a, then f(x) also tends to L.
nodes.by: First used geometrically by Archimedes and Eudoxus; formulated in modern terms by Carl Friedrich Gauss
nodes.note: It is typically used to find the limit of a function by comparing it with two other functions whose limits are known. One example is the limit of sin x / x as x tends to 0, which is used to show that the derivative of the sine function is the cosine function.

nodes.name: Besicovitch inequality
nodes.statement: Give the n-dimensional cube [0,1]ⁿ any Riemannian metric, and for each i let dᵢ be the distance between the i-th pair of opposite faces in that metric. Then the product d₁·d₂·⋯·dₙ is at most the volume of the cube in that metric.
nodes.by: Abram Besicovitch
nodes.note: A more general form holds for an n-dimensional Riemannian manifold with connected boundary that maps smoothly onto the cube with degree 1 on the boundary. The inequality was used to prove systolic inequalities on surfaces.

nodes.name: Lebesgue's dominated convergence theorem
nodes.statement: Let (fₙ) be a sequence of complex-valued measurable functions on a measure space (S, Σ, μ) that converges pointwise to a function f, and suppose there is an integrable function g with |fₙ(x)| ≤ g(x) for all x in S and all n. Then all fₙ and f are integrable, ∫fₙ dμ tends to ∫f dμ, and in fact ∫|fₙ − f| dμ tends to 0.
nodes.by: Named after Lebesgue
nodes.note: The convergence and the domination need only hold almost everywhere. The theorem is one of the main theoretical advantages of Lebesgue integration over Riemann integration.

nodes.name: Fatou's lemma
nodes.statement: Let f₁, f₂, … be measurable functions on a measure space with values in [0, ∞]. Then the integral of their limit inferior is at most the limit inferior of their integrals: ∫ liminf fₙ dμ ≤ liminf ∫ fₙ dμ.
nodes.by: Named after Pierre Fatou
nodes.note: It can be used to prove the Fatou–Lebesgue theorem and Lebesgue's dominated convergence theorem. The inequality can be strict, and it can fail for functions that take negative values without an integrable lower bound.

nodes.name: Chernoff bound
nodes.statement: For a random variable X with moment-generating function M(t) = E(e^{tX}) and any real number a, P(X ≥ a) ≤ M(t)·e^{−ta} for every t > 0, so P(X ≥ a) ≤ inf over t > 0 of M(t)·e^{−ta}. Likewise P(X ≤ a) ≤ M(t)·e^{−ta} for every t < 0, so P(X ≤ a) ≤ inf over t < 0 of M(t)·e^{−ta}.
nodes.by: Herman Chernoff described the method in a 1952 paper, though he attributed it to Herman Rubin; Harald Cramér published an almost identical concept in 1938
nodes.note: It is obtained by applying Markov's inequality to e^{tX}. It is sharper than Markov's or Chebyshev's inequality, and for sums it requires the random variables to be independent.

nodes.name: Weierstrass M-test
nodes.statement: Let (fₙ) be a sequence of real- or complex-valued functions on a set A, and let (Mₙ) be non-negative numbers with |fₙ(x)| ≤ Mₙ for all n ≥ 1 and all x in A. If the series ∑ Mₙ converges, then the series ∑ fₙ(x) converges absolutely and uniformly on A.
nodes.by: Named after Karl Weierstrass
nodes.note: It is analogous to the comparison test for series of numbers. Combined with the uniform limit theorem, it shows that a series of continuous functions on a topological space satisfying the hypothesis converges to a continuous function.

nodes.name: Bochner's tube theorem
nodes.statement: Let ω ⊂ ℝⁿ be a connected open set. Then every function holomorphic on the tube domain Ω = ω + iℝⁿ in ℂⁿ can be extended to a function holomorphic on the convex hull of Ω.
nodes.by: Named after Salomon Bochner
nodes.note: Bochner and Martin (1948) is a classic reference for it. A generalized version for CR functions on tube domains was first proved by Kazlow (1979).

nodes.name: Malgrange–Zerner theorem
nodes.statement: Let P = ℝ + i[0,1), let X be the union over k = 1, …, n of ℝ^{k−1} × P × ℝ^{n−k}, and let W be the convex hull of X. Let f: X → ℂ be locally bounded and infinitely differentiable on X, and suppose that for each k, with the other n − 1 real coordinates fixed, f is holomorphic in the k-th variable z in the interior of P. Then f extends uniquely to a function holomorphic in the interior of W.
nodes.by: Bernard Malgrange, 1961 (unpublished), then Martin Zerner; first published proof in Henry Epstein's lectures (attributed to Broz, Epstein and Glaser)
nodes.note: It generalizes Bochner's tube theorem to tube-like domains whose base is not open. The smoothness assumption was later relaxed to f being continuous on ℝⁿ.

nodes.name: Hairy ball theorem
nodes.statement: There is no non-vanishing continuous tangent vector field on an even-dimensional sphere. For the ordinary 2-sphere, every continuous tangent vector field vanishes at at least one point.
nodes.by: Henri Poincaré for the 2-sphere, 1885; extended to higher even dimensions by L. E. J. Brouwer, 1912
nodes.note: On the torus, whose Euler characteristic is 0, a continuous tangent vector field with no zero does exist.

nodes.name: Generalized Stokes theorem
nodes.statement: Let Ω be an oriented smooth manifold of dimension n with boundary ∂Ω, and let ω be a smooth (n−1)-form on Ω with compact support. Then the integral of ω over the boundary ∂Ω equals the integral of its exterior derivative dω over Ω.
nodes.by: Formulated in its modern form by Élie Cartan, 1945, following earlier work by Vito Volterra, Édouard Goursat and Henri Poincaré
nodes.note: It generalizes the fundamental theorem of calculus, Green's theorem, the classical Stokes' theorem and the divergence theorem.

nodes.name: Lions–Lax–Milgram theorem
nodes.statement: Let H be a Hilbert space, V a normed space, and B : H × V → ℝ a continuous bilinear function. Then two conditions are equivalent. First, for some constant c > 0, the infimum over unit vectors v in V of the supremum over h in H with norm at most 1 of |B(h, v)| is at least c. Second, for each continuous linear functional f on V there is an element h of H with B(h, v) = ⟨f, v⟩ for all v in V.
nodes.by: Named after Jacques-Louis Lions, Peter Lax and Arthur Milgram
nodes.note: It generalizes the Lax–Milgram theorem, which gives conditions for the existence and uniqueness of a weak solution to a boundary value problem.

nodes.name: Chentsov's theorem
nodes.statement: On a statistical manifold, the Fisher information metric is, up to rescaling, the only Riemannian metric that is invariant under sufficient statistics.
nodes.by: Nikolai Chentsov, 1981

nodes.name: Alexandrov's soap bubble theorem
nodes.statement: Let Ω ⊂ ℝⁿ be a bounded connected domain whose boundary Γ = ∂Ω is of class C² and has constant mean curvature. Then Γ is a sphere.
nodes.by: Alexander Danilovich Alexandrov, 1958
nodes.note: In the proof Alexandrov introduced the method of moving planes, later widely used in geometric analysis.

nodes.name: Krylov–Bogolyubov theorem
nodes.statement: Let X be a compact metrizable topological space and F : X → X a continuous map. Then there is a Borel probability measure μ on X that F leaves invariant: μ(F⁻¹(A)) = μ(A) for every Borel set A.
nodes.by: Nikolay Krylov and Nikolay Bogolyubov
nodes.note: A second theorem of the same name gives an invariant probability measure for a time-homogeneous Markov semigroup with the Feller property on a Polish space, when the transition probabilities from some point are uniformly tight.

nodes.name: Propagation of singularities theorem
nodes.statement: Let X be a smooth manifold and P a properly supported pseudodifferential operator on X of class L₁ᵐ(X) (symbols in the Hörmander class S^m_{1,0}), with a real principal symbol p_m that is homogeneous of degree m in ξ. If a distribution u on X satisfies Pu = f, then WF(u) ∖ WF(f), the part of the wavefront set of u outside the wavefront set of f, lies inside the characteristic set of p_m and is invariant under the Hamiltonian flow induced by p_m.
nodes.by: Johannes Jisse Duistermaat and Lars Hörmander, 1972
nodes.note: Also called the Duistermaat–Hörmander theorem, it says that singularities of solutions follow the bicharacteristic flow of the principal symbol of P. Many generalizations have since appeared.

nodes.name: Netto's theorem
nodes.statement: There is no continuous bijection between two smooth manifolds of different dimension. In other words, continuous bijections of smooth manifolds preserve dimension.
nodes.by: Named after Eugen Netto; the case of maps from a higher-dimensional manifold to a one-dimensional manifold was proven by Jacob Lüroth, 1878; Netto, 1878, and Georg Cantor, 1879, gave faulty proofs of the general theorem, which were later corrected
nodes.note: Space-filling curves and Osgood curves show what becomes possible when its conditions are relaxed for maps from one-dimensional spaces to two-dimensional spaces.

nodes.name: Thom's first isotopy lemma
nodes.statement: Let f : M → N be a smooth map between smooth manifolds and S ⊂ M a closed Whitney stratified subset. If f restricted to S is proper and f restricted to each stratum A of S is a submersion, then f restricted to S is a locally trivial fibration.
nodes.by: René Thom
nodes.note: The local trivializations preserve the strata but are generally not smooth. Thom originally considered the case N = ℝ, where the lemma gives an isotopy between fibers.

nodes.name: Thom's second isotopy lemma
nodes.statement: Let f : M → N be a smooth map between smooth manifolds, let S ⊂ M and S' ⊂ N be closed Whitney stratified subsets with f(S) ⊂ S', and let p : S → Z and q : S' → Z be maps to a smooth manifold Z with q∘f = p on S. If f restricted to S and q are proper, q is a submersion on each stratum of S', each stratum of S is mapped by a submersion into a stratum of S', and Thom's condition (a_f) holds for each pair of strata of S, then f is locally trivial over Z: each point z of Z has a neighborhood U with homeomorphisms h₁ : p⁻¹(z) × U → p⁻¹(U) and h₂ : q⁻¹(z) × U → q⁻¹(U) over U such that f∘h₁ = h₂∘(f restricted to p⁻¹(z), times the identity).
nodes.by: René Thom
nodes.note: It is a family version of Thom's first isotopy lemma.

nodes.name: Vitali convergence theorem
nodes.statement: Let (X, 𝒜, μ) be a measure space with μ(X) < ∞, let 1 ≤ p < ∞, let f₁, f₂, … be functions in Lᵖ and let f be a measurable function. Then f lies in Lᵖ and fₙ converges to f in Lᵖ if and only if fₙ converges to f in measure and the functions |fₙ|ᵖ are uniformly integrable, meaning that the largest over n of the integral of |fₙ|ᵖ over the set where |fₙ|ᵖ > M tends to 0 as M → ∞.
nodes.by: Named after Giuseppe Vitali
nodes.note: It generalizes the dominated convergence theorem of Henri Lebesgue. A version for measure spaces of infinite measure adds the condition that for every ε > 0 there is a set of finite measure outside which every integral of |fₙ|ᵖ is below ε.

nodes.name: Wigner's theorem
nodes.statement: Let H and K be complex Hilbert spaces and T a bijection from the rays of H (nonzero vectors up to a nonzero scalar factor) to the rays of K that preserves the quantity |⟨Ψ, Φ⟩| / (‖Ψ‖ ‖Φ‖) for all pairs of rays. Then T is induced by a unitary or antiunitary transformation V : H → K, and if H has dimension at least 2, V is unique up to a phase factor e^{iφ}.
nodes.by: Eugene Wigner, 1931
nodes.note: As a consequence, the representation of a symmetry group on ray space can be lifted to a projective representation or sometimes even an ordinary representation on Hilbert space. If H has dimension 1, uniqueness fails.

nodes.name: Thom–Sebastiani theorem
nodes.statement: Let f(z₁, z₂) = f₁(z₁) + f₂(z₂) be a germ of a function from ℂ^(n₁+n₂) to ℂ, where f₁ and f₂ are germs of holomorphic functions with isolated singularities. Then the vanishing cycle complex of f is isomorphic to the tensor product of those of f₁ and f₂, and the isomorphism respects the monodromy operators: T_f₁ ⊗ T_f₂ = T_f.
nodes.by: Thom and Sebastiani, 1971
nodes.note: The analogue fails in positive characteristic, where Deligne suggested replacing the tensor product by a local convolution product.

nodes.name: Harnack's principle
nodes.statement: Let u₁ ≤ u₂ ≤ … be a sequence of harmonic functions on an open connected subset G of ℝⁿ, nondecreasing at every point. Then the limit either is infinite at every point of G or is finite at every point of G. In the finite case the convergence is uniform on compact sets and the limit is a harmonic function on G.
nodes.note: It is a corollary of Harnack's inequality, and the same argument works for solutions of linear second-order elliptic equations.

nodes.name: Hurwitz's theorem
nodes.statement: Let f_k be holomorphic functions on a connected open set G that converge uniformly on compact subsets of G to a holomorphic function f that is not identically zero on G. If f has a zero of order m at z₀, then for every small enough ρ > 0 and all sufficiently large k (depending on ρ), f_k has exactly m zeros, counted with multiplicity, in the disk |z − z₀| < ρ, and these zeros converge to z₀ as k → ∞.
nodes.by: Named after Adolf Hurwitz
nodes.note: It is used in the proof of the Riemann mapping theorem. The conclusion can fail for a disk that has zeros of f on its boundary.

nodes.name: Kuratowski's intersection theorem
nodes.statement: Let X be a complete metric space. For a subset A of X, let α(A) be the infimum of all r ≥ 0 such that A can be covered by finitely many subsets of X, each of diameter at most r. If A₁ ⊇ A₂ ⊇ … are non-empty closed subsets of X and α(Aₙ) → 0 as n → ∞, then the intersection of all the Aₙ is a non-empty compact set.
nodes.by: Kazimierz Kuratowski, 1930
nodes.note: It generalizes Cantor's intersection theorem by allowing non-compact sets whose non-compactness tends to zero.

nodes.name: Taylor's theorem
nodes.statement: Let k ≥ 1 and let f be a real function of one real variable that is k times differentiable at the point a, with k-th order Taylor polynomial Pₖ(x) = f(a) + f′(a)(x − a) + f″(a)(x − a)²/2! + … + f⁽ᵏ⁾(a)(x − a)ᵏ/k!. Then f(x) − Pₖ(x) = hₖ(x)(x − a)ᵏ with hₖ(x) → 0 as x → a, so the error shrinks faster than (x − a)ᵏ, and Pₖ is the only polynomial of degree at most k with this property.
nodes.by: Brook Taylor stated a version in 1715; an earlier version was mentioned by James Gregory in 1671
nodes.note: Under stronger assumptions on f there are explicit formulas for the error, such as the Lagrange and Cauchy forms of the remainder. It is the starting point of the study of analytic functions.

nodes.name: Morera's theorem
nodes.statement: If f is a continuous, complex-valued function on an open set D in the complex plane, and the integral of f over every closed piecewise C¹ curve in D is 0, then f is holomorphic on D.
nodes.by: Named after Giacinto Morera
nodes.note: The assumption is equivalent to f having an antiderivative on D. The converse holds, for example, when the domain is simply connected; this is Cauchy's integral theorem.

nodes.name: Halanay inequality
nodes.statement: Let t₀ be a real number and τ ≥ 0. Suppose v is a function from [t₀−τ, ∞) to the positive reals such that v′(t) ≤ −αv(t) + β·sup of v(s) over s in [t−τ, t], for all t ≥ t₀, where α and β are constants with α > β > 0. Then there are constants k > 0 and η > 0 such that v(t) ≤ k·e^(−η(t−t₀)) for all t ≥ t₀.
nodes.note: It is a comparison theorem used to analyze the stability of delayed differential equations, for example industrial processes with dead-time and delayed neural networks.

nodes.name: Yan's theorem
nodes.statement: Let (Ω, 𝓕, P) be a probability space, 1 ≤ p < ∞, q the conjugate index of p, B₊ the non-negative bounded random variables, and K a convex subset of L^p that contains 0. Then three conditions are equivalent: (1) for every nonzero non-negative f in L^p there is c > 0 with cf outside the closure of K − B₊; (2) for every event A with P(A) > 0 there is c > 0 with c·I_A outside the closure of K − B₊; (3) there is Z in L^q with Z > 0 almost surely and the supremum of E[ZY] over Y in K finite.
nodes.by: Published by Jia-An Yan and proven for L^1; generalized by Jean-Pascal Ansel to 1 ≤ p < ∞
nodes.note: It is a separation and existence result. In financial mathematics it is used to prove the Kreps-Yan theorem.

nodes.name: Brouwer fixed-point theorem
nodes.statement: Every continuous function from a nonempty compact convex subset of Euclidean space to itself has a fixed point, that is, a point x with f(x) = x. In particular, every continuous function from a closed disk to itself, or from a closed interval to itself, has a fixed point.
nodes.by: Named after L. E. J. Brouwer. Piers Bohl proved the case n = 3 in 1904 and Brouwer proved it in 1909; Jacques Hadamard proved the general case in 1910 (for differentiable maps of the ball), and Brouwer proved it for continuous maps in 1910 or 1911
nodes.note: It is one of the key theorems characterizing the topology of Euclidean spaces and is used in game theory and in the proof of existence of general equilibrium in economics.

nodes.name: Komlós' theorem
nodes.statement: Let ξ₁, ξ₂, … be real-valued random variables on a probability space with sup over n of E|ξₙ| finite. Then there is an integrable random variable ψ and a subsequence (η_k) such that for every further subsequence of (η_k), the averages of its first n terms converge to ψ almost surely as n → ∞.
nodes.by: János Komlós, 1967; generalized by Srishti D. Chatterji, 1970
nodes.note: It is an existence theorem for an integrable random variable, and concerns Cesàro convergence of a subsequence.

nodes.name: Fubini's theorem
nodes.statement: Let X and Y be σ-finite measure spaces, and give X × Y the product measure. If f is a measurable function on X × Y and the integral of |f| over X × Y is finite, then integrating f first over y and then over x, first over x and then over y, or over X × Y at once all give the same value.
nodes.by: Guido Fubini, 1907, proving a conjecture of Beppo Levi; special cases were known earlier to Leonhard Euler and, for bounded measurable functions on a product of intervals, to Henri Lebesgue, 1904
nodes.note: If the integral of |f| is not finite, the two iterated integrals may have different values. Tonelli's theorem is the similar result for non-negative measurable functions.

nodes.name: Rearrangement inequality
nodes.statement: Let x₁ ≤ … ≤ xₙ and y₁ ≤ … ≤ yₙ be real numbers. Then for every permutation σ of 1, …, n, x₁yₙ + x₂yₙ₋₁ + … + xₙy₁ ≤ x₁y_σ(1) + … + xₙy_σ(n) ≤ x₁y₁ + … + xₙyₙ, so pairing the numbers in the same order gives the largest sum and pairing them in opposite order gives the smallest.
nodes.note: The inequality makes no assumption on the signs of the numbers. Many inequalities can be proved with it, such as the arithmetic mean–geometric mean inequality, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and Chebyshev's sum inequality.

nodes.name: Dirichlet's test
nodes.statement: If (aₙ) is a monotonic sequence of real numbers with limit 0, and (bₙ) is a sequence of real or complex numbers with bounded partial sums, then the series ∑ aₙbₙ converges.
nodes.by: Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet, published posthumously in 1862
nodes.note: It is especially useful for proving conditional convergence. The alternating series test is a special case.

nodes.name: Monotone convergence theorem
nodes.statement: Let f₁ ≤ f₂ ≤ f₃ ≤ … be non-negative measurable functions on a measure space, with values allowed to be +∞, increasing at every point. Then their pointwise supremum f is measurable, and the integral of f equals the limit of the integrals of the fₖ, which is also their supremum. Both sides may be +∞, and one is finite exactly when the other is.
nodes.by: Henri Lebesgue and Beppo Levi; Levi proved it in 1906 as a slight generalization of an earlier result by Lebesgue
nodes.note: Fatou's lemma and the dominated convergence theorem follow from it. In its simplest form the theorem says that a non-decreasing sequence of real numbers that is bounded above converges to its supremum.

nodes.name: Helmholtz decomposition theorem
nodes.statement: Every continuously differentiable vector field F on a domain in ℝⁿ that is smooth, or that decays sufficiently rapidly at infinity, can be written as F = G + R. Here G = −∇Φ is the gradient of a twice continuously differentiable scalar potential Φ, so G is curl-free, and R has divergence zero.
nodes.by: First described in three dimensions by George Gabriel Stokes, 1849; Hermann von Helmholtz published his paper in 1858
nodes.note: It is named after Hermann von Helmholtz and is also called the fundamental theorem of vector calculus. If arbitrary growth at infinity is allowed, a decomposition still exists in the distributional sense but is no longer unique.

nodes.name: Integral test for convergence
nodes.statement: Let N be an integer and f a function defined on [N, ∞) that is monotonically decreasing. Then the series ∑ f(n) from n = N to ∞ converges to a real number if and only if the improper integral of f(x) from N to ∞ is finite. In particular, if the integral diverges, the series diverges.
nodes.by: Colin Maclaurin and Augustin-Louis Cauchy
nodes.note: It is also known as the Maclaurin–Cauchy test. The function need not be positive, since a negative decreasing function makes both the series and the integral diverge.

nodes.name: ∂∂̄ lemma
nodes.statement: Let (X, ω) be a compact Kähler manifold and α a closed complex differential form of bidegree (p, q), with p, q ≥ 1, whose de Rham cohomology class is zero. Then there is a form β of bidegree (p−1, q−1) such that α = i∂∂̄β, where ∂ and ∂̄ are the Dolbeault operators of X.
nodes.note: It follows from Hodge theory and the Kähler identities on a compact Kähler manifold. In bidegree (1,1) it lets Kähler forms in the same cohomology class be described by a single function, the Kähler potential.

nodes.name: Transversality theorem
nodes.statement: Let F: X × S → Y be a smooth map of finite-dimensional smooth manifolds, where only X has a boundary, giving the family of maps f_s(x) = F(x, s), and let Z be a submanifold of Y without boundary. If both F and its restriction to the boundary are transverse to Z, then for almost every s in S both f_s and its restriction to the boundary of X are transverse to Z.
nodes.by: Named after René Thom; Thom's original paper on the jet transversality version appeared in 1956
nodes.note: A map is transverse to Z when, at each point sent into Z, the image of its derivative and the tangent space of Z together span the tangent space of Y. Together with the Pontryagin–Thom construction, the theorem is the technical heart of cobordism theory.

nodes.name: Dimension doubling theorem
nodes.statement: Let W be a Brownian motion in dimension d ≥ 2, and for a set A ⊂ [0, ∞) let W(A) be the set of its values at times in A. Then with probability 1, for every set A at once, the Hausdorff dimension of W(A) is twice the Hausdorff dimension of A.
nodes.by: Henry P. McKean Jr., 1955, for each fixed set; Robert Kaufman, 1969, for all sets simultaneously
nodes.note: McKean's theorem gives the same equality almost surely for each fixed set A, with the exceptional null set depending on A. Kaufman's refinement holds for all A at once, so it also applies to random sets.

nodes.name: Hadamard factorization theorem
nodes.statement: Every entire function f of finite order ρ can be written as f(z) = zᵐ · e^(Q(z)) · ∏ₙ E_p(z/aₙ), where m is the order of the zero of f at 0, the aₙ are the nonzero roots of f repeated according to multiplicity, E_p(z) = (1 − z) · e^(z + z²/2 + … + zᵖ/p), p is the smallest non-negative integer for which ∑ 1/|aₙ|^(p+1) converges, and Q is a polynomial. The genus g, the larger of p and the degree of Q, satisfies g ≤ ρ ≤ g + 1.
nodes.by: Named after Jacques Hadamard
nodes.note: It extends the fundamental theorem of algebra and is closely related to the Weierstrass factorization theorem, which does not restrict to entire functions of finite order. It can be used to prove special cases of Picard's little theorem.

nodes.name: Riesz's lemma
nodes.statement: Let Y be a closed vector subspace of a normed space X with Y not equal to X. Then for every α < 1 there is a vector u of length 1 in X whose distance from every point of Y is at least α. If X is a reflexive Banach space, this also holds for α = 1.
nodes.by: Named after Frigyes Riesz
nodes.note: It can be seen as a substitute for orthogonality when the normed space is not an inner product space. It shows that a normed space is finite-dimensional if and only if its closed unit ball is compact.

nodes.name: Radon–Nikodym theorem
nodes.statement: Let μ and ν be two σ-finite measures on the same measurable space (X, Σ). If ν is absolutely continuous with respect to μ, then there is a Σ-measurable function f : X → [0, ∞) such that ν(A) = ∫_A f dμ for every measurable set A.
nodes.by: Johann Radon, 1913 (for ℝⁿ); Otto Nikodym, 1930 (general case)
nodes.note: The function f is called the Radon–Nikodym derivative dν/dμ and is unique up to a μ-null set. In probability theory it gives the probability density function of a random variable.

nodes.name: Egorov's theorem
nodes.statement: Let f₁, f₂, … be measurable functions on a measure space, with values in a separable metric space, and let A be a measurable set of finite measure on which the sequence converges almost everywhere to a function f. Then for every ε > 0 there is a measurable subset B of A with measure less than ε such that the sequence converges to f uniformly on the part of A outside B.
nodes.by: Carlo Severini, 1910; independently Dmitri Egorov, 1911
nodes.note: The condition that A has finite measure is necessary: the indicator functions of the intervals [n, n+1] converge to zero everywhere on the real line, but not uniformly outside any set of finite measure. The theorem can be used to prove Lusin's theorem for integrable functions.

nodes.name: Hopf theorem
nodes.statement: Let M be a compact, connected, oriented manifold of dimension n, and let f and g be continuous maps from M to the n-sphere. Then f and g have the same topological degree if and only if f and g are homotopic.
nodes.by: Named after Heinz Hopf
nodes.note: It says that the topological degree is the only homotopy invariant of continuous maps to spheres.

nodes.name: Kaplansky density theorem
nodes.statement: If A is a self-adjoint algebra of bounded operators on a Hilbert space H, then every operator in the unit ball of the strong-operator closure of A lies in the strong-operator closure of the unit ball of A. Moreover, every self-adjoint operator in the unit ball of the strong-operator closure of A lies in the strong-operator closure of the self-adjoint operators in the unit ball of A.
nodes.by: Irving Kaplansky
nodes.note: It is a fundamental approximation theorem for the strong operator topology. The results also hold for a ball of any radius r > 0 in place of the unit ball.

nodes.name: Dirichlet–Jordan test
nodes.statement: Let f be a complex-valued function with period 2π that is integrable and of bounded variation on [−π, π]. Then at every x the partial sums of its Fourier series converge to the midpoint of the left and right limits of f at x, which equals f(x) where f is continuous. If f is continuous at every point, the convergence is uniform.
nodes.by: Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet, 1829, for piecewise monotone functions; extended by Camille Jordan in the late 19th century to functions of bounded variation
nodes.note: It is one of many conditions for the convergence of Fourier series. A version for Fourier integrals on the real line goes back to Joseph Fourier.

nodes.name: Doob–Dynkin lemma
nodes.statement: Let T be a function from a set Ω to a measurable space (Ω', 𝒜'), and let f be a function from Ω to [0,1]. Then f is measurable with respect to the σ-algebra generated by T (and the Borel sets of [0,1]) if and only if f = g∘T for some 𝒜'-measurable function g from Ω' to [0,1].
nodes.by: Named after Joseph L. Doob and Eugene Dynkin
nodes.note: It is also known as the factorization lemma. It lets conditioning on a random variable be replaced by conditioning on the σ-algebra that the variable generates.

nodes.name: Sobczyk's theorem
nodes.statement: If a separable Banach space X contains the space c₀ of sequences converging to zero as a subspace, then there is a projection from X onto c₀ with norm at most 2.
nodes.by: Andrew Sobczyk, 1941
nodes.note: The theorem is not true for general non-separable Banach spaces. An extension version says that if X is separable and Y is a subspace of X, every bounded linear operator S from Y into c₀ extends to an operator T on all of X with ‖T‖ ≤ 2‖S‖.

nodes.name: Schwartz kernel theorem
nodes.statement: Let X and Y be open sets in ℝⁿ, where test functions are smooth functions with compact support. Every distribution k on X × Y defines a continuous linear map K from the test functions on Y to the distributions on X, informally ⟨Kv, u⟩ = ∫∫ k(x,y) v(y) u(x) dy dx, and conversely every such continuous linear map arises in this way from one and only one distribution k on X × Y, called its kernel.
nodes.by: Laurent Schwartz, 1952
nodes.note: It says that Schwartz distributions have a two-variable theory that includes all reasonable bilinear forms on the space of test functions. Grothendieck developed much of the theory of nuclear spaces while investigating it.

nodes.name: Pyjama problem
nodes.statement: For every ε > 0, however small, the plane can be covered by finitely many rotated copies of the stripe pattern E(ε). Here E(ε) is the set of complex numbers z whose real part lies strictly within ε of an integer, a repeating pattern of stripes of width 2ε.
nodes.by: Posed by Alex Iosevich, Mihail Kolountzakis and Máté Matolcsi, 2006; answered in the affirmative by Freddie Manners, 2015
nodes.note: Manners used an analogy with Furstenberg's ×2, ×3 theorem. Noah Kravitz and James Leng later gave an explicit upper bound on the number of rotations needed, while lower bounds beyond the trivial volume bound remain open.

nodes.name: De Rham theorem
nodes.statement: On a manifold, the map from de Rham cohomology to singular cohomology with real coefficients, given by integrating differential forms over smooth singular chains, is an isomorphism of rings.
nodes.note: It gives an explicit isomorphism between the two cohomologies, connecting analysis and topology more directly. With coefficients in another group, such as the integers, no such isomorphism holds in general.

nodes.name: Poincaré–Hopf theorem
nodes.statement: Let M be a compact differentiable manifold of dimension n and v a continuous vector field on M whose zeros are all isolated; if M has a boundary, v must point in the outward normal direction along it and have no zeros there. Then the sum of the indices of v at its zeros equals the Euler characteristic of M, where the index at a zero x is the degree of the map v/‖v‖ from the boundary of a small ball around x to the (n−1)-sphere.
nodes.by: Henri Poincaré proved the 2-dimensional case; Heinz Hopf proved it in general
nodes.note: The hairy ball theorem is a special case: an even-dimensional sphere has no continuous vector field without zeros.

nodes.name: Whitney embedding theorem
nodes.statement: Every smooth real m-dimensional manifold that is Hausdorff and second-countable, with m > 0, can be smoothly embedded in the 2m-dimensional Euclidean space ℝ²ᵐ.
nodes.by: Hassler Whitney
nodes.note: 2m is the best linear bound, because the real projective spaces of dimension m cannot be embedded in ℝ²ᵐ⁻¹ when m is a power of two. A weaker version says that a continuous map from an n-dimensional manifold to an m-dimensional manifold can be approximated by a smooth embedding when m > 2n.

nodes.name: Künneth theorem
nodes.statement: For topological spaces X and Y and singular homology with coefficients in a field F, in every degree k the homology of the product is a direct sum of tensor products: H_k(X×Y; F) ≅ ⊕_{i+j=k} H_i(X; F) ⊗ H_j(Y; F). For coefficients in a principal ideal domain R, such as the integers, there is instead a natural short exact sequence 0 → ⊕_{i+j=k} H_i(X; R) ⊗_R H_j(Y; R) → H_k(X×Y; R) → ⊕_{i+j=k−1} Tor₁^R(H_i(X; R), H_j(Y; R)) → 0, which splits, though not canonically.
nodes.by: Named after Hermann Künneth
nodes.note: A consequence is that the generating function of the Betti numbers of X × Y is the product of those of X and Y. Künneth theorems of the same form hold in many other homology and cohomology theories, such as complex K-theory.

nodes.name: Mittag-Leffler's theorem
nodes.statement: Let U be an open set in ℂ and E ⊂ U a subset whose limit points, if any, lie on the boundary of U. For each a in E let p_a(z) be a polynomial in 1/(z−a) without constant term, of the form ∑ c_{a,n}/(z−a)^n for n = 1, ..., N_a. Then there is a meromorphic function f on U whose poles are exactly the elements of E and such that f(z) − p_a(z) has only a removable singularity at each a in E. Any other meromorphic function g on U with these properties is f + h for some holomorphic function h on U.
nodes.by: Gösta Mittag-Leffler, who published versions of the theorem in 1876 and 1884
nodes.note: It can be used to express any meromorphic function as a sum of partial fractions. It is a sister to the Weierstrass factorization theorem, which concerns holomorphic functions with prescribed zeros.

nodes.name: Rademacher's theorem
nodes.statement: If U is an open subset of ℝⁿ and f: U → ℝᵐ is locally Lipschitz continuous, then f is differentiable almost everywhere in U. That is, the points of U where f is not differentiable form a set of Lebesgue measure zero.
nodes.by: Named after Hans Rademacher; one of the standard proofs was found by Charles Morrey

nodes.name: Weierstrass factorization theorem
nodes.statement: Let f be an entire function with a zero of order m ≥ 0 at 0, and let a₁, a₂, ... be its non-zero zeros, repeated according to multiplicity. Then there are an entire function g and integers p_n ≥ 0 such that f(z) = zᵐ e^{g(z)} ∏ E_{p_n}(z/a_n), where E₀(z) = 1 − z and E_p(z) = (1 − z)·exp(z + z²/2 + ... + z^p/p).
nodes.by: Named after Karl Weierstrass
nodes.note: It extends the fundamental theorem of algebra, which factors every polynomial into linear factors. For entire functions of finite order, the p_n can be taken equal and g is a polynomial (Hadamard factorization).

nodes.name: Cartwright's theorem
nodes.statement: For every integer p ≥ 1 there is a constant C_p such that every p-valent holomorphic function f(z) = ∑ a_n zⁿ on the disc |z| < 1 satisfies |f(z)| ≤ C_p · max(|a_0|, ..., |a_p|) / (1 − r)^(2p) for all z with |z| ≤ r < 1. Here p-valent means the function takes the same value no more than p times.
nodes.by: Mary Cartwright
nodes.note: It estimates the maximum modulus of a holomorphic function that takes the same value no more than p times on the unit disc.

nodes.name: Schwarz lemma
nodes.statement: Let D be the open unit disk {z : |z| < 1} in the complex plane, and let f: D → ℂ be holomorphic with f(0) = 0 and |f(z)| ≤ 1 on D. Then |f(z)| ≤ |z| for all z in D and |f′(0)| ≤ 1, and if |f(z)| = |z| for some non-zero z or |f′(0)| = 1, then f(z) = az for some complex number a with |a| = 1.
nodes.by: Named after Hermann Amandus Schwarz; the proof first appears in a paper by Carathéodory, where it is attributed to Erhard Schmidt
nodes.note: The Schwarz lemma has opened several branches of complex geometry and is an essential tool in the use of geometric PDE methods in complex geometry.

nodes.name: Pólya's shire theorem
nodes.statement: Let f be a meromorphic function on the complex plane with a nonempty set P of poles, and let E be the set of all zeros of all the successive derivatives of f. If f has only one pole, E has no limit points; if P has at least two points, the limit points of E are exactly the points on the edges of the Voronoi diagram determined by P.
nodes.by: Named after George Pólya
nodes.note: It describes the asymptotic distribution of the zeros of successive derivatives of a meromorphic function and has applications in Nevanlinna theory. The set of limit points does not depend on the orders of the poles.

nodes.name: Tietze extension theorem
nodes.statement: Let X be a normal topological space and A a closed subset of X. Every continuous function f from A to the real numbers can be extended to a continuous function F from X to the real numbers, and if f is bounded, F can be chosen with the same bound.
nodes.by: Special case for finite-dimensional real vector spaces by L. E. J. Brouwer and Henri Lebesgue; extended to all metric spaces by Heinrich Tietze; proved for normal topological spaces by Pavel Urysohn
nodes.note: Also known as the Tietze–Urysohn–Brouwer extension theorem. It is equivalent to Urysohn's lemma and applies to all metric spaces and all compact Hausdorff spaces, since these are normal.

nodes.name: Eilenberg–Zilber theorem
nodes.statement: For topological spaces X and Y there are chain maps F from the chain complex of X×Y to the tensor product of the chain complexes of X and Y, and G in the opposite direction, natural in X and Y, such that FG is the identity and GF is chain-homotopic to the identity. Consequently both complexes have the same homology, and this holds for simplicial or singular chain complexes.
nodes.by: Samuel Eilenberg and Joseph A. Zilber, 1953
nodes.note: It links the homology groups of a product space X×Y to those of X and Y, and is a key ingredient in establishing the Künneth theorem.

nodes.name: Riesz representation theorem
nodes.statement: Let H be a Hilbert space over the real or the complex numbers. For every continuous linear functional φ on H there is exactly one vector f in H with φ(z) = ⟨f | z⟩ for all z in H, and the norm of φ equals the length of f; so H and its continuous dual space are isometrically isomorphic when the scalars are real and isometrically anti-isomorphic when they are complex.
nodes.by: Often attributed simultaneously to Frigyes Riesz and Maurice René Fréchet, 1907
nodes.note: The existence of the representing vector uses the Hilbert projection theorem and so needs completeness. The norm formula alone holds in every inner product space.

nodes.name: Lusin's theorem
nodes.statement: Let f be a measurable function from an interval [a, b] to the complex numbers. Then for every ε > 0 there is a compact set E ⊆ [a, b] with measure greater than b − a − ε such that f restricted to E is continuous. Conversely, an almost-everywhere finite function on [a, b] that agrees with a continuous function except on a set of measure less than ε, for every ε > 0, is measurable.
nodes.by: Named for Nikolai Luzin
nodes.note: In J. E. Littlewood's informal formulation, every measurable function is nearly continuous.

nodes.name: Heine's theorem
nodes.statement: Let f be a real-valued function of one real variable and a an accumulation point of its domain. The limit of f(x) as x approaches a exists and equals L if and only if f(xₙ) converges to L for every sequence xₙ of points of the domain that converges to a with xₙ ≠ a for all n.
nodes.by: Named after Eduard Heine
nodes.note: It lets many properties of limits of functions be derived from the corresponding properties of limits of sequences.

nodes.name: Argument principle
nodes.statement: Let f be meromorphic inside and on a simple closed contour C, oriented counter-clockwise, with no zeros or poles on C. Then the contour integral of f′/f around C, divided by 2πi, equals Z − P, where Z and P are the numbers of zeros and poles of f inside C, counted with multiplicity and order.
nodes.by: Augustin-Louis Cauchy: a similar theorem about zeros only was presented in 1831, and a paper covering both zeros and poles appeared in 1855
nodes.note: A more general form uses winding numbers for a closed curve contractible to a point in an open set where f is meromorphic.

nodes.name: Besicovitch covering theorem
nodes.statement: For each dimension N there is a number c_N, depending only on N, with the following property. If F is a collection of open balls in ℝᴺ that covers a bounded set E so that every point of E is the center of some ball of F, then F contains c_N subcollections, each made of balls that do not overlap, whose balls together cover E.
nodes.by: Named after Abram Samoilovitch Besicovitch
nodes.note: An equivalent form says that some subcollection of F still covers E while every point lies in at most b_N of its balls, for a constant b_N depending only on N. It is used to prove maximal inequalities for general Borel measures.

nodes.name: Freedman's classification
nodes.statement: Every symmetric unimodular bilinear form over the integers is the intersection form of a simply connected, oriented, closed topological 4-manifold. If the form is even (only even entries on the diagonal), exactly one such manifold exists up to orientation-preserving homeomorphism; if it is odd, exactly two exist, and they have different Kirby–Siebenmann invariants.
nodes.by: Michael Freedman, 1982
nodes.note: It classifies simply connected oriented closed topological 4-manifolds up to orientation-preserving homeomorphism by their intersection form and Kirby–Siebenmann invariant. The case of the empty form gives the topological Poincaré conjecture in four dimensions.

nodes.name: Ryll-Nardzewski fixed-point theorem
nodes.statement: Let E be a normed vector space and K a nonempty convex subset of E that is compact under the weak topology. Then every group (equivalently, every semigroup) of affine isometries of K has at least one fixed point, that is, a point fixed by every map in the set.
nodes.by: Announced by Czesław Ryll-Nardzewski; Namioka and Asplund later gave a proof based on a different approach, and Ryll-Nardzewski himself gave a complete proof in the original spirit
nodes.note: The theorem yields the existence of a Haar measure on compact groups.

nodes.name: Uniform boundedness principle
nodes.statement: Let F be a family of continuous linear operators from a Banach space X to a normed space Y. Then the supremum of ‖T(x)‖ over T in F is finite for every x in X if and only if the supremum of the operator norms ‖T‖ over T in F is finite.
nodes.by: Stefan Banach and Hugo Steinhaus, 1927; also proved independently by Hans Hahn
nodes.note: It is also called the Banach–Steinhaus theorem. Together with the Hahn–Banach theorem and the open mapping theorem it is considered a cornerstone of functional analysis.

nodes.name: Chebyshev's sum inequality
nodes.statement: If the real numbers satisfy a₁ ≥ a₂ ≥ … ≥ aₙ and b₁ ≥ b₂ ≥ … ≥ bₙ, then the average of the products aₖbₖ is at least the product of the average of the aₖ and the average of the bₖ. If instead a₁ ≤ a₂ ≤ … ≤ aₙ and b₁ ≥ b₂ ≥ … ≥ bₙ, the inequality is reversed.
nodes.by: Named after Pafnuty Chebyshev
nodes.note: There is also a continuous version for integrable functions on an interval [a, b] that are both non-increasing or both non-decreasing.

nodes.name: Cauchy formula for repeated integration
nodes.statement: Let f be a continuous function on the real line, a a real number and n a positive integer. Then for every x, integrating f n times in succession, each time starting from a, gives the same result as the single integral (1/(n−1)!) ∫ from a to x of (x−t)ⁿ⁻¹ f(t) dt.
nodes.by: Augustin-Louis Cauchy, 1823
nodes.note: It compresses n antiderivatives of a function into a single integral. Replacing n by a non-integer and the factorial by the gamma function gives the Riemann–Liouville integral of fractional calculus.

nodes.name: Faà di Bruno's formula
nodes.statement: If f and g can be differentiated n times, the nth derivative of f(g(x)) is a sum with one term for each way π of splitting the set {1, …, n} into blocks. Each term is f^(|π|)(g(x)) multiplied by the product of g^(|B|)(x) over the blocks B, where |π| is the number of blocks, |B| is the size of block B, and f^(m) is the mth derivative of f.
nodes.by: Named after Faà di Bruno, 1855; first stated by Louis François Antoine Arbogast in a calculus textbook, 1800
nodes.note: It generalizes the chain rule to higher derivatives. When f is the exponential function, the formula expresses the nth derivative of e^g(x) through the complete exponential Bell polynomials.

nodes.name: Parseval's theorem
nodes.statement: Let f be a real-valued function on [−π, π] such that f and f² are integrable, with Fourier series f(x) ~ ½a₀ + ∑ₙ₌₁^∞ (aₙ cos(nx) + bₙ sin(nx)). Then (1/π) ∫₋π^π f(x)² dx = ½a₀² + ∑ₙ₌₁^∞ (aₙ² + bₙ²).
nodes.by: Marc-Antoine Parseval, 1799, as a theorem about series; later applied to Fourier series
nodes.note: In its general form it says that the Fourier transform is unitary: the integral of the square of a function equals the integral of the square of its transform. The most general version of this property is called the Plancherel theorem.

nodes.name: Freudenthal suspension theorem
nodes.statement: Let X be an n-connected pointed space (a pointed CW-complex or pointed simplicial set). The map X → Ω(ΣX), where Ω is the loop functor and Σ the reduced suspension functor, induces a map π_k(X) → π_k(Ω(ΣX)) on homotopy groups. This map is an isomorphism if k ≤ 2n and an epimorphism if k = 2n + 1.
nodes.by: Hans Freudenthal, 1937
nodes.note: It is the fundamental result leading to the stabilization of homotopy groups and ultimately to stable homotopy theory. It is a corollary of the homotopy excision theorem.

nodes.name: Hellinger–Toeplitz theorem
nodes.statement: An everywhere-defined symmetric operator on a Hilbert space is bounded. Here an operator A is symmetric if ⟨Ax|y⟩ = ⟨x|Ay⟩ for all x, y in its domain.
nodes.by: Named after Ernst David Hellinger and Otto Toeplitz
nodes.note: It is an immediate corollary of the closed graph theorem. It implies that unbounded self-adjoint operators, such as the energy operator in quantum mechanics, cannot be defined on the whole Hilbert space.

nodes.name: Arzelà–Ascoli theorem
nodes.statement: Let a sequence of real-valued continuous functions be defined on a closed and bounded interval [a, b]. If the sequence is uniformly bounded (one number M bounds every function at every point) and uniformly equicontinuous, then some subsequence converges uniformly; conversely, if every subsequence has a uniformly convergent subsequence, then the sequence is uniformly bounded and equicontinuous.
nodes.by: Giulio Ascoli proved a weak form with the sufficient condition, 1883–1884; Cesare Arzelà proved the necessary condition and gave the first clear presentation, 1895
nodes.note: It underlies the proofs of the Peano existence theorem, Montel's theorem and the Peter–Weyl theorem. Fréchet generalized it in 1906 to functions on a compact metric space.

nodes.name: Commutative Gelfand–Naimark theorem
nodes.statement: Let A be a commutative C*-algebra and let X be its spectrum: the space of non-zero *-homomorphisms from A to ℂ, with the weak-* topology. Then the Gelfand map, which sends each element a of A to the function φ ↦ φ(a) on X, is an isometric *-isomorphism from A onto C₀(X), the algebra of continuous complex-valued functions on X that vanish at infinity.
nodes.by: Named after I. M. Gelfand; also called the Gelfand–Naimark representation theorem
nodes.note: For a general commutative Banach algebra the Gelfand representation is neither injective nor surjective. The theorem gives the continuous functional calculus for normal elements of a C*-algebra and generalizes diagonalizing a normal matrix.

nodes.name: Symmetry of second derivatives (Schwarz's theorem)
nodes.statement: Let f be a real-valued function on a set Ω ⊆ ℝⁿ, and let p be a point such that some neighbourhood of p lies in Ω and f has continuous second partial derivatives on that neighbourhood. Then for all i and j in {1, …, n}, ∂²f/∂xᵢ∂xⱼ(p) = ∂²f/∂xⱼ∂xᵢ(p), so taking the two partial derivatives in either order gives the same value at p.
nodes.by: First rigorous proof by Schwarz, six years after Lindelöf's 1867 counterexample; flawed proofs had been proposed since Euler and Clairaut, 1740
nodes.note: Equivalently, the Hessian matrix of second partial derivatives is symmetric. Some condition is needed: in 1867 Lindelöf gave a counterexample where the mixed derivatives are not equal.

nodes.name: Runge's theorem
nodes.statement: Let K be a closed subset of the Riemann sphere ℂ ∪ {∞}, let f be holomorphic on an open set containing K, and let A be a set containing at least one point from every connected component of the complement of K in ℂ ∪ {∞}. Then there is a sequence of rational functions that converges uniformly to f on K and whose poles all lie in A. In particular, if K is a compact subset of ℂ whose complement in ℂ is connected, f can be approximated uniformly on K by polynomials.
nodes.by: Carl Runge, 1885
nodes.note: The set A can be chosen freely as long as it meets every connected component of the complement of K. Mergelyan's theorem relaxes the condition on f in the polynomial case.

nodes.name: Lie's third theorem
nodes.statement: Every finite-dimensional Lie algebra 𝔤 over the real numbers is the Lie algebra of some Lie group G.
nodes.by: Named after Sophus Lie, who proved the infinitesimal version; the global form was proved by Élie Cartan
nodes.note: It is part of the Lie group–Lie algebra correspondence. One classical proof uses Ado's theorem, which says every finite-dimensional Lie algebra can be represented by matrices.

nodes.name: Schottky's theorem
nodes.statement: If f is holomorphic in the open unit disk and never takes the values 0 or 1, then |f(z)| can be bounded in terms of z and f(0) alone. Ahlfors gave the explicit bound log|f(z)| ≤ (1+|z|)/(1−|z|) · (7 + max(0, log|f(0)|)).
nodes.by: Schottky, 1904; explicit bound by Ahlfors, 1938
nodes.note: It is a quantitative version of Picard's theorem.

nodes.name: Brezis–Gallouët inequality
nodes.statement: Let Ω ⊂ ℝ² be the interior or the exterior of a bounded domain with regular boundary, or ℝ² itself. Then there is a real constant C depending only on Ω such that for every u in the Sobolev space H²(Ω) that is not almost everywhere 0, the essential supremum of |u| is at most C·a·(1 + √(log(1 + b/a))), where a and b are the H¹ and H² norms of u on Ω.
nodes.by: Named after Haïm Brezis and Thierry Gallouët
nodes.note: It shows that a sufficiently smooth function of two variables is essentially bounded, with a bound that depends only logarithmically on the second derivatives. It is used in the study of partial differential equations.

nodes.name: Peter–Weyl theorem
nodes.statement: For a compact group G, the matrix coefficients of the irreducible representations of G are dense in the space C(G) of continuous complex-valued functions on G (with the uniform norm) and hence in L²(G), and every unitary representation of G on a complex Hilbert space splits into an orthogonal direct sum of irreducible finite-dimensional unitary representations. Moreover, L²(G) is the closed orthogonal direct sum of all irreducible unitary representations, each occurring as many times as its dimension d; if one representative π of each isomorphism class and an orthonormal basis e₁, …, e_d for it are chosen, the functions √d·uᵢⱼ with uᵢⱼ(g) = ⟨π(g)eⱼ, eᵢ⟩ form an orthonormal basis of L²(G).
nodes.by: Hermann Weyl with his student Fritz Peter, 1927
nodes.note: It generalizes facts about the decomposition of the regular representation of a finite group found by Frobenius and Schur. For the group of unit complex numbers it reduces to a standard result on Fourier series.

nodes.name: Marden's theorem
nodes.statement: Suppose the three zeroes z₁, z₂, z₃ of a third-degree polynomial p(z) with complex coefficients are non-collinear. Then there is a unique ellipse inscribed in the triangle with these vertices and tangent to its sides at their midpoints (the Steiner inellipse), and the foci of that ellipse are the zeroes of the derivative of p.
nodes.by: Jörg Siebeck, 1864; named after Morris Marden, who wrote about it in 1945
nodes.note: It locates the zeroes of the derivative more precisely than the Gauss–Lucas theorem, which only says they lie within the triangle.

nodes.name: Hahn decomposition theorem
nodes.statement: For any measurable space (X,Σ) and any signed measure μ defined on the σ-algebra Σ, there exist two Σ-measurable sets P and N with P ∪ N = X and P ∩ N = ∅, such that μ(E) ≥ 0 for every measurable E ⊆ P and μ(E) ≤ 0 for every measurable E ⊆ N. The decomposition is essentially unique: for any other such pair (P',N'), the symmetric differences P △ P' and N △ N' are μ-null sets, meaning every measurable subset of them has measure zero.
nodes.by: Named after the Austrian mathematician Hans Hahn
nodes.note: It implies the Jordan decomposition: every signed measure is in exactly one way the difference μ⁺ − μ⁻ of two positive measures, at least one of them finite, where μ⁺ is zero on measurable subsets of N and μ⁻ is zero on measurable subsets of P for any Hahn decomposition (P,N).

nodes.name: Lumer–Phillips theorem
nodes.statement: Let A be a linear operator defined on a linear subspace D(A) of a Banach space X. Then A generates a contraction semigroup if and only if D(A) is dense in X, A is dissipative, and A − λ₀I is surjective for some λ₀ > 0, where I is the identity operator.
nodes.by: Named after Günter Lumer and Ralph Phillips
nodes.note: It gives a necessary and sufficient condition for a linear operator in a Banach space to generate a contraction semigroup.

nodes.name: Cauchy–Kovalevskaya theorem
nodes.statement: Take a system of m first-order equations in n variables, ∂f/∂x_n = A_1(x,f)·∂f/∂x_1 + … + A_{n−1}(x,f)·∂f/∂x_{n−1} + b(x,f), where the matrix-valued A_i and the vector-valued b are analytic near (0,0), over the real or complex numbers. With the initial condition f = 0 on the hypersurface x_n = 0, there is a neighbourhood of 0 on which this problem has a unique analytic solution f.
nodes.by: A special case by Cauchy, 1842; the full result by Kovalevskaya, 1874
nodes.note: It is the main local existence and uniqueness theorem for analytic partial differential equations with Cauchy initial value problems. Lewy's example shows it does not hold for all smooth functions.

nodes.name: Abel–Dini–Pringsheim theorem
nodes.statement: Let a₀, a₁, a₂, … be positive real numbers whose sum is infinite, and let Sₙ = a₀ + a₁ + … + aₙ. Then ∑ aₙ/Sₙ is infinite, ∑ₙ≥₁ aₙ/(Sₙ·Sₙ₋₁^ε) is finite for every ε > 0, and if aₙ/Sₙ tends to 0, then a₀/S₀ + … + aₙ/Sₙ is asymptotically equal to ln Sₙ.
nodes.by: Niels Henrik Abel proved a weak form of the first part; Ulisse Dini proved the complete first part and a weak form of the second; Alfred Pringsheim proved the second part; the third part is due to Ernesto Cesàro
nodes.note: A consequence is that ∑ aₙ/Sₙᵗ converges for t > 1 and diverges for t ≤ 1, so for every convergence test based on a particular series there is a series about which the test is inconclusive. An equivalent form for convergent series uses the remainders rₙ = aₙ + aₙ₊₁ + … in place of the partial sums.

nodes.name: Kadison transitivity theorem
nodes.statement: Suppose a C*-algebra acts topologically irreducibly on a Hilbert space, y_1, ..., y_n are vectors and x_1, ..., x_n are linearly independent vectors in the space. Then some element A of the algebra satisfies Ax_j = y_j for every j, and if some self-adjoint operator B satisfies Bx_j = y_j, then A can be chosen self-adjoint. In particular, a topologically irreducible action is also algebraically irreducible.
nodes.by: Richard Kadison
nodes.note: It shows that topological and algebraic irreducibility of representations of C*-algebras are equivalent.

nodes.name: Orlicz–Pettis theorem
nodes.statement: Let X be a Hausdorff locally convex topological vector space with dual X*. If a series ∑xₙ in X converges in the weak topology σ(X, X*) along every subseries, then every subseries also converges in the original topology of X. Equivalently, an additive set function on a σ-algebra with values in X that is weakly countably additive is countably additive in the original topology.
nodes.by: W. Orlicz, first for weakly sequentially complete Banach spaces; also proved by Pettis; in locally convex spaces a special case of a theorem of Grothendieck, 1953
nodes.note: W. Orlicz first proved a version for weakly sequentially complete Banach spaces, and Pettis gave a proof because he needed the result to show that weak and strong measures coincide. In locally convex spaces it is a special case of a 1953 theorem of Grothendieck.

nodes.name: Hoeffding's inequality
nodes.statement: Let X₁, …, Xₙ be independent random variables with aᵢ ≤ Xᵢ ≤ bᵢ almost surely, and let Sₙ = X₁ + … + Xₙ. Then for all t > 0, P(Sₙ − E[Sₙ] ≥ t) ≤ exp(−2t² / ∑(bᵢ − aᵢ)²) and P(|Sₙ − E[Sₙ]| ≥ t) ≤ 2·exp(−2t² / ∑(bᵢ − aᵢ)²), where the sums run over i = 1, …, n.
nodes.by: Wassily Hoeffding, 1963
nodes.note: It is a special case of the Azuma–Hoeffding inequality and McDiarmid's inequality. It is similar to the Chernoff bound but tends to be less sharp when the variances are small.

nodes.name: Littlewood's Tauberian theorem
nodes.statement: Suppose the numbers aₙ satisfy aₙ = O(1/n), that is |aₙ| ≤ C/n for some constant C, and ∑ aₙxⁿ tends to s as x increases to 1. Then the series ∑ aₙ converges and its sum is s.
nodes.by: Littlewood, 1911
nodes.note: It strengthens Tauber's theorem, which assumed the stronger condition aₙ = o(1/n). Hardy and Littlewood later weakened the hypothesis to aₙ ≥ −C/n for some constant C.

nodes.name: Sturm's theorem
nodes.statement: Let P be a square-free polynomial with real coefficients, and form the sequence P₀ = P, P₁ = P′, P_{i+1} = −(remainder of P_{i−1} divided by P_i). If V(ξ) is the number of sign changes, ignoring zeros, in P₀(ξ), P₁(ξ), P₂(ξ), …, then for real numbers a < b the number of distinct real roots of P in the interval (a, b] is V(a) − V(b).
nodes.by: Jacques Charles François Sturm, 1829
nodes.note: Applied to the interval of all real numbers, it gives the total number of real roots. It yields the oldest real-root isolation algorithm.

nodes.name: Pontryagin duality theorem
nodes.statement: The Pontryagin dual of a locally compact abelian group is the group of its continuous homomorphisms to the circle group, with pointwise multiplication and the topology of uniform convergence on compact sets. Every locally compact abelian group is naturally isomorphic with its bidual, the dual of its dual.
nodes.by: Lev Pontryagin, 1934, for second-countable groups that are compact or discrete; extended to all locally compact abelian groups by Egbert van Kampen, 1935, and André Weil, 1940
nodes.note: The Fourier inversion theorem is a special case of this theorem.

nodes.name: Mazur–Ulam theorem
nodes.statement: If V and W are normed spaces over ℝ and f: V → W is a surjective isometry (a map onto W that preserves all distances), then f is affine.
nodes.by: Stanisław Mazur and Stanisław Ulam, in response to a question raised by Stefan Banach
nodes.note: For strictly convex spaces the result holds, and is easy, even when the isometry is not surjective.

nodes.name: Blumberg theorem
nodes.statement: For every function f : ℝ → ℝ, however badly behaved, there is a dense subset D of ℝ (a set that meets every interval) such that f restricted to D is continuous.
nodes.by: Henry Blumberg, its discoverer
nodes.note: A topological space on which every real-valued function has a continuous restriction to some dense subset is called a Blumberg space, so the theorem says that ℝ is a Blumberg space.

nodes.name: Chaplygin's theorem
nodes.statement: Consider the problem y′(t) = f(t, y(t)) for t in [t₀, α], with α > t₀ and y(t₀) = y₀, and let u and v be functions continuous on [t₀, α] and smooth on (t₀, α] with u(t₀) < y₀ < v(t₀), u′(t) < f(t, u(t)) and v′(t) > f(t, v(t)) for all t in (t₀, α]. If f is continuous for t in [t₀, α] and u(t) ≤ y ≤ v(t), and there is a constant K > 0 with |f(t, y₁) − f(t, y₂)| ≤ K|y₁ − y₂| for all such t, y₁ and y₂, then the problem has exactly one solution y(t) on [t₀, α], and u(t) < y(t) < v(t) for all t in [t₀, α].
nodes.by: Sergey Chaplygin, 1919
nodes.note: It is one of many comparison theorems. The Chaplygin method solves ordinary differential equations that fit the conditions of the theorem.

nodes.name: Jessen–Wintner theorem
nodes.statement: A random variable that is the sum of an almost surely convergent series of independent discrete random variables is of pure type.
nodes.by: Jessen and Aurel Wintner, 1935

nodes.name: Delzant's theorem
nodes.statement: For every compact connected symplectic manifold of dimension 2n with an effective Hamiltonian action of the n-dimensional torus (a symplectic toric manifold), the image of the moment map is a Delzant polytope in ℝⁿ, and every Delzant polytope arises in this way. Two such manifolds whose moment polytopes agree up to translations and GL(n, ℤ)-transformations are related by a torus-equivariant symplectomorphism, so the moment map gives a bijection between symplectic toric manifolds, up to such symplectomorphisms, and Delzant polytopes.
nodes.by: Thomas Delzant, 1988
