nodes.note: It gives a complete classification of symplectic toric manifolds in terms of a special class of polytopes. The proof is based on symplectic reduction.

nodes.name: Smale conjecture
nodes.statement: The diffeomorphism group of the 3-sphere has the homotopy type of its isometry group, the orthogonal group O(4).
nodes.by: Named after Stephen Smale; proved by Allen Hatcher, 1983
nodes.note: One equivalent form is that the group of diffeomorphisms of the 3-ball that restrict to the identity on the boundary is contractible. The analogous statement fails in dimensions 5 and higher.

nodes.name: Grace–Walsh–Szegő coincidence theorem
nodes.statement: Let f(z₁, …, zₙ) be a polynomial with complex coefficients that is symmetric (unchanged when the variables are permuted) and multi-affine (of degree at most 1 in each variable separately), and let A be a circular region in the complex plane. If A is convex or f has degree n, then for every ζ₁, …, ζₙ in A there is a ζ in A with f(ζ₁, …, ζₙ) = f(ζ, …, ζ).
nodes.by: Named after John Hilton Grace, Joseph L. Walsh and Gábor Szegő

nodes.name: Kolmogorov's two-series theorem
nodes.statement: Let X₁, X₂, … be independent random variables with expected values μₙ and variances σₙ². If the series ∑ μₙ and ∑ σₙ² both converge in ℝ, then ∑ Xₙ converges in ℝ with probability 1.
nodes.note: It follows from Kolmogorov's inequality and is used in one proof of the strong law of large numbers.

nodes.name: Alexandrov's theorem on polyhedra
nodes.statement: If a metric space is geodesic, homeomorphic to a sphere, and locally Euclidean except at finitely many cone points, each of positive angular defect (the defects then sum to 4π), then it is the surface metric of a convex polyhedron in three-dimensional space, which may be degenerate, that is, a flat convex polygon covered on both sides. Any two convex polyhedra with the same surface metric are congruent.
nodes.by: Aleksandr Danilovich Aleksandrov, published in the 1940s
nodes.note: It shows that distinct convex polyhedra have distinct surface metrics, and it characterizes the metric spaces that arise as surface distances of convex polyhedra. Non-convex polyhedra with the same metric can exist.

nodes.name: Landweber exact functor theorem
nodes.statement: For every prime p there are elements v₁, v₂, … of the complex cobordism coefficient ring MU_* such that the following holds. If M_* is a graded MU_*-module and the sequence (p, v₁, v₂, …, vₙ) is regular for M for every p and n, then E_*(X) = MU_*(X) ⊗ M_* (tensor product over MU_*) is a homology theory on CW-complexes.
nodes.by: Named after Peter Landweber
nodes.note: It constructs a homology theory out of a formal group law, reversing the passage from a complex-oriented homology theory to a formal group law. Many homology theories, such as elliptic homology, were first constructed this way.

nodes.name: Chain rule of probability
nodes.statement: For events A₁, …, Aₙ whose intersection does not have probability zero, P(A₁ ∩ A₂ ∩ … ∩ Aₙ) = P(A₁) · P(A₂ | A₁) · P(A₃ | A₁ ∩ A₂) ⋯ P(Aₙ | A₁ ∩ … ∩ Aₙ₋₁), where P(B | A) is the conditional probability of B given A.
nodes.note: For two events it reads P(A ∩ B) = P(B | A) · P(A). It is used in the study of Bayesian networks, which describe a probability distribution in terms of conditional probabilities.

nodes.name: Cohn-Vossen's inequality
nodes.statement: In every complete Riemannian 2-manifold S with finite total curvature and finite Euler characteristic, the integral of the Gaussian curvature K over S with respect to area is at most 2π times the Euler characteristic χ(S). That is, ∬_S K dA ≤ 2πχ(S).
nodes.by: Named after Stefan Cohn-Vossen
nodes.note: It is akin to the Gauss–Bonnet theorem for a compact surface.

nodes.name: Chetaev instability theorem
nodes.statement: Consider a system ẋ = X(x) with an equilibrium point at the origin. Suppose there is a continuously differentiable function V(x) such that the origin is a boundary point of the set G = {x : V(x) > 0}, and there is a neighborhood U of the origin such that V̇, the rate of change of V along the system, is positive at every point of G ∩ U. Then the origin is an unstable equilibrium point of the system.
nodes.by: Named after Nicolai Gurevich Chetaev
nodes.note: It is less restrictive than the Lyapunov instability theorems, since it does not need a complete sphere around the origin on which V and V̇ have the same sign.

nodes.name: Grothendieck–Katz p-curvature conjecture
nodes.statement: Consider the linear differential system dv/dz = A(z)v, where A is an n-by-n matrix of rational functions with rational number coefficients. If for almost all primes p the system reduced modulo p has a full set of algebraic solutions over the finite field with p elements (equivalently, its p-curvature is zero), then the original system has a full set of algebraic function solutions.
nodes.by: Alexander Grothendieck, put forth in public discussion in Spring 1969; first published in a paper by Nicholas Katz, 1972
nodes.note: It is a local-global principle for linear ordinary differential equations. A wide class of cases has been proved by Benson Farb and Mark Kisin.

nodes.name: Hopf lemma
nodes.statement: Let Ω be a bounded domain in ℝⁿ with smooth boundary, and let f be a real-valued function that is continuous on the closure of Ω and harmonic on Ω. If x is a boundary point with f(x) > f(y) for all y in Ω sufficiently close to x, then the one-sided directional derivative of f along the outward normal at x is strictly positive.
nodes.by: Stanisław Zaremba, 1910, for the Laplacian; found independently for elliptic equations by Eberhard Hopf and Olga Oleinik, 1952
nodes.note: It is an important tool in the proof of the maximum principle. It has been generalized to uniformly elliptic operators.

nodes.name: Hsu–Robbins–Erdős theorem
nodes.statement: Let X₁, X₂, ... be independent, identically distributed random variables with mean zero and finite variance, and let Sₙ = X₁ + ⋯ + Xₙ. Then for every ε > 0 the sum over n ≥ 1 of the probabilities P(|Sₙ| > εn) is finite; conversely, for such variables with mean zero this sum can be finite only if the variance is finite.
nodes.by: Pao-Lu Hsu and Herbert Robbins, 1947; the converse, which they conjectured, was proved two years later by Paul Erdős
nodes.note: It strengthens the classical strong law of large numbers in the direction of the Borel–Cantelli lemma.

nodes.name: Hyperbolic law of cosines
nodes.statement: In a hyperbolic plane of Gaussian curvature −1/k², every triangle ABC with angle α at A and side lengths a = BC, b = AC, c = AB satisfies cosh(a/k) = cosh(b/k)·cosh(c/k) − sinh(b/k)·sinh(c/k)·cos α.
nodes.by: Franz Taurinus, 1826; also shown by Nikolai Lobachevsky, 1830
nodes.note: A second law, cos α = −cos β cos γ + sin β sin γ cosh(a/k), shows that the angles of a hyperbolic triangle determine its sides. The first law corresponds to the relativistic velocity addition formula when the sides are read as rapidities.

nodes.name: Ignatov's theorem
nodes.statement: Let X₁, X₂, ... be an infinite sequence of independent and identically distributed random variables, say that the nth term has initial rank r when Xᵢ ≥ Xₙ for exactly r indices i ≤ n, and let Yₖ be the sequence of terms with initial rank k in order of appearance (the kth partial records). Then the sequences Y₁, Y₂, Y₃, ... are independent and identically distributed.
nodes.by: Named after Tzvetan Ignatov (1942–2024), a Bulgarian professor at Sofia University
nodes.note: It is a basic result on the distribution of record values of a stochastic process.

nodes.name: Homotopy excision theorem
nodes.statement: Let (X; A, B) be an excisive triad with C = A ∩ B nonempty, such that the pair (A, C) is (m−1)-connected with m ≥ 2 and the pair (B, C) is (n−1)-connected with n ≥ 1. Then the map from the qth relative homotopy group of (A, C) to that of (X, B) induced by inclusion is bijective for q < m + n − 2 and surjective for q = m + n − 2.
nodes.note: It is a substitute for the absence of excision in homotopy theory. Its most important consequence is the Freudenthal suspension theorem.

nodes.name: Jordan's inequality
nodes.statement: For every x in the interval [0, π/2], (2/π)·x ≤ sin(x) ≤ x.
nodes.by: Named after Camille Jordan
nodes.note: It can be proven through the geometry of circles.

nodes.name: Sendov's conjecture
nodes.statement: Let f(z) = (z − r₁)⋯(z − rₙ) be a polynomial with n ≥ 2 whose roots all lie in the closed unit disk of the complex plane. Then each of the n roots is at distance at most 1 from at least one critical point of f.
nodes.by: Proposed by Blagovest Sendov, 1959; a proof generated using OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Pro was posted by Lech Mazur in 2026 and verified and simplified by Terence Tao
nodes.note: By the Gauss–Lucas theorem the critical points lie in the convex hull of the roots, and so in the unit disk. Earlier proofs covered n < 9 (Brown and Xiang, 1999) and sufficiently large n (Tao, 2020).

nodes.name: Bing metrization theorem
nodes.statement: A topological space X is metrizable if and only if it is regular and T₀ and has a σ-discrete basis. A family of sets is σ-discrete when it is a union of countably many discrete families, a family being discrete when every point has a neighborhood meeting at most one of its members.
nodes.by: R. H. Bing, 1951, independently of the Nagata–Smirnov metrization theorem
nodes.note: It is a common tool for proving other metrization theorems; for example, the Moore metrization theorem follows directly from it.

nodes.name: Willmore conjecture
nodes.statement: For every smooth immersed torus M in ℝ³, the Willmore energy W(M) = ∫ H² dA − ∫ K dA is at least 2π², where H is the mean curvature and K the Gaussian curvature.
nodes.by: Conjectured by Tom Willmore, 1965; proved by Fernando Codá Marques and André Neves, 2012, after Peter Wai-Kwong Li and Shing-Tung Yau proved the non-embedded case in 1982
nodes.note: Marques and Neves proved the embedded case using the Almgren–Pitts min-max theory of minimal surfaces; their proof was published in 2014.

nodes.name: Riesz–Markov–Kakutani representation theorem
nodes.statement: Let X be a locally compact Hausdorff space and ψ a positive linear functional on the space C_c(X) of compactly supported complex-valued continuous functions on X. Then there is exactly one positive Borel measure μ on X with ψ(f) = ∫ f dμ for all f in C_c(X) that is finite on compact sets, outer regular on Borel sets, and inner regular on open sets and on Borel sets of finite measure; it can be taken on a σ-algebra containing the Borel sets on which it is complete.
nodes.by: Riesz, 1909, for continuous functions on the unit interval; extended by Markov, 1938, to some non-compact spaces and by Kakutani, 1941, to compact Hausdorff spaces
nodes.note: It relates linear functionals on spaces of continuous functions to measures. Without the regularity conditions the Borel measure need not be unique.

nodes.name: Vitali–Carathéodory theorem
nodes.statement: Let X be a locally compact Hausdorff space with a Borel measure μ that is finite on every compact set, outer regular, and tight when restricted to any Borel set that is open or of finite mass. If f is in L¹(μ), then for every ε > 0 there are functions u ≤ f ≤ v on X, with u upper-semicontinuous and bounded above and v lower-semicontinuous and bounded below, such that the integral of v − u over X is less than ε.
nodes.by: Named after Giuseppe Vitali and Constantin Carathéodory
nodes.note: It shows that integrable functions can be approximated in L¹ from above and below by lower- and upper-semicontinuous functions.

nodes.name: Wold decomposition
nodes.statement: Every isometry on a Hilbert space is the direct sum of some number of copies of the unilateral shift and a unitary operator, where the unitary part may be absent.
nodes.by: Named after Herman Wold and John von Neumann
nodes.note: In time series analysis, it implies that every stationary discrete-time stochastic process can be decomposed into two uncorrelated processes, one deterministic and the other a moving average process.

nodes.name: Localization theorem
nodes.statement: Let F be a real-valued function that is continuous on an open interval Ω. If the integral of F over every subinterval D contained in Ω is 0, then F(x) = 0 for every x in Ω.
nodes.note: The theorem extends to functions of several variables, with intervals replaced by subdomains.

nodes.name: Snaith's theorem
nodes.statement: The complex K-theory spectrum is identified with the localization of the suspension spectrum of ℂP^∞ away from the Bott element.
nodes.by: Introduced by Victor Snaith

nodes.name: Lickorish–Wallace theorem
nodes.statement: Every closed, orientable, connected 3-manifold can be obtained by Dehn surgery on a framed link in the 3-sphere with ±1 surgery coefficients. Each component of the link can be assumed to be unknotted.
nodes.by: W. B. R. Lickorish and Andrew H. Wallace, independently, in the early 1960s
nodes.note: A corollary is that every closed, orientable 3-manifold bounds a simply-connected compact 4-manifold.

nodes.name: Mercer's theorem
nodes.statement: Let K be a continuous, symmetric, real-valued function on the square [a,b] × [a,b] that is positive-definite, meaning ∑ᵢ∑ⱼ K(xᵢ,xⱼ)cᵢcⱼ ≥ 0 for every finite choice of points xᵢ in [a,b] and real numbers cᵢ. Then the square-integrable functions on [a,b] have an orthonormal basis of eigenfunctions eⱼ of the integral operator φ ↦ ∫ K(x,s)φ(s) ds with eigenvalues λⱼ ≥ 0, the eigenfunctions with λⱼ ≠ 0 are continuous, and K(s,t) = ∑ λⱼ eⱼ(s) eⱼ(t) with absolute and uniform convergence.
nodes.by: James Mercer, 1909
nodes.note: It is used in the theory of integral equations and in the theory of reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces.

nodes.name: Riemann series theorem
nodes.statement: If an infinite series of real numbers is conditionally convergent, then for every real number M its terms can be rearranged by a permutation so that the new series converges to M. They can also be rearranged so that the series diverges to ∞ or to −∞, or fails to approach any limit.
nodes.by: Bernhard Riemann; the dependence of an infinite sum on the order of its terms was observed by Augustin-Louis Cauchy, 1833
nodes.note: It implies that a series of real numbers is absolutely convergent if and only if it is unconditionally convergent.

nodes.name: Markov brothers' inequality
nodes.statement: Let P be a polynomial of degree at most n. Then for every nonnegative integer k, the maximum of |P⁽ᵏ⁾(x)| on −1 ≤ x ≤ 1 is at most n²(n²−1²)(n²−2²)⋯(n²−(k−1)²) / (1·3·5⋯(2k−1)) times the maximum of |P(x)| on −1 ≤ x ≤ 1. The bound is tight, with equality for Chebyshev polynomials of the first kind.
nodes.by: Andrey Markov (case k = 1) and his brother Vladimir Markov (cases k = 2, 3, ...), in the 1890s
nodes.note: It is used to obtain lower bounds in computational complexity theory through the polynomial method.

nodes.name: James's theorem
nodes.statement: A real or complex Banach space X is reflexive if and only if, for every continuous linear functional f on X, there is a point x in the closed unit ball of X with |f(x)| equal to the norm of f.
nodes.by: Robert C. James: for separable Banach spaces in 1957, for general Banach spaces in 1964
nodes.note: A stronger version says that a weakly closed subset C of a Banach space is weakly compact if and only if every continuous linear functional attains a maximum on C. The completeness of the space cannot be dropped.

nodes.name: Auerbach's lemma
nodes.statement: Every n-dimensional normed vector space V has a basis e₁, …, eₙ with ‖eᵢ‖ = 1 for every i, such that the dual basis e¹, …, eⁿ of the dual space V* also has ‖eⁱ‖ = 1 for every i.
nodes.by: Named after Herman Auerbach
nodes.note: It shows that a property of Euclidean spaces holds for all finite-dimensional normed vector spaces. A corollary gives, for every n-dimensional subspace of a normed space, a projection onto it with norm at most n.

nodes.name: Bramble–Hilbert lemma
nodes.statement: Let Ω be a bounded domain in ℝⁿ of diameter d whose boundary is reasonable, for example a domain with the strong cone property, as Bramble and Hilbert assumed (Lipschitz domains qualify), and let 1 ≤ p ≤ ∞. Then there is a constant C depending only on m and Ω, not on p or u, such that every u in the Sobolev space W^m_p(Ω) has a polynomial v of degree at most m − 1 with |u − v|_{W^k_p(Ω)} ≤ C·d^(m−k)·|u|_{W^m_p(Ω)} for every k = 0, …, m, where |·|_{W^k_p} measures the derivatives of order k in the Lᵖ norm.
nodes.by: James H. Bramble and Stephen Hilbert
nodes.note: It bounds the error of approximating a function by a polynomial in terms of its derivatives of order m. It is an essential step in error estimates for the finite element method.

nodes.name: Céa's lemma
nodes.statement: Let V be a real Hilbert space and a : V × V → ℝ a bilinear form with |a(v, w)| ≤ γ‖v‖‖w‖ and a(v, v) ≥ α‖v‖² for all v, w in V, where α, γ > 0. Let L : V → ℝ be a bounded linear operator, let u in V satisfy a(u, v) = L(v) for all v in V, and let u_h in a finite-dimensional subspace V_h satisfy a(u_h, v) = L(v) for all v in V_h. Then ‖u − u_h‖ ≤ (γ/α)‖u − v‖ for all v in V_h.
nodes.by: Jean Céa, in his Ph.D. dissertation
nodes.note: It is a tool for proving error estimates for the finite element method applied to elliptic partial differential equations. It also holds on complex Hilbert spaces with a sesquilinear form and the coercivity condition |a(v, v)| ≥ α‖v‖².

nodes.name: Jordan's lemma
nodes.statement: Let f be a continuous complex-valued function on the semicircle C_R = {Re^{iθ} : θ ∈ [0, π]} of radius R > 0 in the upper half-plane, with f(z) = e^{iaz} g(z) and a > 0. Then |∫ f(z) dz over C_R| ≤ (π/a)·M_R, where M_R is the maximum of |g| on the semicircle. An analogous statement holds for a semicircle in the lower half-plane when a < 0.
nodes.by: Named after Camille Jordan
nodes.note: It is used together with the residue theorem to evaluate contour integrals and improper integrals. Unlike the estimation lemma, its bound does not depend explicitly on the length of the contour.

nodes.name: Urysohn's lemma
nodes.statement: A topological space X is normal if and only if for any two non-empty disjoint closed subsets A and B of X there is a continuous map f : X → [0, 1] with f(A) = {0} and f(B) = {1}.
nodes.by: Named after Pavel Samuilovich Urysohn
nodes.note: It is used to construct continuous functions on normal spaces, and is generalised by the Tietze extension theorem.

nodes.name: Bagpipe theorem
nodes.statement: Every connected surface in which the closure of every countable set is compact (an ω-bounded surface) is the connected sum of a compact connected surface and a finite number of long pipes.
nodes.by: Peter Nyikos
nodes.note: It describes connected ω-bounded surfaces that may fail to be paracompact. It does not cover surfaces that are not ω-bounded, such as the Prüfer manifold.

nodes.name: Poincaré lemma
nodes.statement: Every closed p-form on an open ball in ℝⁿ is exact, for p with 1 ≤ p ≤ n.
nodes.by: Henri Poincaré, 1886
nodes.note: An exact form is necessarily closed, and the lemma gives a sufficient condition for the converse. The same holds on any contractible open subset of a manifold.

nodes.name: Liouville's formula
nodes.statement: Let A(t) be an n×n matrix with real or complex entries for each t in an interval I of the real line, and let Φ be a square-matrix solution of y′ = A(t)y on I, so that Φ′(t) = A(t)Φ(t). If the trace of A (the sum of its diagonal entries) is continuous, then det Φ(t) = det Φ(t₀) · exp(∫ from t₀ to t of tr A(s) ds) for all t and t₀ in I.
nodes.by: Named after Joseph Liouville
nodes.note: Also known as the Abel–Jacobi–Liouville identity. It generalizes Abel's identity and can be used to prove it.

nodes.name: Painlevé conjecture
nodes.statement: For every n ≥ 4, the Newtonian gravitational n-body problem has solutions with a noncollision singularity: at a finite time the forces and accelerations become unbounded, although the positions of the bodies do not tend to a definite limit.
nodes.by: Conjectured by Paul Painlevé in his 1895 Stockholm lectures; proved for n ≥ 5 by Jeff Xia in 1988 and for n = 4 by Jinxin Xue in 2014
nodes.note: Painlevé showed that for n = 3 any solution with a finite time singularity has a collision singularity.

nodes.name: Fubini's theorem on differentiation
nodes.statement: Let I ⊆ ℝ be an interval and let each f_k: I → ℝ (k = 1, 2, 3, …) be an increasing function. If the sum s(x) = ∑ f_k(x) exists for every x in I, then for almost every x in I the derivatives exist and s′(x) = ∑ f_k′(x).
nodes.by: Named after Guido Fubini
nodes.note: Without the assumption that every f_k is increasing, the same conclusion needs a stricter condition such as uniform convergence of the sums of the derivatives. It can be proven using Fatou's lemma and the properties of null sets.

nodes.name: Euler's formula
nodes.statement: For any real number x, e^(ix) = cos x + i sin x, where e is the base of the natural logarithm and i is the imaginary unit. The formula remains valid when x is a complex number.
nodes.by: Leonhard Euler, who derived it around 1740 and first published it in 1748
nodes.note: It links the trigonometric functions to the complex exponential function, and Euler's identity is a special case of it. In 1714 Roger Cotes gave a geometric argument that, after correcting a misplaced factor, amounts to the logarithmic form ix = ln(cos x + i sin x).

nodes.name: Cantor–Dedekind axiom
nodes.statement: The real numbers are order-isomorphic to the linear continuum of geometry. In other words, there is a one-to-one correspondence between real numbers and points on a line.
nodes.by: Emil Artin, in his book Geometric Algebra
nodes.note: It began as an axiom and later became a theorem. Euclidean spaces over the real numbers satisfy the axioms of Euclidean geometry, and from those axioms one can construct a field isomorphic to the real numbers.

nodes.name: Central limit theorem
nodes.statement: Let X₁, X₂, … be independent, identically distributed random variables with expected value μ and finite positive variance σ², and let X̄ₙ be the average of the first n of them. Then, as n tends to infinity, the distribution of √n(X̄ₙ − μ) converges to the normal distribution with mean 0 and variance σ².
nodes.by: Previous versions date back to 1811; the modern form was precisely stated in the 1920s
nodes.note: The result holds whatever the shape of the distribution of the individual variables. Its earliest version is the de Moivre–Laplace theorem, and the requirements of independence and identical distribution can be weakened under certain conditions.

nodes.name: De Moivre's formula
nodes.statement: For any real number x and any integer n, (cos x + i sin x)ⁿ = cos nx + i sin nx, where i is the imaginary unit with i² = −1.
nodes.by: Named after Abraham de Moivre, although he never stated it in his works
nodes.note: It follows from Euler's formula and the exponential law for integer powers. As written it is not valid for non-integer powers n.

nodes.name: L'Hôpital's rule
nodes.statement: Let c be a real number or ±∞, and let f and g be real-valued functions that are differentiable, with g′(x) ≠ 0, at every point of an open interval around c other than c itself (or of an open interval with endpoint c, for a one-sided limit or when c is infinite). If f(x) and g(x) both tend to 0, or |f(x)| and |g(x)| both tend to ∞, as x → c, and f′(x)/g′(x) tends to a limit L that is finite or ±∞, then f(x)/g(x) also tends to L.
nodes.by: Johann Bernoulli found it for the form 0/0 and sent it to Guillaume de l'Hôpital in a letter of 1694; l'Hôpital published it in 1696
nodes.note: It is used to evaluate limits of quotients where both functions tend to zero or both tend to infinity. If the limit of f′/g′ does not exist, the limit of f/g may still exist.

nodes.name: Lebesgue's decomposition theorem
nodes.statement: Let (Ω, Σ) be a measurable space and let μ and ν be σ-finite signed measures on Σ. Then there are uniquely determined σ-finite signed measures ν₀ and ν₁ with ν = ν₀ + ν₁, where ν₀ is absolutely continuous with respect to μ and ν₁ is singular with respect to μ.
nodes.note: It splits a measure into two parts according to its relationship with another measure. Together with the Radon–Nikodym theorem it gives the Lebesgue–Radon–Nikodym theorem.

nodes.name: Rolle's theorem
nodes.statement: Let a < b. If a real function f is continuous on the closed interval [a, b], differentiable on the open interval (a, b), and f(a) = f(b), then there is at least one c in (a, b) with f′(c) = 0.
nodes.by: An early form was stated by Bhāskara II in the 12th century; named after Michel Rolle, whose 1691 proof covered only polynomial functions; first proved in general by Cauchy, 1823
nodes.note: It is a special case of the mean value theorem and is used to prove it. It relies on the completeness of the real numbers and fails over the rational numbers.

nodes.name: Alexander's theorem
nodes.statement: Every knot or link can be represented as a closed braid, that is, a braid in which the corresponding ends of the strings are connected in pairs.
nodes.by: James Waddell Alexander II, 1923
nodes.note: A knot may have many braid representations. Markov's theorem addresses which closed braids represent the same knot type.

nodes.name: Hausdorff paradox
nodes.statement: There is a countable set of points on the sphere S² (the surface of a ball in 3-dimensional space) such that, once it is removed, the rest of the sphere can be divided into three disjoint sets A, B and C for which A, B, C and B ∪ C are all congruent.
nodes.by: Felix Hausdorff, 1914
nodes.note: It implies that the sphere has no finitely additive measure defined on all subsets that gives congruent sets equal measure. Its proof relies on the axiom of choice, and the proof of the Banach–Tarski paradox uses its ideas.

nodes.name: Mergelyan's theorem
nodes.statement: Let K be a compact subset of the complex plane such that the complement of K is connected. Then every continuous function f: K → ℂ whose restriction to the interior of K is holomorphic can be approximated uniformly on K by polynomials.
nodes.by: Sergei Mergelyan, 1951
nodes.note: It generalizes the Weierstrass approximation theorem and Runge's theorem. Mergelyan's proof is constructive and remains the only known constructive proof of the result.

nodes.name: Rising sun lemma
nodes.statement: Let g be a real-valued continuous function on [a,b], let S be the set of x in [a,b] for which some y in (x,b] has g(y) > g(x), and let E = S ∩ (a,b). Then E is open and is a countable union of disjoint intervals (aₖ,bₖ) with g(aₖ) = g(bₖ), except that if aₖ = a lies in S for some k, then g(a) < g(bₖ) for that k. Moreover, if x is in (aₖ,bₖ), then g(x) < g(bₖ).
nodes.by: Frigyes Riesz
nodes.note: It is used in the proof of the Hardy–Littlewood maximal theorem and was a one-dimensional precursor of the Calderón–Zygmund lemma.

nodes.name: Plateau's problem
nodes.statement: Every simple closed curve in space is the boundary of a minimal surface, where the surface is given as a mapping (immersion).
nodes.by: First raised by Joseph-Louis Lagrange, 1760; named after Joseph Plateau; solved independently by Jesse Douglas and Tibor Radó, 1930
nodes.note: Radó's solution held only for rectifiable simple closed curves, while Douglas's held for an arbitrary simple closed curve. The extension to k-dimensional surfaces in n-dimensional space is much harder, and its solutions can have singularities.

nodes.name: Runge's phenomenon
nodes.statement: Let f(x) = 1/(1+25x²) be interpolated at the equidistant points xᵢ = 2i/n − 1 between −1 and 1 by a polynomial Pₙ of degree at most n. Then the largest error of Pₙ on [−1, 1] grows without bound as n increases.
nodes.by: Discovered by Carl Runge
nodes.note: Higher degree does not always improve accuracy: the interpolant oscillates near the ends of the interval. Interpolating at Chebyshev nodes instead makes the error for this function shrink as the degree grows.

nodes.name: Hölder's theorem
nodes.statement: The gamma function does not satisfy any algebraic differential equation whose coefficients are rational functions. That is, for every n ≥ 0 there is no non-zero polynomial P in the variables z, y₀, y₁, ..., yₙ with complex coefficients such that P(z, Γ(z), Γ′(z), ..., Γ⁽ⁿ⁾(z)) = 0 for all complex z that are not zero or negative integers.
nodes.by: Otto Hölder, 1887
nodes.note: It also generalizes to the q-gamma function. Most familiar special functions, such as the Bessel functions, do satisfy such equations, so the gamma function is called transcendentally transcendental.

nodes.name: Kolmogorov's zero–one law
nodes.statement: Let (F_n) be a sequence of independent σ-algebras on a probability space. Then every event in the terminal σ-algebra of the F_n, that is, every tail event, has probability 0 or probability 1.
nodes.by: Named in honor of Andrey Nikolaevich Kolmogorov
nodes.note: It is often easy to show that an event has probability 0 or 1 this way, but hard to decide which of the two it is.

nodes.name: Hilbert's theorem
nodes.statement: There is no complete regular surface of constant negative Gaussian curvature immersed in ℝ³.
nodes.by: David Hilbert, 1901
nodes.note: A different proof was given shortly after by E. Holmgren in 1902. Nikolai Efimov obtained a far-leading generalization in 1975.

nodes.name: Hilbert–Schmidt theorem
nodes.statement: Let A be a bounded, compact, self-adjoint operator on a real or complex Hilbert space H. Then there is a sequence of non-zero real eigenvalues λ₁, …, λ_N, with N equal to the rank of A, such that |λᵢ| is non-increasing and, if N is infinite, λᵢ tends to 0. If each eigenvalue is repeated according to its multiplicity, there is an orthonormal set φ₁, …, φ_N of eigenfunctions with Aφᵢ = λᵢφᵢ. These form an orthonormal basis for the range of A, and Au = ∑ λᵢ⟨φᵢ, u⟩φᵢ for all u in H.
nodes.note: Also known as the eigenfunction expansion theorem. It is useful in solving elliptic boundary value problems in the theory of partial differential equations.

nodes.name: Euler's identity
nodes.statement: e^(iπ) + 1 = 0, where e is Euler's number, the base of natural logarithms, i is the imaginary unit with i² = −1, and π is the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter.
nodes.by: Named after Leonhard Euler; follows directly from Euler's formula, which he first published in 1748
nodes.note: It is the special case x = π of Euler's formula e^(ix) = cos x + i sin x. Euler himself may never have written the identity down.

nodes.name: Poincaré duality
nodes.statement: If M is an n-dimensional oriented closed manifold (compact and without boundary), then for every integer k the kth cohomology group of M is isomorphic to the (n − k)th homology group of M. This holds for any coefficient ring for which M is oriented, and mod 2 without any orientation assumption.
nodes.by: First stated, without proof, by Henri Poincaré in 1893; he gave a new proof in the first two complements to Analysis Situs; it took its modern form in the 1930s with Eduard Čech and Hassler Whitney
nodes.note: For a manifold that is not compact, homology is replaced by Borel–Moore homology or cohomology by cohomology with compact support. One consequence is that every closed odd-dimensional manifold has Euler characteristic zero.

nodes.name: Chain rule
nodes.statement: Let f and g be real-valued functions of one real variable. If g is differentiable at a point c and f is differentiable at g(c), then the composite function f∘g is differentiable at c and (f∘g)′(c) = f′(g(c)) · g′(c).
nodes.by: First used by Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, who mentioned it in a 1676 memoir; the first modern version is believed to appear in Lagrange's 1797 Théorie des fonctions analytiques
nodes.note: In integration, the counterpart of the chain rule is the substitution rule. Faà di Bruno's formula extends it to higher derivatives.

nodes.name: Law of large numbers
nodes.statement: Let X₁, X₂, … be independent and identically distributed random variables whose expected value μ exists and is finite. Then with probability 1 the average (X₁ + ⋯ + Xₙ)/n tends to μ as n grows (strong law), and so for every ε > 0 the probability that this average lies within ε of μ tends to 1 (weak law).
nodes.by: Stated without proof by Gerolamo Cardano; a special form for binary random variables first proved by Jacob Bernoulli, published 1713; the strong law for independent identically distributed variables with an expected value proved by Kolmogorov, 1930
nodes.note: The averages need not converge when there is no finite expected value: averages of Cauchy-distributed samples have the same distribution as a single sample. The strong form implies the weak form.

nodes.name: Hopf–Rinow theorem
nodes.statement: For a connected smooth (finite-dimensional) Riemannian manifold M without boundary, the following are equivalent: the closed and bounded subsets of M are compact; M is a complete metric space; M is geodesically complete. Any one of these implies that any two points of M are joined by a length-minimizing geodesic.
nodes.by: Heinz Hopf and Willi Rinow, 1931
nodes.note: Stefan Cohn-Vossen extended part of it to certain metric spaces. It does not hold for infinite-dimensional manifolds or for Lorentzian manifolds.

nodes.name: Plancherel theorem
nodes.statement: Define the Fourier transform of a function f on the real line by f̂(ξ) = ∫ f(x) e^(−2πixξ) dx. If f belongs to both L¹ and L² (both |f| and |f|² have finite integrals), then f̂ also belongs to L², and the integral of |f(x)|² over the real line equals the integral of |f̂(ξ)|² over the real line.
nodes.by: Michel Plancherel, 1910
nodes.note: It generalizes Parseval's theorem and is used to prove that the Fourier transform is unitary. It also holds on n-dimensional Euclidean space and on locally compact abelian groups.

nodes.name: Rokhlin lemma
nodes.statement: Let T be an invertible, measure-preserving, aperiodic map on a Lebesgue space of total measure 1. Aperiodic means that the points which return to themselves after some number of steps form a set of measure zero. Then for every height N and every ε > 0 there is a measurable set S such that S, TS, …, T^(N−1)S are pairwise disjoint and the part of the space outside their union has measure less than ε.
nodes.by: Vladimir Abramovich Rokhlin, and independently Shizuo Kakutani
nodes.note: Also called the Kakutani–Rokhlin lemma. It is used extensively in ergodic theory, for example in the proof of the Ornstein isomorphism theorem, and has versions for non-invertible maps and for free actions of countable amenable groups.

nodes.name: Hartman–Grobman theorem
nodes.statement: Let du/dt = f(u) with f a smooth map from ℝⁿ to ℝⁿ, and let u* be a hyperbolic equilibrium, meaning f(u*) = 0 and the Jacobian matrix A of f at u* has no eigenvalue with real part zero. Then there is a neighbourhood N of u* and a homeomorphism h from N into ℝⁿ with h(u*) = 0 that, inside N, makes the flow of du/dt = f(u) topologically conjugate to the flow of the linearization dU/dt = AU.
nodes.by: Named after Philip Hartman and David M. Grobman
nodes.note: Near a hyperbolic equilibrium the system behaves qualitatively like its linearization, so the simpler linear system can be used to analyse it. A like result holds for iterated maps and for fixed points on manifolds.

nodes.name: Fundamental theorem of Riemannian geometry
nodes.statement: On any Riemannian or pseudo-Riemannian manifold there is exactly one affine connection that is torsion-free and compatible with the metric. This connection is called the Levi-Civita connection.
nodes.note: The connection can be written explicitly in terms of the metric and its first derivatives, for example by the Koszul formula or the second Christoffel identity.

nodes.name: Banach fixed-point theorem
nodes.statement: Let (X, d) be a non-empty complete metric space and T: X → X a contraction, meaning there is a constant q with 0 ≤ q < 1 such that d(T(x), T(y)) ≤ q·d(x, y) for all x, y in X. Then T has exactly one fixed point x*, and starting from any x₀ in X and setting xₙ = T(xₙ₋₁), the sequence xₙ converges to x*.
nodes.by: Stefan Banach, 1922
nodes.note: It guarantees existence and uniqueness of fixed points and gives a constructive way to find them. A standard application is the proof of the Picard–Lindelöf theorem on solutions of ordinary differential equations.

nodes.name: Banach–Mazur theorem
nodes.statement: Every real, separable Banach space is isometrically isomorphic to a closed subspace of C([0, 1], ℝ), the space of all continuous functions from the unit interval into the real line.
nodes.by: Named after Stefan Banach and Stanisław Mazur
nodes.note: It bounds the complexity of separable Banach spaces by embedding them all into one standard space. Non-separable Banach spaces cannot embed isometrically into it, but every Banach space embeds isometrically into C(K) for some compact Hausdorff space K.

nodes.name: Clairaut's relation
nodes.statement: If γ parametrizes a great circle on the unit sphere, then ρ(γ(t))·sin ψ(γ(t)) is constant, where ρ(P) is the distance from the point P to the z-axis and ψ(P) is the angle between the great circle and the meridian through P. More generally, along any geodesic on a surface of revolution, the distance to the axis of revolution times the sine of the angle with the meridian is constant.
nodes.by: Named after Alexis Claude de Clairaut
nodes.note: It expresses conservation of angular momentum about the axis of revolution for a particle moving along a geodesic with no forces other than those keeping it on the surface.

nodes.name: Eberlein–Šmulian theorem
nodes.statement: Let X be a Banach space and A a subset of X. Then these are equivalent: every sequence of elements of A has a subsequence that is weakly convergent in X; every sequence of elements of A has a weak cluster point in X; the weak closure of A is weakly compact.
nodes.by: Named after William Frederick Eberlein and Witold Lwowitsch Schmulian
nodes.note: It relates three kinds of weak compactness in a Banach space. The weak topology is not metrizable in infinite dimensional spaces, so the equivalence that holds in metric spaces does not apply automatically.

nodes.name: Gelfand–Mazur theorem
nodes.statement: A Banach algebra with unit over the complex numbers in which every nonzero element is invertible is isometrically isomorphic to the complex numbers ℂ. So ℂ is the only complex Banach algebra that is a division algebra.
nodes.by: Named after Israel Gelfand and Stanisław Mazur; first proved by Mazur, who published it without a proof; Gelfand independently published a proof of the complex case a few years later
nodes.note: It follows from the fact that the spectrum of any element of a complex Banach algebra is nonempty. It can be strengthened to say that up to isomorphism the only real Banach division algebras are ℝ, ℂ and the quaternions.

nodes.name: Gelfand–Naimark theorem
nodes.statement: Every C*-algebra is isometrically *-isomorphic to a C*-subalgebra of the bounded operators on some Hilbert space.
nodes.by: Israel Gelfand and Mark Naimark, 1943
nodes.note: It showed that a C*-algebra can be treated as an abstract algebraic object, without reference to particular realizations as an operator algebra.

nodes.name: Hurwitz's automorphisms theorem
nodes.statement: A compact Riemann surface of genus g > 1 has at most 84(g − 1) automorphisms that are orientation-preserving conformal mappings.
nodes.by: Adolf Hurwitz, 1893
nodes.note: A group for which the maximum is achieved is called a Hurwitz group, and the corresponding surface a Hurwitz surface. The bound also holds for algebraic curves over a field of characteristic 0, and in characteristic p > 0 for groups of order coprime to p, but it can fail when p divides the group order.

nodes.name: Kantorovich theorem
nodes.statement: Let F be a differentiable function from an open set X ⊂ ℝⁿ to ℝⁿ whose Jacobian F′ is locally Lipschitz continuous. Take x₀ in X with F′(x₀) invertible, put h₀ = −F′(x₀)⁻¹F(x₀) and x₁ = x₀ + h₀, and suppose the ball B(x₁, ‖h₀‖) lies in X; let M be the Lipschitz constant of F′ on this ball and α₀ = M·‖F′(x₀)⁻¹‖·‖h₀‖. If α₀ ≤ 1/2, then F(x*) = 0 has a solution x* in the closed ball with centre x₁ and radius ‖h₀‖, and Newton's method started at x₀ converges to x* at least linearly.
nodes.by: Leonid Kantorovich, 1948
nodes.note: It resembles the Banach fixed-point theorem but gives existence and uniqueness of a zero rather than a fixed point. A sharper form gives uniqueness of the zero in a larger ball and quadratic convergence.

nodes.name: Fréchet–Kolmogorov theorem
nodes.statement: Let B be a set of functions in L^p(ℝⁿ) with 1 ≤ p < ∞. Then B is relatively compact if and only if two conditions hold uniformly for all f in B: the L^p norm of f(x − h) − f(x) tends to 0 as |h| → 0, and the integral of |f|^p over the region |x| > r tends to 0 as r → ∞.
nodes.by: Named after Maurice René Fréchet and Andrey Kolmogorov
nodes.note: It is an L^p version of the Arzelà–Ascoli theorem, from which it can be deduced. The two conditions already imply that B is bounded, so no separate boundedness assumption is needed.

nodes.name: Malgrange–Ehrenpreis theorem
nodes.statement: Every non-zero linear differential operator with constant coefficients has a Green's function. That is, for every non-zero polynomial P in ℓ variables, the equation P(∂/∂x₁, …, ∂/∂x_ℓ) u = δ, where δ is the Dirac delta function, has a solution u in the sense of distributions.
nodes.by: First proved independently by Ehrenpreis and by Malgrange (1955–1956)
nodes.note: It implies that P(∂)u = f has a solution for every compactly supported distribution f, though not a unique one. The analogue for operators with polynomial coefficients is false, as Lewy's example shows.

nodes.name: Mazur's lemma
nodes.statement: In a normed vector space, every weakly convergent sequence has a sequence of convex combinations of its members that converges strongly to the same limit.
nodes.by: Introduced by Stanisław Mazur
nodes.note: It is used in the proof of Tonelli's theorem.

nodes.name: Sharkovskii's theorem
nodes.statement: Let f be a continuous function from an interval I of the real line to itself. Order the positive integers as follows: first the odd numbers above 1 in increasing order (3, 5, 7, …), then 2 times those odd numbers, then 4 times them, then 8 times them, and so on, and finally the powers of two in decreasing order (…, 8, 4, 2, 1). If f has a periodic point of least period m, and m comes before n in this order, then f also has a periodic point of least period n.
nodes.by: Oleksandr Mykolayovych Sharkovsky, 1964
nodes.note: If f has a periodic point of period 3, it has periodic points of every other period. If f has only finitely many periodic points, all their periods are powers of two.

nodes.name: Casorati–Weierstrass theorem
nodes.statement: Let f be holomorphic on an open set U of the complex plane except at one point z₀ of U, where f has an essential singularity. Then for every neighbourhood V of z₀, every complex number b and every ε > 0, there is a point z ≠ z₀ in V with |f(z) − b| < ε. In other words, arbitrarily close to z₀ the values of f come arbitrarily close to every complex number.
nodes.by: Published by Briot and Bouquet, 1859; by Sokhotski and by Casorati, 1868; by Weierstrass, 1876
nodes.note: Picard's great theorem strengthens it: near z₀, f takes every complex value, with one possible exception, infinitely often. In Russian literature it is called Sokhotski's theorem.

nodes.name: Law of total expectation
nodes.statement: If X is a random variable whose expected value is defined, and Y is any random variable on the same probability space, then E[X] = E[E[X | Y]]. In particular, if the events Aᵢ form a finite or countable partition of the sample space, then E[X] = ∑ E[X | Aᵢ]·Pr(Aᵢ).
nodes.note: It is also called the law of iterated expectations, Adam's law and the tower rule. The conditional expectation E[X | Y] is itself a random variable, a function of Y.

nodes.name: Poincaré recurrence theorem
nodes.statement: Suppose a dynamical system has a phase space of finite volume and its time evolution preserves volume. Then almost every initial state eventually returns arbitrarily close to its starting state, and it does so infinitely many times.
nodes.by: Discussed by Henri Poincaré, 1890; a proof using measure theory was presented by Constantin Carathéodory, 1919
nodes.note: The theorem applies in particular to isolated bounded systems in mechanics when no form of friction is present. It fails on spaces of infinite volume, and it does not guarantee that every single state returns.

nodes.name: Lebesgue differentiation theorem
nodes.statement: Let f be a Lebesgue integrable real or complex-valued function on ℝⁿ. Then for almost every point x, the average of f over a ball B centred at x, that is (1/|B|) times the integral of f over B, tends to f(x) as the diameter of B tends to 0.
nodes.by: Henri Lebesgue; the one-dimensional case in 1904, the general case in 1910
nodes.note: The same holds when balls are replaced by sets of bounded eccentricity, such as cubes. In one dimension it says that F(x) = ∫ f from −∞ to x is almost everywhere differentiable with F′ = f.

nodes.name: Caristi fixed-point theorem
nodes.statement: Let (X, d) be a complete metric space, T : X → X a map, and f : X → [0, ∞) a lower semicontinuous function such that d(x, T(x)) ≤ f(x) − f(T(x)) for every x in X. Then T has a fixed point, that is, a point x₀ with T(x₀) = x₀.
nodes.by: James Caristi and William Arthur Kirk
nodes.note: It generalizes the Banach fixed-point theorem. Its conclusion is equivalent to metric completeness, as proved by Weston (1977).

nodes.name: Kingman's subadditive ergodic theorem
nodes.statement: Let T be a measure-preserving transformation on a probability space (Ω, Σ, μ), and let (gₙ) be a sequence of L¹ functions with g_{n+m}(x) ≤ gₙ(x) + g_m(Tⁿx) for all n, m and x. Then gₙ(x)/n converges to a limit g(x) ≥ −∞ for μ-almost every x, and g is T-invariant. If T is ergodic, g is constant.
nodes.by: Named after John Kingman
nodes.note: It can be seen as a generalization of Birkhoff's ergodic theorem and as a random variable version of Fekete's lemma. It is used to prove statements about Lyapunov exponents.

nodes.name: Sphere theorem (quarter-pinched sphere theorem)
nodes.statement: If M is a complete, simply-connected, n-dimensional Riemannian manifold whose sectional curvature at every tangent 2-plane lies in the interval (1, 4], then M is homeomorphic to the n-sphere.
nodes.by: Conjectured by Heinz Hopf; topological version with optimal pinching proved by Marcel Berger and Wilhelm Klingenberg, 1960
nodes.note: The conclusion fails for the closed interval [1, 4], for example for complex projective space with the Fubini–Study metric. In 2007 Simon Brendle and Richard Schoen used Ricci flow to show that M is diffeomorphic to the standard n-sphere.

nodes.name: Looman–Menchoff theorem
nodes.statement: Let Ω be an open set in the complex plane and f : Ω → ℂ a continuous function whose partial derivatives ∂f/∂x and ∂f/∂y exist everywhere except possibly on a countable set. Then f is holomorphic if and only if it satisfies the Cauchy–Riemann equation ½(∂f/∂x + i ∂f/∂y) = 0.
nodes.by: Named after Herman Looman and Dmitrii Menshov
nodes.note: It generalizes a theorem of Édouard Goursat, which assumes Fréchet differentiability instead of continuity.

nodes.name: QM–AM–GM–HM inequalities
nodes.statement: For positive real numbers x₁,…,xₙ, the harmonic mean is at most the geometric mean, which is at most the arithmetic mean, which is at most the quadratic mean (root mean square): n/(1/x₁+…+1/xₙ) ≤ ⁿ√(x₁⋯xₙ) ≤ (x₁+…+xₙ)/n ≤ √((x₁²+…+xₙ²)/n). Equality holds when x₁ = x₂ = … = xₙ.
nodes.note: The proofs use methods such as induction, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, Lagrange multipliers and Jensen's inequality.

nodes.name: Lévy–Steinitz theorem
nodes.statement: For a series of vectors in a finite-dimensional real Euclidean space, the set of all values to which rearrangements of the series can converge is either empty or a translate v + M of a linear subspace M.
nodes.by: Paul Lévy, in his first published paper at age 19; Ernst Steinitz filled a gap in the proof and gave another proof in 1913

nodes.name: Cousin's theorem
nodes.statement: Let C be a collection of closed subintervals of [a, b] such that for every x in [a, b] there is a δ > 0 for which C contains all subintervals of [a, b] that contain x and have length smaller than δ. Then [a, b] can be split into finitely many non-overlapping intervals [x_{i−1}, x_i], with a = x₀ < x₁ < … < xₙ = b, each of which belongs to C.
nodes.by: Pierre Cousin, 1895
nodes.note: It extends the Heine–Borel theorem on compactness to arbitrary covers of compact subsets of ℝⁿ. It is used in Henstock–Kurzweil integration, where it is known as Cousin's lemma.

nodes.name: Hurewicz theorem
nodes.statement: Let X be a path-connected space and n ≥ 2. If X is (n−1)-connected, meaning πᵢ(X) = 0 for all i < n, then the reduced homology groups H̃ᵢ(X) are 0 for all i < n, the Hurewicz homomorphism πₙ(X) → Hₙ(X) (integer coefficients) is an isomorphism, and the map πₙ₊₁(X) → Hₙ₊₁(X) is onto. For n = 1, the Hurewicz homomorphism induces an isomorphism from the abelianization π₁(X)/[π₁(X), π₁(X)] of the fundamental group onto H₁(X).
nodes.by: Named after Witold Hurewicz; it generalizes earlier results of Henri Poincaré
nodes.note: It links homotopy groups with homology groups through the Hurewicz homomorphism. It implies that homological connectivity equals homotopical connectivity when the latter is at least 1.

nodes.name: Azuma's inequality
nodes.statement: Let X₀, X₁, X₂, … be a martingale or supermartingale with |X_k − X_{k−1}| ≤ c_k almost surely for constants c_k. Then for every positive integer N and every real ε > 0, P(X_N − X₀ ≥ ε) ≤ exp(−ε² / (2 ∑_{k=1}^{N} c_k²)). For a submartingale the same bound holds for P(X_N − X₀ ≤ −ε), and for a martingale P(|X_N − X₀| ≥ ε) ≤ 2 exp(−ε² / (2 ∑_{k=1}^{N} c_k²)).
nodes.by: Named after Kazuoki Azuma and Wassily Hoeffding; Hoeffding proved it for independent variables and observed that his argument extends to martingale differences, 1963
nodes.note: It is a concentration result for martingales with bounded differences. A general form applied to the Doob martingale gives McDiarmid's inequality.

nodes.name: Monotone class theorem
nodes.statement: The smallest monotone class containing an algebra of sets G is exactly the smallest σ-algebra containing G.
nodes.note: It is used as a type of transfinite induction to prove other theorems, such as Fubini's theorem.

nodes.name: Thom conjecture
nodes.statement: Let C be a smooth algebraic curve of degree d in the complex projective plane. If Σ is any smoothly embedded connected curve representing the same homology class as C, then the genus g of Σ satisfies g ≥ (d−1)(d−2)/2.
nodes.by: Named after René Thom; first proved by Peter Kronheimer and Tomasz Mrowka, October 1994
nodes.note: The proof used Seiberg–Witten invariants. The bound equals the genus of C given by the genus–degree formula, so C has the smallest genus in its homology class.

nodes.name: Intermediate value theorem
nodes.statement: Let f be a continuous real-valued function defined on the closed interval [a, b] of real numbers, and let s be a number between f(a) and f(b). Then there is some x between a and b with f(x) = s.
nodes.by: First proved by Bernard Bolzano, 1817; Augustin-Louis Cauchy gave the modern formulation and a proof, 1821
nodes.note: The theorem depends on, and is equivalent to, the completeness of the real numbers. Bolzano's theorem, that a continuous function with values of opposite sign on an interval has a root there, is a corollary.

nodes.name: Riesz–Thorin theorem
nodes.statement: Let T be a linear operator on complex-valued functions between σ-finite measure spaces, and let 1 ≤ p₀, p₁, q₀, q₁ ≤ ∞. If T maps L^(p₀) boundedly into L^(q₀) with norm M₀ and L^(p₁) boundedly into L^(q₁) with norm M₁, then for every 0 < θ < 1 it maps L^(p_θ) boundedly into L^(q_θ) with norm at most M₀^(1−θ)·M₁^θ, where 1/p_θ = (1−θ)/p₀ + θ/p₁ and 1/q_θ = (1−θ)/q₀ + θ/q₁.
nodes.by: Marcel Riesz, 1927, for the case p₀ ≤ q₀ and p₁ ≤ q₁; extended to all exponents by Olof Thorin, 1938, expanded in his 1948 thesis
nodes.note: It lets one prove bounds for the harder Lᵖ spaces from two simpler cases such as L¹, L² and L^∞. The Marcinkiewicz theorem is similar but also applies to a class of non-linear maps.

nodes.name: Fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations
nodes.statement: If a continuous function f on an open interval (a, b) satisfies ∫ f(x)h(x) dx = 0, integrated from a to b, for all compactly supported smooth functions h on (a, b), then f is identically zero.
nodes.note: It is used to turn the weak, integrated form of the extremum condition into a differential equation, for example to derive the Euler–Lagrange equation. This is the basic version; several other versions are in use.

nodes.name: Poincaré–Bendixson theorem
nodes.statement: For a differentiable real dynamical system on an open subset of the plane, every non-empty compact ω-limit set of an orbit that contains only finitely many fixed points is a fixed point, a periodic orbit, or a connected set made of finitely many fixed points together with homoclinic and heteroclinic orbits connecting them.
nodes.by: A weaker version conceived by Poincaré, 1892; complete proof given by Bendixson, 1901
nodes.note: It implies that a two-dimensional continuous dynamical system cannot have a strange attractor. It does not apply to discrete dynamical systems.

nodes.name: Chebyshev's inequality
nodes.statement: Let X be a random variable with finite, non-zero variance σ² and mean μ. Then for every real number k > 0, the probability that X differs from μ by at least kσ is at most 1/k².
nodes.by: First formulated and first proved by Irénée-Jules Bienaymé, 1853; more generally proved by Pafnuty Chebyshev, 1867
nodes.note: It is also called the Bienaymé–Chebyshev inequality. It applies to any probability distribution with a defined mean and variance, can be used to prove the weak law of large numbers, and generalizes to measure spaces.

nodes.name: Universal coefficient theorem
nodes.statement: For every topological space X, every abelian group A and every i, there is a short exact sequence 0 → H_i(X,ℤ)⊗A → H_i(X,A) → Tor₁(H_{i−1}(X,ℤ),A) → 0 in singular homology. The first map is induced by the bilinear map H_i(X,ℤ)×A → H_i(X,A), and the sequence splits, though not naturally, so the integral homology groups of X determine its homology groups with coefficients in A.
nodes.note: The usual proof is a piece of homological algebra about chain complexes of free abelian groups. A similar theorem for cohomology uses the Ext functor in place of Tor.

nodes.name: Dubins–Spanier theorem
nodes.statement: Let U be a set with a σ-algebra of measurable subsets, and let V₁, …, Vₙ be real-valued value measures on it that are countably additive and nonatomic. Fix k, and for each partition of U into k measurable pieces X₁, …, X_k form the n×k matrix whose entry (i, j) is Vᵢ(Xⱼ). Then the set of all these matrices is compact and convex.
nodes.by: Published by Lester Dubins and Edwin Spanier, 1961; already proved earlier by Dvoretzky, Wald and Wolfowitz
nodes.note: Convexity implies that a consensus partition exists, in which all partners value each piece j at exactly a given weight wⱼ. Compactness implies that utilitarian-optimal and leximin-optimal divisions exist.

nodes.name: Kuratowski–Ryll-Nardzewski measurable selection theorem
nodes.statement: Let X be a Polish space with Borel σ-algebra B(X), let (Ω, F) be a measurable space and let ψ be a multifunction on Ω whose values are nonempty closed subsets of X. If for every open subset U of X the set {ω : ψ(ω) ∩ U ≠ ∅} belongs to F, then ψ has a selection that is F-B(X)-measurable.
nodes.by: Named after Kazimierz Kuratowski and Czesław Ryll-Nardzewski
nodes.note: Many classical selection results follow from this theorem, and it is widely used in mathematical economics and optimal control.

nodes.name: Poincaré–Miranda theorem
nodes.statement: Let f₁, …, fₙ be continuous real-valued functions of n variables on the cube [−1,1]ⁿ. Suppose that for each i, fᵢ is nonpositive where xᵢ = −1 and nonnegative where xᵢ = 1. Then there is a point in the cube at which all the functions are zero.
nodes.by: Conjectured by Henri Poincaré, 1883; Carlo Miranda showed in 1940 that it is equivalent to the Brouwer fixed-point theorem
nodes.note: It generalises the intermediate value theorem from one function of one variable to n functions of n variables.

nodes.name: Lusternik–Schnirelmann theorem
nodes.statement: If the n-dimensional sphere Sⁿ is covered by n+1 closed sets, then at least one of these sets contains a pair of antipodal points x and −x.
nodes.by: Lazar Lyusternik and Lev Schnirelmann, 1930
nodes.note: It can be proved from the Borsuk–Ulam theorem. It implies that the Lusternik–Schnirelmann category of real projective space ℝPⁿ is at least n+1, and it equals n+1.

nodes.name: Kolmogorov–Arnold representation theorem
nodes.statement: Every continuous function f from [0,1]ⁿ to ℝ can be written as f(x₁,…,xₙ) = ∑ from q=0 to 2n of Φ_q(∑ from p=1 to n of φ_{q,p}(x_p)). The inner functions φ_{q,p} are continuous functions of one variable that do not depend on f, and the outer functions Φ_q are continuous functions of one variable that depend on f.
nodes.by: Vladimir Arnold and Andrey Kolmogorov; Kolmogorov's paper on representation by functions of one variable and addition, 1957
nodes.note: It solved a constrained form of Hilbert's thirteenth problem. In a sense it shows that the only true continuous function of several variables is the sum.

nodes.name: Littlewood's 4/3 inequality
nodes.statement: For every bilinear form B on c₀ × c₀ with real or complex values, where c₀ is the space of scalar sequences that converge to zero, (∑ over i,j ≥ 1 of |B(e_i,e_j)|^(4/3))^(3/4) ≤ √2 ‖B‖. Here e_i is the sequence with 1 in place i and 0 elsewhere, and ‖B‖ is the supremum of |B(x₁,x₂)| over all sequences x₁, x₂ whose terms all have absolute value at most 1.
nodes.by: Named after John Edensor Littlewood
nodes.note: The exponent 4/3 cannot be improved by a smaller exponent, and for real scalars the constant √2 is sharp. The Bohnenblust–Hille inequality extends it to multilinear maps.

nodes.name: Janiszewski's theorem
nodes.statement: Let A and B be closed subsets of the extended plane whose intersection is connected. If two points can be joined by a path that avoids A and also by a path that avoids B, then they can be joined by a path that avoids both A and B.
nodes.by: Named after Zygmunt Janiszewski
nodes.note: It has been used as a tool for proving the Jordan curve theorem and in complex function theory.

nodes.name: Theorem of the three geodesics
nodes.statement: Every Riemannian surface that is topologically a sphere has at least three simple closed geodesics, that is, closed geodesics that do not cross themselves.
nodes.by: Conjectured by Henri Poincaré, 1905; proof published by Lazar Lyusternik and Lev Schnirelmann, 1929, with a flawed step; a universally accepted proof was given by Grayson in the 1980s, following a suggestion of Karen Uhlenbeck
nodes.note: The theorem is sharp: a sphere has infinitely many closed geodesics, but only three are guaranteed to have no self-intersections.

nodes.name: Browder–Minty theorem
nodes.statement: Let X be a real, separable, reflexive Banach space with continuous dual X*. If T: X → X* is bounded, continuous, coercive and monotone, then T is surjective. That is, for each continuous linear functional g in X* there is a solution u in X of T(u) = g. T need not be linear.
nodes.by: Felix Browder and George J. Minty, who proved it independently

nodes.name: Principal orbit type theorem
nodes.statement: Let a compact Lie group G act smoothly on a connected differentiable manifold M. Then there is a unique isotropy type (a conjugacy class of isotropy groups) such that the set of points of M whose isotropy groups lie in that type is open and dense.
nodes.note: The principal orbit type is the space G/H, where H is a subgroup in that isotropy type.

nodes.name: Pisier–Ringrose inequality
nodes.statement: Let γ be a bounded linear mapping of one C*-algebra 𝔄 into another C*-algebra 𝔅. Then for every finite set A₁, …, Aₙ of elements of 𝔄, ‖∑ (γ(Aⱼ)*γ(Aⱼ) + γ(Aⱼ)γ(Aⱼ)*)‖ ≤ 4 ‖γ‖² ‖∑ (Aⱼ*Aⱼ + AⱼAⱼ*)‖.
nodes.by: Gilles Pisier, 1978, affirming a conjecture of John Ringrose
nodes.note: It is an extension of the Grothendieck inequality.

nodes.name: Wiener–Lévy theorem
nodes.statement: Let F(θ) = ∑ c_k e^(ikθ), θ in [0, 2π], be an absolutely convergent Fourier series, so that ∑ |c_k| < ∞. If the values of F lie on a curve C, and H is an analytic (not necessarily single-valued) function of a complex variable that is regular at every point of C, then H(F(θ)) also has an absolutely convergent Fourier series.
nodes.by: Paul Lévy, generalizing a result of Norbert Wiener
nodes.note: Wiener's earlier 1/f theorem says that if f has an absolutely convergent Fourier series and is never zero, then 1/f also has one.

nodes.name: Arakelyan's theorem
nodes.statement: Let Ω be an open subset of the complex plane, E a relatively closed subset of Ω, and Ω* the Alexandroff compactification of Ω. Every function f continuous on E and holomorphic in the interior of E can be approximated on E to within any ε > 0 by a function g holomorphic on Ω (|g − f| < ε on E) if and only if Ω* ∖ E is connected and locally connected.
nodes.note: It generalizes Mergelyan's theorem from compact subsets of an open set to relatively closed subsets.

nodes.name: Denjoy–Riesz theorem
nodes.statement: Every compact totally disconnected subset of the plane is a subset of a Jordan arc, that is, a continuous image of the unit interval without self-intersections.
nodes.by: Credited by Kuratowski (1968) to Frigyes Riesz, 1906, and Arnaud Denjoy, 1910; Riesz argued incorrectly for a stronger claim, and Denjoy claimed a proof with little detail
nodes.note: Moore and Kline proved a generalization that characterizes the subsets of the plane that can lie in a Jordan arc. Applied to a two-dimensional Smith–Volterra–Cantor set, the theorem gives a Jordan arc of positive area.

nodes.name: Kadison–Singer problem
nodes.statement: Let B be the algebra of all continuous linear operators on the Hilbert space ℓ² and D the algebra of all diagonal continuous linear operators on ℓ². Then every pure state on D has exactly one extension to a state on B.
nodes.by: Posed by Richard Kadison and Isadore Singer, 1959; proved by Adam Marcus, Daniel Spielman and Nikhil Srivastava, 2013
nodes.note: Joel Anderson showed in 1979 that the problem is equivalent to his paving conjecture about operators on finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces.

nodes.name: Heine–Borel theorem
nodes.statement: A subset of Euclidean space ℝⁿ is compact, meaning every open cover of it has a finite subcover, if and only if it is closed and bounded.
nodes.by: Named after Eduard Heine and Émile Borel. Borel in 1895 was the first to state and prove a form of it, restricted to countable covers; Pierre Cousin (1895), Lebesgue (1898) and Schoenflies (1900) generalized it to arbitrary covers
nodes.note: It is sometimes also called the Borel–Lebesgue lemma.

nodes.name: Bernstein's theorem for polynomials
nodes.statement: For every complex polynomial P(z) of degree n, the maximum of |P′(z)| on the unit circle |z| = 1 is at most n times the maximum of |P(z)| on the unit circle. Equality holds if and only if P(z) = αzⁿ.
nodes.by: Sergei Bernstein
nodes.note: Paul Erdős conjectured, and Peter Lax proved, that the factor n can be replaced by n/2 when P has no zeros in |z| < 1.

nodes.name: Ionescu-Tulcea theorem
nodes.statement: Start with a probability space and a sequence of measurable spaces, where each space after the first comes with a Markov kernel from the product of all earlier spaces. Then there is a unique probability measure on the infinite product space whose restriction to each finite stage is the measure built from the initial measure and the kernels up to that stage.
nodes.by: Cassius Ionescu-Tulcea, 1949
nodes.note: It goes beyond the existence of countable product measures, since the individual events may be dependent.

nodes.name: Lax equivalence theorem
nodes.statement: For a linear consistent finite difference method applied to a well-posed linear initial value problem, the method is convergent if and only if it is stable. Here stable means Lax–Richtmyer stable: a matrix norm of the matrix used in the iteration is at most 1.
nodes.by: Peter Lax; also called the Lax–Richtmyer theorem, after Peter Lax and Robert D. Richtmyer
nodes.note: Consistency is easy to check and stability is usually easier to show than convergence, so convergence is usually shown through this theorem.

nodes.name: nth-term test
nodes.statement: For an infinite series a₁ + a₂ + a₃ + … of real numbers, if aₙ does not tend to 0 as n → ∞ (the limit is not 0 or does not exist), then the series diverges. The same holds in any normed vector space.
nodes.note: The converse is false: the harmonic series diverges although its terms tend to 0. In p-adic analysis the condition is also sufficient for convergence.

nodes.name: Hardy–Littlewood inequality
nodes.statement: If f and g are nonnegative measurable real functions on n-dimensional space ℝⁿ that vanish at infinity, then the integral of f(x)g(x) over ℝⁿ is at most the integral of f*(x)g*(x). Here f* and g* are the symmetric decreasing rearrangements of f and g: for every r > 0 the set where f* > r is a ball centred at the origin with the same volume as the set where f > r, and likewise for g*.
nodes.by: Named after G. H. Hardy and John Edensor Littlewood
nodes.note: It is proved by writing f and g with the layer cake representation and exchanging the order of integration with Fubini's theorem.

nodes.name: Jordan curve theorem
nodes.statement: Every simple closed curve in the plane (a continuous loop that does not cross itself) divides the plane into exactly two regions: a bounded interior and an unbounded exterior. Every continuous path from a point of one region to a point of the other must cross the curve.
nodes.by: Camille Jordan, 1887, who published the first claimed proof; Bernard Bolzano had earlier been the first to formulate a precise conjecture
nodes.note: For decades the first rigorous proof was credited to Oswald Veblen, but Thomas C. Hales and others have argued that Jordan's proof was essentially correct. Hales made the first formal computer proof in HOL Light in 2005.

nodes.name: Routh–Hurwitz stability criterion
nodes.statement: Let f be a polynomial of degree n with real coefficients and a positive leading coefficient. All roots of f have negative real parts if and only if the n determinants Δ₁, …, Δₙ of the top-left square corners of its Hurwitz matrix (an n×n matrix filled with the coefficients of f) are all positive.
nodes.by: Edward John Routh, 1876 (recursive test); Adolf Hurwitz, independently, 1895 (determinant form)
nodes.note: A polynomial meeting the criterion is called a Hurwitz polynomial; if the leading coefficient is negative, the determinants must alternate in sign instead. Routh's test is an equivalent and more efficient way to compute the Hurwitz determinants, and it decides whether a linear system is stable without solving it.

nodes.name: Carathéodory's extension theorem
nodes.statement: Let R be a ring of sets on a set X, and let μ be a pre-measure on R: a function from R to [0, +∞] with μ(∅) = 0 such that μ(A) = ∑ μ(Aᵢ) whenever a set A in R is the disjoint union of countably many sets A₁, A₂, … in R. Then μ extends to a measure on the σ-algebra generated by R, and this extension is unique if μ is σ-finite.
nodes.by: Named after Constantin Carathéodory
nodes.note: It leads, for example, to the Lebesgue measure. It is also known as the Hahn–Kolmogorov extension theorem.

nodes.name: Convolution theorem
nodes.statement: If u and v are integrable functions on ℝⁿ (in L¹(ℝⁿ)) and the Fourier transform is defined by U(f) = ∫ u(x) e^(−2πi f·x) dx, then the convolution u*v is also integrable and its Fourier transform equals U(f)·V(f) for every f. With other normalizations of the Fourier transform, constant factors such as 2π or √(2π) appear in the formula.
nodes.note: Convolution in one domain, such as time, corresponds to pointwise multiplication in the other, such as frequency. Versions hold for Fourier series, sequences, the discrete Fourier transform, the Laplace transform and tempered distributions.

nodes.name: Bloch's theorem
nodes.statement: Let f be a holomorphic function on the closed unit disk |z| ≤ 1 with |f′(0)| = 1. Then there is a disk S inside the unit disk on which f is biholomorphic (one-to-one with a holomorphic inverse), and f(S) contains a disk of radius 1/72.
nodes.by: Named after André Bloch
nodes.note: It gives a lower bound on the size of a disk in which an inverse to a holomorphic function exists. The bound 1/72 is not the best possible, and the best constant, Bloch's constant, is still unknown.

nodes.name: Browder fixed-point theorem
nodes.statement: Let K be a non-empty, convex, closed, bounded set in a uniformly convex Banach space. If f maps K into itself and is non-expansive, meaning ‖f(x) − f(y)‖ ≤ ‖x − y‖ for all x, y in K, then f has a fixed point.
nodes.by: Felix Browder and, independently, William Kirk, 1965
nodes.note: It refines the Banach fixed-point theorem for uniformly convex Banach spaces.

nodes.name: Alexander's subbase lemma
nodes.statement: Let X be a topological space with a subbase S. A subset K of X is compact if and only if every cover of K by sets from S has a finite subcover.
nodes.by: James Waddell Alexander II
nodes.note: The lemma is typically used to prove Tychonoff's theorem.

nodes.name: Bohr–Mollerup theorem
nodes.statement: The gamma function is the only positive function f on the interval x > 0 that satisfies f(1) = 1 and f(x + 1) = x f(x) for x > 0 and is logarithmically convex.
nodes.by: Harald Bohr and Johannes Mollerup
nodes.note: The theorem was first published in a textbook on complex analysis, because Bohr and Mollerup thought it had already been proved.

nodes.name: Lovelock's theorem
nodes.statement: In four-dimensional spacetime, any symmetric, divergence-free tensor A^{μν} whose components are functions of the metric tensor and its first and second derivatives, and are linear in the second derivatives, has the form A^{μν} = a G^{μν} + b g^{μν}, where a and b are constants and G^{μν} is the Einstein tensor.
nodes.by: David Lovelock, 1971
nodes.note: It says that a local gravitational action containing only second derivatives of the four-dimensional spacetime metric can only give the Einstein field equations as equations of motion.

nodes.name: Euler–Maclaurin formula
nodes.statement: Let m and n be natural numbers, p a positive integer, and f a real or complex valued function that is p times continuously differentiable on [m, n]. Then f(m + 1) + f(m + 2) + ⋯ + f(n) − ∫ₘⁿ f(x) dx = ∑ₖ₌₁ᵖ (Bₖ/k!)(f⁽ᵏ⁻¹⁾(n) − f⁽ᵏ⁻¹⁾(m)) + Rₚ, where Bₖ is the kth Bernoulli number (with B₁ = 1/2) and the remainder is Rₚ = (−1)ᵖ⁺¹ ∫ₘⁿ f⁽ᵖ⁾(x) Pₚ(x)/p! dx, with Pₚ the periodized Bernoulli function.
nodes.by: Discovered independently by Leonhard Euler and Colin Maclaurin, around 1735
nodes.note: It is used to approximate integrals by finite sums or to evaluate sums and series using integrals. Faulhaber's formula for the sum of powers is an immediate consequence.

nodes.name: Universal chord theorem
nodes.statement: If a function f is continuous on [a,b] and f(a) = f(b), then for every positive integer n there is some x with a ≤ x ≤ b − (b−a)/n such that f(x) = f(x + (b−a)/n).
nodes.by: Paul Lévy, 1934
nodes.note: It was published as a generalization of Rolle's theorem. It does not hold when (b−a)/n is replaced by a length that is not of this form.

nodes.name: Glivenko's theorem
nodes.statement: Let μ₁, μ₂, … and μ be probability distributions with characteristic functions φ₁, φ₂, … and φ. If φₙ converges to φ almost everywhere, then μₙ converges to μ in the sense of probability distributions.
nodes.by: Named after Glivenko

nodes.name: Knaster–Kuratowski–Mazurkiewicz lemma
nodes.statement: Take a simplex with n vertices labelled 1, …, n, and n closed subsets C₁, …, Cₙ of it such that, for every set I of labels, the convex hull of the vertices with labels in I is covered by the union of the sets Cᵢ with i in I. Then all n sets have a point in common.
nodes.by: Knaster, Kuratowski and Mazurkiewicz, 1929
nodes.note: It can be proved from Sperner's lemma and can be used to prove the Brouwer fixed-point theorem.

nodes.name: Goldbach–Euler theorem
nodes.statement: The sum of 1/(p − 1) over all perfect powers p (numbers such as 4, 8, 9, 16, 25, 27, 32), excluding 1 and counting each such number only once, converges to 1: 1/3 + 1/7 + 1/8 + 1/15 + 1/24 + 1/26 + 1/31 + … = 1.
nodes.by: First published by Euler, 1737; Euler attributed the result to a letter from Goldbach
nodes.note: Goldbach's original proof was not rigorous by modern standards. Its method of sieving out powers resembles the factorization used to derive Euler's product formula for the Riemann zeta function.

nodes.name: Leibniz integral rule
nodes.statement: Suppose f(x, t) and its partial derivative ∂f/∂x are continuous on a region of the (x, t)-plane containing the range of integration, and a(x) and b(x) are finite and differentiable. Then d/dx ∫ from a(x) to b(x) of f(x, t) dt = f(x, b(x))·b′(x) − f(x, a(x))·a′(x) + ∫ from a(x) to b(x) of ∂f/∂x(x, t) dt; when a and b are constants, only the last integral remains.
nodes.by: Named after Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz
nodes.note: Under suitable conditions it lets one interchange integration and partial differentiation, which is useful for differentiating integral transforms. The first fundamental theorem of calculus is a special case.

nodes.name: Crofton formula
nodes.statement: For a rectifiable plane curve γ, let n_γ(φ, p) be the number of points where γ meets the oriented line with direction φ and signed distance p from the origin. Then the length of γ equals one quarter of the integral of n_γ(φ, p) over all oriented lines, with respect to dφ dp.
nodes.by: Named after Morgan Crofton (1826–1915)
nodes.note: It relates the length of a curve to the expected number of times a random line intersects it. A version exists for codimension 1 surfaces in ℝⁿ.

nodes.name: Zorich's theorem
nodes.statement: Every locally homeomorphic quasiregular mapping f from ℝⁿ to ℝⁿ with n ≥ 3 is a homeomorphism of ℝⁿ.
nodes.by: Conjectured by M. A. Lavrentev, 1938; proved by Vladimir A. Zorich, 1967
nodes.note: There is no such result for n = 2, as the exponential function shows.

nodes.name: Goldstine theorem
nodes.statement: Let X be a Banach space. Then the image of the closed unit ball B of X under the canonical embedding into the closed unit ball B'' of the bidual space X'' is a weak*-dense subset of B''.
nodes.by: Named after Herman Goldstine
nodes.note: The same conclusion for the norm topology is never true if X is not reflexive.

nodes.name: Kantorovich inequality
nodes.statement: Let p_i ≥ 0 and 0 < a ≤ x_i ≤ b for i = 1, …, n. Then (∑ p_i x_i)(∑ p_i / x_i) ≤ (a+b)²/(4ab) · (∑ p_i)² − (a−b)²/(4ab) · m, where m is the smallest value of (∑_{i∈X} p_i − ∑_{j∈Y} p_j)² over all ways of splitting {1, …, n} into two disjoint sets X and Y.
nodes.by: Named after Leonid Kantorovich
nodes.note: It is used in convergence analysis, where it bounds the convergence rate of Cauchy's steepest descent. A matrix version is due to Marshall and Olkin (1990).

nodes.name: Loewner's torus inequality
nodes.statement: Every Riemannian metric on the 2-torus satisfies sys² ≤ (2/√3) · area, where sys is the systole, the least length of a noncontractible loop. The constant 2/√3 is the best possible.
nodes.by: Charles Loewner, 1949
nodes.note: The constant 2/√3 is the Hermite constant in dimension 2. Equality holds exactly when the metric is flat and homothetic to the equilateral torus.

nodes.name: Abel's identity
nodes.statement: Take the equation y'' + p(x)y' + q(x)y = 0 on an interval I, where p and q are continuous, real- or complex-valued functions. For any two solutions y₁ and y₂, the Wronskian W = y₁y₂' − y₁'y₂ satisfies W(x) = W(x₀)·exp(−∫ from x₀ to x of p(t) dt) for all x and x₀ in I.
nodes.by: Named after Niels Henrik Abel
nodes.note: It lets one find one solution from another, and it is useful for equations such as Bessel's equation where the Wronskian is hard to compute directly.

nodes.name: Summation by parts
nodes.statement: For two sequences f and g, the sum over k = m, …, n of f_k(g_(k+1) − g_k) equals (f_(n+1)g_(n+1) − f_m g_m) minus the sum over k = m, …, n of g_(k+1)(f_(k+1) − f_k). The identity is purely algebraic and holds in any field.
nodes.by: Niels Henrik Abel, 1826
nodes.note: It is a discrete analogue of integration by parts and is also called Abel's lemma or the Abel transformation.

nodes.name: Abel's theorem for power series
nodes.statement: Let G(x) = ∑ a_k x^k (k from 0 to ∞) be a power series with real coefficients a_k, and suppose that ∑ a_k converges. Then G(x) tends to ∑ a_k as x approaches 1 from the left.
nodes.by: Niels Henrik Abel, 1826
nodes.note: The same holds for complex power series if z approaches 1 within a single Stolz sector. Without that restriction the limit may fail to exist.

nodes.name: Green's theorem
nodes.statement: Let C be a positively oriented, piecewise smooth, simple closed curve in a plane and D the region bounded by C. If L and M are functions of (x, y) defined on an open region containing D and have continuous partial derivatives there, then the line integral ∮_C (L dx + M dy), taken counterclockwise, equals the double integral over D of (∂M/∂x − ∂L/∂y) dA.
nodes.by: Named after George Green, who stated a similar result in 1828; Augustin-Louis Cauchy stated it in 1846; first proved by Bernhard Riemann, 1851
nodes.note: It is the two-dimensional special case of Stokes' theorem.

nodes.name: Estimation lemma
nodes.statement: Let f be a continuous complex-valued function on a contour Γ, and suppose |f(z)| ≤ M for all z on Γ. Then the absolute value of the contour integral of f over Γ is at most M times the arc length of Γ.
nodes.note: It is also known as the ML inequality. It is most commonly used in contour integration to show that the integral over part of a contour goes to zero as z goes to infinity.

nodes.name: Borel–Carathéodory theorem
nodes.statement: Let f be analytic on the closed disc of radius R centered at the origin, and let r < R. Then the maximum of |f(z)| over |z| ≤ r is at most 2r/(R−r) times the supremum of the real part Re f(z) over |z| ≤ R, plus (R+r)/(R−r) times |f(0)|.
nodes.by: Named for Émile Borel and Constantin Carathéodory
nodes.note: It shows that an analytic function may be bounded by its real part. It is an application of the maximum modulus principle and is used, for example, in the proof of the Hadamard factorization theorem.

nodes.name: Dehn's lemma
nodes.statement: If a piecewise-linear map of a disk into a 3-manifold has its singularity set in the interior of the disk, then there is another piecewise-linear map of the disk that is an embedding and agrees with the original map on the boundary of the disk.
