nodes.by: Claimed by Dehn, 1910, but Kneser found a gap in 1929; proved by Papakyriakopoulos, 1957, using work by Johansson, 1938
nodes.note: Papakyriakopoulos proved it with his tower construction and generalized it to the loop theorem and the sphere theorem. Shapiro and Whitehead gave a substantially simpler proof in 1958.

nodes.name: Gauss's lemma (Riemannian geometry)
nodes.statement: Let M be a Riemannian manifold with its Levi-Civita connection and p a point of M. The exponential map at p sends every sufficiently small sphere centered at 0 in the tangent space at p to a set that is perpendicular to every geodesic starting at p.
nodes.note: It lets the exponential map be understood as a radial isometry and is fundamental in the study of geodesic convexity and normal coordinates.

nodes.name: Lebesgue's lemma
nodes.statement: Let V be a normed vector space, U a subspace of V, and P a linear projection onto U. Then for every v in V, ‖v − Pv‖ ≤ (1 + ‖P‖) · inf{‖v − u‖ : u in U}.
nodes.note: It bounds the error of approximating by a linear projection in terms of the best possible error in the subspace and the operator norm of the projection. The proof is a one-line application of the triangle inequality.

nodes.name: Scheffé's lemma
nodes.statement: Let f₁, f₂, … be integrable functions on a measure space (X, Σ, μ) that converge almost everywhere to an integrable function f. Then ∫|fₙ − f| dμ → 0 if and only if ∫|fₙ| dμ → ∫|f| dμ.
nodes.by: Special case of a theorem by Frigyes Riesz, 1928; Henry Scheffé published a proof for probability densities in 1947
nodes.note: The proof rests on the triangle inequality and Fatou's lemma. The Brezis–Lieb lemma is a quantitative version of it.

nodes.name: Vitali covering lemma
nodes.statement: Let F be a collection of balls of positive radius in ℝ^d whose radii are bounded. Then F contains a countable subcollection G of pairwise disjoint balls such that every ball B in F meets some ball C in G with B contained in 5C, the ball with the same center as C and five times its radius.
nodes.by: Named after Giuseppe Vitali
nodes.note: It is an intermediate step in the proof of the Vitali covering theorem and is used to prove the Hardy–Littlewood maximal inequality. It can fail if the radii are unbounded, and the constant 5 can be replaced by any constant larger than 3 but not by 3.

nodes.name: Fekete's lemma
nodes.statement: Let a₁, a₂, … be a sequence of real numbers with aₙ₊ₘ ≤ aₙ + aₘ for all positive integers n and m. Then aₙ/n converges to the infimum of aₙ/n over all n ≥ 1, and this infimum may be −∞.
nodes.by: Michael Fekete, 1923
nodes.note: It gives the linear growth rate of subadditive sequences. Corollaries cover superadditive and submultiplicative sequences, for example the connective constant for self-avoiding walks on a lattice.

nodes.name: Irrationality of π
nodes.statement: The number π is irrational: it cannot be written as a fraction a/b where a and b are integers (with b not zero).
nodes.by: Johann Heinrich Lambert, 1768; later proofs by Charles Hermite (1873), Mary Cartwright, Ivan Niven (1947), Nicolas Bourbaki and Miklós Laczkovich
nodes.note: Ferdinand von Lindemann proved in 1882 that π is not just irrational but transcendental. Lambert's proof uses a continued fraction for tan x and shows that tan x is irrational for every nonzero rational x.

nodes.name: Divergence theorem
nodes.statement: Let V be a compact subset of ℝⁿ with a piecewise smooth boundary S, and let F be a continuously differentiable vector field defined on a neighborhood of V. Then the volume integral of the divergence of F over V equals the surface integral of F over S taken with the outward pointing unit normal, which is the flux of F out of V.
nodes.by: Discovered by Joseph-Louis Lagrange, 1762; first proof of the general theorem by Mikhail Ostrogradsky, 1826
nodes.note: In one dimension it is equivalent to the fundamental theorem of calculus, and in two dimensions it is equivalent to Green's theorem.

nodes.name: Kolmogorov extension theorem
nodes.statement: Let T be an interval. Suppose that for each finite sequence of distinct times t₁, …, t_k in T there is a probability measure on (ℝⁿ)^k, and that these measures are consistent under permuting the times and under dropping extra times (marginalising over ℝⁿ). Then there is a probability space and a stochastic process X: T × Ω → ℝⁿ whose finite-dimensional distributions are exactly these measures.
nodes.by: Credited to Percy John Daniell and Andrey Nikolaevich Kolmogorov
nodes.note: One can take the underlying space to be (ℝⁿ)^T with the canonical process. When T is uncountable, the resulting measure is defined only on the product σ-algebra.

nodes.name: Excision theorem
nodes.statement: Let X be a topological space and U ⊆ A ⊆ X subspaces. If the closure of U is contained in the interior of A, then the inclusion of the pair (X ∖ U, A ∖ U) into (X, A) induces isomorphisms between their relative homology groups.
nodes.note: It is taken as one of the Eilenberg–Steenrod axioms. It is used to derive the Mayer–Vietoris sequence and the suspension theorem for homology.

nodes.name: Balian–Low theorem
nodes.statement: Let g be a square-integrable function on the real line, and let g_{m,n}(x) = e^(2πimbx) g(x − na) for integers m and n, where a, b > 0 and ab = 1. If the functions g_{m,n} form an orthonormal basis of L²(ℝ), then either ∫ x²|g(x)|² dx = ∞ or ∫ ξ²|ĝ(ξ)|² dξ = ∞, where ĝ is the Fourier transform of g and both integrals are over the whole real line.
nodes.by: Named after Roger Balian and Francis E. Low
nodes.note: Roughly, there is no window function that is well localized in both time and frequency for an exact Gabor frame.

nodes.name: Bernstein's theorem on monotone functions
nodes.statement: Every real-valued function f on [0, ∞) that is completely monotone is the Laplace transform of a non-negative finite Borel measure μ on [0, ∞), that is f(t) = ∫₀^∞ e^(−tx) dμ(x). Complete monotonicity means that f is continuous on [0, ∞), infinitely differentiable on (0, ∞), and (−1)ⁿ times the n-th derivative of f is ≥ 0 for every n ≥ 0 and every t > 0.
nodes.by: Sergei Bernstein, 1928; David Widder discussed similar results in 1931, found independently
nodes.note: It is also known as the Bernstein–Widder theorem or the Hausdorff–Bernstein–Widder theorem. The Schoenberg–Williamson theorem is its finite-order version.

nodes.name: Borel's lemma
nodes.statement: Let U be an open set in ℝⁿ and f₀, f₁, … a sequence of smooth functions on U. If I is any open interval in ℝ containing 0 (possibly I = ℝ), then there exists a smooth function F(t, x) on I×U such that the k-th partial derivative of F with respect to t at (0, x) equals f_k(x), for all k ≥ 0 and all x in U.
nodes.by: Named after Émile Borel
nodes.note: It is an important result used in the theory of asymptotic expansions and partial differential equations.

nodes.name: Budan's theorem
nodes.statement: Let p be a nonzero polynomial with real coefficients and ℓ < r real numbers, and for each real h let v_h(p) be the number of sign changes, ignoring zeros, in the sequence of coefficients of the polynomial p(x + h). Then v_ℓ(p) − v_r(p) − N is a nonnegative even integer, where N is the number of real roots of p in the half-open interval (ℓ, r], counted with multiplicity.
nodes.by: François Budan de Boislaurent, 1807; a similar theorem was published independently by Joseph Fourier, 1820
nodes.note: It generalizes Descartes's rule of signs, and when v_ℓ(p) − v_r(p) ≤ 1 it gives the exact number of roots in (ℓ, r]. Fourier's equivalent version uses the values of the successive derivatives of p at ℓ and r instead of the coefficients of p(x + h).

nodes.name: Dold–Thom theorem
nodes.statement: For a connected CW complex X and every n, the n-th homotopy group of the infinite symmetric product of X is isomorphic to the n-th reduced homology group of X.
nodes.by: Dold and Thom
nodes.note: Unlike the Hurewicz theorem, it allows homology to be reduced directly to homotopy. The requirement that X be a CW complex cannot simply be dropped.

nodes.name: Donsker's theorem
nodes.statement: Let X₁, X₂, … be independent random variables that all have the same distribution function F, and let Fₙ be the empirical distribution function of the first n of them. Then Gₙ(x) = √n (Fₙ(x) − F(x)), viewed as a random element of the Skorokhod space D(−∞, ∞), converges in distribution as n → ∞ to a Gaussian process G with mean zero and covariance min{F(s), F(t)} − F(s)F(t), which can be written as G(x) = B(F(x)) for a standard Brownian bridge B.
nodes.by: Monroe D. Donsker stated and proved it, not quite correctly, in 1952; Skorokhod and Kolmogorov gave a correct form in 1956
nodes.note: It is also called Donsker's invariance principle or the functional central limit theorem. In its random walk form, the rescaled partial sums of independent identically distributed variables with mean 0 and variance 1 converge in distribution to a standard Brownian motion.

nodes.name: F. and M. Riesz theorem
nodes.statement: Let μ be a measure on the circle whose Fourier–Stieltjes coefficients, the integral of e^(−inθ) against μ(dθ)/(2π), are zero for all n < 0. Then μ is absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure dθ.
nodes.by: Frigyes Riesz and Marcel Riesz, 1916
nodes.note: Any part of a measure on the circle that is not absolutely continuous can be detected by its Fourier coefficients. This formulation follows Walter Rudin's Real and Complex Analysis; the brothers' original statements are rather different.

nodes.name: Fáry–Milnor theorem
nodes.statement: If a closed curve in three-dimensional space is smooth enough to have a curvature κ at each point, and its total absolute curvature, the integral of |κ| along the curve, is at most 4π, then the curve is an unknot. The condition is sufficient but not necessary: some unknots have total curvature greater than 4π.
nodes.by: Proved independently by István Fáry in 1949 and John Milnor in 1950
nodes.note: It was later shown to follow from the existence of quadrisecants.

nodes.name: Glaeser's continuity theorem
nodes.statement: Let f be a function of class C² from an open set U in ℝⁿ to the non-negative reals. Then √f is of class C¹ in U if and only if the first and second order partial derivatives of f vanish at the zeros of f.
nodes.by: Georges Glaeser, 1963; later simplified by Jean Dieudonné

nodes.name: Lax–Wendroff theorem
nodes.statement: If a conservative numerical scheme for a hyperbolic system of conservation laws converges, then it converges towards a weak solution.
nodes.by: Named after Peter Lax and Burton Wendroff

nodes.name: Mahler's theorem
nodes.statement: Let Δ be the forward difference operator, (Δf)(x) = f(x+1) − f(x). A function f: ℤ_p → ℚ_p is continuous if and only if its Newton series converges to f everywhere, that is, f(x) = ∑ over n ≥ 0 of (Δⁿf)(0) · C(x,n) for all x in ℤ_p, where C(x,n) = x(x−1)⋯(x−n+1)/n!. Equivalently, a series ∑ aₙ C(x,n) defines a continuous function if and only if aₙ → 0 in ℚ_p as n → ∞.
nodes.by: Mahler, 1958
nodes.note: It is the p-adic counterpart to the Stone–Weierstrass theorem for continuous real-valued functions on a closed interval.

nodes.name: Müntz–Szász theorem
nodes.statement: Let S be a set of positive integers and 0 < a < b. The powers xⁿ with n in S span a dense subset of the space of continuous complex-valued functions on [a, b] with the uniform norm if and only if the sum of 1/n over n in S diverges; on an interval [0, b] the same holds provided the constant function 1 = x⁰ is also included.
nodes.by: Form conjectured by Sergei Bernstein; proved by Herman Müntz, 1914, and Otto Szász, 1916
nodes.note: It shows to what extent the Weierstrass theorem on polynomial approximation survives when some coefficients are forced to be zero. The same result holds for any strictly increasing sequence of positive real exponents.

nodes.name: Poincaré–Birkhoff theorem
nodes.statement: Every area-preserving, orientation-preserving homeomorphism of an annulus that rotates the two boundaries in opposite directions has at least two fixed points.
nodes.by: Henri Poincaré, 1912, who proved it for some special cases; the general case was proved by George D. Birkhoff, 1913

nodes.name: Radó's theorem on Riemann surfaces
nodes.statement: Every connected Riemann surface is second-countable, which means its topology has a countable base.
nodes.by: Radó, 1925
nodes.note: The Prüfer surface has no countable base for its topology, so it cannot have the structure of a Riemann surface. In higher dimensions the analogue is false: there are 2-dimensional connected complex manifolds that are not second-countable.

nodes.name: Rellich–Kondrachov theorem
nodes.statement: Let Ω ⊆ ℝⁿ be an open, bounded Lipschitz domain, let 1 ≤ p < n, and set p* = np/(n − p). Then the Sobolev space W^{1,p}(Ω) is continuously embedded in L^{p*}(Ω) and is compactly embedded in L^q(Ω) for every 1 ≤ q < p*.
nodes.by: Named after Franz Rellich and Vladimir Iosifovich Kondrashov; Rellich proved the L² theorem and Kondrashov the L^p theorem
nodes.note: It implies that every uniformly bounded sequence in W^{1,p}(Ω) has a subsequence that converges in L^q(Ω). It can be used to prove the Poincaré inequality.

nodes.name: Steinhaus theorem
nodes.statement: If A is a Lebesgue-measurable set in ℝⁿ whose Lebesgue measure is not zero, then the difference set A − A = {a − b : a, b ∈ A} contains an open neighbourhood of the origin.
nodes.by: Hugo Steinhaus; the general version for locally compact groups was first proved by André Weil
nodes.note: The general version says that if G is a locally compact group and A ⊂ G has positive left Haar measure, then {ab⁻¹ : a, b ∈ A} contains an open neighbourhood of the identity. A corollary is that every measurable proper subgroup of (ℝ, +) has measure zero.

nodes.name: Synge's theorem
nodes.statement: Let M be a closed Riemannian manifold with positive sectional curvature. If M is even-dimensional and orientable, then M is simply connected. If M is odd-dimensional, then M is orientable.
nodes.by: John Lighton Synge, 1936
nodes.note: It follows that a closed even-dimensional manifold can carry a positively curved Riemannian metric only if its fundamental group has one or two elements.

nodes.name: Wielandt theorem
nodes.statement: The gamma function is the only function f on the half-plane H = {z ∈ ℂ : Re z > 0} that is holomorphic on H, satisfies f(1) = 1 and f(z+1) = z f(z) for all z in H, and is bounded on the strip {z ∈ ℂ : 1 ≤ Re z ≤ 2}.
nodes.by: Named after Helmut Wielandt
nodes.note: It characterizes the gamma function, defined for Re z > 0 by Γ(z) = ∫ from 0 to ∞ of t^(z−1) e^(−t) dt.

nodes.name: Whitehead theorem
nodes.statement: Let f: X → Y be a continuous map between CW complexes that is a weak homotopy equivalence, meaning that it gives a bijection between the path components of X and of Y and isomorphisms πₙ(X, x) → πₙ(Y, f(x)) for every point x of X and every n ≥ 1. Then f is a homotopy equivalence, so it has a homotopy inverse g: Y → X.
nodes.by: J. H. C. Whitehead, 1949
nodes.note: It fails for general topological spaces: the Warsaw circle has all homotopy groups zero but is not homotopy equivalent to a point. Combined with the Hurewicz theorem, it shows that a map between simply connected CW complexes inducing isomorphisms on all integral homology groups is a homotopy equivalence.

nodes.name: Invariance of domain
nodes.statement: If U is an open subset of ℝⁿ and f : U → ℝⁿ is an injective continuous map, then f(U) is open in ℝⁿ and f is a homeomorphism between U and f(U).
nodes.by: L. E. J. Brouwer, 1912
nodes.note: The proof uses algebraic topology, notably the Brouwer fixed point theorem. One consequence is that ℝⁿ is not homeomorphic to ℝᵐ if n ≠ m.

nodes.name: Gromov's non-squeezing theorem
nodes.statement: In ℝ²ⁿ with the standard symplectic form dx₁∧dy₁ + ... + dxₙ∧dyₙ, if there is a symplectic embedding of the ball of radius r (the points with distance less than r from the origin) into the cylinder of radius R (the points with x₁² + y₁² < R²), then r ≤ R.
nodes.by: Mikhail Gromov, 1985
nodes.note: Symplectic maps preserve volume, but the theorem shows that being symplectic is much more restrictive than being volume-preserving. It is also known as the principle of the symplectic camel.

nodes.name: Hilbert projection theorem
nodes.statement: For every vector x in a Hilbert space H and every nonempty closed convex subset C of H, there is exactly one vector m in C such that ‖m − x‖ ≤ ‖c − x‖ for every c in C; that is, exactly one point of C is closest to x.

nodes.name: M. Riesz extension theorem
nodes.statement: Let E be a real vector space, F a vector subspace of E and K a convex cone in E, and suppose every y in E can be written as y = x + k with x in F and k in K. Then every linear functional on F that is non-negative on F ∩ K has a linear extension to all of E that is non-negative on all of K.
nodes.by: Marcel Riesz
nodes.note: Without the condition that every y in E is of the form x + k, a positive linear functional on a subspace need not have a positive extension. The Hahn–Banach theorem can be deduced from it, and Riesz proved it while studying the problem of moments.

nodes.name: Weierstrass preparation theorem
nodes.statement: Let f be an analytic function of several complex variables (z, z₂, ..., zₙ) near the origin with f(0,...,0) = 0, whose power series has some term involving only z. Then near the origin f = W·h, where h is analytic with h(0,...,0) ≠ 0, and W = zᵏ + g_{k−1}zᵏ⁻¹ + ... + g₀ is a monic polynomial in z whose coefficients gᵢ are analytic functions of z₂, ..., zₙ that are zero at the origin.
nodes.by: Named after Weierstrass; Carl Siegel disputed the attribution
nodes.note: Fixing small values of the other variables and solving W(z) = 0 gives the zeros of f near the origin as continuously varying branches, so f cannot have an isolated zero. It is equivalent to the Weierstrass division theorem.

nodes.name: Collage theorem
nodes.statement: Let L be a nonempty compact subset of a complete metric space, and let w₁, …, w_N be contractions forming an iterated function system with contractivity factor s, where 0 ≤ s < 1. If the Hausdorff distance between L and the union of the sets w_n(L) is at most ε, then the Hausdorff distance between L and the attractor A of the system is at most ε/(1 − s).
nodes.note: Informally, if L is close to being stabilized by the system, then L is also close to being its attractor. It is typically used in fractal compression.

nodes.name: Wiener's Tauberian theorem
nodes.statement: Let f be an integrable function on the real line. The linear combinations of translations x ↦ f(x + a) of f are dense in L¹(ℝ), so that they approximate every integrable function arbitrarily well, if and only if the Fourier transform of f has no real zeros.
nodes.by: Norbert Wiener, 1932
nodes.note: In L²(ℝ) the corresponding condition is that the real zeros of the Fourier transform form a set of Lebesgue measure zero. Gelfand gave a new proof using the theory of Banach algebras.

nodes.name: Karamata's inequality
nodes.statement: Let f be a convex real-valued function on an interval I of the real line, and let x₁ ≥ x₂ ≥ … ≥ xₙ and y₁ ≥ y₂ ≥ … ≥ yₙ be numbers in I such that x₁ + … + xᵢ ≥ y₁ + … + yᵢ for every i from 1 to n − 1 and x₁ + … + xₙ = y₁ + … + yₙ. Then f(x₁) + … + f(xₙ) ≥ f(y₁) + … + f(yₙ).
nodes.by: Named after Jovan Karamata
nodes.note: It generalizes the discrete form of Jensen's inequality, which is the case where every yᵢ equals the mean of the xᵢ. For a concave f the inequality is reversed.

nodes.name: Ky Fan inequality
nodes.statement: If x₁, …, xₙ are real numbers with 0 ≤ xᵢ ≤ 1/2 for every i, then the geometric mean of the xᵢ divided by the geometric mean of the numbers 1 − xᵢ is at most the arithmetic mean of the xᵢ divided by the arithmetic mean of the numbers 1 − xᵢ. Equality holds if and only if x₁ = x₂ = … = xₙ.
nodes.by: Published by Edwin F. Beckenbach and Richard E. Bellman, 1961, who attribute it to an unpublished result by Ky Fan
nodes.note: It is a special case of Levinson's inequality and resembles the inequality of arithmetic and geometric means.

nodes.name: Seifert–Van Kampen theorem
nodes.statement: Let X be a topological space that is the union of two open, path-connected subspaces U₁ and U₂ whose intersection is path-connected and nonempty, and let x₀ be a point in the intersection. Then X is path-connected, and the fundamental group of X at x₀ is the free product of the fundamental groups of U₁ and U₂ with amalgamation of the fundamental group of U₁ ∩ U₂.
nodes.by: Named after Herbert Seifert and Egbert van Kampen
nodes.note: It can be used to compute the fundamental group of spaces that are constructed out of simpler ones.

nodes.name: Carleman's inequality
nodes.statement: For every sequence a₁, a₂, a₃, … of non-negative real numbers, ∑ₙ₌₁^∞ (a₁a₂⋯aₙ)^(1/n) ≤ e · ∑ₙ₌₁^∞ aₙ, where e is Euler's number. The constant e cannot be replaced by any smaller number, and if ∑aₙ converges and some aₙ is non-zero, the inequality is strict.
nodes.by: Torsten Carleman, 1923
nodes.note: Carleman used it to prove the Denjoy–Carleman theorem on quasi-analytic classes. It can also be derived from Hardy's inequality by letting the exponent p tend to infinity.

nodes.name: Riemann–Roch theorem
nodes.statement: Let X be a connected compact Riemann surface of genus g with canonical divisor K, and let D be a divisor on X. Then ℓ(D) − ℓ(K − D) = deg(D) − g + 1, where ℓ(D) is the dimension of the space of meromorphic functions h on X for which every coefficient of (h) + D is non-negative.
nodes.by: Riemann, 1857 (as Riemann's inequality); definitive form after work of his student Roch, 1865
nodes.note: It computes the dimension of the space of meromorphic functions with prescribed zeros and allowed poles. Since ℓ(K − D) is never negative, ℓ(D) ≥ deg(D) − g + 1, which is Riemann's inequality.

nodes.name: Picone identity
nodes.statement: Suppose u and v solve the self-adjoint equations (p₁u′)′ + q₁u = 0 and (p₂v′)′ + q₂v = 0. Then for all x with v(x) ≠ 0, ((u/v)(p₁u′v − p₂uv′))′ = (q₂ − q₁)u² + (p₁ − p₂)u′² + p₂(u′ − v′u/v)².
nodes.by: Named after Mauro Picone; introduced in 1910
nodes.note: It gives an almost immediate proof of the Sturm comparison theorem and is used to prove the Sturm–Picone comparison theorem.

nodes.name: Loop theorem
nodes.statement: Let M be a 3-dimensional manifold with boundary ∂M. If there is a map f from the disc D² to M that takes the boundary circle ∂D² into ∂M, and f restricted to ∂D² is not nullhomotopic in ∂M, then there is an embedding of the disc with the same property.
nodes.by: Christos Papakyriakopoulos, 1956; a more general version is due to John Stallings
nodes.note: It generalizes Dehn's lemma and was first proven in the same work as Dehn's lemma and the Sphere theorem.

nodes.name: Tube lemma
nodes.statement: Let X be any topological space and Y a compact space. If an open set in X × Y contains a slice {x} × Y, then it also contains a tube U × Y around that slice, with U open in X; equivalently, the projection map X × Y → X is closed.
nodes.note: Also called Wallace's theorem. It is used to prove that a product of finitely many compact spaces is compact, and it fails without compactness of Y: in the plane, the open set |xy| < 1 contains {0} × ℝ but no tube.

nodes.name: Hartogs's extension theorem
nodes.statement: Let G be an open subset of ℂⁿ with n ≥ 2, let K be a compact subset of G, and let f be holomorphic on G \ K. If G \ K is connected, then f extends to a unique holomorphic function F on G.
nodes.by: First version proved by Friedrich Hartogs, 1906
nodes.note: It shows that an isolated singularity of a holomorphic function of more than one complex variable is always removable. The theorem fails for one variable, as f(z) = 1/z on ℂ without 0 shows.

nodes.name: Poisson summation formula
nodes.statement: Let s be a smooth complex valued function on ℝ that decays at infinity with all its derivatives (a Schwartz function), and let S be its Fourier transform, S(ξ) = ∫ s(x) e^(−2πiξx) dx. Then the sum of s(n) over all integers n equals the sum of S(k) over all integers k.
nodes.by: Discovered by Siméon Denis Poisson
nodes.note: It relates the Fourier series coefficients of the periodic summation of a function to values of the function's Fourier transform. It is used to derive functional equations such as that of the Riemann zeta function.

nodes.name: Tameness theorem
nodes.statement: Every complete hyperbolic 3-manifold with finitely generated fundamental group is topologically tame, that is, homeomorphic to the interior of a compact 3-manifold.
nodes.by: Conjectured by Albert Marden, 1974; proved by Ian Agol, 2004, and independently by Danny Calegari and David Gabai
nodes.note: It implies the Ahlfors measure conjecture. Before its proof it was called the Marden conjecture or the tame ends conjecture.

nodes.name: Brunn–Minkowski theorem
nodes.statement: Let n ≥ 1, let μ be the Lebesgue measure (volume) on ℝⁿ, and let A and B be nonempty compact subsets of ℝⁿ. Then μ(A + B)^(1/n) ≥ μ(A)^(1/n) + μ(B)^(1/n), where A + B = {a + b : a in A, b in B} is the Minkowski sum, and the inequality also holds when A, B and A + B are only assumed to be measurable and nonempty.
nodes.by: Hermann Brunn, 1887, and Hermann Minkowski, 1896, for convex sets; Lazar Lyusternik, 1935, for compact sets
nodes.note: It is equivalent to the multiplicative form μ(λA + (1 − λ)B) ≥ μ(A)^λ μ(B)^(1−λ) for λ in [0, 1]. The Prékopa–Leindler inequality is a functional generalization of that form.

nodes.name: Sturm–Picone comparison theorem
nodes.statement: Let p₁, p₂, q₁, q₂ be real-valued continuous functions on [a, b] with 0 < p₂(x) ≤ p₁(x) and q₁(x) ≤ q₂(x). Let u be a non-trivial solution of (p₁y′)′ + q₁y = 0 with successive roots z₁ and z₂, and let v be a non-trivial solution of (p₂y′)′ + q₂y = 0; then either v has a zero strictly between z₁ and z₂, or v = λu for some real number λ.
nodes.by: Jacques Charles François Sturm, 1836 (first part); Mauro Picone, 1910 (second part)
nodes.note: When the two equations are identical it gives the Sturm separation theorem. Picone proved his part using the Picone identity.

nodes.name: Simplicial approximation theorem
nodes.statement: Let f be a continuous map between finite simplicial complexes |K| and |L|. Then there is a number n₀ such that for every n ≥ n₀, after n barycentric subdivisions of K there is a simplicial map s that approximates f, meaning that |s|(x) lies in the smallest closed simplex of L containing f(x) for every x. Such an approximation is homotopic to f.
nodes.by: First proved by L.E.J. Brouwer
nodes.note: It put the homology theory of the time on a rigorous basis by showing that the effect of continuous maps on homology groups can be expressed in a finitary way.

nodes.name: Kuratowski embedding
nodes.statement: Let (X,d) be a metric space with a chosen point x₀, and let C_b(X) be the Banach space of all bounded continuous real-valued functions on X with the supremum norm. Then the map Φ sending x to the function y ↦ d(x,y) − d(x₀,y) is an isometry from X into C_b(X).
nodes.by: Kazimierz Kuratowski; a very close variation already appears in papers of Fréchet
nodes.note: It lets any metric space be viewed as a subset of a Banach space, which has extra structure such as addition of points and completeness.

nodes.name: Helly's selection theorem
nodes.statement: Let (f_n) be a sequence of increasing functions from a real interval I into the real line, uniformly bounded: there are real numbers a and b with a ≤ f_n ≤ b for every n. Then the sequence has a subsequence that converges pointwise.
nodes.by: Named after the Austrian mathematician Eduard Helly
nodes.note: It is a sequential compactness theorem for uniformly bounded monotone functions. In probability theory it implies compactness of a tight family of measures.

nodes.name: Fourier inversion theorem
nodes.statement: Let f: ℝ → ℂ and let its Fourier transform be (𝓕f)(ξ) = ∫ e^(−2πiyξ) f(y) dy. If both f and 𝓕f are absolutely integrable (in the Lebesgue sense) and f is continuous at the point x, then f(x) = ∫ e^(2πixξ) (𝓕f)(ξ) dξ, so f can be recovered from its Fourier transform.
nodes.note: Versions of the theorem also hold under more general conditions, although the integrals may then not converge in the ordinary sense.

nodes.name: Mostow rigidity theorem
nodes.statement: Let M and N be complete hyperbolic manifolds of finite volume, both of the same dimension n ≥ 3. Every isomorphism between their fundamental groups is induced by a unique isometry from M to N, so the geometry of such a manifold is determined by its fundamental group.
nodes.by: Proven for closed manifolds by Mostow, 1968; extended to finite volume manifolds by Prasad, 1973 (all dimensions at least 3) and by Marden, 1974 (dimension 3)
nodes.note: For n > 2 the space of complete hyperbolic structures on a finite volume hyperbolic n-manifold is a single point. A hyperbolic surface of genus g > 1 instead has a moduli space of dimension 6g − 6.

nodes.name: Skorokhod's representation theorem
nodes.statement: Let μₙ be probability measures on a metric space S that converge weakly to a probability measure μ∞ on S whose support is separable. Then there are S-valued random variables Xₙ on a common probability space, with the law of Xₙ equal to μₙ for every n including n = ∞, such that Xₙ converges to X∞ almost surely.
nodes.by: Named after A. V. Skorokhod
nodes.note: It represents a weakly convergent sequence of probability measures as the laws of a pointwise convergent sequence of random variables.

nodes.name: Peetre's inequality
nodes.statement: For any real number t and any vectors x and y in ℝⁿ, ((1 + |x|²) / (1 + |y|²))^t ≤ 2^|t| · (1 + |x − y|²)^|t|.
nodes.by: Jaak Peetre, 1959

nodes.name: Soul theorem
nodes.statement: If (M, g) is a complete connected non-compact Riemannian manifold with nonnegative sectional curvature, then there exists a closed, totally convex, totally geodesic embedded submanifold whose normal bundle is diffeomorphic to M.
nodes.by: Jeff Cheeger and Detlef Gromoll, 1972
nodes.note: It largely reduces the study of complete manifolds of non-negative sectional curvature to the compact case. It generalizes a 1969 result of Gromoll and Wolfgang Meyer.

nodes.name: Positive energy theorem
nodes.statement: Let (M, g, k) be an initial data set satisfying the dominant energy condition, where (M, g) is an oriented, smooth, complete three-dimensional Riemannian manifold without boundary with finitely many ends, each asymptotically flat: in suitable coordinates the metric differs from the Euclidean one by terms bounded by a constant times 1/|x|, its first and second derivatives by constants times 1/|x|² and 1/|x|³, and the scalar curvature, k and the trace of k decay at the further rates the theorem specifies. Then the ADM energy of every end is nonnegative, and if in addition the third and fourth derivatives of that difference are bounded by constants times 1/|x|⁴ and some end has ADM energy zero, then M has only one end, M is diffeomorphic to ℝ³, and Minkowski space is a development of (M, g, k).
nodes.by: Richard Schoen and Shing-Tung Yau, 1979 and 1981; another proof by Edward Witten, 1981
nodes.note: It is also known as the positive mass theorem. Schoen used it in 1984 to complete the solution of the Yamabe problem, and Hubert Bray used it to prove the Riemannian Penrose inequality.

nodes.name: Minkowski problem
nodes.statement: A non-negative Borel measure μ on the unit sphere Sⁿ⁻¹ is the surface area measure of some convex body in ℝⁿ if and only if μ has its centroid at the origin and is not concentrated on a great subsphere. The convex body is then determined by μ uniquely up to translation.
nodes.by: Hermann Minkowski, Aleksandr Danilovich Aleksandrov, Werner Fenchel and Børge Jessen
nodes.note: The surface area measure of a convex body is the pushforward of the (n−1)-dimensional Hausdorff measure on its boundary under the Gauss map. In 1953 Louis Nirenberg published a solution of the Minkowski problem in Euclidean 3-space, where the problem asks for a strictly convex surface with prescribed Gaussian curvature.

nodes.name: Classification of Fatou components
nodes.statement: Let f = P(z)/Q(z) be a rational function on the extended complex plane with max(deg P, deg Q) ≥ 2. Then every periodic component U of the Fatou set of f is exactly one of the following: a component containing an attracting periodic point; a parabolic component; a Siegel disc, which is simply connected and on which f is analytically conjugate to a rotation of the unit disc by an irrational angle; or a Herman ring, which is an annulus on which f is analytically conjugate to a rotation of a round annulus by an irrational angle.
nodes.note: For transcendental functions there are further types of component: Baker domains, on which the iterates tend to an essential singularity, and wandering domains, which are not eventually periodic.

nodes.name: Olech theorem
nodes.statement: Let ẋ = f(x) be a system of two differential equations with x = (x₁, x₂) in ℝ² and with 0 as an equilibrium point. Suppose that at every point of ℝ² the trace of the Jacobian matrix of f is negative and its determinant is positive, and that either (∂f¹/∂x₁)(∂f²/∂x₂) ≠ 0 at every point or (∂f¹/∂x₂)(∂f²/∂x₁) ≠ 0 at every point. Then the equilibrium 0 is uniformly globally asymptotically stable.
nodes.by: Czesław Olech, 1963, based on joint work with Philip Hartman

nodes.name: Liberman's lemma
nodes.statement: Let γ be a minimizing geodesic with unit speed on the surface of a convex body K in Euclidean space, and let p be any point of K. Then the function that sends t to the square of the distance from p to γ(t), minus t², is concave.
nodes.by: Named after Joseph Liberman

nodes.name: Morse–Palais lemma
nodes.statement: Let H be a real Hilbert space, U an open neighbourhood of 0 in H, and f : U → ℝ a function that is k+2 times continuously differentiable for some k ≥ 1, with f(0) = 0 and 0 a non-degenerate critical point, meaning that the second derivative of f at 0 gives an isomorphism of H with its continuous dual. Then there are a neighbourhood V of 0 in U, a diffeomorphism φ : V → V that is Cᵏ with Cᵏ inverse, and an invertible symmetric operator A : H → H such that f(x) = ⟨Aφ(x), φ(x)⟩ for all x in V.
nodes.by: Marston Morse in the finite-dimensional case; generalized to Hilbert spaces by Richard Palais and Stephen Smale
nodes.note: It plays a crucial role in Morse theory.

nodes.name: Initial value theorem
nodes.statement: Let F(s) = ∫₀^∞ f(t)e^(−st) dt be the one-sided Laplace transform of f. If f is bounded on (0, ∞), or merely f(t) = O(e^(ct)) for some constant c, and f(t) has a limit as t tends to 0 from above, then that limit equals the limit of sF(s) as s tends to ∞.
nodes.note: It relates expressions in the frequency domain to the behavior in the time domain as time approaches zero.

nodes.name: Vysochanskij–Petunin inequality
nodes.statement: Let X be a random variable with a unimodal distribution and finite variance, let α be a real number, and let ρ = √E[(X−α)²]. Then for any r > 0, Pr(|X−α| ≥ r) ≤ 4ρ²/(9r²) when r ≥ √(8/3)·ρ, and Pr(|X−α| ≥ r) ≤ 4ρ²/(3r²) − 1/3 when r ≤ √(8/3)·ρ.
nodes.note: It refines Chebyshev's inequality by the factor 4/9, made possible by unimodality. Taking α as the mean μ and r = λσ gives Pr(|X−μ| ≥ λσ) ≤ 4/(9λ²) for every λ > √(8/3).

nodes.name: Jackson's inequality
nodes.statement: If f is a complex-valued function on [0, 2π], periodic with period 2π, that is r times differentiable and satisfies |f^(r)(x)| ≤ 1 for all x, then for every positive integer n there is a trigonometric polynomial T of degree at most n−1 with |f(x) − T(x)| ≤ C(r)/n^r for all x in [0, 2π], where C(r) depends only on r.
nodes.by: Dunham Jackson
nodes.note: The smoother the function is, the better it can be approximated by polynomials. The Akhiezer–Krein–Favard theorem gives the sharp value of C(r), and Bernstein's theorem gives a converse.

nodes.name: Steffensen's inequality
nodes.statement: Let f: [a, b] → ℝ be non-negative, monotonically decreasing and integrable, and let g: [a, b] → [0, 1] be integrable. With k = ∫ₐᵇ g(x) dx, we have ∫ from b−k to b of f(x) dx ≤ ∫ₐᵇ f(x)g(x) dx ≤ ∫ from a to a+k of f(x) dx.
nodes.by: Named after Johan Frederik Steffensen

nodes.name: Phragmén–Lindelöf principle
nodes.statement: Let S be the horizontal strip of complex numbers z whose imaginary part lies strictly between −π/2 and π/2. If f is holomorphic on S and continuous on S together with its two boundary lines, satisfies |f(z)| ≤ 1 on those boundary lines, and satisfies |f(z)| < exp(A·exp(c·|Re z|)) for all z in S for some real constants c < 1 and A < ∞, then |f(z)| ≤ 1 for all z in S.
nodes.by: Lars Edvard Phragmén and Ernst Leonard Lindelöf, 1908
nodes.note: The conclusion fails when c = 1. A version for sectors of the complex plane gives a complex-analytic proof of Hardy's uncertainty principle, and Carlson's theorem is an application of the principle.

nodes.name: Carathéodory's theorem
nodes.statement: Every conformal mapping from the unit disk onto a region of the complex plane bounded by a Jordan curve (a closed curve that does not cross itself) extends continuously to a homeomorphism from the unit circle onto that Jordan curve.
nodes.by: Constantin Carathéodory, 1913
nodes.note: It extends the Riemann mapping theorem and is one of Carathéodory's results on prime ends and the boundary behaviour of univalent holomorphic functions.

nodes.name: Schwarz reflection principle
nodes.statement: Suppose F is continuous on the closed upper half plane (Im z ≥ 0), holomorphic on the open upper half plane (Im z > 0), and real-valued on the real axis. Then setting F(z̄) equal to the complex conjugate of F(z) for each z in the upper half plane extends F to a function that is analytic on the whole complex plane.
nodes.by: Proved by Hermann Schwarz
nodes.note: The principle is easy to prove from Morera's theorem, and the same method gives versions that allow singularities, for example for meromorphic functions. The principle also adapts to harmonic functions.

nodes.name: Hilbert–Arnold problem
nodes.statement: In a generic family of smooth vector fields on the sphere, smoothly parameterized over a compact set in finite dimensional Euclidean space, the number of limit cycles is bounded by one number for all parameter values.
nodes.by: Formulated by Vladimir Arnold and Yulij Ilyashenko in the 1980s
nodes.note: The problem is historically related to Hilbert's sixteenth problem. It reduces to a local problem about bifurcations of polycycles, which has been solved for families with one and two parameters.

nodes.name: Hadamard gap theorem
nodes.statement: Let n₀ < n₁ < n₂ < … be positive integers with lim inf n_(k+1)/n_k > 1, and let a_k be complex numbers such that the power series f(z) = ∑ a_k z^(n_k) has radius of convergence 1. Then the unit circle is a natural boundary of f, so f cannot be continued analytically across any point of the circle.
nodes.by: Jacques Hadamard, 1892
nodes.note: It is a special case of both the Fabry gap theorem and Ostrowski's overconvergence theorem.

nodes.name: Edge-of-the-wedge theorem
nodes.statement: Let C be an open cone in ℝⁿ with vertex at the origin and E an open subset of ℝⁿ, and form the wedge W of points x + iy with x in E and y in C, and the opposite wedge W′ of points x + iy with x in E and −y in C. If f is continuous on W together with E and W′, and holomorphic on W and on W′, then f extends to a holomorphic function on a neighborhood of E in ℂⁿ.
nodes.by: Formulated and first proved by Nikolay Bogoliubov, 1956; named by Hans-Joachim Bremermann, Reinhard Oehme and John G. Taylor, who also demonstrated it in 1958
nodes.note: It is used in quantum field theory to construct the analytic continuation of Wightman functions. In one dimension it says that a continuous function on the complex plane that is holomorphic on the upper and lower half-planes is holomorphic everywhere.

nodes.name: Denjoy's theorem on rotation number
nodes.statement: Let f be an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of the circle whose rotation number θ is irrational, and suppose its derivative is positive and is a continuous function of bounded variation. Then f is topologically conjugate to the irrational rotation by θ, and every orbit of f is dense in the circle.
nodes.by: Denjoy, 1932
nodes.note: Every C² diffeomorphism satisfies the hypothesis on the derivative. Denjoy also gave an example of a C¹ diffeomorphism with an irrational rotation number that is not conjugate to a rotation.

nodes.name: Kirszbraun theorem
nodes.statement: Let U be a subset of a Hilbert space H₁, let H₂ be another Hilbert space, and let f: U → H₂ be Lipschitz-continuous. Then there is a Lipschitz-continuous map F: H₁ → H₂ that extends f and has the same Lipschitz constant as f.
nodes.by: Mojżesz David Kirszbraun, 1934; reproved by Frederick Valentine, 1945
nodes.note: The corresponding statement for Banach spaces is not true in general, not even for finite-dimensional Banach spaces.

nodes.name: Liouville's theorem on conformal mappings
nodes.statement: Every smooth conformal mapping on a domain of ℝⁿ, where n > 2, can be expressed as a composition of translations, homotheties, orthogonal transformations and inversions, that is, it is a Möbius transformation in n dimensions.
nodes.by: Joseph Liouville, 1850
nodes.note: It is a rigidity theorem that severely limits the conformal mappings in ℝ³ and higher dimensions. In ℝ² conformal mappings can be much more complicated.

nodes.name: Meusnier's theorem
nodes.statement: All curves on a surface that pass through a given point p and have the same tangent line at p have the same normal curvature at p, and their osculating circles form a sphere.
nodes.by: Jean Baptiste Meusnier, announced 1776, published 1785

nodes.name: Novikov's compact leaf theorem
nodes.statement: Every smooth codimension-one foliation of a closed 3-manifold whose universal covering space is not contractible has a compact leaf. In particular, every smooth codimension-one foliation of the 3-sphere S³ has a compact leaf, which is a torus T² bounding a solid torus with the Reeb foliation.
nodes.by: Sergei Novikov, 1964 for the 3-sphere, as conjectured earlier by Charles Ehresmann, and 1965 for any closed 3-manifold
nodes.note: In the 1965 form the compact leaf has genus at most 1. Ehresmann's conjecture for S³ was known to hold for all known examples, including the Reeb foliation.

nodes.name: Routh–Hurwitz theorem
nodes.statement: Let f be a polynomial of degree n with complex coefficients and no roots on the imaginary axis, and let p and q be its numbers of roots, counted with multiplicity, in the left and right half-planes. Then p − q equals 1/π times the change in the argument of f(iy) as y runs from −∞ to +∞, and it also equals w(+∞) − w(−∞), where w(x) is the number of sign variations of the generalized Sturm chain obtained by the Euclidean algorithm from the real and imaginary parts P₀(y) and P₁(y) of f(iy).
nodes.by: Named after Edward John Routh and Adolf Hurwitz; proved in 1895
nodes.note: It gives the Routh–Hurwitz stability criterion: f has all its roots in the left half-plane exactly when p − q = n. The equality p − q = w(+∞) − w(−∞) is a complex counterpart of Sturm's theorem.

nodes.name: Reeb sphere theorem
nodes.statement: Let M be a closed, oriented, connected manifold of dimension n ≥ 2 that admits a C¹ transversely oriented codimension-one foliation whose set of singularities is non-empty and consists only of centers. Then the foliation has exactly two singular points and M is homeomorphic to the sphere Sⁿ.
nodes.by: Named after Georges Reeb
nodes.note: It is a consequence of the Reeb stability theorem. In 1978 Edward Wagneur extended it to Morse foliations with saddles, showing that the number of centers is at most the number of saddles plus 2.

nodes.name: Reeb stability theorem
nodes.statement: Let F be a C¹ codimension-one foliation of a closed manifold M. If some leaf of F is compact and has finite fundamental group, then every leaf of F is compact and has finite fundamental group.
nodes.by: Named after Georges Reeb
nodes.note: If F is also transversely orientable, every leaf is diffeomorphic to the given one and M fibres over the circle with the leaves as fibres. The global theorem is false for foliations of codimension greater than one.

nodes.name: Sazonov's theorem
nodes.statement: Let G and H be Hilbert spaces and T a bounded linear operator from G to H. If T is a Hilbert–Schmidt operator, then T is γ-radonifying, meaning that the pushforward of the canonical Gaussian cylinder set measure on G is a genuine measure on H.
nodes.by: Named after Vyacheslav Sazonov
nodes.note: The converse also holds. The result matters in the study of stochastic processes and the Malliavin calculus.

nodes.name: No-wandering-domain theorem
nodes.statement: Let f be a rational map from the Riemann sphere to itself with degree at least 2. Then for every component U of the Fatou set of f, the sequence U, f(U), f(f(U)), … eventually becomes periodic, so f has no wandering domain.
nodes.by: Conjectured by Fatou; proved by Dennis Sullivan, 1985
nodes.note: The theorem does not hold for arbitrary maps: the transcendental map f(z) = z + 2π sin(z) has wandering domains. It extends to transcendental entire and meromorphic functions with finitely many singular values.

nodes.name: Stone's theorem on one-parameter unitary groups
nodes.statement: Let (Uₜ), t ∈ ℝ, be a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group on a Hilbert space: unitary operators with Uₜ₊ₛ = UₜUₛ for all real s, t and Uₜψ → Uₛψ as t → s for every vector ψ. Then there is a unique, possibly unbounded, self-adjoint operator A with Uₜ = e^(itA) for all t, and conversely, for every self-adjoint operator A the operators Uₜ = e^(itA) form a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group.
nodes.by: Proved by Stone
nodes.note: The operator A is called the infinitesimal generator of the group, and it is bounded exactly when t ↦ Uₜ is norm-continuous. Von Neumann (1932) showed that strong continuity can be relaxed to weak measurability, at least when the Hilbert space is separable.

nodes.name: Hardy's theorem
nodes.statement: Let f be a non-constant holomorphic function on the open disc of radius R centred at zero in the complex plane, and for 0 < r < R let I(r) be the average of |f(re^(iθ))| over θ from 0 to 2π. Then I(r) is strictly increasing and is a convex function of log r.

nodes.name: Monodromy theorem
nodes.statement: Let f be a complex-analytic function on an open disk centred at a point P, and let Q be another point. If γₛ, for s in [0, 1], is a family of curves from P to Q such that γₛ(t) depends continuously on (s, t) and f can be analytically continued along every γₛ, then the analytic continuations of f along γ₀ and γ₁ give the same values at Q.
nodes.note: A consequence also called the monodromy theorem says that if f can be continued along every curve from P in an open simply connected set W containing the disk, then f extends to a complex-analytic function on all of W.

nodes.name: Schur test
nodes.statement: Let X and Y be measurable spaces and T an integral operator Tf(x) = ∫_Y K(x,y) f(y) dy with non-negative kernel K. If there are functions p(x) > 0 and q(y) > 0 and numbers α, β > 0 with ∫_Y K(x,y) q(y) dy ≤ α p(x) for almost all x and ∫_X p(x) K(x,y) dx ≤ β q(y) for almost all y, then T extends to a continuous operator from L² to L² with operator norm at most √(αβ).
nodes.by: Named after Issai Schur
nodes.note: In the original version T is a matrix and α = β = 1. Young's inequality for integral operators is a similar statement for Lᵖ to L^q operator norms.

nodes.name: 2π theorem
nodes.statement: Let M be a cusped hyperbolic 3-manifold with disjoint horoball neighbourhoods chosen for each cusp. A Dehn filling of M in which each filling slope has length greater than 2π results in a 3-manifold with a complete metric of negative sectional curvature. This metric can be chosen to agree with the original hyperbolic metric outside the horoball neighbourhoods.
nodes.by: Gromov and Thurston
nodes.note: In 2000 it was improved by the 6 theorem, which says that Dehn filling along slopes of length greater than 6 gives a hyperbolike 3-manifold.

nodes.name: Abel's inequality
nodes.statement: Let a₁, …, aₙ be a nonincreasing or nondecreasing sequence of real numbers, let b₁, …, bₙ be real or complex numbers, and let B_k = b₁ + … + b_k. If the a's are nondecreasing, then |∑ a_k b_k| ≤ max|B_k|·(|aₙ| + aₙ − a₁). If they are nonincreasing, then |∑ a_k b_k| ≤ max|B_k|·(|aₙ| − aₙ + a₁). In particular, if they are nonincreasing and nonnegative, then |∑ a_k b_k| ≤ max|B_k|·a₁.
nodes.by: Named after Niels Henrik Abel
nodes.note: It follows from Abel's transformation, the discrete version of integration by parts.

nodes.name: Product rule
nodes.statement: If two functions u and v are differentiable at a point x, then their product u·v is also differentiable at x, and (u·v)′(x) = u′(x)·v(x) + u(x)·v′(x). In Leibniz's notation, d(uv)/dx = (du/dx)·v + u·(dv/dx).
nodes.by: Credited to Gottfried Leibniz; J. M. Child argues it is due to Isaac Barrow
nodes.note: It extends to products of three or more functions and to higher-order derivatives of a product.

nodes.name: Stokes' theorem
nodes.statement: Let Σ be a smooth oriented surface in ℝ³ with boundary curve ∂Σ, and let F be a vector field with continuous first-order partial derivatives on Σ. Then the circulation of F around ∂Σ equals the surface integral of the curl of F over Σ.
nodes.by: First appears in a letter from William Thomson to George Stokes, 2 July 1850; Stokes set it as a question on the 1854 Smith's Prize examination
nodes.note: It is also called the Kelvin–Stokes theorem and is a special case of the generalized Stokes theorem.

nodes.name: Acyclic models theorem
nodes.statement: Let F and V be covariant functors from a category to chain complexes of R-modules over a ring R, both zero in negative degrees. Suppose F is free, with F_k having a basis in a set of models M_k for each k ≥ 0, and V is acyclic at these models, meaning H_k(V(M)) = 0 for all k > 0 and all M in M_k ∪ M_(k+1). Then every natural transformation H₀(F) → H₀(V) induces a natural chain map F → V, and this chain map is unique up to natural chain homotopy.
nodes.by: Developed by Samuel Eilenberg and Saunders MacLane
nodes.note: It can be used to show that two homology theories are isomorphic, and to prove the Eilenberg–Zilber theorem.

nodes.name: Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem
nodes.statement: Every infinite bounded sequence in ℝⁿ has a convergent subsequence. Equivalently, a subset of ℝⁿ is sequentially compact if and only if it is closed and bounded.
nodes.by: Named after Bernard Bolzano and Karl Weierstrass; first proved by Bolzano in 1817 as a lemma in the proof of the intermediate value theorem, and proven again by Weierstrass some fifty years later
nodes.note: It is also called the sequential compactness theorem.

nodes.name: Ahlfors measure conjecture
nodes.statement: The limit set of a finitely generated Kleinian group is either the whole Riemann sphere or has measure zero.
nodes.by: Introduced by Lars Ahlfors, who proved the case of a finite-sided fundamental domain; proved for topologically tame groups by Richard Canary; the general case follows from Marden's tameness conjecture, proved independently by Ian Agol and by Danny Calegari and David Gabai
nodes.note: Canary also showed that when the limit set is the whole sphere, the action of the group on it is ergodic.

nodes.name: Ahlfors finiteness theorem
nodes.statement: If Γ is a finitely generated Kleinian group with region of discontinuity Ω, then Ω/Γ has a finite number of components. Each component is a compact Riemann surface with a finite number of points removed.
nodes.by: Lars Ahlfors, apart from a gap that was filled by Greenberg
nodes.note: A quantitative refinement, the Bers area inequality, bounds Area(Ω/Γ) by 4π(N − 1) for a non-elementary Kleinian group with N generators.

nodes.name: Akhiezer's theorem
nodes.statement: Let f be an entire function of exponential type τ with f(x) ≥ 0 for real x. Then the following are equivalent: (1) there is an entire function F of exponential type τ/2, with all its zeros in the closed upper half plane, such that f(z) = F(z) times the complex conjugate of F(z̄); (2) the sum of |Im(1/zₙ)| over the zeros zₙ of f is finite.
nodes.by: Naum Akhiezer
nodes.note: The Fejér–Riesz theorem is a special case.

nodes.name: Stirling's approximation
nodes.statement: n! is asymptotic to √(2πn) · (n/e)ⁿ, meaning the ratio of the two sides tends to 1 as n tends to infinity.
nodes.by: First discovered by Abraham de Moivre in 1721 with an unspecified constant; James Stirling showed in 1730 that the constant is √(2π)
nodes.note: It can be derived from the Euler–Maclaurin formula together with Wallis' product. It is the first term of the Stirling series, an asymptotic expansion that does not converge.

nodes.name: Denjoy–Luzin theorem
nodes.statement: If a trigonometric series converges absolutely on a set of positive measure, then the sum of its coefficients converges absolutely, and in particular the trigonometric series converges absolutely everywhere.
nodes.by: Introduced independently by Denjoy and Luzin, 1912

nodes.name: Analyst's traveling salesman theorem
nodes.statement: For a set E in the plane, let β(E) be the diameter of E plus the sum, over all dyadic squares Q with side l(Q), of β_E(3Q)² · l(Q), where 3Q is the square with the same center and three times the side and 2β_E(3Q) · l(3Q) is the width of the smallest rectangle containing the part of E inside 3Q. There is a constant C > 0 such that every plane set E with β(E) < ∞ lies on a curve of length at most C · β(E), and conversely every rectifiable curve Γ satisfies β(Γ) < C · H¹(Γ), where H¹ is the one-dimensional Hausdorff measure.
nodes.by: Peter Jones; extended to ℝᵈ by Kate Okikiolu and to Hilbert spaces by Raanan Schul
nodes.note: It answers which plane sets are subsets of rectifiable curves of finite length. Okikiolu showed the same theorem in ℝᵈ for d > 1, and Schul's Hilbert space version has a constant independent of dimension.

nodes.name: Analytic Fredholm theorem
nodes.statement: Let G be an open connected subset of the complex numbers and H a real or complex Hilbert space. Let B be a map from G to the bounded linear operators on H that is analytic (the complex derivative exists at every point of G) and such that B(λ) is a compact operator for each λ in G. Then either (I − B(λ)) has no inverse for any λ in G, or it has an inverse for every λ in G outside a discrete subset S of G (a set with no limit points in G). In the second case λ ↦ (I − B(λ))⁻¹ is analytic on G \ S, and for λ in S the equation B(λ)ψ = ψ has a finite-dimensional family of solutions.
nodes.by: Named after Erik Ivar Fredholm
nodes.note: It is the basis of the Fredholm alternative and the Hilbert–Schmidt theorem.

nodes.name: Analyticity of holomorphic functions
nodes.statement: A complex function that is differentiable at every point of some open disk centered at a is, in some open disk centered at a, equal to a convergent power series. Conversely, a function that is a convergent power series in an open disk centered at a is differentiable at every point of such a disk.
nodes.by: The argument was first given by Cauchy
nodes.note: Corollaries include the identity theorem and the fact that holomorphic functions are infinitely differentiable.

nodes.name: Anderson's theorem
nodes.statement: Let K be a convex body in ℝⁿ with K = −K. Let f: ℝⁿ → ℝ be non-negative, symmetric (f(x) = f(−x)) and integrable over ℝⁿ, with convex super-level sets {x : f(x) ≥ t} for every t ≥ 0. Then for any 0 ≤ c ≤ 1 and y in ℝⁿ, the integral of f(x + cy) over K is at least the integral of f(x + y) over K.
nodes.by: Named after Theodore Wilbur Anderson
nodes.note: The integral over K does not decrease when K is translated towards the origin. It also has an application to probability theory.

nodes.name: Annulus theorem
nodes.statement: If h is a homeomorphism of ℝⁿ to itself that maps the unit ball B into its interior, then the region B minus h(interior of B) is homeomorphic to the annulus S^(n−1)×[0,1].
nodes.by: Proved in dimension 2 by Radó (1924), in dimension 3 by Moise (1952), in dimensions at least 5 by Kirby (1969) and in dimension 4 by Quinn (1982)
nodes.note: It was formerly called the annulus conjecture. It is trivial in dimensions 0 and 1, and it is equivalent to the stable homeomorphism conjecture, which says that every orientation-preserving homeomorphism of ℝⁿ is stable.

nodes.name: Area theorem (conformal mapping)
nodes.statement: Suppose f is analytic and injective on the punctured open unit disk (the points z with 0 < |z| < 1), and there f(z) = 1/z + ∑ aₙzⁿ, summed over n ≥ 0. Then ∑ n|aₙ|² ≤ 1, summed over n ≥ 0.
nodes.note: It is called the area theorem because its proof uses the notion of area. It is often used to prove the Koebe 1/4 theorem.

nodes.name: Abel's test
nodes.statement: If ∑aₙ is a convergent series of real numbers and (bₙ) is a monotone and bounded sequence, then the series ∑aₙbₙ also converges.
nodes.by: Niels Henrik Abel, 1826
nodes.note: It is mainly useful for series ∑aₙ that do not converge absolutely, and it can be proved by summation by parts. A related version for power series is used in complex analysis.

nodes.name: Artstein's theorem
nodes.statement: A nonlinear control-affine system ẋ = f(x) + ∑ gᵢ(x)uᵢ (sum over i = 1 to m) has a differentiable control-Lyapunov function if and only if it admits a regular stabilizing feedback u(x), that is, a locally Lipschitz function on ℝⁿ without the origin.
nodes.by: Zvi Artstein, 1983; constructive version by Eduardo D. Sontag, 1989
nodes.note: Artstein's original proof is nonconstructive. Sontag's version exhibits the feedback explicitly.

nodes.name: Askey–Gasper inequality
nodes.statement: Let β ≥ 0 and −1 ≤ x ≤ 1. The sum over k from 0 to n of P_k^(α,β)(x) / P_k^(β,α)(1), where P_k^(α,β) is a Jacobi polynomial, is at least 0 if and only if α + β ≥ −2.
nodes.by: Askey and Gasper, 1976
nodes.note: In its special case β = 0, with α a non-negative integer, Louis de Branges used it in his proof of the Bieberbach conjecture. Ekhad gave a short proof in 1993.

nodes.name: Atiyah–Segal completion theorem
nodes.statement: Let G be a compact Lie group and X a G-CW-complex. The projection X×EG → X induces an isomorphism of prorings from the completion of the G-equivariant K-theory of X, taken with respect to the augmentation ideal I of the representation ring of G, to the K-theory of (X×EG)/G.
nodes.by: Michael Atiyah, 1961 for finite groups; Michael Atiyah and Graeme Segal, 1969 for the general case
nodes.note: When X is a point, it gives an isomorphism between the K-theory of the classifying space BG and the completion of the representation ring R(G).

nodes.name: Atkinson's theorem
nodes.statement: Let H be a Hilbert space. A bounded operator T on H has finite-dimensional kernel, an adjoint with finite-dimensional kernel and closed range (that is, T is Fredholm) if and only if there are a bounded operator S and compact operators C₁ and C₂ with TS = I + C₁ and ST = I + C₂.
nodes.by: Named after Frederick Valentine Atkinson
nodes.note: Equivalently, T is Fredholm if and only if its projection in the Calkin algebra is invertible.

nodes.name: Atkinson–Mingarelli theorem
nodes.statement: Consider a Sturm–Liouville eigenvalue problem on a closed bounded interval with real piecewise continuous coefficients p, q, w and separated boundary conditions with real coefficients. Suppose p has finitely many sign changes and the positive part (w/p)₊ = max{w/p, 0} and negative part (w/p)₋ = max{−w/p, 0} are not identically zero. Then there are infinitely many eigenvalues 0 < λ₁⁺ < λ₂⁺ < … tending to ∞ and infinitely many 0 > λ₁⁻ > λ₂⁻ > … tending to −∞, with λₙ⁺ ~ n²π² / (∫ √(w/p)₊ dx)² and λₙ⁻ ~ −n²π² / (∫ √(w/p)₋ dx)² as n → ∞, the integrals running over the interval.
nodes.by: Frederick Valentine Atkinson and A. B. Mingarelli, 1987
nodes.note: The asymptotic formulas are Atkinson and Mingarelli's solution of Jörgens' conjecture. The theorem also holds when 1/p, q and w are only Lebesgue integrable.

nodes.name: Aubin–Lions lemma
nodes.statement: Let X₀ ⊆ X ⊆ X₁ be Banach spaces, where X₀ is compactly embedded in X and X is continuously embedded in X₁. For 1 ≤ p, q ≤ ∞ let W be the set of u in L^p([0,T]; X₀) whose derivative u̇ lies in L^q([0,T]; X₁). If p < ∞, the embedding of W into L^p([0,T]; X) is compact. If p = ∞ and q > 1, the embedding of W into C([0,T]; X) is compact.
nodes.by: Named after Jean-Pierre Aubin and Jacques-Louis Lions; Aubin's original proof assumed X₀ and X₁ reflexive, and Simon removed this assumption
nodes.note: It is a compactness criterion used to show that approximate solutions of nonlinear evolution equations have a convergent subsequence. It is also called the Aubin–Lions–Simon lemma.

nodes.name: Babenko–Beckner inequality
nodes.statement: Let 1 < p ≤ 2 and 1/p + 1/q = 1. The norm of the n-dimensional Fourier transform ℱ from Lᵖ(ℝⁿ) to L^q(ℝⁿ) equals (p^(1/p) / q^(1/q))^(n/2), so ‖ℱf‖_q ≤ (p^(1/p) / q^(1/q))^(n/2) ‖f‖_p for every f in Lᵖ(ℝⁿ). In one dimension, with g(y) = ∫ e^(−2πixy) f(x) dx the Fourier transform of f, this reads (√q ∫|g(y)|^q dy)^(1/q) ≤ (√p ∫|f(x)|^p dx)^(1/p).
nodes.by: Babenko, 1961, for even integer values of q; William E. Beckner, 1975, for all q ≥ 2
nodes.note: It is a sharpened form of the Hausdorff–Young inequality and has applications to uncertainty principles in the Fourier analysis of L^p spaces.

nodes.name: Babuška–Lax–Milgram theorem
nodes.statement: Let U and V be real Hilbert spaces and B : U × V → ℝ a continuous bilinear functional. Suppose that for some c > 0 and all u in U, the supremum of |B(u, v)| over ‖v‖ = 1 is at least c‖u‖, and that for every nonzero v in V, the supremum of |B(u, v)| over ‖u‖ = 1 is greater than 0. Then for every f in the dual space V*, there is a unique u_f in U with B(u_f, v) = ⟨f, v⟩ for all v in V, and ‖u_f‖ ≤ ‖f‖ / c.
nodes.by: J. Nečas, 1962
nodes.note: It generalizes the Lax–Milgram theorem of Peter Lax and Arthur Milgram by dropping the requirement that U and V be the same space. Nečas' proof extends to U a Banach space and V a reflexive Banach space.

nodes.name: Banach–Stone theorem
nodes.statement: Let X and Y be compact Hausdorff spaces, and let T : C(X) → C(Y) be a surjective linear isometry between the Banach spaces of continuous real- or complex-valued functions with the supremum norm. Then there is a homeomorphism φ : Y → X and a continuous function g on Y with |g(y)| = 1 for all y, such that (Tf)(y) = g(y)·f(φ(y)) for all y in Y and f in C(X). In particular, if C(X) and C(Y) are isometrically isomorphic, then X and Y are homeomorphic.
nodes.by: Stefan Banach proved the case of compact metric spaces; Marshall Stone extended it to compact Hausdorff spaces
nodes.note: It recovers a compact Hausdorff space from the Banach space structure of its continuous functions, without using their multiplicative structure.

nodes.name: Barratt–Priddy theorem
nodes.statement: Let Map₀(Sⁿ, Sⁿ) be the space of continuous maps from the n-sphere to itself that fix a basepoint and have degree 0. For n ≥ 2k there is a natural isomorphism between the k-th homology of the symmetric group Σₙ and the k-th homology of Map₀(Sⁿ, Sⁿ), and this holds with any coefficients.
nodes.by: Named after Michael Barratt, Stewart Priddy, and Daniel Quillen
nodes.note: Both sides are independent of n in this range. The theorem is also stated as a relation between the sphere spectrum and the classifying spaces of the symmetric groups via Quillen's plus construction.

nodes.name: Behnke–Stein theorem
nodes.statement: The union of an increasing sequence of domains of holomorphy G_k ⊂ ℂⁿ, where G_k ⊂ G_{k+1}, is again a domain of holomorphy.
nodes.by: Heinrich Behnke and Karl Stein, 1938
nodes.note: It also holds for Stein manifolds, but it is not known whether it holds for Stein spaces. Historically it was used to solve the Levi problem.

nodes.name: Beltrami's theorem
nodes.statement: Any connected pseudo-Riemannian manifold that is locally projectively flat has constant curvature.
nodes.by: Eugenio Beltrami, whose original proof covered the two-dimensional Riemannian case
nodes.note: It is the converse of the fact that every pseudo-Riemannian manifold of constant curvature is locally projectively flat. It concerns determining a metric from its geodesics.

nodes.name: Berger's isoembolic inequality
nodes.statement: Let (M, g) be a closed m-dimensional Riemannian manifold with injectivity radius inj(M), and let c_m be the volume of the standard m-dimensional sphere of radius one. Then vol(M) ≥ c_m (inj(M)/π)^m, with equality if and only if (M, g) is isometric to the m-sphere with its usual round metric.
nodes.by: Marcel Berger, derived from an inequality proved by Jerry Kazdan
nodes.note: Kazdan's inequality is sometimes called the Berger–Kazdan inequality. The original work appears in the appendices of Arthur Besse's book on manifolds all of whose geodesics are closed.

nodes.name: Bernstein's problem
nodes.statement: Let f be a function of n − 1 real variables defined on all of ℝⁿ⁻¹ whose graph is a minimal surface in ℝⁿ, that is, f satisfies the minimal surface equation. When n ≤ 8, f must be a polynomial of degree 1, but for every n ≥ 9 there are such functions whose graphs are not hyperplanes.
nodes.by: Named after Sergei Natanovich Bernstein, who solved the case n = 3 in 1914; extended by De Giorgi (1965), Almgren (1966) and Simons (1968) up to n ≤ 8; Bombieri, De Giorgi and Giusti (1969) showed it fails for n ≥ 9
nodes.note: Simons showed in 1968 that a certain cone in ℝ⁸ is locally stable and asked whether it is globally area-minimizing. Bombieri, De Giorgi and Giusti showed that it is.

nodes.name: Bernstein's theorem (approximation theory)
nodes.statement: Let f be a complex-valued 2π-periodic function, r a positive integer and 0 < α < 1. Suppose there are a number k(f) > 0 and trigonometric polynomials P_n of degree n, for every n ≥ n₀, with sup |f(x) − P_n(x)| ≤ k(f) / n^(r+α). Then f = P_{n₀} + φ, where φ has a bounded r-th derivative that is α-Hölder continuous.
nodes.by: Sergei Bernstein, 1912 (first results of this type)
nodes.note: It is a converse to Jackson's theorem.

nodes.name: Berry–Robbins problem
nodes.statement: There is a continuous map from configurations of n points in ℝ³ to the flag manifold U(n)/Tⁿ that is compatible with the action of the symmetric group on n points.
nodes.by: Posed by Berry and Robbins, 1997; solved positively by Atiyah, 2000

nodes.name: Nakano vanishing theorem
nodes.statement: Let M be a compact complex manifold of complex dimension n with a holomorphic line bundle F, and let Ω^p(F) be the sheaf of holomorphic (p,0)-forms with values in F. If the first Chern class of F is negative, then the cohomology group H^q(M; Ω^p(F)) is zero whenever q + p < n; if it is positive, the group is zero whenever q + p > n.
nodes.note: Also called the Akizuki–Nakano vanishing theorem, it generalizes the Kodaira vanishing theorem.

nodes.name: Yau's conjecture
nodes.statement: Every closed Riemannian 3-manifold contains infinitely many smooth closed immersed minimal surfaces.
nodes.by: Posed by Shing-Tung Yau, 1982; first resolved by Fernando Codá Marques and André Neves for positive Ricci curvature; proved for all metrics by Antoine Song
nodes.note: The proofs use min-max theory, a form of infinite dimensional Morse theory for the area functional.

nodes.name: Markov theorem
nodes.statement: Take a braid β in the braid group Bₙ and a braid β′ in the braid group Bₘ. Their closures are equivalent links if and only if β′ can be obtained from β by a sequence of these operations: conjugating in Bₙ; replacing a braid in Bₙ by its product with σₙ or σₙ⁻¹ in Bₙ₊₁; and the inverse of that second operation.
nodes.by: Proved by Andrei Andreevich Markov Jr.; the first complete proof is in Joan Birman's 1974 monograph Braids, Links, and Mapping Class Groups
nodes.note: It gives necessary and sufficient conditions for two braids to have closures that are equivalent knots or links. Alexander's theorem says every knot or link is the closure of a braid.

nodes.name: Solèr's theorem
nodes.statement: Let K be a division ring with a conjugation x ↦ x* (so (x + y)* = x* + y*, (xy)* = y*x* and (x*)* = x), and let V be a vector space over K with a non-degenerate Hermitian form that is orthomodular, meaning that S + S⊥ is the whole space for every closed subspace S. If V has an infinite orthonormal set, then K is the real numbers, the complex numbers or the quaternions, and V is a Hilbert space over it.
nodes.by: Proved by Maria Pia Solèr
nodes.note: The result is significant for quantum logic and the foundations of quantum mechanics. It is also an important step in the Heunen–Kornell axiomatisation of the category of Hilbert spaces.

nodes.name: Bihari–LaSalle inequality
nodes.statement: Let u and f be non-negative continuous functions on [0, ∞), let w be a continuous non-decreasing function on [0, ∞) with w(x) > 0 for x > 0, and let α be a non-negative constant. If u(t) ≤ α + ∫₀ᵗ f(s) w(u(s)) ds for all t ≥ 0, then u(t) ≤ G⁻¹(G(α) + ∫₀ᵗ f(s) ds) for t in [0, T], where G(x) = ∫ from x₀ to x of dy/w(y) with x₀ > 0, G⁻¹ is its inverse, and T is chosen so that G(α) + ∫₀ᵗ f(s) ds lies in the domain of G⁻¹ for all t in [0, T].
nodes.by: Joseph P. LaSalle, 1949, and Imre Bihari, 1956
nodes.note: It is a nonlinear generalization of Grönwall's lemma.

nodes.name: Dieudonné's theorem
nodes.statement: Let X be a locally convex space and A, B nonempty closed convex subsets of X. If either A or B is locally compact and the intersection of the recession cones of A and B is a linear subspace, then A − B is closed.
nodes.by: Named after Jean Dieudonné
nodes.note: It gives conditions under which the Minkowski sum of closed sets is closed.

nodes.name: Bipolar theorem
nodes.statement: Let X be a topological vector space with continuous dual X′, and for A ⊆ X let the polar A° be the set of all x′ in X′ with |x′(a)| ≤ 1 for every a in A. Then the bipolar of A, the set of all x in X with |x′(x)| ≤ 1 for every x′ in A°, equals the closure of the convex balanced hull of A in the weak topology σ(X, X′), the weakest vector space topology on X making all functionals in X′ continuous.
nodes.note: The bipolar theorem can be seen as a special case of the Fenchel–Moreau theorem. In convex analysis a version for cones says that a nonempty convex cone has the closure of itself as its bipolar.

nodes.name: Birkhoff–Kellogg invariant-direction theorem
nodes.statement: Let U be a bounded open neighborhood of 0 in an infinite-dimensional normed linear space V, and let F: ∂U → V be a compact map with ‖F(x)‖ ≥ α for some α > 0 and all x in ∂U. Then there exist some x₀ in ∂U and some λ > 0 with x₀ = λF(x₀), so F has an invariant direction.
nodes.by: Named after G. D. Birkhoff and O. D. Kellogg
nodes.note: It generalizes the Brouwer fixed-point theorem. It and its generalizations by Schauder and Leray have applications to partial differential equations.

nodes.name: Bishop–Gromov inequality
nodes.statement: Let M be a complete n-dimensional Riemannian manifold whose Ricci curvature satisfies Ric ≥ (n − 1)K for a real constant K, and let M_K be the complete n-dimensional simply connected space of constant sectional curvature K. Then for any p in M and any p_K in M_K, the ratio Vol B(p, r) / Vol B(p_K, r) of the volumes of balls of radius r is non-increasing on (0, ∞), and in particular Vol B(p, r) ≤ Vol B(p_K, r).
nodes.by: Named after Richard L. Bishop and Mikhail Gromov; the volume bound Vol B(p, r) ≤ Vol B(p_K, r) was first proved by Bishop
nodes.note: It is closely related to Myers' theorem and is the key point in the proof of Gromov's compactness theorem.

nodes.name: Björling problem
nodes.statement: Let c(s) be a real analytic curve in ℝ³ over an interval I with c′(s) ≠ 0, and let n(s) be a unit vector field along c with c′(s)·n(s) = 0, where the power series of c and n converge on a simply connected domain Ω containing I. Then the surface X(u, v) = Re( c(w) − i ∫ from w₀ to w of n(w) × c′(w) dw ), with w = u + iv in Ω and base point w₀ in I, is minimal, and it is the unique minimal surface through c with normal n along c.
nodes.by: Posed and solved by Emanuel Gabriel Björling, with further refinement by Hermann Schwarz
nodes.note: The solution extends the surface from the curve by complex analytic continuation. Applied to a cycloid it gives Catalan's minimal surface.

nodes.name: Bochner identity
nodes.statement: Let M and N be Riemannian manifolds and u : M → N a harmonic map. Then ½Δ(|∇u|²) = |∇(du)|² + ⟨Ric_M ∇u, ∇u⟩ − ⟨Riem_N(u)(∇u, ∇u)∇u, ∇u⟩, where du is the derivative of u, ∇ the gradient, Δ the Laplace–Beltrami operator, Riem_N the Riemann curvature tensor on N and Ric_M the Ricci curvature tensor on M.
nodes.by: Named after the American mathematician Salomon Bochner
nodes.note: It is an identity concerning harmonic maps between Riemannian manifolds.

nodes.name: Bochner's theorem
nodes.statement: On a locally compact abelian group G with dual group Ĝ, every normalized continuous positive-definite function f : G → ℂ (with f equal to 1 at the unit of G) is the Fourier transform of a unique probability measure μ on Ĝ, that is, f(g) = ∫ ξ(g) dμ(ξ). Conversely, the Fourier transform of a probability measure on Ĝ is a normalized continuous positive-definite function.
nodes.by: Named after Salomon Bochner; the case of sequences was first established by Gustav Herglotz
nodes.note: The theorem gives a one-to-one correspondence between such functions and probability measures on the dual group.

nodes.name: Bochner's theorem on Killing vector fields
nodes.statement: Every Killing vector field on a compact Riemannian manifold with negative Ricci curvature is zero. Consequently the isometry group of the manifold is finite.
nodes.by: Salomon Bochner, 1946
nodes.note: It follows from Bochner's result that on a connected Riemannian manifold of negative Ricci curvature the length of a nonzero Killing vector field cannot have a local maximum.

nodes.name: Bonnet theorem
nodes.statement: Let D be an open region in ℝ², and let g and h be smooth symmetric 2-tensors on D, with g positive-definite, that satisfy the Gauss–Codazzi equations. Then D is covered by open sets that can be smoothly embedded in ℝ³ with first fundamental form g and second fundamental form h, and each such embedding is unique up to a rigid motion of ℝ³.
nodes.by: Pierre Ossian Bonnet, 1867
nodes.note: It is a local converse to the fact that the two fundamental forms of a surface in three-dimensional Euclidean space satisfy the Gauss–Codazzi equations. It is a corollary of the Frobenius theorem.

nodes.name: Borell–Brascamp–Lieb inequality
nodes.statement: Let 0 < λ < 1, let −1/n ≤ p ≤ +∞, and let f, g, h : ℝⁿ → [0, +∞) be integrable functions with h((1−λ)x + λy) ≥ M_p(f(x), g(y), λ) for all x and y. Here M_p(a, b, λ) = ((1−λ)a^p + λb^p)^(1/p) if ab ≠ 0, M_p(a, b, λ) = 0 if ab = 0, and M_0(a, b, λ) = a^(1−λ) b^λ. Then ∫h ≥ M_q(∫f, ∫g, λ) with q = p/(np+1), where q is taken to be −∞ when p = −1/n and 1/n when p = +∞.
nodes.by: Proved for p > 0 by Henstock and Macbeath, 1953; general version by Brascamp and Lieb, 1976, and independently by Borell, 1975
nodes.note: The case p = 0 is known as the Prékopa–Leindler inequality.

nodes.name: Bott periodicity theorem
nodes.statement: The homotopy groups of the direct limit U(∞) of the unitary groups are periodic with period 2: πᵢ(U(∞)) ≅ πᵢ₊₂(U(∞)) for i ≥ 0, with π₀ = 0 and π₁ ≅ ℤ. For the direct limit O(∞) of the orthogonal groups, the period is 8: πᵢ(O(∞)) ≅ πᵢ₊₈(O(∞)) for i ≥ 0.
nodes.by: Bott, 1959
nodes.note: It is of foundational significance for K-theory of stable complex vector bundles and for the stable homotopy groups of spheres. Bott's original proof used Morse theory.

nodes.name: Riemann–Hurwitz formula
nodes.statement: Let π: S′ → S be a surjective complex analytic map of degree N between compact connected Riemann surfaces, and let e_P be the ramification index at a point P of S′. Then χ(S′) = N·χ(S) − ∑(e_P − 1), summed over the points P of S′, where only finitely many terms are nonzero. Equivalently, 2g(S′) − 2 = N(2g(S) − 2) + ∑(e_P − 1), where g is the genus.
nodes.by: Named after Bernhard Riemann and Adolf Hurwitz
nodes.note: It corrects the formula χ(S′) = N·χ(S) for unramified coverings to allow for sheets coming together at ramification points.

nodes.name: Schoenflies theorem
nodes.statement: If C is a simple closed curve in the plane ℝ², then there is a homeomorphism f of ℝ² onto itself such that f(C) is the unit circle. In particular, the curve separates the plane into a bounded inside and an unbounded outside that are homeomorphic to the inside and outside of a standard circle.
nodes.by: Arthur Schoenflies; elementary proofs in Newman (1939), Cairns (1951), Moise (1977) and Thomassen (1992)
nodes.note: It is a sharpening of the Jordan curve theorem and holds only in two dimensions. In three dimensions Alexander's horned sphere is a counterexample.

nodes.name: Branching theorem
nodes.statement: Let X and Y be Riemann surfaces, f : X → Y a non-constant holomorphic map, a a point of X and b = f(a). Then there is a natural number k and charts ψ₁ on X and ψ₂ on Y with ψ₁(a) = ψ₂(b) = 0 such that ψ₂ ∘ f ∘ ψ₁⁻¹ is the map z ↦ z^k.
nodes.note: The number k is called the multiplicity of f at a. If k > 1, the point a is called a branch point of f.

nodes.name: Brown's representability theorem
nodes.statement: Let F be a contravariant functor from the homotopy category of pointed connected CW complexes to sets. If F turns every wedge sum of complexes into the product of the corresponding sets, and satisfies the Mayer–Vietoris axiom (whenever a CW complex W is covered by subcomplexes U and V, any u in F(U) and v in F(V) that restrict to the same element of F(U ∩ V) both come from one element of F(W)), then there is a CW complex C with F(Z) ≅ Hom(Z, C) naturally in Z; conversely, every functor represented by a CW complex has these two properties.
nodes.by: Edgar H. Brown, 1962
nodes.note: Applied to singular cohomology H^i(X, A) with i > 0, it shows that Eilenberg–MacLane spaces K(A, i) exist. The theorem is false without the restriction to pointed connected spaces.

nodes.name: Cameron–Martin theorem
nodes.statement: Let i: H → E be an abstract Wiener space with abstract Wiener measure γ on the separable Banach space E, and let h be in H. Then shifting γ by the vector i(h) gives a measure equivalent to γ, with Radon–Nikodym derivative exp(⟨h, x⟩~ − ½‖h‖²_H), where ⟨h, x⟩~ is the Paley–Wiener integral.
nodes.by: Named after Robert Horton Cameron and W. T. Martin
nodes.note: The formula holds only for shifts by vectors in the Cameron–Martin space i(H): γ is quasi-invariant under a shift by v exactly when v lies in i(H). It leads to an integration by parts formula used in Malliavin calculus.

nodes.name: Carathéodory's existence theorem
nodes.statement: Consider y′(t) = f(t, y(t)) with y(t₀) = y₀, where y takes values in ℝⁿ and f is defined on the rectangle |t − t₀| ≤ a, |y − y₀| ≤ b.
