If f is continuous in y for each fixed t, measurable in t for each fixed y, and satisfies |f(t, y)| ≤ m(t) on the rectangle for some Lebesgue-integrable function m ≥ 0 on [t₀ − a, t₀ + a], then the equation has a solution in the extended sense (an absolutely continuous function that satisfies the equation almost everywhere and the initial condition) in a neighborhood of the initial condition.
nodes.by: Named after Constantin Carathéodory
nodes.note: It generalizes Peano's existence theorem, which requires the right-hand side to be continuous, and covers some discontinuous equations.

nodes.name: Carathéodory kernel theorem
nodes.statement: Let f_n be holomorphic one-to-one (univalent) functions on the unit disk D with f_n(0) = 0 and f_n′(0) > 0. Then f_n converges uniformly on compact subsets of D to a function f if and only if the image sets U_n = f_n(D) converge to their kernel (every subsequence has the same kernel) and this kernel is not the whole plane ℂ; in that case f = 0 if the kernel is {0}, and otherwise f is univalent on D and maps D onto the kernel.
nodes.by: Constantin Carathéodory, 1912
nodes.note: It has wide application in the theory of univalent functions and provides the geometric basis for the Loewner differential equation.

nodes.name: Carlson's theorem
nodes.statement: Let f be an entire function with |f(z)| ≤ C·e^(τ|z|) for all complex z, for some real constants C and τ, and suppose there is c < π with |f(iy)| ≤ C·e^(c|y|) for all real y. If f(n) = 0 for every non-negative integer n, then f is identically zero.
nodes.by: Fritz David Carlson
nodes.note: Informally, two different analytic functions that do not grow very fast at infinity cannot coincide at the integers. It is typically invoked to justify the uniqueness of a Newton series expansion.

nodes.name: Cartan's lemma (potential theory)
nodes.statement: Let μ be a finite positive Borel measure on the complex plane with μ(ℂ) = n, and let u(z) = (1/2π) ∫ log|z − ζ| dμ(ζ) be its logarithmic potential. For every H in (0, 1) there are discs with radii r_i such that ∑ r_i < 5H and u(z) ≥ (n/2π) log(H/e) for all z outside the union of these discs.
nodes.by: Named after Henri Cartan
nodes.note: It bounds the measure and complexity of the set on which a logarithmic Newtonian potential is small.

nodes.name: Cartan–Hadamard theorem
nodes.statement: The universal covering space of a connected complete Riemannian manifold of dimension n with non-positive sectional curvature is diffeomorphic to ℝⁿ. In fact, the exponential map at any point of such a manifold is a covering map.
nodes.by: Hans Carl Friedrich von Mangoldt for surfaces, 1881, and independently Jacques Hadamard, 1898; generalized to Riemannian manifolds by Élie Cartan, 1928
nodes.note: It was generalized to a wide class of metric spaces by Mikhail Gromov in 1987.

nodes.name: Cartan–Kuranishi prolongation theorem
nodes.statement: Given an exterior differential system on a manifold M, after a finite number of prolongations the system is either in involution (it admits at least one 'large' integral manifold) or is impossible.
nodes.by: Conjectured by Élie Cartan, who made several attempts to prove it in 1946; proved by Masatake Kuranishi, 1957
nodes.note: It is used in infinite-dimensional Lie theory.

nodes.name: Cartan–Kähler theorem
nodes.statement: Let (M, I) be a real analytic exterior differential system, and let P ⊆ M be a connected, k-dimensional, real analytic, regular integral manifold of I with r(P) ≥ 0, meaning its tangent spaces extend to higher dimensional integral elements. If there is a real analytic submanifold R ⊆ M of codimension r(P) containing P such that T_pR ∩ H(T_pP) has dimension k + 1 for all p in P, then there exists a locally unique connected, (k+1)-dimensional, real analytic integral manifold X ⊆ M of I with P ⊆ X ⊆ R.
nodes.by: Named after Élie Cartan and Erich Kähler
nodes.note: The proof uses the Cauchy–Kovalevskaya theorem, so the analyticity assumption is necessary.

nodes.name: Cellular approximation theorem
nodes.statement: Every continuous map f : X → Y between CW-complexes is homotopic to a cellular map, that is, a map taking the n-skeleton of X into the n-skeleton of Y for all n. If f is already cellular on a subcomplex A of X, the homotopy can be chosen to be stationary on A.
nodes.note: It gives at once that the homotopy group πₙ(Sᵏ) is trivial when n < k.

nodes.name: Cheng's eigenvalue comparison theorem
nodes.statement: Let M be a Riemannian manifold of dimension n, let p be a point of M, and let r be less than the injectivity radius of p. For each real k let N(k) be the simply connected space form of dimension n with constant sectional curvature k. If the sectional curvature of M is at most k, then the first Dirichlet eigenvalue of the geodesic ball of radius r in N(k) is at most the first Dirichlet eigenvalue of the geodesic ball B_M(p, r). If instead Ric(X, X) ≥ k(n−1)|X|² for every vector field X, then the inequality is reversed: the first eigenvalue of the ball in N(k) is at least that of B_M(p, r).
nodes.by: Shiu-Yuen Cheng, 1975
nodes.note: In general terms, the larger a domain is, the smaller its first Dirichlet eigenvalue. For k = −1 and inj(p) = ∞ it gives McKean's inequality.

nodes.name: Choi's theorem on completely positive maps
nodes.statement: For a linear map Φ from n×n complex matrices to m×m complex matrices, the following are equivalent: Φ is n-positive, meaning (id ⊗ Φ)(A) is positive whenever A is a positive element of ℂⁿˣⁿ ⊗ ℂⁿˣⁿ; the nm×nm matrix C_Φ = ∑ E_ij ⊗ Φ(E_ij) is positive semi-definite, where E_ij has 1 in entry ij and 0 elsewhere; Φ is completely positive.
nodes.by: M.-D. Choi, 1975
nodes.note: C_Φ is sometimes called the Choi matrix of Φ. An infinite-dimensional algebraic generalization is known as Belavkin's "Radon–Nikodym" theorem for completely positive maps.

nodes.name: Chow–Rashevsky theorem
nodes.statement: Any two points of a connected sub-Riemannian manifold, endowed with a bracket generating distribution, are connected by a horizontal path in the manifold.
nodes.by: Named after Wei-Liang Chow, who proved it in 1939, and Rashevsky, who proved it independently in 1938
nodes.note: An equivalent form is that the topology induced by the Carnot–Carathéodory metric is equivalent to the intrinsic topology of the manifold. The ball–box theorem is a stronger statement that implies it.

nodes.name: Grönwall's inequality
nodes.statement: Let I be an interval [a, ∞), [a, b] or [a, b) with a < b, let β and u be continuous real functions on I with β ≥ 0, and let α be a real function on I whose negative part is integrable on every closed bounded subinterval of I. If u(t) ≤ α(t) + ∫ₐᵗ β(s)u(s) ds for all t in I, then u(t) ≤ α(t) + ∫ₐᵗ α(s)β(s)·exp(∫ₛᵗ β(r) dr) ds for all t in I, and if α is also non-decreasing, then u(t) ≤ α(t)·exp(∫ₐᵗ β(s) ds).
nodes.by: Thomas Hakon Grönwall, 1919 (the integral form with constant α and β); Richard Bellman proved a slightly more general integral form in 1943
nodes.note: It bounds a function that satisfies a differential or integral inequality by the solution of the corresponding equation, and is used to prove uniqueness of solutions of initial value problems. In differential form, u′ ≤ βu implies u(t) ≤ u(a)·exp(∫ₐᵗ β(s) ds).

nodes.name: Commutant lifting theorem
nodes.statement: Let T be a contraction on a Hilbert space H, let U be its minimal unitary dilation acting on a Hilbert space K, and let R be an operator on H commuting with T. Then there is an operator S on K commuting with U such that R Tⁿ = P_H S Uⁿ restricted to H for all n ≥ 0, and ‖S‖ = ‖R‖, where P_H is the projection from K onto H.
nodes.by: Sz.-Nagy and Foias
nodes.note: It is used to prove several interpolation results, among them the Nevanlinna-Pick interpolation theorem.

nodes.name: Commutation theorem for traces
nodes.statement: Let M be a von Neumann algebra acting on a Hilbert space H, with a unit vector Ω such that MΩ is dense in H, M′Ω is dense in H (M′ being the commutant of M, the operators that commute with every element of M), and (abΩ, Ω) = (baΩ, Ω) for all a, b in M. If J is the conjugate-linear map with J(aΩ) = a*Ω for a in M, then the commutant M′ equals JMJ.
nodes.by: Francis Joseph Murray and John von Neumann, 1930s
nodes.note: The same equality holds for a von Neumann algebra with a faithful semifinite trace acting on L²(M, τ). The non-tracial generalisation, Tomita–Takesaki theory, was developed in the late 1960s.

nodes.name: Complex conjugate root theorem
nodes.statement: If P is a polynomial in one variable with real coefficients, and a + bi is a root of P with a and b real numbers, then its complex conjugate a − bi is also a root of P.
nodes.note: Together with the fundamental theorem of algebra it follows that a real polynomial of odd degree has at least one real root. That fact can also be proved with the intermediate value theorem.

nodes.name: Conley–Zehnder theorem
nodes.statement: A Hamiltonian diffeomorphism of a standard symplectic torus of dimension 2n has at least 2n+1 fixed points, which is one plus the cup-length of the torus. If all its fixed points are non-degenerate, it has at least 2^(2n) fixed points, the rank of the homology of the torus.
nodes.by: Named after Charles C. Conley and Eduard Zehnder; conjectured by Vladimir Arnold
nodes.note: It was known as the Arnold conjecture on fixed points of symplectomorphisms, and Andreas Floer and others extended it to more general closed symplectic manifolds. The non-degeneracy condition is generic in the C^1-topology.

nodes.name: Continuous mapping theorem
nodes.statement: Let Xₙ and X be random elements with values in a metric space S, and let g map S to another metric space S′ so that X falls with probability 0 into the set of points where g is discontinuous. If Xₙ converges to X in distribution, in probability, or almost surely, then g(Xₙ) converges to g(X) in the same sense.
nodes.by: Henry Mann and Abraham Wald, 1943
nodes.note: It extends the fact that continuous functions map convergent sequences of numbers to convergent sequences. It is sometimes called the Mann–Wald theorem.

nodes.name: Contraction principle (large deviations theory)
nodes.statement: Let X and Y be Hausdorff topological spaces, and let (με) be a family of probability measures on X satisfying the large deviation principle with rate function I. Let T: X → Y be continuous, let νε be the push-forward of με by T, and let J(y) be the infimum of I(x) over all x with T(x) = y, with the infimum over the empty set taken as +∞. Then J is a rate function on Y, J is a good rate function if I is, and (νε) satisfies the large deviation principle on Y with rate function J.
nodes.note: It shows how a large deviation principle on one space carries over to another space through a continuous function.

nodes.name: Corona theorem
nodes.statement: The open unit disc is dense in the spectrum of H^∞, the algebra of bounded holomorphic functions on the open unit disc. Equivalently, functions f_1,...,f_n in H^∞ generate the unit ideal if and only if there is some δ > 0 such that |f_1| + ... + |f_n| ≥ δ everywhere in the unit disc.
nodes.by: Conjectured by Kakutani, 1941; proved by Carleson, 1962
nodes.note: Newman showed that it can be reduced to an interpolation problem, which Carleson then proved.

nodes.name: Boole's inequality
nodes.statement: For any finite or countable set of events, the probability that at least one of them happens is no greater than the sum of the probabilities of the individual events. The same holds for arbitrary measures, as countable subadditivity.
nodes.by: Named after George Boole
nodes.note: It is also known as the union bound.

nodes.name: Cotlar–Stein almost orthogonality lemma
nodes.statement: Let E and F be Hilbert spaces and T_j (j ≥ 1) bounded linear operators from E to F. Put a_jk = ‖T_j T_k*‖ and b_jk = ‖T_j* T_k‖, and let A = sup_j ∑_k √a_jk and B = sup_j ∑_k √b_jk. If A and B are both finite, then the series ∑ T_j converges in the strong operator topology and ‖∑ T_j‖ ≤ √(AB).
nodes.by: Mischa Cotlar, 1955 (self-adjoint, mutually commuting case); a more general version by Elias Stein
nodes.note: It bounds the operator norm of an operator that decomposes into almost orthogonal pieces. Cotlar used it to show that the Hilbert transform is continuous on L² without the Fourier transform.

nodes.name: Jensen's inequality
nodes.statement: If X is an integrable real-valued random variable (one with a finite mean) and φ is a convex function, then φ(E[X]) ≤ E[φ(X)]. For two points this says f(t·x₁ + (1−t)·x₂) ≤ t·f(x₁) + (1−t)·f(x₂) for every convex f and every t in [0,1], so the secant line of a convex function lies above its graph.
nodes.by: Otto Hölder, 1889, for doubly-differentiable functions; proved by Johan Jensen, 1906
nodes.note: The inequality is reversed for concave functions. Taking φ = log gives the arithmetic-mean/geometric-mean inequality.

nodes.name: Kakutani fixed-point theorem
nodes.statement: Let S be a non-empty, compact, convex subset of a Euclidean space ℝⁿ. Let φ assign to each point x of S a non-empty convex subset φ(x) of S, such that φ has a closed graph. Then φ has a fixed point, that is, a point x with x ∈ φ(x).
nodes.by: Shizuo Kakutani, 1941
nodes.note: It generalizes the Brouwer fixed point theorem to set-valued functions and was used by John Nash in his description of Nash equilibria.

nodes.name: Curtis–Hedlund–Lyndon theorem
nodes.statement: For a finite alphabet, a function from the shift space (all bi-infinite sequences of symbols) to itself is the transition function of a one-dimensional cellular automaton if and only if it is continuous in the Cantor topology and commutes with the shift map.
nodes.by: Named after Morton L. Curtis, Gustav A. Hedlund and Roger Lyndon; stated by Hedlund in his 1969 paper, which credited Curtis and Lyndon as co-discoverers
nodes.note: The theorem fails for infinite alphabets. One consequence is that the reverse dynamics of a reversible cellular automaton can also be described by a cellular automaton.

nodes.name: Cyclic surgery theorem
nodes.statement: Let M be a compact, connected, orientable, irreducible three-manifold whose boundary is a torus T, and suppose M is not a Seifert-fibered space. If r and s are slopes on T whose Dehn fillings both have cyclic fundamental group, then the distance between r and s, the minimal number of times two simple closed curves in T representing them must intersect, is at most 1; consequently at most three Dehn fillings of M have cyclic fundamental group.
nodes.by: Marc Culler, Cameron Gordon, John Luecke and Peter Shalen, 1987

nodes.name: Carathéodory–Jacobi–Lie theorem
nodes.statement: Let M be a 2n-dimensional symplectic manifold with symplectic form ω, let p be a point of M and r ≤ n. If f₁, ..., f_r are smooth functions on an open neighborhood V of p whose differentials are linearly independent at each point and which are pairwise in involution, meaning {fᵢ, fⱼ} = 0 for the Poisson bracket, then there are functions f_{r+1}, ..., f_n, g₁, ..., g_n on an open neighborhood U ⊂ V of p such that ω = ∑ dfᵢ ∧ dgᵢ on U, so that (fᵢ, gᵢ) is a symplectic chart of M.
nodes.note: It generalizes Darboux's theorem.

nodes.name: Dawson–Gärtner theorem
nodes.statement: Let X be the projective limit of a projective system of Hausdorff topological spaces Y_j, with p_j the projection from X to Y_j, and let (μ_ε) be a family of probability measures on X. If for each j the push-forward measures of μ_ε under p_j satisfy the large deviation principle on Y_j with good rate function I_j, then (μ_ε) satisfies the large deviation principle on X with good rate function I(x) = sup over j of I_j(p_j(x)).
nodes.note: It allows a large deviation principle on a smaller topological space to be transported to a larger one.

nodes.name: De Rham–Weil theorem
nodes.statement: Let F be a sheaf on a topological space X and let F• be a resolution of F by acyclic sheaves. Then the q-th sheaf cohomology group H^q(X, F) is isomorphic to H^q(F•(X)), the q-th cohomology of the complex of global sections of the resolution.
nodes.note: It follows from the more general fact that derived functors may be computed using acyclic resolutions instead of only injective resolutions.

nodes.name: Denjoy–Wolff theorem
nodes.statement: Let f be a holomorphic function from the open unit disc D into D that is not an automorphism of D. Then there is a unique point z in the closure of D such that the iterates of f tend to z uniformly on compact subsets of D, and if z lies in D it is the unique fixed point of f.
nodes.by: Arnaud Denjoy and Julius Wolff, independently, 1926

nodes.name: Denjoy–Luzin–Saks theorem
nodes.statement: Every function of generalized bounded variation in the restricted sense has a derivative almost everywhere.
nodes.by: A weaker form proved by N. N. Luzin and A. Denjoy; strengthened by S. Saks, 1937
nodes.note: The theorem also gives further conditions on the set of values of the function where the derivative does not exist.

nodes.name: Denjoy–Young–Saks theorem
nodes.statement: If f is a real-valued function defined on an interval, then except possibly on a set of measure 0, at each point one of four cases holds for the Dini derivatives D⁺f, D⁻f, D₊f, D₋f: f has a finite derivative; or D⁺f = D₋f is finite, D⁻f = ∞ and D₊f = −∞; or D⁻f = D₊f is finite, D⁺f = ∞ and D₋f = −∞; or D⁻f = D⁺f = ∞ and D₋f = D₊f = −∞.
nodes.by: A. Denjoy, 1915, for continuous functions; extended by Grace Chisholm Young, 1917, to measurable functions and by S. Saks, 1924, to arbitrary functions
nodes.note: It gives the possibilities for the Dini derivatives of a function that hold almost everywhere.

nodes.name: Disc theorem
nodes.statement: Two smooth embeddings of a closed k-disc into a connected smooth n-manifold are ambient isotopic, provided that when k = n the two embeddings are equioriented.
nodes.by: Palais, 1960
nodes.note: It implies that the connected sum of smooth oriented manifolds is well defined. It is a different result from the disc embedding theorem proved by Freedman in 1982.

nodes.name: Disintegration theorem
nodes.statement: Let X and Y be Polish spaces, μ a Borel probability measure on Y, π: Y → X a Borel-measurable function, and ν = π_*(μ) the pushforward measure. Then there is a family of Borel probability measures μ_x on Y, uniquely determined ν-almost everywhere, such that x ↦ μ_x(B) is Borel measurable for each Borel set B, μ_x is concentrated on the fiber π⁻¹(x) for ν-almost all x, and for every Borel-measurable f: Y → [0,∞] the integral of f over Y with respect to μ equals the integral over X, with respect to ν, of the integrals of f over π⁻¹(x) with respect to μ_x.
nodes.note: It is related to the existence of conditional probability measures, and is in a sense the opposite process to constructing a product measure.

nodes.name: Kochen–Specker theorem
nodes.statement: In a Hilbert space of dimension three or more, the quantum observables cannot all be given definite values that do not depend on the measurement context and that respect the functional relations between compatible observables. In particular, the projection operators cannot each be given the value 0 or 1 so that, for every orthogonal basis, exactly one of the projections onto the basis vectors has the value 1.
nodes.by: John S. Bell, 1966; Simon B. Kochen and Ernst Specker, 1967
nodes.note: It shows that no non-contextual hidden-variable model can reproduce the predictions of quantum theory, and it complements Bell's theorem. Kochen and Specker used a set of 117 projection operators; later and simpler proofs, such as those by Mermin and Peres, often work only from dimension four.

nodes.name: Von Neumann bicommutant theorem
nodes.statement: Let M be an algebra of bounded operators on a Hilbert space H that contains the identity operator and is closed under taking adjoints. Then the closures of M in the weak operator topology and in the strong operator topology are equal, and both equal the bicommutant M′′ of M.
nodes.by: Named after von Neumann
nodes.note: It connects the algebraic and topological sides of operator theory. The resulting algebra is called the von Neumann algebra generated by M.

nodes.name: Donaldson's theorem
nodes.statement: If the intersection form of a closed, oriented, smooth 4-manifold is definite, then it is diagonalizable over the integers. A positive definite form diagonalizes to the identity matrix and a negative definite form to the negative identity matrix.
nodes.by: Simon Donaldson
nodes.note: The original version required the manifold to be simply connected. It was later improved to apply to 4-manifolds with any fundamental group.

nodes.name: Doob–Meyer decomposition theorem
nodes.statement: On a filtered probability space satisfying the usual conditions, a right-continuous submartingale X of class D can be written uniquely as X = M + A, where M is a uniformly integrable martingale and A is a predictable, right-continuous, increasing process with A₀ = 0. The decomposition is unique up to indistinguishability.
nodes.by: Conjectured by Joseph L. Doob; proved by Paul-André Meyer in publications of 1962 and 1963
nodes.note: It carries the discrete-time Doob decomposition theorem of 1953 over to continuous time.

nodes.name: Double bubble theorem
nodes.statement: In three-dimensional space, for any two given volumes, the shape that encloses and separates them with the least possible surface area is the standard double bubble: three spherical surfaces meeting at angles of 120° on a common circle. When the two volumes are equal, the middle surface is a flat disk.
nodes.by: Formulated in the 19th century; equal-volume case by Joel Hass and Roger Schlafly, announced 1995; full proof by Hutchings, Morgan, Ritoré and Ros, announced 2000 and published 2002
nodes.note: It extends the isoperimetric inequality, by which the least-surface-area enclosure of a single volume is a sphere. Reichardt published the generalization to all higher dimensions in 2008.

nodes.name: Thurston's double limit theorem
nodes.statement: Quasi-Fuchsian groups of a fixed genus correspond to points (g, h) in T×T, where T is the Teichmüller space of that genus. Suppose a sequence of such groups corresponds to points (g_i, h_i), where g_i and h_i converge to two points of the Thurston boundary of T, the space of projective measured laminations. If every nonzero measured lamination has positive intersection number with at least one of these two points, then the sequence of groups has a subsequence that converges algebraically.
nodes.by: Thurston, 1998
nodes.note: It is a major step in Thurston's proof of the hyperbolization theorem for manifolds that fiber over the circle.

nodes.name: Double suspension theorem
nodes.statement: The double suspension S²X of a homology sphere X is a topological sphere.
nodes.by: James W. Cannon (1979) and Robert D. Edwards
nodes.note: If X is a piecewise-linear homology sphere but not a sphere, its double suspension gives a triangulation of a topological sphere that is not piecewise-linear.

nodes.name: Douglas' lemma
nodes.statement: For bounded operators A and B on a Hilbert space H, the following are equivalent: (1) the range of A is contained in the range of B; (2) AA* ≤ λ²BB* for some λ ≥ 0; (3) A = BC for some bounded operator C on H. When these hold, there is a unique such C with ‖C‖² = inf{μ : AA* ≤ μBB*}, ker A = ker C, and range C contained in the closure of the range of B*.
nodes.by: Generally attributed to Ronald G. Douglas
nodes.note: It relates factorization, range inclusion and majorization of Hilbert space operators.

nodes.name: Picard–Lindelöf theorem
nodes.statement: Let D be a closed rectangle in ℝ × ℝⁿ with (t₀, y₀) in its interior, and let f: D → ℝⁿ be continuous in t and Lipschitz continuous in y, with a Lipschitz constant independent of t. Then for some ε > 0, the initial value problem y′(t) = f(t, y(t)), y(t₀) = y₀ has a unique solution on the interval [t₀−ε, t₀+ε].
nodes.by: Named after Émile Picard, Ernst Lindelöf, Rudolf Lipschitz and Augustin-Louis Cauchy
nodes.note: The conditions are sufficient but not necessary. The theorem is also known as the Cauchy–Lipschitz theorem and the existence and uniqueness theorem.

nodes.name: Dunford–Schwartz theorem
nodes.statement: Let T be a linear operator from L¹ to L¹ with ‖T‖₁ ≤ 1 and ‖T‖∞ ≤ 1. Then for every f in L¹ the averages (1/n)∑ₖ Tᵏf, with k from 0 to n−1, converge almost everywhere as n tends to infinity.
nodes.by: Named after Nelson Dunford and Jacob T. Schwartz
nodes.note: The statement is no longer true when the bound on ‖T‖∞ is relaxed to 1+ε.

nodes.name: Dvoretzky's theorem
nodes.statement: For every natural number k and every ε > 0 there is a natural number N(k, ε) such that every normed space (X, ‖·‖) of dimension N(k, ε) has a k-dimensional subspace E with a Euclidean norm |·| satisfying |x| ≤ ‖x‖ ≤ (1+ε)|x| for every x in E.
nodes.by: Aryeh Dvoretzky, early 1960s, answering a question of Alexander Grothendieck; a new proof by Vitali Milman in 1971
nodes.note: Equivalently, every high-dimensional bounded symmetric convex set has low-dimensional sections that are approximately ellipsoids. Milman's new proof was one of the starting points for the development of asymptotic geometric analysis.

nodes.name: Earle–Hamilton fixed-point theorem
nodes.statement: Let D be a connected open subset of a complex Banach space X and let f be a holomorphic mapping of D into itself such that the image f(D) is bounded in norm and the distance between points of f(D) and points in the exterior of D is bounded below by a positive constant. Then f has a unique fixed point x in D, and for any point y in D the iterates fⁿ(y) converge to x.
nodes.by: Clifford Earle and Richard S. Hamilton, 1968
nodes.note: The proof shows that f is a contraction for the Carathéodory metric on D, so that the Banach fixed-point theorem applies.

nodes.name: Eckmann–Hilton argument
nodes.statement: Let a set X carry two binary operations ∘ and ⊗, each with an identity element, such that (a⊗b)∘(c⊗d) = (a∘c)⊗(b∘d) for all a, b, c, d in X. Then the two operations are equal, and are commutative and associative.
nodes.by: Named after Beno Eckmann and Peter Hilton, who used it in a 1962 paper
nodes.note: It can be used to prove that the higher homotopy groups are commutative. Associativity and a shared identity element need not be assumed, since both follow.

nodes.name: Ehrenpreis conjecture
nodes.statement: For every K greater than 1, any two closed Riemann surfaces of genus at least 2 have finite-degree covers that are K-quasiconformal, that is, the covers are arbitrarily close in the Teichmüller metric.
nodes.by: Conjectured by Leon Ehrenpreis; a proof was announced by Jeremy Kahn and Vladimir Markovic in January 2011
nodes.note: The proof used the authors' proof of the Surface subgroup conjecture and a newly developed "good pants homology" theory.

nodes.name: Ehrling's lemma
nodes.statement: Let X, Y and Z be Banach spaces, where X is compactly embedded in Y and Y is continuously embedded in Z. Then for every ε > 0 there is a constant C(ε) such that ‖x‖_Y ≤ ε‖x‖_X + C(ε)‖x‖_Z for all x in X.
nodes.by: Named after Gunnar Ehrling
nodes.note: It is often used to show that certain norms on Sobolev spaces are equivalent. It is also known as Lions' lemma.

nodes.name: Eisenbud–Levine–Khimshiashvili signature formula
nodes.statement: Let X be a real analytic vector field on ℝⁿ with components f₁, …, fₙ and an algebraically isolated zero at 0 (one that stays isolated over the complex numbers). Let B_X be the finite-dimensional real algebra of analytic function germs at 0 modulo the ideal generated by f₁, …, fₙ, and let ℓ be any linear map from B_X to ℝ that is positive on the class of the Jacobian determinant of (f₁, …, fₙ); then the Poincaré–Hopf index of X at 0 equals the signature of the bilinear form β(g, h) = ℓ(g·h) on B_X.
nodes.by: Named after David Eisenbud, Harold I. Levine and George Khimshiashvili
nodes.note: It computes the index of a vector field with tools from commutative algebra. For the plane field (x³ − 3xy²)∂/∂x + (3x²y − y³)∂/∂y it gives index +3, which agrees with a direct topological computation.

nodes.name: Eisenstein's theorem
nodes.statement: Suppose a formal power series ∑ aₙtⁿ with rational coefficients has a non-zero radius of convergence in the complex plane and represents an algebraic function there. Then there is a non-zero integer A such that all the numbers A^(n+1)·aₙ are integers.
nodes.by: Gotthold Eisenstein, 1852
nodes.note: It shows, for example, that the exponential function must be transcendental.

nodes.name: Montel's theorem
nodes.statement: Every locally uniformly bounded family of holomorphic functions on an open subset of the complex numbers is normal. Locally uniformly bounded means that on each compact subset all functions of the family share one common bound.
nodes.by: Named after Paul Montel
nodes.note: It is the analogue of Liouville's theorem for families of functions and has also been called the Stieltjes–Osgood theorem. A stronger version says that a family of holomorphic functions that all omit the same two values is normal.

nodes.name: Ellis–Numakura lemma
nodes.statement: If S is a non-empty semigroup with a topology such that S is a compact space and the product is semi-continuous, then S has an idempotent element, that is, an element p with pp = p.
nodes.by: Named after Robert Ellis and Katsui Numakura
nodes.note: Applied to the Stone–Čech compactification βN of the natural numbers, where the product is only semi-continuous, it shows that βN has idempotent elements.

nodes.name: Ending lamination theorem
nodes.statement: Hyperbolic 3-manifolds with finitely generated fundamental groups are determined by their topology together with certain end invariants, which are geodesic laminations on some surfaces in the boundary of the manifold.
nodes.by: Conjectured by Thurston, 1982; proved for Kleinian surface groups by Minsky (2010) and Brock, Canary and Minsky (2012), which with the Tameness theorem gives the general case
nodes.note: It generalizes the Mostow rigidity theorem to hyperbolic manifolds of infinite volume. It was the eleventh of Thurston's twenty-four questions.

nodes.name: Banach–Alaoglu theorem
nodes.statement: For every normed vector space, the closed unit ball of its continuous dual space (the space of continuous linear functionals on it) is compact in the weak* topology, the topology of pointwise convergence.
nodes.by: Leonidas Alaoglu published the proof of the general case in 1940; Stefan Banach proved it in 1932 for separable normed spaces, considering only sequential compactness
nodes.note: A common proof identifies the unit ball with a closed subset of a product of compact sets and applies Tychonoff's theorem. In 1912 Helly proved a special case for the dual space of C([a, b]).

nodes.name: Equioscillation theorem
nodes.statement: Let f be a continuous function from [a, b] to ℝ. A polynomial g of degree ≤ n makes the largest distance max |f(x) − g(x)| over [a, b] as small as possible among all polynomials of degree ≤ n if and only if there are n + 2 points a ≤ x₀ < x₁ < ⋯ < xₙ₊₁ ≤ b with f(xᵢ) − g(xᵢ) = σ(−1)ⁱ‖f − g‖∞ for every i, where σ is either −1 or +1.
nodes.by: Attributed to Chebyshev
nodes.note: The best polynomial oscillates above and below f at these points, by the same amount each time. The Remez algorithm is the most common way to compute such approximations.

nodes.name: Erdős–Turán inequality
nodes.statement: Let μ be a probability measure on the unit circle ℝ/ℤ and n a natural number. Then the supremum over all arcs A of the circle of |μ(A) − Lebesgue measure of A| is at most C(1/n + ∑ₖ₌₁ⁿ |μ̂(k)|/k), where μ̂(k) = ∫ exp(2πikθ) dμ(θ) are the Fourier coefficients of μ and C > 0 is a numerical constant.
nodes.by: Paul Erdős and Pál Turán, 1948
nodes.note: Applied to the measures given by a sequence of real numbers taken mod 1, it bounds the discrepancy of the sequence and gives a quantitative form of Weyl's criterion for equidistribution.

nodes.name: Farrell–Markushevich theorem
nodes.statement: Let Ω be a bounded domain in the complex plane whose boundary is a simple closed Jordan curve. Then every square-integrable holomorphic function on Ω can be approximated in mean square arbitrarily closely by complex polynomials, that is, the polynomials are dense in the Bergman space of Ω.
nodes.by: O. J. Farrell and A. I. Markushevich, independently, 1934
nodes.note: The Gram–Schmidt process can then build an orthonormal basis of the Bergman space, which gives an explicit Bergman kernel and an explicit Riemann mapping function for the domain.

nodes.name: Fatou conjecture
nodes.statement: The quadratic family of maps from the complex plane to itself is hyperbolic for an open dense set of parameters.
nodes.by: Named after Pierre Fatou

nodes.name: Fatou–Lebesgue theorem
nodes.statement: Let f₁, f₂, … be real-valued measurable functions on a measure space (S, Σ, μ). If there is a Lebesgue-integrable function g on S with |fₙ| ≤ g for all natural numbers n, then every fₙ, the pointwise limit inferior and the pointwise limit superior of the fₙ are integrable, and ∫ liminf fₙ dμ ≤ liminf ∫ fₙ dμ ≤ limsup ∫ fₙ dμ ≤ ∫ limsup fₙ dμ.
nodes.by: Named after Pierre Fatou and Henri Léon Lebesgue
nodes.note: If the sequence of functions converges pointwise, the inequalities become equalities and the theorem reduces to Lebesgue's dominated convergence theorem.

nodes.name: Favard's theorem
nodes.statement: Let y₀, y₁, … be polynomials where yₙ has degree n and y₀ = 1. If they satisfy a three-term recurrence yₙ₊₁ = (x − cₙ)yₙ − dₙyₙ₋₁ for some numbers cₙ and dₙ, then there is exactly one linear functional Λ with Λ(1) = 1 such that Λ(yₘyₙ) = 0 whenever m ≠ n, and Λ is positive definite if and only if all cₙ are real and all dₙ are positive.
nodes.by: Introduced in the theory of orthogonal polynomials by Favard, 1935, and Shohat, 1938; essentially the same theorem was used earlier by Stieltjes in the theory of continued fractions
nodes.note: It is roughly a converse of the fact that orthogonal polynomials for a positive weight function satisfy a three-term recurrence relation. It is also called the Shohat–Favard theorem.

nodes.name: Fekete–Szegő inequality
nodes.statement: Let f(z) = z + a₂z² + a₃z³ + ⋯ be a univalent analytic function on the unit disk and let 0 ≤ λ < 1. Then |a₃ − λa₂²| ≤ 1 + 2exp(−2λ/(1−λ)).
nodes.by: Fekete and Szegő, 1933
nodes.note: It is related to the Bieberbach conjecture. Finding similar estimates for other classes of functions is called the Fekete–Szegő problem.

nodes.name: Lagrange inversion theorem
nodes.statement: Suppose z = f(w), where f is analytic at a point a and f′(a) ≠ 0. Then the equation can be solved as w = g(z) = a + ∑ gₙ (z − f(a))ⁿ / n! (sum over n ≥ 1), where gₙ is the limit as w → a of dⁿ⁻¹/dwⁿ⁻¹ [ ((w − a)/(f(w) − f(a)))ⁿ ], and this series has a non-zero radius of convergence, so g is analytic in a neighbourhood of f(a).
nodes.by: Proved by Lagrange and generalized by Hans Heinrich Bürmann, both in the late 18th century
nodes.note: It gives the Taylor series of the inverse function of an analytic function and is a special case of the inverse function theorem. Without the claims about analyticity the formula also holds for formal power series.

nodes.name: Fenchel's duality theorem
nodes.statement: Let X and Y be Banach spaces, f: X → ℝ ∪ {+∞} and g: Y → ℝ ∪ {+∞} convex functions, and A: X → Y a bounded linear map. Let p* be the infimum of f(x) + g(Ax) over X and d* the supremum of −f*(A*y*) − g*(−y*) over the dual of Y. Then p* ≥ d*. If f and g are lower semi-continuous and 0 lies in the algebraic interior of dom g − A dom f, or if A dom f contains a point where g is continuous, then p* = d*, and if d* is finite the supremum is attained.
nodes.by: Named after Werner Fenchel
nodes.note: Here f* and g* are the convex conjugates of f and g, and A* is the adjoint operator.

nodes.name: Fenchel's theorem
nodes.statement: The total absolute curvature of a closed smooth space curve is at least 2π. Equivalently, its average curvature is at least 2π/L, where L is the length of the curve, and equality holds exactly for the plane convex curves.
nodes.by: Werner Fenchel, 1929
nodes.note: The Fáry–Milnor theorem strengthens it: a nontrivially knotted closed smooth simple space curve has total absolute curvature greater than 4π.

nodes.name: Fenchel–Moreau theorem
nodes.statement: Let X be a Hausdorff locally convex space and f an extended real valued function on X. Then f equals its biconjugate f** if and only if f is proper, lower semi-continuous and convex, or f is identically +∞, or f is identically −∞.
nodes.by: Named after Werner Fenchel and Jean Jacques Moreau
nodes.note: Every function satisfies f** ≤ f. The theorem can be seen as a generalization of the bipolar theorem and is used in duality theory to prove strong duality.

nodes.name: Glivenko–Cantelli theorem
nodes.statement: Let X₁, X₂, … be independent and identically distributed real random variables with cumulative distribution function F. Then the empirical distribution function Fₙ of X₁, …, Xₙ converges uniformly to F almost surely as n grows.
nodes.by: Valery Glivenko and Francesco Cantelli, 1933
nodes.note: For each fixed x, the convergence of Fₙ(x) to F(x) follows from the strong law of large numbers. The theorem strengthens this to uniform convergence.

nodes.name: Fernique's theorem
nodes.statement: Let X be a separable Banach space and μ a centred Gaussian measure on X, that is, a probability measure on the Borel sets of X such that every bounded linear functional ℓ : X → ℝ pushes μ forward to a normal distribution with zero mean. Then there is α > 0 such that the integral of exp(α‖x‖²) over X with respect to μ is finite, so in particular ‖x‖ has finite moments of every order k ≥ 0.
nodes.by: Xavier Fernique, 1970
nodes.note: It extends the finite-dimensional result that a Gaussian random variable has exponential tails.

nodes.name: Fiber bundle construction theorem
nodes.statement: Let X and F be topological spaces and G a topological group acting continuously on F from the left. Given an open cover {Uᵢ} of X and continuous maps tᵢⱼ : Uᵢ ∩ Uⱼ → G on every nonempty overlap with tᵢₖ(x) = tᵢⱼ(x)tⱼₖ(x) for all x in Uᵢ ∩ Uⱼ ∩ Uₖ, there is a fiber bundle E → X with fiber F and structure group G that is trivializable over {Uᵢ} with transition functions tᵢⱼ, and if G acts faithfully on F this bundle is unique up to isomorphism.
nodes.note: A similar theorem holds for smooth manifolds, Lie groups and smooth transition maps. It is used in the associated bundle construction, where the fiber of a given bundle is replaced while all other data stay the same.

nodes.name: Gromov's filling area conjecture
nodes.statement: Among orientable compact Riemannian surfaces whose boundary is a closed curve of given length, and in which the distance between any two boundary points is the same along the surface as along the boundary curve, the hemisphere has the smallest area.
nodes.by: Mikhail Gromov, 1983
nodes.note: Gromov proved it for surfaces homeomorphic to a disk, and it is also known for surfaces of genus one. It becomes false if Finsler 2-chains with rational coefficients are allowed as fillings.

nodes.name: Fraňková–Helly selection theorem
nodes.statement: Let X be a separable Hilbert space and (fₙ) a sequence of regulated functions [0,T] → X with the supremum norm. Suppose that for every ε > 0 there is L_ε > 0 such that each fₙ differs by less than ε in supremum norm from some function uₙ of bounded variation with |uₙ(0)| + Var(uₙ) ≤ L_ε; then some subsequence converges weakly in X, at every t in [0,T], to a regulated function f.
nodes.by: Dana Fraňková, 1991
nodes.note: It generalizes Helly's selection theorem for functions of bounded variation to regulated functions, for which Helly's theorem itself fails.

nodes.name: Freudenthal spectral theorem
nodes.statement: Let E be a Riesz space with the principal projection property and e a positive element of E. Then every f in the principal ideal generated by e is the e-uniform limit of an increasing sequence of e-simple functions and also of a decreasing sequence of e-simple functions, where an e-simple function is a real linear combination of pairwise disjoint components of e.
nodes.by: Hans Freudenthal, 1936
nodes.note: The Radon–Nikodym theorem, the Poisson formula and the spectral theorem for normal operators can be derived from it as special cases.

nodes.name: Discontinuities of monotone functions
nodes.statement: A monotone real-valued function defined on an interval of real numbers has at most countably many discontinuities, and all of them are jump discontinuities.
nodes.by: Called Froda's theorem in some recent works; Alexandru Froda gave an elementary proof in his 1929 dissertation, stating that the result was already well known
nodes.note: Alexandru Froda stated in 1929 that the result was already well known. Earlier work on discontinuities appears in the 1875 memoir of Jean Gaston Darboux.

nodes.name: Frostman's lemma
nodes.statement: Let A be a Borel subset of ℝⁿ and let s > 0. Then the s-dimensional Hausdorff measure of A is positive if and only if there is a Borel measure μ on ℝⁿ with μ(A) > 0 such that μ(B(x,r)) ≤ r^s for every ball B(x,r) with centre x in ℝⁿ and radius r > 0.
nodes.by: Otto Frostman, 1935, for closed sets; the generalization to Borel sets requires the theory of Suslin sets
nodes.note: It is a tool for estimating the Hausdorff dimension of sets such as fractals.

nodes.name: Fuglede's theorem
nodes.statement: Let T and N be bounded operators on a complex Hilbert space, with N normal. If TN = NT, then TN* = N*T, where N* is the adjoint of N.
nodes.by: Bent Fuglede, 1950
nodes.note: Normality of N is necessary. Calvin Richard Putnam extended the result in 1951 to operators with MT = TN for normal M and N.

nodes.name: Gaussian isoperimetric inequality
nodes.statement: Among all sets of a given Gaussian measure in n-dimensional Euclidean space, half-spaces have the minimal Gaussian boundary measure. Precisely, for every measurable set A ⊂ ℝⁿ with standard Gaussian measure γⁿ, the limit inferior as ε → 0⁺ of (γⁿ(A_ε) − γⁿ(A))/ε is at least φ(Φ⁻¹(γⁿ(A))), where A_ε is the set of points at distance at most ε from A, φ is the standard normal density and Φ its cumulative distribution function.
nodes.by: Boris Tsirelson and Vladimir Sudakov, and later independently Christer Borell
nodes.note: The original proofs were based on Paul Lévy's spherical isoperimetric inequality. The inequality also follows from Ehrhard's inequality.

nodes.name: Gelfand–Naimark–Segal construction
nodes.statement: Let A be a C*-algebra. If π is a *-representation of A on a Hilbert space and ξ is a cyclic vector of norm 1, then a ↦ ⟨π(a)ξ, ξ⟩ is a state of A (a positive linear functional of norm 1). Conversely, every state ρ of A arises this way: there is a *-representation π with a unit cyclic vector ξ such that ρ(a) = ⟨π(a)ξ, ξ⟩ for all a, and this representation is essentially uniquely determined by ρ.
nodes.by: Named after Israel Gelfand, Mark Naimark and Irving Segal; Segal recognized the construction implicit in Gelfand and Naimark's 1943 paper and presented it in sharpened form
nodes.note: The construction is at the heart of the proof of the Gelfand–Naimark theorem, which characterizes C*-algebras as algebras of operators. The GNS representation of a state is irreducible exactly when the state is pure.

nodes.name: Geroch's splitting theorem
nodes.statement: Every globally hyperbolic spacetime has a Cauchy surface S, and a homeomorphism from the spacetime to S × ℝ can be chosen so that every slice S × {t} is a Cauchy surface and every curve {p} × ℝ is a continuous timelike curve.
nodes.by: Robert Geroch, 1970; improved by A. N. Bernal and M. Sánchez
nodes.note: It gives a topological characterization of globally hyperbolic spacetimes. Bernal and Sánchez proved a global smooth splitting and a global Cauchy orthogonal splitting.

nodes.name: Bing–Borsuk conjecture
nodes.statement: Every n-dimensional homogeneous absolute neighborhood retract space is a topological manifold.
nodes.by: R. H. Bing and Karol Borsuk, 1965; they proved it for n = 1 and 2
nodes.note: Włodzimierz Jakobsche showed in 1978 that the 3-dimensional version of the conjecture implies the Poincaré conjecture.

nodes.name: Cohn's theorem
nodes.statement: Let p(z) be a self-inversive polynomial of degree n, that is, p(z) = ω p*(z) for some complex number ω with |ω| = 1, where p*(z) = zⁿ times the complex conjugate of p(1/z̄). Then p(z) and the reciprocal polynomial of its derivative, q*(z) = z^(n−1) times the complex conjugate of p′(1/z̄), have the same number of roots in the open unit disk |z| < 1.
nodes.note: It is useful for studying the distribution of the roots of self-inversive and self-reciprocal polynomials in the complex plane.

nodes.name: Tennis ball theorem
nodes.statement: Any smooth (twice continuously differentiable) curve on the surface of a sphere that divides the sphere into two equal-area parts without touching or crossing itself has at least four inflection points, points at which the curve does not consistently bend to only one side of its tangent line.
nodes.by: First published under this name by Vladimir Arnold, 1994; a special case of a theorem of Joel L. Weiner, 1977
nodes.note: A closely related result appears in a 1968 paper by Beniamino Segre. The theorem is analogous to the four-vertex theorem for plane curves.

nodes.name: Ladyzhenskaya–Babuška–Brezzi condition
nodes.statement: Let V and Q be Hilbert spaces, a: V × V → ℝ and b: V × Q → ℝ continuous bilinear forms, f a continuous linear functional on V and g one on Q, and suppose a(v, v) ≥ α‖v‖² for some α > 0 and all v with b(v, q) = 0 for every q in Q. If there is β > 0 such that for every q the supremum of b(v, q)/‖v‖ over nonzero v in V is at least β‖q‖, then there is exactly one pair u in V, p in Q with a(u, v) + b(v, p) = f(v) and b(u, q) = g(q) for all v and q, and ‖u‖ + ‖p‖ ≤ C(‖f‖ + ‖g‖) for some constant C.
nodes.note: It gives criteria for when a discretization of a saddle point problem, such as those arising from Stokes flow, is stable.

nodes.name: Gleason's theorem
nodes.statement: Let H be a finite-dimensional Hilbert space over the real or complex numbers (or a quaternionic module) of dimension at least 3. If f assigns to each projection onto a unit vector a number from 0 to 1 so that the values for the vectors of any orthonormal basis add up to 1, then there is a positive-semidefinite operator ρ with trace 1 such that f(Π) = Tr(Πρ) for every such projection Π.
nodes.by: Andrew M. Gleason, 1957, answering a question posed by George W. Mackey
nodes.note: It derives the Born rule of quantum physics from noncontextual probability assignments and rules out noncontextual hidden-variable theories. In dimension 2 it fails: Kadison showed there is a probability measure there that does not come from a density operator.

nodes.name: Goldberg–Sachs theorem
nodes.statement: A vacuum solution of the Einstein field equations admits a shear-free null geodesic congruence if and only if its Weyl tensor is algebraically special.
nodes.by: Stated by Goldberg and Sachs
nodes.note: The theorem is often used when searching for algebraically special vacuum solutions. Dain and Moreschi showed that the corresponding statement fails in linearized gravity.

nodes.name: Gordon–Luecke theorem
nodes.statement: If the complements of two tame knots in the 3-sphere are homeomorphic, then the knots are equivalent, meaning that some self-homeomorphism of the 3-sphere takes one knot to the other. In particular, any homeomorphism between the knot complements takes a meridian to a meridian.
nodes.by: Cameron Gordon and John Luecke, 1989
nodes.note: It follows from the result that no nontrivial Dehn surgery on a nontrivial knot in the 3-sphere can yield the 3-sphere. The analogous claim for links is false.

nodes.name: Gromov's compactness theorem
nodes.statement: Let (X_i, d_i) be a sequence of compact metric spaces whose diameters are all below one common bound. Suppose that for every ε > 0 there is a natural number N such that every X_i can be covered by N balls of radius ε. Then the sequence has a subsequence that converges in the Gromov–Hausdorff distance.
nodes.by: Mikhael Gromov, 1981
nodes.note: Its role in the theory of Gromov–Hausdorff convergence is analogous to the role of the Arzelà–Ascoli theorem in the theory of uniform convergence. For closed Riemannian manifolds with a common lower bound on Ricci curvature and a common upper bound on diameter, the covering condition holds automatically.

nodes.name: Gromov's inequality for complex projective space
nodes.statement: For every Riemannian metric on complex projective space ℂPⁿ, (stsys₂)ⁿ ≤ n! · vol₂ₙ(ℂPⁿ), where the stable 2-systole stsys₂ is the infimum of the areas of rational 2-cycles representing the class of the complex projective line ℂP¹ ⊂ ℂPⁿ in 2-dimensional homology. Equality is attained by the symmetric Fubini–Study metric.
nodes.by: Gromov, 1981 (Theorem 4.36)
nodes.note: The proof relies on the Wirtinger inequality for exterior 2-forms. For n = 2 it is an analog of Pu's inequality for the real projective plane.

nodes.name: Gromov's systolic inequality for essential manifolds
nodes.statement: Let M be a closed essential Riemannian manifold of dimension n, and let sysπ₁(M) be the least length of a non-contractible loop on M. Then (sysπ₁(M))ⁿ ≤ Cₙ · vol(M), where Cₙ is a universal constant depending only on n. A closed manifold is essential if its fundamental class (with integer coefficients if it is orientable, with coefficients modulo 2 otherwise) defines a nonzero element in the homology of its fundamental group.
nodes.by: M. Gromov, 1983
nodes.note: It can be viewed as a non-optimal generalisation of Loewner's torus inequality and Pu's inequality for the real projective plane. Examples of essential manifolds include aspherical manifolds, real projective spaces and lens spaces.

nodes.name: Grothendieck inequality
nodes.statement: There is a constant K_G, the same for every n, such that for every n × n matrix M with |∑ M_ij s_i t_j| ≤ 1 for all numbers s_i, t_j of absolute value at most 1, also |∑ M_ij ⟨S_i, T_j⟩| ≤ K_G for all vectors S_i, T_j in the unit ball of a Hilbert space. The matrix, the numbers and the Hilbert space are either all real or all complex.
nodes.by: Alexander Grothendieck, 1953
nodes.note: There are separate real and complex Grothendieck constants. Grothendieck proved π/2 ≤ K_G ≤ sinh(π/2) for the real constant, and the inequality is used to approximate the cut norm of a matrix efficiently by semidefinite programming.

nodes.name: Grunsky's theorem
nodes.statement: If f is a univalent holomorphic function on the unit disc with f(0) = 0, then for every r ≤ tanh(π/4) the image of the disc |z| < r is starlike with respect to 0, meaning it is closed under multiplication by real numbers in (0,1).
nodes.by: Helmut Grunsky
nodes.note: It follows from Grunsky's inequality |log(zf′(z)/f(z))| ≤ log((1 + |z|)/(1 − |z|)) for univalent f on the unit disc with f(0) = 0.

nodes.name: Walsh–Lebesgue theorem
nodes.statement: Let K be a compact subset of the Euclidean plane ℝ² whose complement in ℝ² is connected. Then every real-valued continuous function on the boundary of K can be approximated uniformly on that boundary by real-valued harmonic polynomials in x and y.
nodes.by: Joseph L. Walsh, 1929, using results proved by Lebesgue in 1907
nodes.note: It has been generalized to Riemann surfaces and to ℝⁿ.

nodes.name: Cauchy's limit theorem
nodes.statement: If a sequence (aₙ) converges to a, then the arithmetic means (a₁ + ⋯ + aₙ)/n also converge to a.
nodes.by: Augustin-Louis Cauchy, 1821
nodes.note: The arithmetic means are also called Cesàro means. It is a special case of the Stolz–Cesàro theorem, and its converse fails: the means can converge while the sequence does not.

nodes.name: Milnor–Wood inequality
nodes.statement: Let π: E → Σ_g be a flat oriented topological circle bundle over a closed oriented surface Σ_g of genus g ≥ 1. Then the Euler number of the bundle satisfies |e(π)| ≤ 2g − 2, and for flat oriented linear circle bundles the bound is |e(π)| ≤ g − 1.
nodes.by: John Milnor, 1958 (linear bundles); John W. Wood, 1971 (topological bundles)
nodes.note: Wood's theorem implies Milnor's older result. Either statement can be meant by the name Milnor–Wood inequality.

nodes.name: Hadwiger's theorem
nodes.statement: Every valuation v on the compact convex sets in ℝⁿ that is continuous in the Hausdorff metric and unchanged by translations and rotations is a combination v(S) = c₀W₀(S) + c₁W₁(S) + … + cₙWₙ(S) of the quermassintegrals with constants cⱼ. The quermassintegrals are defined by Steiner's formula; W₀ is the volume, W₁ is proportional to the surface measure and Wₙ₋₁ to the mean width.
nodes.by: Hugo Hadwiger
nodes.note: It characterises the valuations on convex bodies in ℝⁿ. As a corollary, such a valuation that is homogeneous of degree j is a multiple of Wₙ₋ⱼ.

nodes.name: Kolmogorov continuity theorem
nodes.statement: Let (S,d) be a complete separable metric space and X a stochastic process on [0,∞) with values in S. If for every time T > 0 there are positive constants α, β, K with E[d(Xₜ, Xₛ)^α] ≤ K|t − s|^(1+β) for all 0 ≤ s, t ≤ T, then X has a modification that is sample-continuous and equals X at each time t ≥ 0 with probability 1, and its paths are locally γ-Hölder-continuous for every 0 < γ < β/α.
nodes.by: Credited to Andrey Nikolaevich Kolmogorov
nodes.note: For Brownian motion on ℝⁿ the constants α = 4, β = 1, K = n(n + 2) work.

nodes.name: Solvability criterion for the Hamburger moment problem
nodes.statement: A sequence (m₀, m₁, m₂, …) is the sequence of moments mₙ = ∫ xⁿ dμ(x) of some positive Borel measure μ on the real line if and only if ∑ m_{j+k} c_j conj(c_k) ≥ 0 for every sequence of complex numbers c_j with only finitely many nonzero terms.
nodes.by: Named after Hans Ludwig Hamburger
nodes.note: The Stieltjes, Vorobyev and Hausdorff moment problems are similar but replace the real line by [0,∞) or by a bounded interval.

nodes.name: Hanner's inequalities
nodes.statement: Let f and g be in L^p(E), where E is any measure space. If 1 ≤ p ≤ 2, then ‖f+g‖ₚᵖ + ‖f−g‖ₚᵖ ≥ (‖f‖ₚ + ‖g‖ₚ)ᵖ + |‖f‖ₚ − ‖g‖ₚ|ᵖ; for 2 ≤ p < ∞ the inequality is reversed, and for p = 2 it becomes an equality, the parallelogram rule.
nodes.by: Olof Hanner, proof published 1956
nodes.note: They give a simpler way of proving the uniform convexity of L^p spaces for 1 < p < ∞ than the approach proposed by James A. Clarkson in 1936.

nodes.name: Hardy–Littlewood Tauberian theorem
nodes.statement: Let a₀, a₁, a₂, … be a sequence of numbers with every aₙ ≥ 0. If the sum of aₙ·e^(−ny) over n ≥ 0 is asymptotically equivalent to 1/y as y decreases to 0, then the partial sums a₀ + a₁ + … + aₙ are asymptotically equivalent to n as n → ∞.
nodes.by: G. H. Hardy and J. E. Littlewood, 1914; a new and much simpler proof by Jovan Karamata, 1930
nodes.note: It relates the asymptotics of the partial sums of a series to the asymptotics of its Abel summation. Hardy and Littlewood used it in 1915 to prove the prime number theorem.

nodes.name: Hartogs–Rosenthal theorem
nodes.statement: If K is a compact subset of the complex plane with Lebesgue measure zero, then every continuous complex-valued function on K can be uniformly approximated by rational functions.
nodes.by: Friedrich Hartogs and Arthur Rosenthal, 1931
nodes.note: It has been widely applied, particularly in operator theory.

nodes.name: Hausdorff moment problem
nodes.statement: A sequence (m₀, m₁, m₂, ...) is the sequence of moments mₙ = ∫₀¹ xⁿ dμ(x) of some Borel measure μ on the closed interval [0, 1] if and only if it is completely monotonic. That means Δᵏ mₙ ≥ 0 for all n, k ≥ 0, where Δ mₙ = mₙ − mₙ₊₁ and Δᵏ mₙ = ∑ from i = 0 to k of (k choose i)(−1)ⁱ mₙ₊ᵢ.
nodes.by: Felix Hausdorff, 1921
nodes.note: On the bounded interval [0, 1] the solution is unique whenever it exists, unlike in the Stieltjes and Hamburger moment problems on a half-line and on the whole line.

nodes.name: Hausdorff–Young inequality
nodes.statement: Let 1 < p ≤ 2 and let p′ be given by 1/p + 1/p′ = 1. For every function f in L^p((0,1)), with Fourier coefficients c(n) = ∫₀¹ f(t)e^(−2πint) dt, the inequality (∑ over all integers n of |c(n)|^p′)^(1/p′) ≤ (∫₀¹ |f(t)|^p dt)^(1/p) holds.
nodes.by: Young, 1913, for Fourier series; extended by Hausdorff, 1923
nodes.note: It follows from the Plancherel theorem combined with the Riesz–Thorin theorem, and extends to multidimensional Fourier series and to the Fourier transform on ℝⁿ for p in [1, 2]. The condition p ≤ 2 is essential.

nodes.name: Heine's identity
nodes.statement: For every real number z > 1, 1/√(z − cos ψ) = (√2/π) ∑ Q_{m−1/2}(z) e^(imψ), where the sum runs over all integers m and Q_{m−1/2} is a Legendre function of the second kind.
nodes.by: Named after Eduard Heine
nodes.note: It is a Fourier expansion of a reciprocal square root. The identity generalizes to arbitrary half-integer powers of z − cos ψ, with coefficients involving the gamma function and associated Legendre functions.

nodes.name: Helly–Bray theorem
nodes.statement: Let F and F₁, F₂, ... be cumulative distribution functions on the real line. If Fₙ converges weakly to F, then the integral of g with respect to Fₙ converges to the integral of g with respect to F, for every bounded, continuous function g from ℝ to ℝ (the integrals are Riemann–Stieltjes integrals).
nodes.by: Named after Eduard Helly and Hubert Evelyn Bray
nodes.note: It does not imply that E(Xₙ) → E(X), since g(x) = x is not bounded. A more general version for probability measures on a set S is sometimes taken as the definition of weak convergence of measures.

nodes.name: Fejér's theorem
nodes.statement: Let f be a continuous function on ℝ with period 2π, let sₙ(f,x) be the partial sums of its Fourier series, and let σₙ(f,x) = (s₀(f,x) + s₁(f,x) + … + sₙ₋₁(f,x))/n be their averages. Then σₙ(f,x) converges to f(x) as n → ∞, uniformly in x.
nodes.by: Named after the Hungarian mathematician Lipót Fejér
nodes.note: The result fails if the averages σₙ are replaced by the partial sums sₙ, since there are functions whose Fourier series fails to converge at some point. A more general form holds for functions in L¹(−π, π) at points where the left and right limits exist.

nodes.name: Andreotti–Grauert theorem
nodes.statement: Let X be a complex analytic space, not necessarily reduced, and F a coherent analytic sheaf on X. If X is q-pseudoconvex, then Hⁱ(X, F) is finite-dimensional over ℂ for i ≥ q. If X is q-pseudoconcave, then Hⁱ(X, F) is finite-dimensional for i < codh(F) − q. If X is q-complete, then Hⁱ(X, F) = 0 for i ≥ q.
nodes.by: Aldo Andreotti and Hans Grauert, 1962
nodes.note: It gives conditions for cohomology groups of coherent sheaves to vanish or to be finite-dimensional.

nodes.name: Fundamental theorem of curves
nodes.statement: Every regular curve in three-dimensional space with non-zero curvature has its shape and size completely determined by its curvature and torsion, taken as functions of arc length. Two such curves with the same curvature and torsion differ only in position, that is, they are congruent.
nodes.note: From the curvature and torsion, the tangent, normal and binormal vectors follow from the Frenet–Serret formulas, and integrating the tangent recovers the curve.

nodes.name: Hilbert's lemma
nodes.statement: Take a smooth surface in three-dimensional space and a point p on it, with principal curvatures k and m and Gaussian curvature K. If k has a local maximum at p, m has a local minimum at p, and k is strictly greater than m at p, then K(p) ≤ 0.
nodes.by: Proposed by David Hilbert at the end of the 19th century
nodes.note: It may be used to prove Liebmann's theorem that a compact surface with constant Gaussian curvature must be a sphere.

nodes.name: Hilbert's nineteenth problem
nodes.statement: Solutions of regular problems in the calculus of variations are always analytic. That is, if F(p, q, z; x, y) is an analytic function of all its arguments, satisfies the ellipticity condition F_pp·F_qq − (F_pq)² > 0 on its second partial derivatives and suitable growth conditions, then every real-valued function z(x, y) that minimizes ∬ F(∂z/∂x, ∂z/∂y, z; x, y) dx dy is analytic.
nodes.by: Posed by David Hilbert, 1900; solved independently by Ennio De Giorgi and John Forbes Nash, Jr. in the late 1950s
nodes.note: The answer is affirmative for a single scalar unknown, but counterexamples from 1968 show that vector-valued solutions and solutions of single elliptic equations of order greater than two need not be analytic.

nodes.name: Hilton's theorem
nodes.statement: The loop space of a wedge of spheres is homotopy-equivalent to a product, in general with infinitely many factors, of loop spaces of spheres.
nodes.by: Hilton, 1955; generalized by Milnor, 1972
nodes.note: Milnor showed more generally that the loop space of the suspension of a wedge of spaces can be written as an infinite product of loop spaces of suspensions of smash products.

nodes.name: Liouville's theorem (complex analysis)
nodes.statement: Every bounded entire function is constant. That is, if f is holomorphic on the whole complex plane and there is a positive number M with |f(z)| ≤ M for all complex z, then f is constant.
nodes.by: Named after Joseph Liouville; first proven by Cauchy, 1844
nodes.note: Picard's little theorem improves it: every entire function whose image omits two or more complex numbers must be constant.

nodes.name: Sard's theorem
nodes.statement: Let f: ℝⁿ → ℝᵐ be k times continuously differentiable, where k ≥ max{n − m + 1, 1}, and let X be the set of points where the Jacobian matrix of f has rank less than m. Then the image f(X) has Lebesgue measure 0 in ℝᵐ. The same holds, with the same condition on k, for maps from an n-dimensional to an m-dimensional differentiable manifold.
nodes.by: Anthony P. Morse, 1939 (case m = 1); Arthur Sard, 1942 (general case)
nodes.note: A smooth map may have many critical points but has few critical values. In topology it is often used to show that a non-constant smooth map has at least one regular value.

nodes.name: Kolmogorov–Arnold–Moser theorem
nodes.statement: Take an integrable Hamiltonian system, whose motions run quasiperiodically on invariant tori, and assume it satisfies the non-degeneracy condition. Under a sufficiently weak perturbation, the invariant tori whose frequency vector ω is sufficiently irrational (Diophantine: for some γ, τ > 0, |ω·k| ≥ γ/‖k‖^τ for every nonzero integer vector k) are not destroyed but only deformed, and the motion on them stays quasiperiodic.
nodes.by: Andrey Kolmogorov, 1954; proved and extended by Jürgen Moser, 1962 (smooth twist maps), and Vladimir Arnold, 1963 (analytic Hamiltonian systems)
nodes.note: As a consequence, for a large set of initial conditions the motion remains quasiperiodic forever. Tori that the perturbation destroys become invariant Cantor sets, called Cantori.

nodes.name: Hitchin–Thorpe inequality
nodes.statement: Let M be a closed, oriented, four-dimensional smooth manifold. If M has a Riemannian metric that is an Einstein metric, then χ(M) ≥ (3/2)|τ(M)|, where χ(M) is the Euler characteristic and τ(M) is the signature of M.
nodes.by: First stated by John Thorpe in a footnote to a 1969 paper; rediscovered by Nigel Hitchin, who in 1974 gave a complete characterization of the equality case
nodes.note: It restricts the topology of 4-manifolds that carry an Einstein metric. The converse fails: in 1995 LeBrun and Sambusetti found infinitely many 4-manifolds that satisfy the strict inequality but carry no Einstein metric.

nodes.name: Koebe quarter theorem
nodes.statement: If f is an injective analytic function from the unit disk D onto a subset of the complex plane, then the image of f contains the disk with centre f(0) and radius |f′(0)|/4.
nodes.by: Conjectured by Paul Koebe, 1907; proved by Ludwig Bieberbach, 1916
nodes.note: The Koebe function shows that the constant 1/4 cannot be increased.

nodes.name: Holmgren's uniqueness theorem
nodes.statement: Let Ω be a connected open set in ℝⁿ that an analytic hypersurface Σ splits into two nonempty connected open parts Ω₋ and Ω₊, and let P be a linear differential operator with real-analytic coefficients such that Σ is noncharacteristic for P at every point. If u is a distribution on Ω with Pu = 0 in Ω and u vanishes in Ω₋, then u vanishes in an open neighbourhood of Σ.
nodes.by: Named after Erik Albert Holmgren
nodes.note: It is a uniqueness result for linear equations with real-analytic coefficients. It complements the Cauchy–Kowalevski theorem, which by itself does not exclude solutions that are not real-analytic.

nodes.name: Hopf maximum principle
nodes.statement: Let u be a C² function on an open connected domain Ω in ℝⁿ satisfying Lu = ∑ a_ij ∂²u/∂x_i∂x_j + ∑ b_i ∂u/∂x_i ≥ 0. Here the symmetric matrix a_ij is locally uniformly positive definite and the coefficients a_ij, b_i are locally bounded. If u takes a maximum value M in Ω, then u is constant, equal to M.
nodes.by: Eberhard Hopf, 1927
nodes.note: It generalizes the maximum principle for harmonic functions, which was already known to Gauss in 1839.

nodes.name: Dini's theorem
nodes.statement: Let X be a compact topological space and let (fₙ) be a monotone sequence (increasing or decreasing) of continuous real-valued functions on X that converges pointwise to a continuous function f: X → ℝ. Then the convergence is uniform.
nodes.by: Named after Ulisse Dini
nodes.note: The limit function must be continuous, and this cannot be inferred from the other hypotheses: xⁿ on [0,1] is a counterexample.

nodes.name: Hyperbolization theorem
nodes.statement: If M is a compact, irreducible, atoroidal Haken 3-manifold whose boundary has Euler characteristic zero, then the interior of M has a complete hyperbolic structure of finite volume.
nodes.by: Thurston; proofs published by Otal (1996, 1998) and Kapovich (2009)
nodes.note: It implies that closed atoroidal Haken manifolds are hyperbolic. Thurston never published a complete proof.

nodes.name: Identity theorem for Riemann surfaces
nodes.statement: Let X and Y be Riemann surfaces with X connected, and let f and g be holomorphic maps from X to Y. If f and g agree on a subset of X that has a limit point, then f = g on the whole of X.
nodes.note: A holomorphic function is completely determined by its values on any subset of its domain that has a limit point.

nodes.name: Shapiro inequality
nodes.statement: Let n be a natural number that is even and at most 12, or odd and at most 23, and let x₁, …, xₙ be positive numbers. Then the sum of xᵢ/(xᵢ₊₁ + xᵢ₊₂) over i = 1, …, n is at least n/2, where xₙ₊₁ = x₁ and xₙ₊₂ = x₂.
nodes.by: Proposed by Harold S. Shapiro, 1954
nodes.note: A special case is Nesbitt's inequality. For larger n the inequality fails, and Vladimir Drinfeld determined in 1971 the constant γ ≈ 0.9891 in the strict lower bound γn/2.

nodes.name: Increment theorem
nodes.statement: Suppose a function f is differentiable at x and Δx is infinitesimal. Then Δy = f′(x)Δx + εΔx for some infinitesimal ε, where Δy = f(x + Δx) − f(x). If Δx ≠ 0, this means Δy/Δx is infinitely close to f′(x).
nodes.note: A similar theorem holds in standard calculus, where ε is a function of Δx with limit 0 as Δx approaches 0.

nodes.name: Pestov–Ionin theorem
nodes.statement: Every simple closed plane curve that is twice continuously differentiable and has curvature at most one at every point encloses a disk of radius one.
nodes.by: Named for Pestov and Ionin, who published a version for non-convex twice differentiable curves in 1959; a version for convex curves was published by Wilhelm Blaschke in 1916
nodes.note: It is also called the moon in a puddle theorem. It does not generalize to higher dimensions.

nodes.name: Peano kernel theorem
nodes.statement: Let L be a linear functional on the space of functions that are differentiable on (a,b) and of bounded variation on [a,b]. Suppose L gives 0 on every polynomial of degree at most ν, and that L can be exchanged with integration over θ from a to b for every function g(x,θ) that is ν+1 times continuously differentiable in each variable. Let k(θ) = L[(x−θ)₊^ν], where (x−θ)₊^ν is (x−θ)^ν for x ≥ θ and 0 otherwise. If k also belongs to this space, then for every ν+1 times continuously differentiable f, Lf = (1/ν!) ∫ₐᵇ k(θ) f^(ν+1)(θ) dθ.
nodes.by: Attributed to Giuseppe Peano
nodes.note: It gives error bounds for a wide class of numerical approximations, such as numerical quadratures, that are exact for all polynomials of degree at most ν.

nodes.name: Titu's lemma
nodes.statement: For any real numbers a₁, …, aₙ and positive real numbers b₁, …, bₙ, a₁²/b₁ + a₂²/b₂ + … + aₙ²/bₙ ≥ (a₁ + a₂ + … + aₙ)² / (b₁ + b₂ + … + bₙ).
nodes.by: Published independently by Nairi Sedrakyan, 1997; Arthur Engel, 1998; Titu Andreescu, 2003
nodes.note: Also known as Bergström's inequality, Engel's form or Sedrakyan's inequality. It is a direct consequence of the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality.

nodes.name: Anderson–Kadec theorem
nodes.statement: Every infinite-dimensional, separable Fréchet space is homeomorphic to ℝ^ℕ, the product of countably many copies of the real line. In particular, any two infinite-dimensional separable Banach spaces are homeomorphic as topological spaces.
nodes.by: Mikhail Kadec, 1966, and Richard Davis Anderson
nodes.note: The proof starts from Kadec's result that every infinite-dimensional separable Banach space is homeomorphic to ℝ^ℕ.

nodes.name: Wiener's lemma
nodes.statement: Let μ be a finite complex Borel measure on the unit circle whose point masses are c_j. Then (1/(2N+1)) ∑ |μ̂(n)|² over n from −N to N, the average of its squared Fourier–Stieltjes coefficients, tends to ∑ |c_j|² as N → ∞, and likewise for a finite complex Borel measure on the real line, (1/(2R)) ∫ |μ̂(ξ)|² dξ over [−R, R] tends to ∑ |c_j|² as R → ∞.
nodes.by: First discovered by Norbert Wiener
nodes.note: It relates the asymptotic behaviour of the Fourier coefficients of a measure to its discrete part. As a consequence, a probability measure on the circle is a Dirac mass exactly when this limit equals 1.

nodes.name: Lions–Magenes lemma
nodes.statement: Let X₀, X and X₁ be Hilbert spaces with X₀ ⊆ X ⊆ X₁, where X₀ is continuously embedded in X, X is continuously embedded in X₁, and X₁ is the dual space of X₀. If for some T > 0 a function u is in L²([0, T]; X₀) and its time derivative u̇ is in L²([0, T]; X₁), then u is almost everywhere equal to a function continuous from [0, T] into X, and (1/2) d/dt ‖u‖²_X = ⟨u̇, u⟩ in the sense of scalar distributions on (0, T).
nodes.note: It gives a criterion for moving a time derivative of a function out of its action as a functional on the function itself. It does not extend to u̇ ∈ Lq with 1/p + 1/q > 1, which is why the energy equality for weak solutions of the 3-dimensional Navier–Stokes equations is not known.

nodes.name: Laplace's principle
nodes.statement: Let A be a Lebesgue-measurable subset of ℝᵈ and let φ: ℝᵈ → ℝ be a measurable function with ∫_A e^(−φ(x)) dx < ∞. Then, as θ → ∞, (1/θ) log ∫_A e^(−θφ(x)) dx tends to −(the essential infimum of φ over A).
nodes.note: It is similar to Varadhan's lemma. It can be used in statistical mechanics to find the limiting behaviour of a system as the temperature tends to absolute zero.

nodes.name: Lyusternik–Fet theorem
nodes.statement: On every compact Riemannian manifold there exists a closed geodesic.
nodes.by: Lazar Lyusternik and Abram Ilyich Fet, 1951

nodes.name: Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma
nodes.statement: Given 0 < ε < 1, a set X of N points in ℝⁿ, and an integer k > 8(ln N)/ε², there is a linear map f from ℝⁿ to ℝᵏ such that (1−ε)‖u−v‖² ≤ ‖f(u)−f(v)‖² ≤ (1+ε)‖u−v‖² for all points u, v in X.
nodes.by: Named after William B. Johnson and Joram Lindenstrauss
nodes.note: A set of points in a high-dimensional space can be mapped into a much lower dimension with distances nearly preserved. The classical proof uses a random orthogonal projection.

nodes.name: Closed range theorem
nodes.statement: Let X and Y be Banach spaces, let T be a closed linear operator from a dense domain D(T) in X to Y, and let T′ be its transpose. Then the following are equivalent: the range of T is closed in Y; the range of T′ is closed in the dual X′; the range of T equals the set of y in Y with ⟨x*, y⟩ = 0 for all x* in the null space of T′; the range of T′ equals the set of x* in X′ with ⟨x*, y⟩ = 0 for all y in the null space of T.
nodes.by: Stefan Banach, 1932
nodes.note: The range of T always lies in the annihilator of the null space of T′, and the range of T′ always lies in the annihilator of the null space of T. The non-trivial part is the opposite inclusion.

nodes.name: Kachurovskii's theorem
nodes.statement: Let K be a convex subset of a Banach space V and let f from K to ℝ ∪ {+∞} be Fréchet differentiable at each point of K, with derivative df(x). Then the following are equivalent: f is convex; df(x)(y − x) ≤ f(y) − f(x) for all x and y in K; and (df(x) − df(y))(x − y) ≥ 0 for all x and y in K, that is, df is monotone.
nodes.note: It relates the convexity of a function on a Banach space to the monotonicity of its Fréchet derivative.

nodes.name: Kallman–Rota inequality
nodes.statement: If A is the infinitesimal generator of a one-parameter contraction semigroup on a Banach space, then ‖Af‖² ≤ 4‖f‖‖A²f‖.
nodes.by: Kallman and Rota, 1970
nodes.note: It generalizes the Landau–Kolmogorov inequality to Banach spaces.

nodes.name: Karoubi conjecture
nodes.statement: For C* algebras spatially tensored with the algebra of compact operators, the algebraic and topological K-theories coincide.
nodes.by: Conjectured by Max Karoubi; proved by Andrei Suslin and Mariusz Wodzicki
nodes.note: It was first a conjecture of Max Karoubi and was later proved.

nodes.name: Kato's conjecture
nodes.statement: For a uniformly elliptic operator L = −div(A∇) with complex, bounded, measurable coefficients on ℝⁿ, in any dimension n, the domain of the square root of L is the Sobolev space H¹(ℝⁿ), and ‖√L f‖₂ is comparable to ‖∇f‖₂.
nodes.by: Posed by Tosio Kato, 1953; proved by Pascal Auscher, Steve Hofmann, Michael Lacey, Alan McIntosh and Philippe Tchamitchian, 2001

nodes.name: Katětov–Tong insertion theorem
nodes.statement: Let X be a normal topological space and let g, h: X → ℝ be functions with g upper semicontinuous, h lower semicontinuous and g ≤ h. Then there is a continuous function f: X → ℝ with g ≤ f ≤ h.
nodes.by: Proved independently by Miroslav Katětov and Hing Tong in the 1950s
nodes.note: It is the first of many classical insertion theorems and implies the Tietze extension theorem and Urysohn's lemma.

nodes.name: Kharitonov's theorem
nodes.statement: Let p(s) = a₀ + a₁s + … + aₙsⁿ have real coefficients, each free to take any value in a given interval lᵢ ≤ aᵢ ≤ uᵢ, where the interval for the leading coefficient aₙ does not contain 0. Then every such polynomial is stable (all its roots have negative real parts) if and only if the four Kharitonov polynomials are stable, whose coefficients follow the patterns l₀, l₁, u₂, u₃, l₄, l₅, …; u₀, u₁, l₂, l₃, u₄, u₅, …; l₀, u₁, u₂, l₃, l₄, u₅, …; and u₀, l₁, l₂, u₃, u₄, l₅, ….
nodes.by: V. L. Kharitonov, 1978
nodes.note: Although infinitely many polynomials are in the family, only four need to be tested, for instance with the Routh–Hurwitz criterion.

nodes.name: Khintchine inequality
nodes.statement: For each p in (0, ∞) there are constants A_p, B_p > 0 depending only on p such that, for every nonzero square-summable sequence x = (x₁, x₂, ...) and independent random signs ε₁, ε₂, ... (each +1 or −1 with equal probability), (E|∑ εₙxₙ|^p)^(1/p) divided by the ℓ² norm of x lies between A_p and B_p.
nodes.by: Named after Aleksandr Khinchin; the sharp values of the constants were found by Haagerup
nodes.note: It says a randomly signed sum of numbers has size close to the square root of the sum of their squares, with bounded error.

nodes.name: Lagrange's identity
nodes.statement: For any twice differentiable (class C²) functions u and v of n variables, v·L[u] − u·L*[v] = ∇·M, where L[u] = ∑ a_ij ∂²u/∂x_i∂x_j + ∑ b_i ∂u/∂x_i + c·u and L*[v] = ∑ ∂²(a_ij·v)/∂x_i∂x_j − ∑ ∂(b_i·v)/∂x_i + c·v, with sums over i, j from 1 to n. The vector M has components M_i = ∑_j a_ij (v ∂u/∂x_j − u ∂v/∂x_j) + u·v (b_i − ∑_j ∂a_ij/∂x_j).
nodes.by: Named after Joseph Louis Lagrange
nodes.note: It gives the boundary terms arising from integration by parts of a self-adjoint linear differential operator and is fundamental in Sturm–Liouville theory. Integrated over a bounded region with the divergence theorem, it gives Green's second identity.

nodes.name: Killing–Hopf theorem
nodes.statement: Every complete connected Riemannian manifold of constant curvature is isometric to a quotient of a sphere, Euclidean space, or hyperbolic space by a group acting freely and properly discontinuously.
nodes.by: Killing, 1891, and Hopf, 1926
nodes.note: These manifolds are called space forms.

nodes.name: Kline sphere characterization
nodes.statement: If a nondegenerate locally connected metric continuum is separated by every simple closed curve in it but by no pair of points, then it is a two-dimensional sphere.
nodes.by: Named after John Robert Kline; proved by R. H. Bing, who also gave an alternate proof using brick partitioning
nodes.note: A simple closed curve in a two-dimensional sphere separates it into two pieces, while removing a pair of points leaves it connected. The theorem says that these two properties characterize the sphere.

nodes.name: Kobayashi–Hitchin correspondence
nodes.statement: A holomorphic vector bundle over a compact complex manifold with metric 2-form ω admits a Hermite–Einstein metric if and only if it is slope polystable, that is, a direct sum of slope stable bundles of the same slope. When the manifold is not Kähler, stability is defined using a Gauduchon metric, and every metric on a compact complex manifold is conformal to one.
nodes.by: Conjectured independently by Shoshichi Kobayashi and Nigel Hitchin in the early 1980s; proved by Simon Donaldson for algebraic surfaces, 1985, by Karen Uhlenbeck and Shing-Tung Yau for compact Kähler manifolds, by Buchdahl for compact complex surfaces, 1987, and by Jun Li and Yau for arbitrary compact complex manifolds
nodes.note: It is also called the Donaldson–Uhlenbeck–Yau theorem and generalises the Narasimhan–Seshadri theorem for compact Riemann surfaces. For irreducible bundles, slope polystability may be replaced with slope stability.

nodes.name: Kostant's convexity theorem
nodes.statement: Let K be a connected compact Lie group with maximal torus T and Weyl group W, with Lie algebras 𝔨 and 𝔱, and let P be the orthogonal projection of 𝔨 onto 𝔱 for some Ad-invariant inner product on 𝔨. Then for every X in 𝔱, the image P(Ad(K)·X) is the convex polytope whose vertices are the points w(X), where w runs over the Weyl group.
nodes.by: Kostant, 1973
nodes.note: It generalizes a result of Schur, Horn and Thompson for Hermitian matrices, and is a special case of a more general result for symmetric spaces.

nodes.name: Krener's theorem
nodes.statement: Let q̇ = f(q,u) be a smooth control system on a finite-dimensional manifold M, with control u in a set U, and let F be the family of vector fields f(·,u) for u in U.
