If, at a point q in M, the vectors g(q) for g in the Lie algebra generated by F fill the whole tangent space T_qM, then q belongs to the closure of the interior of the attainable set from q.
nodes.by: Attributed to Arthur J. Krener
nodes.note: It implies that every attainable set of a bracket-generating system has nonempty interior, and that every attainable set has nonempty interior in the topology of its orbit.

nodes.name: Kuiper's theorem
nodes.statement: For an infinite-dimensional complex Hilbert space H, with the norm topology on operators, every map from a finite complex Y to the space GL(H) of invertible bounded operators on H is homotopic to a constant. In particular GL(H) is weakly contractible, meaning all its homotopy groups are trivial.
nodes.by: Nicolaas Kuiper, first for separable Hilbert space; the restriction of separability was later lifted
nodes.note: The result has important uses in topological K-theory. An immediate consequence is that every Hilbert bundle is a trivial bundle.

nodes.name: Kuratowski's closure-complement problem
nodes.statement: Starting from any subset of any topological space and repeatedly applying closure and complement, one obtains at most 14 distinct sets. Some subsets of some spaces, for example certain subsets of the real line with its usual topology, give exactly 14.
nodes.by: Kazimierz Kuratowski, 1922
nodes.note: The 14 closure-complement operations form a monoid under composition, called the Kuratowski monoid.

nodes.name: Kőnig's theorem
nodes.statement: Let f(x) = ∑ cₙxⁿ with c₀ ≠ 0 be meromorphic on |x| < R with exactly one pole in that disk, a simple pole at x = r. Then cₙ/cₙ₊₁ = r + o(σⁿ⁺¹) for any σ with 0 < σ < 1 and |r| < σR. In particular cₙ/cₙ₊₁ tends to r as n → ∞.
nodes.by: Named after Gyula Kőnig
nodes.note: It is used in root finding algorithms such as Newton's method and Householder's method.

nodes.name: Kōmura's theorem
nodes.statement: Let X be a reflexive Banach space and let φ : [0, T] → X be absolutely continuous. Then φ is strongly differentiable almost everywhere, its derivative φ′ lies in the Bochner space L¹([0, T]; X), and φ(t) = φ(0) + ∫₀ᵗ φ′(s) ds for all 0 ≤ t ≤ T.
nodes.note: It is a substantial generalization of Lebesgue's theorem on the differentiability of the indefinite integral.

nodes.name: Ladyzhenskaya's inequality
nodes.statement: Let Ω be a Lipschitz domain in ℝⁿ with n = 2 or 3, and let u be a real-valued weakly differentiable function on Ω that vanishes on the boundary in the sense of trace. Then there is a constant C depending only on Ω such that ‖u‖_L⁴ ≤ C ‖u‖_L²^(1/2) ‖∇u‖_L²^(1/2) when n = 2, and ‖u‖_L⁴ ≤ C ‖u‖_L²^(1/4) ‖∇u‖_L²^(3/4) when n = 3.
nodes.by: Olga Aleksandrovna Ladyzhenskaya, 1958
nodes.note: Ladyzhenskaya introduced the two-dimensional inequality to prove existence and uniqueness of long-time solutions to the Navier–Stokes equations in two spatial dimensions. Both versions are special cases of the Gagliardo–Nirenberg interpolation inequality.

nodes.name: Last geometric statement of Jacobi
nodes.statement: For any point p on an ellipsoid that is not an umbilical point, the caustic from p has exactly four cusps.
nodes.by: Conjectured by Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi; proved rigorously by Itoh and Kiyohara, 2004
nodes.note: Numerical experiments had indicated the statement was true before it was proved. It has since been extended to a wider class of surfaces beyond the ellipsoid.

nodes.name: Lauricella's theorem
nodes.statement: A normal orthogonal set {uₖ} is closed if and only if, for each function of a known closed normal orthogonal set {vₖ}, the formal series of that function in terms of {uₖ} converges in the mean to that function.
nodes.by: Giuseppe Lauricella, 1912
nodes.note: It gives a condition for checking the closure of a set of orthogonal functions.

nodes.name: Law of the unconscious statistician
nodes.statement: Let X be a random variable and g a measurable real-valued function such that g(X) has a finite expected value. If X is discrete with probability mass function p_X, then E[g(X)] is the sum of g(x)·p_X(x) over all possible values x of X (this sum converges absolutely), and if X has a probability density function f_X, then E[g(X)] is the integral of g(x)·f_X(x) over all real x.
nodes.note: In greater generality X can be a random element of any measurable space, and the law becomes a general theorem about Lebesgue integration relative to a pushforward measure.

nodes.name: Lefschetz duality
nodes.statement: Let M be an orientable compact manifold of dimension n with boundary ∂M, and let z in Hₙ(M, ∂M; ℤ) be its fundamental class. Then cap product with z gives isomorphisms of Hᵏ(M, ∂M; ℤ) with Hₙ₋ₖ(M; ℤ), and of Hₖ(M, ∂M; ℤ) with Hⁿ⁻ᵏ(M; ℤ), for all k.
nodes.by: Solomon Lefschetz, 1926
nodes.note: The boundary can be empty, so Poincaré duality is a special case. Lefschetz introduced relative homology at the same time, for application to the Lefschetz fixed-point theorem.

nodes.name: Bernstein's lethargy theorem
nodes.statement: Let V₁ ⊂ V₂ ⊂ … be a strictly ascending sequence of finite-dimensional linear subspaces of a Banach space X, and let ε₁ ≥ ε₂ ≥ … be a decreasing sequence of real numbers tending to zero. Then there exists a point x in X whose distance to Vᵢ is exactly εᵢ for every i.
nodes.note: Lethargy theorems quantify the difficulty of approximating general functions by functions of special form, such as polynomials.

nodes.name: Lie–Palais theorem
nodes.statement: Let 𝔤 be a finite-dimensional Lie algebra and M a closed manifold, that is a compact smooth manifold without boundary. Then any infinitesimal action of 𝔤 on M by vector fields integrates to a smooth action of a finite-dimensional Lie group G on M. If M has a boundary, the same holds when the action preserves the boundary, so that the vector fields on the boundary are tangent to it.
nodes.by: Palais, 1957, as a global form of an earlier local theorem due to Sophus Lie
nodes.note: It is a partial converse to the fact that a smooth action of a Lie group induces an infinitesimal action of its Lie algebra.

nodes.name: Limit comparison test
nodes.statement: Let Σaₙ and Σbₙ be two series with aₙ ≥ 0 and bₙ > 0 for all n. If the limit of aₙ/bₙ as n → ∞ equals some c with 0 < c < ∞, then either both series converge or both diverge.

nodes.name: Lindelöf's lemma
nodes.statement: With the standard topology on the real line, every open subset of the real line is a countable union of open intervals.
nodes.by: Named after Ernst Leonard Lindelöf
nodes.note: The name is also used for the more general statement that every open cover of a second-countable space has a countable subcover, so every second-countable space is a Lindelöf space.

nodes.name: Schauder fixed-point theorem
nodes.statement: Let K be a nonempty convex closed subset of a Hausdorff locally convex topological vector space V. If f is a continuous map of K into itself and f(K) is contained in a compact subset of K, then f has a fixed point.
nodes.by: Conjectured by Juliusz Schauder, who proved special cases such as Banach spaces, 1930; Tychonoff proved the case of compact convex K, 1934; B. V. Singbal proved the general case where K may be non-compact
nodes.note: It extends the Brouwer fixed-point theorem to spaces that may be of infinite dimension.

nodes.name: Lefschetz fixed-point theorem
nodes.statement: Let f be a continuous map from a compact triangulable space X to itself, and let its Lefschetz number be the alternating sum over n ≥ 0 of (−1)ⁿ times the trace of the map that f induces on the homology Hₙ(X, ℚ). If this number is nonzero, then f has a fixed point.
nodes.by: Solomon Lefschetz, 1926
nodes.note: This is the weak version. A stronger version, the Lefschetz–Hopf theorem, counts fixed points by their fixed-point index when their number is finite. It generalizes the Brouwer fixed-point theorem.

nodes.name: Fredholm alternative
nodes.statement: Let K be a compact linear operator on a Banach space and let λ be a non-zero complex number. Then either λ is an eigenvalue of K, or K − λ·Id is invertible; for example, for an integral kernel K(x,y) that is square integrable on [a,b]×[a,b], either λφ(x) − ∫ₐᵇ K(x,y)φ(y) dy = 0 has a non-trivial solution, or λφ(x) − ∫ₐᵇ K(x,y)φ(y) dy = f(x) has a solution for every f.
nodes.by: Named after Ivar Fredholm
nodes.note: In finite dimensions it says that a linear map T from a space to itself is either surjective, and then bijective, or has a kernel of positive dimension. It is also used to solve linear elliptic boundary value problems.

nodes.name: Darboux's theorem
nodes.statement: If f is a real-valued differentiable function on an open interval I, then its derivative f′ has the intermediate value property. For any a and b in I and any value y between f′(a) and f′(b), there is a point x between a and b with f′(x) = y, so the image of an interval under f′ is an interval.
nodes.note: Even when f′ is not continuous, the theorem restricts how f′ can behave on any closed interval. The condition is necessary for a function to be a derivative but not sufficient.

nodes.name: Loomis–Whitney inequality
nodes.statement: Fix d ≥ 2. For each j from 1 to d let g_j be a non-negative function in L^(d−1)(ℝ^(d−1)), and let π_j delete the j-th coordinate of a point of ℝ^d. Then the integral over ℝ^d of the product of the g_j(π_j(x)) is at most the product of the L^(d−1) norms of the g_j.
nodes.by: Lynn Harold Loomis and Hassler Whitney, 1949
nodes.note: The original 1949 version says that a measurable set E in ℝ^d satisfies |E| ≤ ∏ |π_j(E)|^(1/(d−1)), so its size is bounded by the sizes of its (d−1)-dimensional projections. The functional form is a generalization and a special case of the Brascamp–Lieb inequality.

nodes.name: Lyapunov–Malkin theorem
nodes.statement: Consider the system ẋ = Ax + X(x,y), ẏ = Y(x,y), where x ∈ ℝᵐ, y ∈ ℝⁿ, A is a real m×m matrix and X, Y are higher-order nonlinear terms. If all eigenvalues of A have negative real parts and X(x,y), Y(x,y) vanish when x = 0, then the solution x = 0, y = 0 is stable with respect to (x,y) and asymptotically stable with respect to x, and every solution starting close enough to it has x(t) → 0 and y(t) → c for some constant c as t → ∞.
nodes.by: Named after Aleksandr Lyapunov and Malkin
nodes.note: For example, the system ẋ = −x + x²y, ẏ = xy² satisfies its hypotheses, and its trajectories near (0,0) converge to points of the form (0,c).

nodes.name: Malgrange preparation theorem
nodes.statement: Let f(t,x) be a smooth complex function of t ∈ ℝ and x ∈ ℝⁿ near the origin, and let k be the smallest integer such that f and its t-derivatives of order below k vanish at the origin while the k-th t-derivative does not. Then near the origin f = c(t,x)(tᵏ + a_{k−1}(x)tᵏ⁻¹ + ⋯ + a₀(x)), where c and the a_i are smooth and c is nonzero at the origin.
nodes.by: Conjectured by René Thom and proved by Malgrange
nodes.note: It is an analogue of the Weierstrass preparation theorem for smooth functions. If f is real the functions c and a_i can be taken real, but unlike in the Weierstrass theorem they are not unique.

nodes.name: Malliavin's absolute continuity lemma
nodes.statement: Let μ be a finite Borel measure on ℝⁿ. Suppose that for every x in ℝⁿ there is a constant C(x) such that |∫ Dφ(y)(x) dμ(y)| ≤ C(x)·‖φ‖∞ for every infinitely differentiable function φ: ℝⁿ → ℝ with compact support, where Dφ(y) is the Fréchet derivative of φ at y and ‖φ‖∞ its supremum norm. Then μ is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure on ℝⁿ.
nodes.by: Paul Malliavin
nodes.note: It plays a foundational role in the regularity theorems of the Malliavin calculus.

nodes.name: Marcinkiewicz interpolation theorem
nodes.statement: Let T be a linear operator with ‖Tf‖ in weak L^p at most N_p‖f‖_p and ‖Tf‖ in weak L^q at most N_q‖f‖_q. Then for every r strictly between p and q, T is bounded from L^r to L^r, with ‖Tf‖_r ≤ γ N_p^δ N_q^(1−δ) ‖f‖_r, where δ = p(q−r)/(r(q−p)) and γ = 2(r(q−p)/((r−p)(q−r)))^(1/r).
nodes.by: Marcinkiewicz, 1939; published by Antoni Zygmund in 1956 together with a generalization of his own
nodes.note: It resembles the Riesz–Thorin theorem but also applies to quasilinear operators, at the cost of a norm bound that grows to infinity as r approaches p or q. It shows, for example, that the Hilbert transform is bounded on L^p for 1 < p < 2.

nodes.name: Margulis lemma
nodes.statement: Let X be a simply-connected manifold of non-positive bounded sectional curvature. There are constants C, ε > 0 such that for any discrete subgroup Γ of the isometry group of X and any point x in X, the subgroup generated by the set of g in Γ with d(x, gx) < ε contains a nilpotent subgroup of index less than C.
nodes.by: Named after Grigory Margulis
nodes.note: Within a fixed radius, the Margulis constant, the orbits of such a group cannot be too complicated. It yields the thick-thin decomposition of finite-volume hyperbolic manifolds.

nodes.name: Martingale central limit theorem
nodes.statement: Let X₁, X₂, … be a martingale with E[X_{t+1} − X_t | X₁,…,X_t] = 0, with |X_{t+1} − X_t| ≤ k for a fixed bound k and all t and |X₁| ≤ k, all almost surely; let σ_t² = E[(X_{t+1} − X_t)² | X₁,…,X_t], assume σ₁² + σ₂² + … = ∞ with probability 1, and let τ_ν be the least t with σ₁² + … + σ_t² ≥ ν. Then X_{τ_ν}/√ν converges in distribution to the normal distribution with mean 0 and variance 1 as ν → ∞.
nodes.note: It generalizes the central limit theorem from sums of independent identically distributed random variables to martingales. This is a simple version of the theorem.

nodes.name: Martingale representation theorem
nodes.statement: Let B be a Brownian motion on a standard filtered probability space and let G_t be the augmented filtration it generates. Every square integrable random variable X that is measurable with respect to G_∞ can be written as X = E(X) + ∫₀^∞ C_s dB_s for some predictable process C adapted to G_t, and consequently E(X | G_t) = E(X) + ∫₀^t C_s dB_s.
nodes.note: The theorem only asserts that the representation exists and does not help to find it explicitly. It can be used to establish the existence of a hedging strategy in finance.

nodes.name: Mashreghi–Ransford inequality
nodes.statement: Let (aₙ) be a sequence of complex numbers, and let bₙ = ∑ C(n,k)·aₖ and cₙ = ∑ (−1)ᵏ C(n,k)·aₖ, with sums over k from 0 to n. If for some β > 1 both bₙ = O(βⁿ) and cₙ = O(βⁿ) as n → ∞, then aₙ = O(αⁿ) with α = √(β² − 1), and there is a universal constant κ such that limsup |aₙ|/αⁿ ≤ κ·(limsup |bₙ|/βⁿ)^(1/2)·(limsup |cₙ|/βⁿ)^(1/2).
nodes.by: J. Mashreghi and T. Ransford
nodes.note: The precise value of κ is unknown, but it satisfies 2/√3 ≤ κ ≤ 2.

nodes.name: Massera's lemma
nodes.statement: Let g: [0, ∞) → ℝ be positive, continuous and strictly decreasing with g(t) → 0 as t → ∞, and let h: [0, ∞) → ℝ be positive, continuous and nondecreasing. Then there is a function G: [0, ∞) → [0, ∞) such that G and its derivative G′ are class-K functions defined for all t ≥ 0, and there are positive constants k₁, k₂ such that for every continuous u with 0 ≤ u(t) ≤ g(t) for all t ≥ 0, ∫₀^∞ G(u(t)) dt ≤ k₁ and ∫₀^∞ G′(u(t))h(t) dt ≤ k₂.
nodes.by: José Luis Massera, 1949
nodes.note: It is used to construct a converse Lyapunov function that proves the stability of a dynamical system.

nodes.name: Maximal ergodic theorem
nodes.statement: Let (X, B, μ) be a probability space, T: X → X a (possibly noninvertible) measure-preserving transformation, and f an integrable real function in L¹(μ). Let f* be the supremum over N ≥ 1 of the averages (1/N)·∑_{i=0}^{N−1} f∘Tⁱ; then for any real λ, the integral of f over the set where f* > λ is at least λ times the measure of that set.
nodes.note: It is used to prove the point-wise ergodic theorem.

nodes.name: Maximum theorem
nodes.statement: Let X and Θ be topological spaces, f: X × Θ → ℝ continuous, and C a correspondence giving for each θ a nonempty compact set C(θ) ⊆ X; let f*(θ) = sup{f(x,θ) : x ∈ C(θ)} and let C*(θ) be the set of x in C(θ) with f(x,θ) = f*(θ). If C is continuous (both upper and lower hemicontinuous) at every θ, then f* is continuous and C* is upper hemicontinuous with nonempty compact values, so the supremum is a maximum.
nodes.by: Claude Berge, 1959
nodes.note: It gives conditions for an optimized value and its set of maximizers to depend continuously on parameters. It supplies the continuity and compactness needed to apply the Brouwer or Kakutani fixed-point theorems to consumer demand.

nodes.name: Max–min inequality
nodes.statement: For any function f from Z × W to the real numbers, the supremum over z in Z of the infimum over w in W of f(z, w) is at most the infimum over w in W of the supremum over z in Z of f(z, w).
nodes.note: Equality does not hold for every function, for example f(z, w) = sin(z + w). A theorem giving conditions that guarantee equality is called a minimax theorem.

nodes.name: Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem
nodes.statement: Suppose a function x(t) has a Fourier transform X(f) that is zero for all frequencies f with |f| ≥ B. If x is sampled at equally spaced times at a rate f_s larger than 2B samples per second, the samples determine x completely, so x can be reconstructed exactly from them; equivalently, perfect reconstruction is guaranteed when B < f_s/2.
nodes.by: First proven by Kinnosuke Ogura, 1920, according to a 2011 historical review; named after Harry Nyquist and Claude Shannon
nodes.note: It bridges continuous-time signals and discrete-time signals, and it leads to a formula, the Whittaker–Shannon interpolation formula, for reconstructing the original function from the samples.

nodes.name: McShane's identity
nodes.statement: For a once punctured torus with a complete, finite-volume hyperbolic structure, the sum of 1/(1 + e^ℓ(γ)) over all unoriented simple closed geodesics γ equals 1/2, where ℓ(γ) is the hyperbolic length of γ.
nodes.note: The identity was generalized by Maryam Mirzakhani in her PhD thesis.

nodes.name: Measurable Riemann mapping theorem
nodes.statement: If μ is a bounded measurable function on ℂ with ‖μ‖∞ < 1, then the Beltrami equation ∂f/∂z̄ = μ·∂f/∂z has a unique solution f that is a quasiconformal homeomorphism of ℂ fixing the points 0, 1 and ∞. A similar result holds with ℂ replaced by the unit disk.
nodes.by: Lars Ahlfors and Lipman Bers, 1960
nodes.note: Despite its name, it is not a direct generalization of the Riemann mapping theorem. It concerns quasiconformal mappings and solutions of the Beltrami equation.

nodes.name: Mellin inversion theorem
nodes.statement: Suppose φ(s) is analytic in the strip a < Re(s) < b, tends to zero uniformly as Im(s) → ±∞, and has an absolutely convergent integral along each vertical line Re(s) = c with c between a and b. Then the function f(x) = (1/2πi)∫ x^(−s) φ(s) ds, taken along such a line, has Mellin transform φ(s) = ∫₀^∞ x^(s−1) f(x) dx. Conversely, if f is piecewise continuous on the positive reals, takes the midpoint value at jump discontinuities, and its Mellin transform integral converges absolutely for a < Re(s) < b, then f is recovered from its Mellin transform by the inverse Mellin transform.
nodes.by: Named after Hjalmar Mellin
nodes.note: The results follow by relating the Mellin transform to the Fourier transform by a change of variables and applying a version of the Fourier inversion theorem.

nodes.name: Milman's reverse Brunn–Minkowski inequality
nodes.statement: There is a constant C, independent of n, such that for any two centrally symmetric convex bodies K and L in ℝⁿ there are volume-preserving linear maps φ and ψ from ℝⁿ to itself such that for all real s, t > 0, vol(sφK + tψL)^{1/n} ≤ C·(s·vol(φK)^{1/n} + t·vol(ψL)^{1/n}). One of the maps may be chosen to be the identity.
nodes.by: Vitali Milman
nodes.note: It reverses the Brunn–Minkowski inequality by bounding the volume of the Minkowski sum of two bodies from above in terms of their volumes. Without the linear maps no such bound is possible.

nodes.name: Milman–Pettis theorem
nodes.statement: Every uniformly convex Banach space is reflexive.
nodes.by: Proved independently by D. Milman, 1938, and B. J. Pettis, 1939; a different proof by S. Kakutani, 1939; a shorter proof by John R. Ringrose, 1959
nodes.note: Mahlon M. Day (1941) gave examples of reflexive Banach spaces that are not isomorphic to any uniformly convex space.

nodes.name: Mingarelli identity
nodes.statement: For i = 1, …, n let xᵢ be the solution on [a, b] of (pᵢ(t)xᵢ′)′ + qᵢ(t)xᵢ = 0 with xᵢ(a) = 1 and xᵢ′(a) = Rᵢ, and assume every xᵢ(t) ≠ 0 on (a, b]. With Δ the forward difference in the index i (Δxᵢ = xᵢ₊₁ − xᵢ, and likewise for pᵢ, qᵢ and pᵢrᵢ), rᵢ = xᵢ′/xᵢ, W(xᵢ, xⱼ) = xᵢ′xⱼ − xᵢxⱼ′ and binomial coefficients C(n−1, k), the value of xₙ₋₁²·Δⁿ⁻¹(p₁r₁) at b minus its value at a equals ∫ₐᵇ (xₙ₋₁′)²·Δⁿ⁻¹(p₁) dt − ∫ₐᵇ xₙ₋₁²·Δⁿ⁻¹(q₁) dt − ∑ₖ₌₀ⁿ⁻¹ C(n−1, k)(−1)ⁿ⁻ᵏ⁻¹ ∫ₐᵇ pₖ₊₁·W(xₖ₊₁, xₙ₋₁)²/xₖ₊₁² dt.
nodes.note: It extends the Picone identity, to which it reduces when n = 2, from two to three or more second-order equations. It leads to a comparison theorem for three equations that extends the Sturm–Picone comparison theorem.

nodes.name: Minlos's theorem
nodes.statement: A cylindrical measure on the dual of a nuclear space is a Radon measure if its Fourier transform is continuous.
nodes.by: Named after Robert Adol'fovich Minlos
nodes.note: It can be proved using Sazonov's theorem.

nodes.name: Moise's theorem
nodes.statement: Every topological 3-manifold has an essentially unique piecewise-linear structure and an essentially unique smooth structure.
nodes.by: Edwin E. Moise
nodes.note: The analogue in dimension 4 and above is false. Some topological 4-manifolds, such as the E8 manifold, have no piecewise-linear structure.

nodes.name: Moreau's theorem
nodes.statement: Let H be a Hilbert space and φ: H → ℝ ∪ {+∞} a proper, convex, lower semi-continuous functional, with subderivative A = ∂φ, and for α > 0 let J_α = (id + αA)⁻¹ be the resolvent and A_α = (id − J_α)/α the Yosida approximation. Then φ_α(x) = inf over y in H of (‖y − x‖²/(2α) + φ(y)) equals (α/2)‖A_α x‖² + φ(J_α x), φ_α is convex and Fréchet differentiable with derivative A_α, and for each x in H, φ_α(x) increases to φ(x) as α → 0.
nodes.by: Named after Jean-Jacques Moreau
nodes.note: It shows that sufficiently well-behaved convex functionals on Hilbert spaces are differentiable, with derivative well approximated by the Yosida approximation.

nodes.name: Mostow–Palais theorem
nodes.statement: If a manifold is acted on by a compact Lie group with finitely many orbit types, then it can be embedded, compatibly with the group action (equivariantly), into some finite-dimensional orthogonal representation of the group.
nodes.by: Mostow and Palais, 1957
nodes.note: It is an equivariant version of the Whitney embedding theorem.

nodes.name: Mountain pass theorem
nodes.statement: Let I be a continuously differentiable functional from a Hilbert space H to the reals whose derivative I′ is Lipschitz continuous on bounded subsets of H, which satisfies the Palais–Smale compactness condition, with I[0] = 0, with I[u] ≥ a whenever ‖u‖ = r for some positive constants r and a, and with I[v] ≤ 0 for some v in H with ‖v‖ > r. Then the number c, the infimum over all continuous paths g from [0,1] to H with g(0) = 0 and g(1) = v of the maximum of I[g(t)] for 0 ≤ t ≤ 1, is a critical value of I.
nodes.by: Antonio Ambrosetti and Paul Rabinowitz
nodes.note: It shows the existence of a saddle point. It is unusual because many theorems concern the existence of extrema but few concern saddle points.

nodes.name: Mumford's compactness theorem
nodes.statement: For fixed genus g > 1 and fixed ε > 0, the space of compact Riemann surfaces of genus g with no closed geodesics of length less than ε in the Poincaré metric is compact.
nodes.by: Mumford, 1971
nodes.note: It was proved as a consequence of a theorem on the compactness of sets of discrete subgroups of semisimple Lie groups, which generalizes Mahler's compactness theorem.

nodes.name: Nachbin's theorem
nodes.statement: Let Ψ(t) = Ψ₀ + Ψ₁t + Ψ₂t² + ⋯ with every Ψₙ > 0 and Ψₙ₊₁/Ψₙ → 0 as n → ∞. A function f(z) = f₀ + f₁z + f₂z² + ⋯ is of Ψ-type τ (τ is the infimum of the numbers τ′ for which |f(z)| ≤ M·Ψ(τ′|z|) holds for some constant M as |z| → ∞ in every direction) if and only if the limit superior of |fₙ/Ψₙ|^(1/n) as n → ∞ equals τ.
nodes.by: Named after Leopoldo Nachbin
nodes.note: It gives the domain of convergence of the generalized Borel transform, also called Nachbin summation. It is related to the root test and the Cauchy–Hadamard theorem.

nodes.name: Naimark's dilation theorem
nodes.statement: Let X be a compact Hausdorff space, H a Hilbert space, and E a regular positive operator-valued measure on the Borel sets of X whose values are bounded operators on H. Then there are a Hilbert space K, a bounded operator V: K → H and a self-adjoint spectral (projection-valued) measure F on X with values operators on K, such that E(B) = V F(B) V* for every Borel set B.
nodes.by: Mark Naimark, 1943
nodes.note: It characterizes positive operator valued measures. It can be viewed as a consequence of the Stinespring dilation theorem.

nodes.name: Nielsen–Thurston classification
nodes.statement: Let S be a compact orientable surface of genus at least two and f : S → S a homeomorphism. Then there is a map g isotopic to f such that at least one of the following holds: g is periodic (some power of g is the identity), g is reducible (it preserves some finite union of disjoint simple closed curves on S), or g is pseudo-Anosov.
nodes.by: William Thurston, completing work initiated by Nielsen (1944)
nodes.note: A pseudo-Anosov homeomorphism is never periodic or reducible. A reducible homeomorphism can be analyzed further by cutting the surface along the preserved curves.

nodes.name: Novikov conjecture
nodes.statement: Let G be a discrete group with classifying space BG, let M be a closed oriented n-dimensional manifold, let f: M → BG be any continuous map, and let x be any class in Hⁿ⁻⁴ⁱ(BG; ℚ). Then the higher signature ⟨f*(x) ∪ Lᵢ(M), [M]⟩, where Lᵢ is the i-th Hirzebruch L-polynomial in the Pontryagin classes of M, is an invariant of the oriented homotopy type of M: if h: M′ → M is an orientation preserving homotopy equivalence, the higher signature for f∘h equals that for f.
nodes.by: Sergei Novikov, 1965
nodes.note: The conjecture has been proved for finitely generated abelian groups. It is not known whether it holds for all groups, and no counterexamples are known.

nodes.name: Oka's lemma
nodes.statement: In a domain of holomorphy in ℂⁿ, the function −log d(z) is plurisubharmonic, where d(z) is the distance from z to the boundary.
nodes.by: Kiyoshi Oka
nodes.note: This property shows that the domain is pseudoconvex. The lemma was first shown for the Hartogs domain in two variables.

nodes.name: Ornstein isomorphism theorem
nodes.statement: Two Bernoulli schemes with the same Kolmogorov entropy are isomorphic.
nodes.by: Donald Ornstein, 1970
nodes.note: In 1959 Sinai and Kolmogorov had shown that Bernoulli schemes with different entropy cannot be isomorphic. The theorem shows that many systems thought to be unrelated are isomorphic.

nodes.name: Oseledets theorem
nodes.statement: Let μ be an ergodic invariant measure on the phase space X of a dynamical system, and let C be a cocycle of n×n matrices such that for each time t the maps x ↦ log‖C(x,t)‖ and x ↦ log‖C(x,t)⁻¹‖ are integrable with respect to μ. Then for μ-almost all x and each non-zero vector u in ℝⁿ, the limit λ = lim (1/t) log(‖C(x,t)u‖ / ‖u‖) as t → ∞ exists. It depends on u but not on x, and takes up to n different values, called the Lyapunov exponents. Moreover, if λ₁ > … > λₘ are the different limits, there are subspaces ℝⁿ = R₁ ⊃ … ⊃ Rₘ ⊃ Rₘ₊₁ = {0}, depending on x, such that the limit is λᵢ for u in Rᵢ but not in Rᵢ₊₁.
nodes.by: Valery Oseledets, 1965
nodes.note: It provides the theoretical background for computing Lyapunov exponents of a nonlinear dynamical system. A different proof was found by M. S. Raghunathan.

nodes.name: Osgood's lemma
nodes.statement: A continuous function of several complex variables that is holomorphic in each variable separately is itself holomorphic.
nodes.by: William Fogg Osgood, 1899
nodes.note: The continuity assumption can be dropped, but that stronger form is much harder to prove and is known as Hartogs' theorem. There is no analogue for real variables.

nodes.name: Pasting lemma
nodes.statement: Let X and Y be both closed or both open subsets of a topological space A with A = X ∪ Y, and let B be a topological space. If f: A → B is continuous when restricted to X and when restricted to Y, then f is continuous.
nodes.note: It is used to glue continuous functions together, as in piecewise functions and in concatenating paths to build the fundamental group. The analogue for infinitely many closed sets is false in general.

nodes.name: Peetre theorem
nodes.statement: Let M be a smooth manifold and E, F vector bundles on M. Let D be a linear morphism of sheaves from the smooth sections of E to the smooth sections of F whose support never grows, that is, supp Ds ⊆ supp s for every smooth section s. Then every point p of M has a neighborhood U and an integer k (depending on U) such that D is a differential operator of order k over U.
nodes.by: Jaak Peetre, 1959
nodes.note: It characterises differential operators by their effect on generalized function spaces, without mentioning differentiation explicitly.

nodes.name: Peixoto's theorem
nodes.statement: Among smooth flows on surfaces (compact two-dimensional manifolds), the structurally stable ones are characterized by four properties. The set of non-wandering points consists only of periodic orbits and fixed points. The fixed points are finite in number and all hyperbolic equilibrium points. There are finitely many attracting or repelling periodic orbits. There are no saddle-to-saddle connections. Moreover, the structurally stable flows form an open set in the space of all flows with the C¹ topology.
nodes.by: Maurício Peixoto

nodes.name: Phragmén–Brouwer theorem
nodes.statement: Let X be a normal, connected, locally connected topological space. Then these are equivalent: (1) whenever A and B are disjoint closed subsets whose union separates X, either A or B separates X; (2) X is unicoherent, meaning that whenever X is the union of two closed connected subsets, their intersection is connected or empty.
nodes.by: Introduced by Lars Edvard Phragmén and Luitzen Egbertus Jan Brouwer
nodes.note: The theorem remains true with the weaker condition that A and B be separated.

nodes.name: Pinsker's inequality
nodes.statement: For two probability distributions P and Q on a measurable space, the total variation distance δ(P,Q), the supremum of |P(A) − Q(A)| over measurable events A, is at most the square root of half the Kullback–Leibler divergence D(P‖Q) measured in nats: δ(P,Q) ≤ √(½ D(P‖Q)).
nodes.by: Named after Mark Semenovich Pinsker, who first proved it with a greater constant; proved in the form above independently by Kullback, Csiszár and Kemperman
nodes.note: The inequality is tight up to constant factors. In terms of the total variation norm of P − Q it reads ‖P − Q‖ ≤ √(2 D(P‖Q)).

nodes.name: Preimage theorem
nodes.statement: Let X and Y be smooth manifolds and f : X → Y a smooth map. If y is a regular value of f (the differential of f is surjective at every point of f⁻¹(y)), then f⁻¹(y) is a smoothly and properly embedded submanifold of X whose codimension equals the dimension of Y, and whose tangent space at each point x is the kernel of the differential of f at x.
nodes.note: It is a variation of the implicit function theorem and is also called the regular value theorem. There is also a complex version for holomorphic maps.

nodes.name: Preissmann's theorem
nodes.statement: If a closed manifold has a Riemannian metric of negative sectional curvature, then every non-trivial abelian subgroup of its fundamental group is isomorphic to the additive group of integers ℤ. Moreover, the fundamental group itself is not abelian.
nodes.by: Alexandre Preissmann, 1943
nodes.note: It implies that the n-dimensional torus admits no Riemannian metric of strictly negative sectional curvature. It is a special case of the flat torus theorem.

nodes.name: Projection-slice theorem
nodes.statement: In two dimensions, projecting a function onto a line and then taking the Fourier transform of that projection gives the same result as taking the two-dimensional Fourier transform of the function and slicing it through the origin, parallel to the projection line. In N dimensions, the Fourier transform of the projection onto an m-dimensional linear submanifold equals the m-dimensional slice of the N-dimensional Fourier transform through the origin, parallel to the projection submanifold.
nodes.by: Ronald N. Bracewell first derived the technique in 1956 for a radio-astronomy problem
nodes.note: It is used in the analysis of medical CT scans to recover a three-dimensional density from its x-ray projections.

nodes.name: Prokhorov's theorem
nodes.statement: Let S be a separable metric space and 𝒫(S) the set of probability measures on its Borel sets, with the topology of weak convergence. Then 𝒫(S) is metrizable, and every tight collection K in 𝒫(S) has a sequentially compact closure; if S is also complete (a Polish space), the converse holds, so K is tight if and only if its closure is sequentially compact.
nodes.by: Credited to Yuri Vasilyevich Prokhorov
nodes.note: It relates tightness of measures to relative compactness, and hence weak convergence, in the space of probability measures. Prokhorov considered probability measures on complete separable metric spaces.

nodes.name: Property P conjecture
nodes.statement: A knot in the 3-sphere has Property P if every 3-manifold obtained by non-trivial Dehn surgery on the knot is not simply-connected. Every knot in the 3-sphere except the unknot has Property P.
nodes.by: Research started by R. H. Bing, who popularized the name and the conjecture; a proof was announced in 2004
nodes.note: If a knot has Property P, then one cannot construct a counterexample to the Poincaré conjecture by surgery along that knot.

nodes.name: Pu's inequality
nodes.statement: Every Riemannian surface M homeomorphic to the real projective plane satisfies Area(M) ≥ (2/π) · Systole(M)², where the systole is the length of the shortest loop in M that cannot be contracted to a point. Equality holds exactly when M is obtained from a Euclidean sphere of radius L/π by identifying each point with its antipode, where L is the systole.
nodes.by: Pao Ming Pu, in his 1950 thesis, published 1952
nodes.note: Pu's paper also stated Loewner's inequality for the first time, a similar result for Riemannian metrics on the torus.

nodes.name: Interior extremum theorem
nodes.statement: Let f be a function from an open interval (a, b) to ℝ, and let x₀ in (a, b) be a point where f has a local extremum. If f is differentiable at x₀, then f′(x₀) = 0.
nodes.by: Named after Pierre de Fermat, who proposed a similar method for finding maxima and minima in his treatises Maxima et minima
nodes.note: It gives a necessary but not sufficient condition for a local extremum, since some stationary points are not local extrema.

nodes.name: Quotient of subspace theorem
nodes.statement: Let X be an N-dimensional normed space. Then there are subspaces Z ⊂ Y ⊂ X such that the quotient space E = Y/Z has dimension at least cN, and there is a positive quadratic form Q on E with √Q(e)/K ≤ ‖e‖ ≤ K√Q(e) for all e in E, where ‖e‖ is the induced norm. Here c > 0 and K > 1 are universal constants that do not depend on N.
nodes.by: Discovered by Vitali Milman
nodes.note: The induced norm of a class e is the smallest norm of an element y in e. The constant c can be made arbitrarily close to 1 at the expense of making K large.

nodes.name: Radó–Kneser–Choquet theorem
nodes.statement: Let f be an orientation-preserving homeomorphism of the unit circle |z| = 1 in ℂ. Then the Poisson integral of f is a harmonic function on the open unit disk that extends continuously to f on the circle, and it is an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of the open unit disk.
nodes.by: Posed as a problem by Tibor Radó and solved by Hellmuth Kneser, 1926; rediscovered with a different proof by Gustave Choquet, 1945
nodes.note: Choquet also generalized the result to homeomorphisms from the unit circle onto a simple Jordan curve bounding a convex region.

nodes.name: Hadamard three-circle theorem
nodes.statement: Let f be holomorphic on the annulus r₁ ≤ |z| ≤ r₃, and let M(r) be the maximum of |f(z)| on the circle |z| = r. Then log M(r) is a convex function of log r, and it is strictly convex unless f has the form c·z^λ for constants c and λ; equivalently, for radii r₁ < r₂ < r₃, log(r₃/r₁)·log M(r₂) ≤ log(r₃/r₂)·log M(r₁) + log(r₂/r₁)·log M(r₃).
nodes.by: Attributed by Harald Bohr and Edmund Landau to Jacques Hadamard, 1896, who published no proof; statement and proof given by J. E. Littlewood, 1912
nodes.note: It can be deduced directly from Hadamard's three-line theorem.

nodes.name: Rauch comparison theorem
nodes.statement: Let γ and γ̃ be unit speed geodesic segments on [0, T] in Riemannian manifolds M and M̃, where γ̃(0) has no conjugate points along γ̃, and let J and J̃ be normal Jacobi fields along γ and γ̃ with J(0) = 0, J̃(0) = 0 and |D_t J(0)| = |D̃_t J̃(0)|. If for each t the sectional curvature of every 2-plane at γ(t) containing γ'(t) is at most the sectional curvature of every 2-plane at γ̃(t) containing γ̃'(t), then |J(t)| ≥ |J̃(t)| for all t in [0, T].
nodes.by: Harry Rauch, 1951
nodes.note: It relates the sectional curvature of a manifold to the rate at which geodesics spread apart. Usually one of the two manifolds is a comparison model of constant curvature.

nodes.name: Ham sandwich theorem
nodes.statement: For every positive integer n, given n measurable objects of finite measure (for example bounded measurable sets) in n-dimensional Euclidean space, a single (n − 1)-dimensional affine hyperplane divides each of them into two halves of equal measure, such as equal volume. This holds even if the objects overlap.
nodes.by: Proposed by Hugo Steinhaus and first proved by Stefan Banach in dimension 3 (published in a 1938 note); n-dimensional version proved by Arthur H. Stone and John Tukey, 1942
nodes.note: The standard proof reduces it to the Borsuk–Ulam theorem. In two dimensions it is known as the pancake theorem.

nodes.name: Remez inequality
nodes.statement: Let σ be a positive number, and consider the polynomials p of degree n with |p(x)| ≤ 1 on some set of measure at least 2 inside the interval [−1, 1+σ]. Among these, the largest possible supremum of |p(x)| over [−1, 1+σ] equals that of the Chebyshev polynomial Tₙ over the same interval, which is Tₙ(1+σ).
nodes.by: Evgeny Yakovlevich Remez, 1936
nodes.note: The bound is attained by the Chebyshev polynomials. The Pólya inequality on sub-level sets of polynomials is one of its corollaries.

nodes.name: Remmert–Stein theorem
nodes.statement: Let F be an analytic set of dimension less than k in a complex manifold D, and let M be an analytic subset of D − F all of whose components have dimension at least k. Then the closure of M is either analytic or contains F.
nodes.by: Reinhold Remmert and Karl Stein, 1953
nodes.note: The condition on the dimensions is necessary. Chow's theorem, that every projective complex analytic space is a projective algebraic variety, is a consequence.

nodes.name: Representer theorem
nodes.statement: Let k be a positive-definite real-valued kernel on a non-empty set with reproducing kernel Hilbert space H_k, and take training data (x₁, y₁), …, (xₙ, yₙ) with real yᵢ, a strictly increasing function g: [0, ∞) → ℝ and any error function E with values in ℝ ∪ {∞}. Then every f* in H_k that minimizes E((x₁, y₁, f(x₁)), …, (xₙ, yₙ, f(xₙ))) + g(‖f‖) has the form f*(·) = α₁k(·, x₁) + … + αₙk(·, xₙ) with real numbers α₁, …, αₙ.
nodes.by: Schölkopf, Herbrich and Smola
nodes.note: It generalizes the first representer theorem, due to Kimeldorf and Wahba for squared loss with regularizer λ‖f‖². It reduces an infinite-dimensional minimization to a search for n coefficients.

nodes.name: Hölder's inequality
nodes.statement: Let p and q be numbers between 1 and ∞ with 1/p + 1/q = 1, where 1/∞ counts as 0. Then for all measurable real- or complex-valued functions f and g on a measure space, ∫|fg| dμ ≤ (∫|f|^p dμ)^(1/p) · (∫|g|^q dμ)^(1/q), where for p = ∞ the factor is the essential supremum of |f| and 0 · ∞ counts as 0.
nodes.by: Leonard James Rogers, 1888, in a slightly different form; another proof by Otto Hölder, 1889
nodes.note: The special case p = q = 2 gives a form of the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality. It is used to prove the Minkowski inequality, which is the triangle inequality in L^p spaces.

nodes.name: Riemannian Penrose inequality
nodes.statement: Let (M, g) be an asymptotically flat Riemannian 3-manifold with nonnegative scalar curvature and ADM mass m, and let A be the area of its outermost minimal surface, which may have several connected components. Then m ≥ √(A / 16π).
nodes.by: Conjectured by Roger Penrose; proved by Gerhard Huisken and Tom Ilmanen in 1997 when A is the area of the largest component; first complete proof by Hubert Bray, 1999
nodes.note: It is a special case of the Penrose inequality and a generalization of the positive mass theorem. Equality holds only for a slice of the Schwarzschild spacetime outside its outermost minimal surface.

nodes.name: Rokhlin's theorem
nodes.statement: If a smooth, orientable, closed 4-manifold has a spin structure (equivalently, its second Stiefel–Whitney class vanishes), then the signature of its intersection form on the second cohomology group is divisible by 16.
nodes.by: Vladimir Rokhlin, 1952
nodes.note: The K3 surface, with signature −16, shows that 16 cannot be improved. The theorem fails for merely topological manifolds: Freedman's E8 manifold has signature 8.

nodes.name: Bendixson–Dulac theorem
nodes.statement: Suppose there is a C¹ function φ(x, y) such that ∂(φf)/∂x + ∂(φg)/∂y has the same nonzero sign almost everywhere in a simply connected region of the plane. Then the system dx/dt = f(x, y), dy/dt = g(x, y) has no nonconstant periodic solutions lying entirely within that region.
nodes.by: Ivar Bendixson, 1901; refined by Henri Dulac, 1923
nodes.note: Here "almost everywhere" means everywhere except possibly on a set of measure 0, such as a point or a line.

nodes.name: Russo–Dye theorem
nodes.statement: In a unital C*-algebra, the closure of the convex hull of the unitary elements is the closed unit ball.
nodes.by: B. Russo and H. A. Dye, 1966
nodes.note: In a unital *-Banach algebra, the closed unit ball is contained in the closed convex hull of the unitary elements.

nodes.name: Peano existence theorem
nodes.statement: Let D be an open subset of ℝ×ℝ and f: D → ℝ a continuous function. Then every initial value problem y′(t) = f(t, y(t)), y(t₀) = y₀ with (t₀, y₀) in D has a solution defined on some neighbourhood of t₀. The solution need not be unique.
nodes.by: Giuseppe Peano, first published 1886 with an incorrect proof; correct proof by Peano, 1890. Also named after Augustin-Louis Cauchy
nodes.note: The Picard–Lindelöf theorem assumes Lipschitz continuity and also gives uniqueness. The theorem does not extend straightforwardly to a general Hilbert space.

nodes.name: Gauss–Bonnet theorem
nodes.statement: Let M be a compact two-dimensional Riemannian manifold with boundary ∂M, let K be its Gaussian curvature and k_g the geodesic curvature of ∂M. Then the integral of K over M plus the integral of k_g along ∂M equals 2π times the Euler characteristic χ(M). If the boundary is only piecewise smooth, the boundary integral also includes the angles by which the smooth portions turn at the corners.
nodes.by: Named after Carl Friedrich Gauss, who developed a version but never published it, and Pierre Ossian Bonnet, who published a special case in 1848
nodes.note: It links the curvature of a surface to its underlying topology. Compactness is essential: the formula fails for the open unit disc.

nodes.name: Schröder–Bernstein theorem for measurable spaces
nodes.statement: Let X and Y be measurable spaces. If there are injective bimeasurable maps f from X to Y and g from Y to X (maps that are measurable and send measurable sets to measurable sets), then X and Y are isomorphic, that is, there is a bimeasurable bijection between them.
nodes.note: It is the counterpart for measurable spaces of the Cantor–Bernstein–Schroeder theorem of set theory. It is used to prove that two measurable spaces are isomorphic, for example the real line and the plane, and it is used in the proof of Kuratowski's theorem.

nodes.name: Schur's lemma
nodes.statement: Let (M, g) be a smooth Riemannian manifold of dimension n ≥ 3. If there is a function κ on M such that the Ricci curvature at every point p equals κ(p) times the metric, then κ is constant on each connected component of M.
nodes.note: It follows in one step from the twice-contracted second Bianchi identity, which gives dκ = (n/2) dκ. The dimension restriction matters: every two-dimensional Riemannian manifold without constant curvature is a counterexample.

nodes.name: Scott core theorem
nodes.statement: Every 3-manifold (not necessarily compact) with finitely generated fundamental group contains a compact three-dimensional submanifold, called the compact core or Scott core, whose inclusion map induces an isomorphism on fundamental groups.
nodes.by: G. Peter Scott, 1973
nodes.note: In particular, a finitely generated 3-manifold group is finitely presentable. A simplified proof was given by Rubinstein and Swarup (1990), and a stronger uniqueness statement by Harris and Scott (1996).

nodes.name: Segal's Burnside ring conjecture
nodes.statement: In its weak form: for every finite group G, there is an isomorphism from the inverse limit over k of the stable cohomotopy groups π_S⁰ of the k-skeleton of the classifying space BG (with a disjoint basepoint added) to the completion of the Burnside ring of G with respect to its augmentation ideal.
nodes.by: Conjectured by Graeme Segal in the mid 1970s; proved by Gunnar Carlsson, 1984
nodes.note: It is still commonly called the Segal conjecture, although it now has the status of a theorem. It has several formulations, not all of which are equivalent, and this is a weak form.

nodes.name: Serre–Swan theorem
nodes.statement: Let M be a smooth manifold (not necessarily compact) and E a smooth vector bundle of finite rank over M. Then the space Γ(E) of smooth sections of E is a finitely generated projective module over the algebra C^∞(M) of smooth real-valued functions on M. When M is connected, the converse also holds: every finitely generated projective module over C^∞(M) arises in this way from some smooth vector bundle on M.
nodes.by: Richard Swan, 1962 (smooth version); the original algebraic version was proved by Jean-Pierre Serre, 1955
nodes.note: It relates vector bundles to projective modules, which gives the intuition that projective modules are like vector bundles. Serre's original version concerns vector bundles on algebraic varieties, and Swan also proved a version for continuous vector bundles on compact Hausdorff spaces.

nodes.name: Shadowing lemma
nodes.statement: Let Λ be a hyperbolic invariant set of a diffeomorphism f. There is a neighborhood U of Λ such that for every δ > 0 there is an ε > 0 with this property: for every finite or infinite sequence x₁, x₂, … of points in U in which each point lies within ε of the image under f of the previous one, there is a true orbit y₁, y₂, … with yₙ₊₁ = f(yₙ) such that each xₙ lies within δ of yₙ.
nodes.note: Informally, a numerically computed trajectory with rounding errors on every step is shadowed by a true trajectory with a slightly altered initial position.

nodes.name: Sherman–Takeda theorem
nodes.statement: If A is a C*-algebra, then its double dual is a W*-algebra, and is isomorphic to the weak closure of A in the universal representation of A.
nodes.by: Announced by Sherman, 1950; proved by Takeda, 1954
nodes.note: The double dual of A is called the universal enveloping W*-algebra of A.

nodes.name: Exponential shift theorem
nodes.statement: Let a be a constant and P(D) a polynomial in the differentiation operator D = d/dx. Then for every sufficiently differentiable function y, P(D)(e^(ax) y) = e^(ax) P(D + a) y.
nodes.note: It allows one to remove the exponential from under the D-operators, and the same rule is applied to inverse operators 1/P(D). It speeds up computing higher derivatives of a product with an exponential and helps solve linear differential equations whose characteristic polynomial has repeated roots.

nodes.name: Hirzebruch signature theorem
nodes.statement: For every smooth closed oriented manifold M of dimension 4n, the signature of M (the signature of the intersection form on its 2n-th cohomology group) equals the n-th L-polynomial in the Pontryagin classes p₁(M), …, pₙ(M), evaluated on the fundamental class of M. This number, the L-genus, is a linear combination of Pontryagin numbers; for n = 1 it is p₁/3.
nodes.by: Friedrich Hirzebruch, 1954
nodes.note: René Thom had earlier proved that the signature is some linear combination of Pontryagin numbers; Hirzebruch found the exact formula. It was used in the proof of the Hirzebruch–Riemann–Roch theorem.

nodes.name: Silverman–Toeplitz theorem
nodes.statement: An infinite matrix (a_ij) with complex entries defines a regular matrix summability method, that is, a linear sequence transformation preserving limits of convergent sequences, if and only if three conditions hold: every column sequence converges to 0, the row sums converge to 1, and the absolute row sums are bounded.
nodes.by: First proved by Otto Toeplitz
nodes.note: Cesàro summation is an example of a regular matrix summability method.

nodes.name: Extreme value theorem
nodes.statement: If a real-valued function f is continuous on the closed and bounded interval [a,b], then f attains a maximum and a minimum, each at least once. That is, there are numbers c and d in [a,b] with f(d) ≤ f(x) ≤ f(c) for all x in [a,b].
nodes.by: Originally proven by Bernard Bolzano in the 1830s, unpublished until 1930; a formulation due to Karl Weierstrass covers continuous functions on non-empty compact spaces
nodes.note: It is more specific than the boundedness theorem and is used to prove Rolle's theorem.

nodes.name: Siu's semicontinuity theorem
nodes.statement: For a closed positive current on a complex manifold and any constant c, the points where its Lelong number is at least c form a complex subvariety. In particular the Lelong number is semicontinuous.
nodes.by: Conjectured by Harvey and King, 1972; proved by Siu, 1973
nodes.note: Demailly generalized the theorem in 1987 to more general versions of the Lelong number.

nodes.name: Skoda–El Mir theorem
nodes.statement: Let X be a complex manifold and E a closed complete pluripolar set in X. If Θ is a closed positive current on X ∖ E that is locally integrable around E, then the trivial extension of Θ to X is closed on X.
nodes.by: Skoda, El Mir and Sibony

nodes.name: Skorokhod's first embedding theorem
nodes.statement: Let X be a real-valued random variable with expected value 0 and finite variance, and let W be a canonical real-valued Wiener process. Then there is a stopping time τ with respect to the natural filtration of W such that W_τ has the same distribution as X, E[τ] = E[X²] and E[τ²] ≤ 4 E[X⁴].
nodes.by: Named after A. V. Skorokhod
nodes.note: It lets one regard a random variable as a Wiener process (Brownian motion) evaluated at a stopping time. A second embedding theorem does the same for the partial sums of a sequence of independent, identically distributed random variables.

nodes.name: Slepian's lemma
nodes.statement: Let X = (X₁,…,Xₙ) and Y = (Y₁,…,Yₙ) be Gaussian random vectors in ℝⁿ with mean zero, with E[Xᵢ²] = E[Yᵢ²] for every i, and with E[XᵢXⱼ] ≤ E[YᵢYⱼ] for i ≠ j. Then for all real numbers u₁,…,uₙ, the probability that Xᵢ ≤ uᵢ for all i is at most the probability that Yᵢ ≤ uᵢ for all i.
nodes.by: David Slepian, 1962
nodes.note: The result is a Gaussian comparison inequality. It is not true in general for other random variables, even those with expectation 0.

nodes.name: Smith conjecture
nodes.statement: If f is a diffeomorphism of the 3-sphere of finite order, then the fixed point set of f cannot be a nontrivial knot.
nodes.by: Smith showed related results (1939) and asked the question in Eilenberg (1949); the order 2 case was proved by Waldhausen, 1969; the general case was described by Bass and Morgan, 1984
nodes.note: The statement is false for continuous involutions of the 3-sphere, where the fixed circle can be wildly embedded. In dimensions 4 and above the analogue is false.

nodes.name: Minkowski inequality
nodes.statement: Let S be a measure space and let 1 ≤ p ≤ ∞. If f and g are in Lᵖ(S), then f + g is in Lᵖ(S) and ‖f + g‖ₚ ≤ ‖f‖ₚ + ‖g‖ₚ. For 1 < p < ∞, equality holds if and only if f = λg for some λ ≥ 0 or g = 0.
nodes.by: Named after Hermann Minkowski
nodes.note: It is the triangle inequality for the Lᵖ norm, which makes Lᵖ spaces normed vector spaces.

nodes.name: Atiyah–Bott fixed-point theorem
nodes.statement: Let f be a smooth map of a closed manifold M to itself whose graph meets the diagonal transversally, and let T be an endomorphism of an elliptic complex on M built from bundle maps φ_j : f⁻¹(E_j) → E_j. Then the Lefschetz number L(T), the alternating sum of the traces of T on the homology of the complex, equals the sum over the fixed points x of f of (∑_j (−1)^j trace φ_{j,x}) / δ(x), where δ(x) is the determinant of I − Df at x.
nodes.by: Michael Atiyah and Raoul Bott, 1960s
nodes.note: Specializing to the de Rham complex gives the original Lefschetz fixed-point formula. A well-known application is a simple proof of the Weyl character formula.

nodes.name: Sphere theorem (3-manifolds)
nodes.statement: Let M be an orientable 3-manifold whose second homotopy group π₂(M) is not the trivial group. Then some non-zero element of π₂(M) is represented by an embedding of the 2-sphere S² into M.
nodes.by: Papakyriakopoulos, 1957
nodes.note: The embedding can be chosen piecewise linear. A more general version, the projective plane theorem, is due to David B. A. Epstein.

nodes.name: Spijker's lemma
nodes.statement: The image of a circle under a complex rational map whose numerator and denominator both have degree at most n has length at most 2nπ.
nodes.note: It can be used to derive a sharp bound version of the Kreiss matrix theorem.

nodes.name: Splitting lemma (functions)
nodes.statement: Let f be a smooth function germ from (ℝⁿ, 0) to (ℝ, 0) with a critical point at 0. Let V be a subspace of ℝⁿ such that the restriction of f to V is non-degenerate, let B be the Hessian matrix of this restriction, and let W be any complementary subspace to V; then near 0 there is a change of coordinates Φ(x, y) = (φ(x, y), y), with x in V and y in W, and a smooth function h on W such that f∘Φ(x, y) = ½ xᵀBx + h(y).
nodes.by: René Thom
nodes.note: It is often called the parametrized Morse lemma and is the gradient version of the implicit function theorem.

nodes.name: Stallings–Zeeman theorem
nodes.statement: Let M be a finite simplicial complex of dimension m ≥ 5 that has the homotopy type of the m-dimensional sphere and is locally piecewise linearly homeomorphic to m-dimensional Euclidean space. Then M is homeomorphic to the m-sphere by a map that is piecewise linear except possibly at a single point x, so that M minus x is piecewise linearly homeomorphic to ℝᵐ.
nodes.by: Named after John R. Stallings and Christopher Zeeman
nodes.note: It is used in the proof of the Poincaré conjecture for dimension greater than or equal to five.

nodes.name: Stein–Strömberg theorem
nodes.statement: Let M be the Hardy–Littlewood maximal operator on ℝⁿ, which sends a real-valued function f to the function whose value at x is the supremum over r > 0 of the average of |f| over the open ball of radius r centred at x. Then for each p > 1 there is a constant C_p > 0, not depending on n, such that ‖Mf‖ ≤ C_p‖f‖ in the L^p norm for all natural numbers n and all f in L^p(ℝⁿ).
nodes.by: Named after Elias M. Stein and Jan-Olov Strömberg
nodes.note: The result is foundational in the study of the problem of differentiation of integrals.

nodes.name: Popoviciu's inequality
nodes.statement: If f is a convex function from an interval I of real numbers to the real numbers, then for any three points x, y, z in I, (f(x) + f(y) + f(z))/3 + f((x + y + z)/3) ≥ (2/3)·[f((x + y)/2) + f((y + z)/2) + f((z + x)/2)]. For continuous f, this inequality holds for all x, y, z in I exactly when f is convex.
nodes.by: Tiberiu Popoviciu, 1965
nodes.note: It is similar to Jensen's inequality. When f is strictly convex, the inequality is strict except for x = y = z.

nodes.name: Stinespring dilation theorem
nodes.statement: Let A be a unital C*-algebra, H a Hilbert space and Φ: A → B(H) a completely positive map into the bounded operators on H. Then there are a Hilbert space K, a unital *-homomorphism π: A → B(K) and a bounded operator V: H → K such that Φ(a) = V*π(a)V for all a in A, and ‖Φ(1)‖ = ‖V‖².
nodes.by: Named after W. Forrest Stinespring
nodes.note: It shows that every completely positive map is a *-representation followed by a map of the form T ↦ V*TV. The converse holds trivially, so the theorem classifies completely positive maps.

nodes.name: Stone–von Neumann theorem
nodes.statement: Let U(t) and V(s) be strongly continuous one-parameter groups of unitary operators on a separable Hilbert space H that act jointly irreducibly and satisfy the Weyl relation U(t)V(s) = e^(−ist)V(s)U(t) for all real s and t. Then there is a unitary operator W: L²(ℝ) → H such that W*U(t)W is multiplication by e^(itx) and W*V(s)W is translation by s, so the pair is unitarily equivalent to the standard position and momentum representation.
nodes.by: Named after Marshall Stone and John von Neumann
nodes.note: It was a key step in proving that Heisenberg's matrix mechanics is unitarily equivalent to Schrödinger's wave mechanics. It extends directly to n degrees of freedom.

nodes.name: Structure theorem for Gaussian measures
nodes.statement: Every strictly positive Gaussian measure γ on a separable Banach space E comes from an abstract Wiener space: there are a separable Hilbert space H and a map i from H to E that is an abstract Wiener space, with γ equal to the pushforward by i of the canonical Gaussian cylinder set measure on H.
nodes.by: Kallianpur–Satô–Stefan and Dudley–Feldman–le Cam, 1970s
nodes.note: An earlier result of Hiroshi Satô shows that any Gaussian measure on a separable Banach space is an abstract Wiener measure in the sense of L. Gross.

nodes.name: Sturm separation theorem
nodes.statement: Let u and v be two non-trivial, continuous, linearly independent solutions of a homogeneous second order linear differential equation in real variables. If x₀ and x₁ are successive roots of u, then v has exactly one root in the open interval (x₀, x₁).
nodes.by: Named after Jacques Charles François Sturm
nodes.note: The zeros of two linearly independent solutions alternate. It is a special case of the Sturm-Picone comparison theorem.

nodes.name: Surface subgroup conjecture
nodes.statement: The fundamental group of every closed, irreducible 3-manifold with infinite fundamental group has a surface subgroup, that is, a subgroup that is the fundamental group of a closed surface other than the 2-sphere.
nodes.by: Stated by Friedhelm Waldhausen; the remaining case of closed hyperbolic 3-manifolds was proved by Jeremy Kahn and Vladimir Markovic, announced 2009, published 2012
nodes.note: Assuming the geometrization conjecture, the only open case was that of closed hyperbolic 3-manifolds. It is Problem 3.75 in Robion Kirby's problem list.

nodes.name: Heine–Cantor theorem
nodes.statement: A continuous function between two metric spaces is uniformly continuous if its domain is compact. In particular, every continuous function from a closed bounded interval to the real numbers is uniformly continuous.
nodes.by: Named after Eduard Heine and Georg Cantor

nodes.name: Sz.-Nagy dilation theorem
nodes.statement: Every contraction T on a Hilbert space H has a unitary dilation U to a Hilbert space K containing H, meaning that Tⁿ = P_H Uⁿ restricted to H for all n ≥ 0, where P_H is the projection from K onto H. If K is minimal, meaning the linear span of the sets UⁿH is dense in K, the dilation is unique up to unitary equivalence.
nodes.by: Béla Szőkefalvi-Nagy

nodes.name: Liouville's theorem (Hamiltonian mechanics)
nodes.statement: In a Hamiltonian system, where positions qᵢ and momenta pᵢ change in time according to Hamilton's equations, the phase-space distribution function ρ is constant along the trajectories of the system (dρ/dt = 0). Equivalently, the flow of the system preserves volume in phase space.
nodes.by: Named after Joseph Liouville
nodes.note: It applies to conservative systems, where friction is absent or can be ignored, and fails for a damped harmonic oscillator. In symplectic geometry it says the Hamiltonian flow preserves the volume form, and in fact the symplectic form itself.

nodes.name: T(1) theorem
nodes.statement: Let T be a continuous operator from Schwartz functions on ℝⁿ to tempered distributions, given by a standard kernel. Then T extends to a bounded operator on the Hilbert space L²(ℝⁿ) if and only if T(1) and T*(1) are of bounded mean oscillation and T is weakly bounded.
nodes.by: David and Journé, 1984
nodes.note: The name refers to a condition on the distribution T(1), which is T applied to the function 1.

nodes.name: Talagrand's concentration inequality
nodes.statement: Let Ω = Ω₁ × Ω₂ × ⋯ × Ωₙ be a product space with a product probability measure, and let A be a subset of Ω. Then for any t ≥ 0, Pr[A] · Pr[Aᶜₜ] ≤ e^(−t²/4), where Aₜ is the set of points x with ρ(A,x) ≤ t, Aᶜₜ is its complement, and ρ(A,x) is Talagrand's convex distance: the largest, over weight vectors α with α₁² + ⋯ + αₙ² ≤ 1, of the smallest total weight of the coordinates in which x differs from a point y of A.
nodes.by: Michel Talagrand
nodes.note: It is an isoperimetric-type inequality for product probability spaces and one of the manifestations of the concentration of measure phenomenon.

nodes.name: Tonelli's theorem in functional analysis
nodes.statement: Let Ω be a bounded domain in ℝⁿ and let f: ℝᵐ → ℝ ∪ {±∞} be continuous. For functions u: Ω → ℝᵐ define F[u] = ∫_Ω f(u(x)) dx. Then F is sequentially weakly lower semicontinuous on L^p(Ω) for 1 < p < ∞, and weakly-* lower semicontinuous on L^∞(Ω), if and only if f is convex.
nodes.by: Attributed to Leonida Tonelli
nodes.note: Roughly, weak lower semicontinuity of an integral functional is equivalent to convexity of the integral kernel.

nodes.name: Tonelli–Hobson test
nodes.statement: Let f be a real-valued measurable function on ℝ². If either iterated integral of |f(x,y)| (integrating over x first, or over y first) is finite, then f is Lebesgue-integrable on ℝ².
nodes.by: Named after Leonida Tonelli and E. W. Hobson
nodes.note: It is often used to establish that Fubini's theorem may be applied to f.

nodes.name: Trigonometric moment problem
nodes.statement: Let c₀, …, cₙ be complex numbers, and set c₋ₖ = conj(cₖ) for k ≥ 1. There is a distribution function σ on [0, 2π] with cₖ = (1/2π) ∫ e^(−ikθ) dσ(θ) for k = 0, …, n if and only if the (n+1) × (n+1) Hermitian Toeplitz matrix whose entry in row i and column j is c_(j−i) is positive semi-definite.
nodes.note: This is the solvability criterion for the truncated problem, where only finitely many coefficients are given. When the Toeplitz matrix is invertible, the truncated problem has infinitely many solutions.

nodes.name: Trudinger's theorem
nodes.statement: Let Ω be a bounded domain in ℝⁿ satisfying the cone condition, let mp = n and p > 1, and set A(t) = exp(t^(n/(n−m))) − 1. Then the Sobolev space W^(m,p)(Ω) embeds in the Orlicz space L_A(Ω).
nodes.by: Named after Neil Trudinger (and Jürgen Moser)
nodes.note: It gives an inequality between a Sobolev space norm and an Orlicz space norm, and is a limiting case of Sobolev embedding.

nodes.name: Twisted Poincaré duality
nodes.statement: For a compact connected manifold M of dimension d, the trace map from the top-degree de Rham cohomology with values in the orientation bundle, H^d(M; o(M)), to ℝ is an isomorphism. The cup product pairing of H^k(M; ℝ) with H^(d−k)(M; o(M)) into H^d(M; o(M)) ≅ ℝ is non-degenerate.
nodes.note: It removes the restriction of Poincaré duality to oriented manifolds. When M is oriented the orientation bundle is trivial and the usual Poincaré duality results.

nodes.name: Uniform limit theorem
nodes.statement: Let X be a topological space and Y a metric space. If a sequence of continuous functions fₙ : X → Y converges uniformly to f : X → Y, then f is continuous.
nodes.note: The theorem fails for pointwise convergence: the functions xⁿ on [0, 1] are continuous but converge pointwise to a discontinuous function.

nodes.name: Varadhan's lemma
nodes.statement: Let X be a regular topological space and (Z_ε) a family of random variables in X whose laws satisfy the large deviation principle with a good rate function I: X → [0, +∞]. Let φ: X → ℝ be continuous and satisfy either the tail condition (the limit as M → ∞ of the limsup as ε → 0 of ε log E[exp(φ(Z_ε)/ε) 1(φ(Z_ε) ≥ M)] equals −∞) or, for some γ > 1, the moment condition (the limsup as ε → 0 of ε log E[exp(γφ(Z_ε)/ε)] is finite); then the limit as ε → 0 of ε log E[exp(φ(Z_ε)/ε)] equals the supremum over x in X of φ(x) − I(x).
nodes.by: Named after S. R. Srinivasa Varadhan
nodes.note: It describes the asymptotic behaviour of φ(Z_ε) as ε becomes small in terms of the rate function.

nodes.name: Vietoris–Begle mapping theorem
nodes.statement: Let X and Y be compact metric spaces and let f: X → Y be surjective and continuous. If every fiber f⁻¹(y) has vanishing reduced Vietoris homology in degrees 0 to n−1, then the induced map f_* on reduced Vietoris homology is an isomorphism in degrees r ≤ n−1 and a surjection for r = n.
nodes.by: Named after Leopold Vietoris and Edward G. Begle; the statement is as formulated by Stephen Smale
nodes.note: As stated, the theorem does not hold for singular homology. The closed topologist's sine curve and a segment have isomorphic Vietoris homology but different singular homology.

nodes.name: Virtually Haken conjecture
nodes.statement: Every compact, orientable, irreducible three-dimensional manifold with infinite fundamental group has a finite cover that is a Haken manifold.
nodes.by: Usually attributed to Friedhelm Waldhausen, 1968, although he did not formally state it; proved by Ian Agol, announced 2012
nodes.note: After Perelman's proof of the geometrization conjecture, the conjecture remained open only for hyperbolic 3-manifolds. Agol's proof built on work of Daniel Wise and collaborators and on the solution of the surface subgroup conjecture by Kahn and Markovic.

nodes.name: Vitale's random Brunn–Minkowski inequality
nodes.statement: Let X be a random non-empty compact set in ℝⁿ with E[‖X‖] < ∞, where ‖K‖ is the largest length of a vector in K, and let E[X] be the set of expectations E[V] of all random vectors V that lie in X with probability 1 and have E‖V‖ < ∞. Then vol(E[X])^(1/n) ≥ E[vol(X)^(1/n)], where vol is n-dimensional Lebesgue measure.
nodes.by: Richard Vitale
nodes.note: It generalizes the classical Brunn–Minkowski inequality for compact subsets of ℝⁿ to random compact sets. When X takes only two values K and L, it reduces to the original Brunn–Minkowski inequality.

nodes.name: Vitali–Hahn–Saks theorem
nodes.statement: Let (λₙ) be a sequence of finite complex measures on a measurable space such that λₙ(B) has a limit λ(B) for every measurable set B. Then λ is a finite complex measure. If a finite measure m satisfies λₙ ≪ m for all n, then λ ≪ m, and for every ε > 0 there is a δ > 0 such that m(B) < δ implies |λₙ(B)| < ε for all n.
nodes.by: Introduced by Vitali (1907), Hahn (1922), and Saks (1933)
nodes.note: It also holds for finite signed measures. The densities dλₙ/dm are uniformly integrable and converge weakly in L¹.

nodes.name: Bessel's inequality
nodes.statement: Let H be a Hilbert space and e₁, e₂, … an orthonormal sequence in H. Then for every vector x in H, the sum over k of |⟨x, eₖ⟩|² is less than or equal to ‖x‖².
nodes.by: Named after F. W. Bessel, who derived a special case of it in 1828
nodes.note: It generalizes the Pythagorean theorem to infinite-dimensional spaces. When the orthonormal sequence is a complete orthonormal basis, it becomes an equality known as Parseval's identity.

nodes.name: Von Neumann's theorem
nodes.statement: Let G and H be Hilbert spaces and T an unbounded operator from G into H that is closed and densely defined. Then T*T, where T* is the adjoint of T, is also densely defined and self-adjoint.

nodes.name: Von Neumann's inequality
nodes.statement: For a contraction T acting on a Hilbert space and a polynomial p, the norm of p(T) is at most the supremum of |p(z)| over z in the unit disk.
nodes.by: John von Neumann
nodes.note: Equivalently, the polynomial functional calculus map of a fixed contraction is itself a contraction.

nodes.name: Watson's lemma
nodes.statement: Let 0 < T ≤ ∞ and φ(t) = t^λ g(t), where λ > −1, g(0) ≠ 0 and g has derivatives of every order near t = 0. Suppose either that |φ(t)| < K·e^(bt) for all t > 0 with constants K and b, or that ∫₀ᵀ |φ(t)| dt < ∞. Then ∫₀ᵀ e^(−xt) φ(t) dt is finite for all sufficiently large x, and as x → ∞ it has the asymptotic expansion ∑ g⁽ⁿ⁾(0) Γ(λ+n+1) / (n! x^(λ+n+1)), summed over n ≥ 0.
nodes.by: G. N. Watson, 1918
nodes.note: It gives, for example, the behaviour of the confluent hypergeometric function ₁F₁(a, b, x) for large x when 0 < a < b.

nodes.name: Weyl's lemma
nodes.statement: Let Ω be an open subset of ℝⁿ. If a locally integrable function u on Ω satisfies ∫ u Δφ dx = 0 for every smooth function φ with compact support in Ω, then, after redefinition on a set of measure zero, u is smooth and satisfies Δu = 0 at every point of Ω.
nodes.by: Named after Hermann Weyl
nodes.note: It shows that harmonic functions are smooth in the interior, and says nothing about the boundary. It is a special case of elliptic or hypoelliptic regularity.

nodes.name: Weyl–Schouten theorem
nodes.statement: Let M be a pseudo-Riemannian manifold of dimension n. If n ≥ 4, M is conformally flat, meaning that around every point it has isothermal coordinates, if and only if its Weyl tensor is zero; if n = 3, M is conformally flat in this sense if and only if its Schouten tensor is a Codazzi tensor.
nodes.by: Named after Hermann Weyl and Jan Arnoldus Schouten
nodes.note: For n = 2 every manifold is conformally flat, which was known before the work of Weyl and Schouten. The theorem and its proof are entirely local, so the topology of the manifold plays no role.

nodes.name: Whitney extension theorem
nodes.statement: Let A be a closed subset of ℝⁿ and let f_α be functions on A, one for each multi-index α with |α| ≤ m, such that for every point a of A each f_α(x) differs from the Taylor polynomial of order m − |α| built at y from the functions f_(α+β) by an amount that is o(|x − y|^(m−|α|)), uniformly as x and y in A tend to a. Then there is a function F of class C^m on ℝⁿ with D^αF = f_α on A for every such α (so F = f₀ on A), and F is real-analytic at every point of ℝⁿ outside A.
nodes.by: Hassler Whitney, 1934
nodes.note: It is a partial converse to Taylor's theorem. Whitney used the Whitney covering lemma to prove it.

nodes.name: Whitney immersion theorem
nodes.statement: For m > 1, every smooth m-dimensional manifold that is Hausdorff and second-countable has a one-to-one immersion in Euclidean 2m-space, and an immersion, not necessarily one-to-one, in Euclidean (2m−1)-space. Every smooth m-dimensional manifold, also for m = 1, can be immersed in the (2m−1)-dimensional sphere.
nodes.by: Named after Hassler Whitney

nodes.name: Wiener–Ikehara theorem
nodes.statement: Let A(x) be a non-negative, nondecreasing function defined for 0 ≤ x < ∞. Suppose that f(s) = ∫₀^∞ A(x) e^(−xs) dx converges for Re(s) > 1, and that for some non-negative number c the function f(s) − c/(s−1) extends to a continuous function on Re(s) ≥ 1. Then e^(−x) A(x) tends to c as x goes to infinity.
nodes.by: Shikao Ikehara, 1931
nodes.note: It is a special case of Wiener's Tauberian theorems. It can be used to prove the prime number theorem from the fact that the Riemann zeta function has no zeros on the line of real part one.

nodes.name: Wirtinger's representation and projection theorem
nodes.statement: Let F be square-integrable over the unit disc |z| < 1, meaning the integral of |F(z)|² over the disc is finite. Then among the holomorphic functions f in the subspace H₂ of L², the unique one that minimizes the integral of |F(z) − f(z)|² over the disc is f(z) = (1/π) ∬ F(ζ) dS / (1 − ζ̄z)², for |z| < 1, with the integral taken over |ζ| < 1.
nodes.by: Wilhelm Wirtinger, 1932
nodes.note: The formula gives the orthogonal projection from L² onto H₂ and is an analog of the Cauchy integral formula with the square of the Cauchy kernel. Mkhitar Djrbashian extended it to weighted spaces in 1948.

nodes.name: Zahorski's theorem
nodes.statement: A subset of the real line is the set of points where some continuous real-valued function fails to be differentiable if and only if it is the union of a G_δ set and a G_δσ set of measure zero.
nodes.by: Named after Zahorski; proved in 1939 and first published in 1941

nodes.name: Zeeman conjecture
nodes.statement: For every finite contractible 2-dimensional CW complex K, the space K × [0,1] is collapsible.
nodes.by: Christopher Zeeman
nodes.note: The conjecture implies the Poincaré conjecture and the Andrews–Curtis conjecture. It can be restated as the claim that for every 2-complex homotopy equivalent to a point, some barycentric subdivision of its product with [0,1] is collapsible.

nodes.name: Zig-zag lemma
nodes.statement: In an abelian category, every short exact sequence 0 → A → B → C → 0 of chain complexes gives boundary maps δₙ: Hₙ(C) → Hₙ₋₁(A) that, together with the maps induced on homology, form a long exact sequence of homology groups.
nodes.note: It can be regarded as a generalization of the Mayer–Vietoris sequence. A variant is commonly known as the snake lemma.

nodes.name: Śleszyński–Pringsheim theorem
nodes.statement: If (aₙ) and (bₙ) are sequences of real numbers with |bₙ| ≥ |aₙ| + 1 for all n, then the continued fraction a₁/(b₁ + a₂/(b₂ + a₃/(b₃ + …))) converges absolutely to a number x with |x| ≤ 1.
nodes.by: Ivan Śleszyński and Alfred Pringsheim, late 19th century
nodes.note: Absolute convergence here means that the series of differences between consecutive convergents converges absolutely.

nodes.name: Basel problem
nodes.statement: The sum of the reciprocals of the squares of the natural numbers is exactly π²/6, that is, 1/1² + 1/2² + 1/3² + ⋯ = π²/6, which is approximately 1.644934.
nodes.by: First posed by Pietro Mengoli, 1650; solved by Leonhard Euler, 1734; Euler produced an accepted proof in 1741
nodes.note: Euler's first arguments used manipulations that were not justified at the time. Two random integers from 1 to n are coprime with a probability that approaches 6/π², the reciprocal of this sum, as n grows.

nodes.name: Girsanov theorem
nodes.statement: Let (Ω, F, P) be a probability space with a complete, right-continuous filtration, and let X be a continuous local martingale adapted to it, with stochastic exponential Z = exp(X − ½[X]), where [X] is the quadratic variation of X. If Z is a martingale, then for any T > 0 the formula Q(A) = ∫_A Z_T dP defines a probability measure on F_T, and for every continuous local martingale M under P, the process M − [M, X] is a continuous local martingale under Q on [0, T].
nodes.by: Results of this type first proved by Robert Horton Cameron and W. T. Martin in the 1940s and by Igor Girsanov in 1960; extended to the general form by Érik Lenglart, 1977
nodes.note: It gives the key result that if Q is absolutely continuous with respect to P, then every P-semimartingale is also a Q-semimartingale. In financial mathematics it is used to convert from the physical measure to the risk-neutral measure.

nodes.name: Cauchy's residue theorem
nodes.statement: Let U be a simply connected open subset of the complex plane containing finitely many points a₁, …, aₙ, and let f be holomorphic on U with those points removed. For every closed rectifiable curve γ in U that avoids the points, the integral of f around γ equals 2πi times the sum over k of the winding number of γ around aₖ times the residue of f at aₖ.
nodes.note: It generalizes the Cauchy integral theorem and Cauchy's integral formula, and is often used to compute real integrals and infinite series.

nodes.name: Frobenius theorem
nodes.statement: A smooth subbundle E of the tangent bundle of a manifold M is integrable if and only if it arises from a regular foliation of M, that is, M splits into submanifolds (leaves) whose tangent spaces are exactly the spaces given by E. Here E is called integrable (involutive) if, for any two vector fields X and Y taking values in E, their Lie bracket [X,Y] also takes values in E.
nodes.by: First proven by Alfred Clebsch and Feodor Deahna, Deahna giving the sufficient conditions and Clebsch the necessary ones; named after Ferdinand Georg Frobenius, who applied it to Pfaffian systems
nodes.note: It generalizes the existence theorem for ordinary differential equations, which gives integral curves of a single vector field. One-dimensional subbundles coming from a nowhere zero vector field are always integrable.

nodes.name: Markov's inequality
nodes.statement: If X is a nonnegative random variable and a > 0, then the probability that X is at least a is at most the expectation of X divided by a: P(X ≥ a) ≤ E(X)/a.
nodes.by: Named after Andrey Markov, although it appeared earlier in the work of his teacher Pafnuty Chebyshev
nodes.note: The bound cannot be improved in general: for each positive constant some random variable gives equality. Chebyshev's inequality follows from it.

nodes.name: Lebesgue's density theorem
nodes.statement: Let A ⊆ ℝⁿ be a Lebesgue measurable set. For almost every point x of ℝⁿ, the share of the ball of radius ε around x that lies in A (the measure of A ∩ B_ε(x) divided by the measure of B_ε(x)) tends to 0 or to 1 as ε → 0, and for almost every point x of A it tends to 1.
nodes.note: It is a particular case of the Lebesgue differentiation theorem. The set of points where the density is neither 0 nor 1 can be nonempty, as on the boundary of a square, but it has measure zero.

nodes.name: Borsuk–Ulam theorem
nodes.statement: Every continuous function from an n-sphere into n-dimensional Euclidean space maps some pair of antipodal points to the same point. Two points on a sphere are antipodal if they lie in exactly opposite directions from the center.
nodes.by: First proved by Karol Borsuk, 1933, who attributed the formulation of the problem to Stanisław Ulam; first mentioned by Lyusternik and Shnirel'man, 1930
nodes.note: It has several equivalent statements in terms of odd functions. For example, a continuous odd function from the n-sphere to n-dimensional Euclidean space has a zero.

nodes.name: Dupin's theorem
