nodes.statement: In a threefold orthogonal system of surfaces, the intersection curve of any two surfaces from different pencils is a curvature line. A threefold orthogonal system consists of three pencils of surfaces such that any two surfaces from different pencils intersect orthogonally.
nodes.by: Named after the French mathematician Charles Dupin
nodes.note: A curvature line is a curve on a surface that has at every point the direction of a principal curvature.

nodes.name: De Branges's theorem
nodes.statement: Let f be a holomorphic, one-to-one function on the open unit disk with f(0) = 0 and f′(0) = 1, with Taylor series f(z) = z + ∑ aₙzⁿ (n ≥ 2). Then |aₙ| ≤ n for all n ≥ 2.
nodes.by: Posed by Bieberbach, 1916; proved by de Branges, 1985
nodes.note: It is also known as the Bieberbach conjecture. The bound is sharp: the Koebe function has aₙ = n for all n, and equality for some n ≥ 2 holds only for rotated Koebe functions.

nodes.name: Stromquist–Woodall theorem
nodes.statement: Take a circular cake, the interval [0,1] with its endpoints identified, and n continuous measures on it, one for each person's valuation. Then for every fraction w in [0,1] there is a subset that every person values at exactly the fraction w of the total value, and this subset is a union of at most n − 1 intervals, so 2n − 2 cuts suffice.
nodes.by: Named after Stromquist and Woodall, who also proved that the bound n − 1 is tight
nodes.note: If the cake is not circular, the subset may be a union of up to n intervals.

nodes.name: Cantor's intersection theorem
nodes.statement: A decreasing nested sequence of non-empty, closed and bounded subsets of the real numbers has a non-empty intersection.
nodes.by: Named after Georg Cantor
nodes.note: The real-number version follows from the general topological statement about compact sets, but is typically used as a lemma in proving the Heine–Borel theorem. It fails for open bounded sets, for unbounded closed sets, and in the rational numbers.

nodes.name: Cauchy's convergence test
nodes.statement: A series a₀ + a₁ + a₂ + ⋯ of real or complex numbers converges if and only if for every ε > 0 there is a natural number N such that |aₙ₊₁ + aₙ₊₂ + ⋯ + aₙ₊ₚ| < ε for all n > N and all p ≥ 1.
nodes.by: Augustin-Louis Cauchy, 1821
nodes.note: It works because the real and complex numbers are complete, so a series converges exactly when its partial sums form a Cauchy sequence. Cauchy published it in his textbook Cours d'Analyse.

nodes.name: Cauchy–Hadamard theorem
nodes.statement: For a power series ∑ cₙ(z − a)ⁿ in one complex variable, with a and cₙ complex, the radius of convergence R at the point a satisfies 1/R = limsup |cₙ|^(1/n). If the limsup is ∞, the series does not converge near a; if it is 0, the radius of convergence is ∞ and the series converges on the entire plane.
nodes.by: Augustin-Louis Cauchy, 1821; rediscovered by Jacques Hadamard, who first published it in 1888
nodes.note: It describes the radius of convergence of a power series. A version for several complex variables also holds.

nodes.name: Mahler's inequality
nodes.statement: For any positive numbers x₁,…,xₙ and y₁,…,yₙ, ((x₁ + y₁)(x₂ + y₂)⋯(xₙ + yₙ))^(1/n) ≥ (x₁x₂⋯xₙ)^(1/n) + (y₁y₂⋯yₙ)^(1/n). In words, the geometric mean of the sums is at least the geometric mean of the x's plus the geometric mean of the y's.
nodes.by: Named after Kurt Mahler
nodes.note: It follows from the inequality of arithmetic and geometric means.

nodes.name: Ehresmann's lemma
nodes.statement: Let f: M → N be a smooth map between smooth manifolds that is a surjective submersion and a proper map. Then f is a locally trivial fibration.
nodes.by: Charles Ehresmann
nodes.note: The properness condition always holds when M is compact. The result has many variants.

nodes.name: Harnack's inequality
nodes.statement: Let f be a non-negative function on a closed ball in ℝⁿ with radius R and centre x₀, continuous on the ball and harmonic in its interior. Then for every point x with |x − x₀| = r < R, (1 − r/R)/(1 + r/R)ⁿ⁻¹ · f(x₀) ≤ f(x) ≤ (1 + r/R)/(1 − r/R)ⁿ⁻¹ · f(x₀).
nodes.by: Introduced by Harnack, 1887
nodes.note: It is used to prove Harnack's theorem on the convergence of sequences of harmonic functions. Serrin and Moser generalized it to solutions of elliptic or parabolic partial differential equations.

nodes.name: Blumenthal's zero–one law
nodes.statement: Let X be an adapted right continuous Feller process on [0,∞) whose starting value X₀ is constant with probability one. Then every event in the germ sigma algebra of X at time 0 (the events determined by the path of X on every interval [0, s] with s > 0) has probability 0 or 1.
nodes.by: Named after Robert McCallum Blumenthal
nodes.note: Loosely, a right continuous Feller process that starts from a deterministic point also has deterministic initial movement. The law extends to any process with the Markov property with respect to the right continuous filtration.

nodes.name: Borel–Cantelli lemma
nodes.statement: For any sequence of events, if the sum of their probabilities is finite, then the probability that infinitely many of them occur is 0. If the events are independent and the sum of their probabilities is infinite, then the probability that infinitely many of them occur is 1.
nodes.by: Émile Borel and Francesco Paolo Cantelli, in the first decades of the 20th century
nodes.note: It follows that the probability that infinitely many of a sequence of independent events occur is always 0 or 1, so the lemma is often called a zero-one law. It is a standard tool for proving the strong law of large numbers.

nodes.name: Young's inequality for products
nodes.statement: For non-negative numbers a and b and exponents α and β with 0 ≤ α, β ≤ 1 and α + β = 1, a^α · b^β ≤ αa + βb. Equality holds if and only if a = b or {α, β} = {0, 1}.
nodes.by: Named after William Henry Young
nodes.note: It can be used to prove Hölder's inequality, and it is widely used to estimate nonlinear terms in the theory of partial differential equations.

nodes.name: Cauchy's integral formula
nodes.statement: Let U be an open subset of the complex plane, let a closed disk D lie completely inside U, and let f be holomorphic on U. If γ is the boundary circle of D, oriented counterclockwise, then for every point a in the interior of D, f(a) = (1/2πi) ∮ f(z)/(z − a) dz over γ. Moreover f is infinitely differentiable, with f⁽ⁿ⁾(a) = (n!/2πi) ∮ f(z)/(z − a)ⁿ⁺¹ dz.
nodes.by: Named after Augustin-Louis Cauchy
nodes.note: It shows that a holomorphic function on a disk is determined by its values on the boundary, and that holomorphic functions are analytic.

nodes.name: Alternating series test
nodes.statement: An alternating series converges when its terms decrease monotonically in absolute value and approach zero in the limit.
nodes.by: Gottfried Leibniz, discussed in an unpublished work of 1676
nodes.note: The test is sufficient but not necessary: some convergent alternating series fail its first condition.

nodes.name: Riemann mapping theorem
nodes.statement: If U is a non-empty simply connected open subset of the complex plane ℂ that is not all of ℂ, then there is a biholomorphic map from U onto the open unit disk {z : |z| < 1}. A biholomorphic map is a bijective holomorphic map whose inverse is also holomorphic.
nodes.by: Stated by Bernhard Riemann, 1851, assuming a piecewise smooth boundary; first rigorous proof by William Fogg Osgood, 1900
nodes.note: Henri Poincaré proved that the map is unique once a chosen point z₀ of U is sent to 0 and the argument of the derivative at z₀ is fixed. Riemann's own proof relied on the Dirichlet principle and was flawed.

nodes.name: Muirhead's inequality
nodes.statement: For positive real numbers x₁, …, xₙ and real exponents a = (a₁, …, aₙ), let [a] be the average, over all n! orderings σ of the x's, of the products x_σ₁^a₁ ⋯ x_σₙ^aₙ. Then [a] ≤ [b] for all positive x₁, …, xₙ if and only if a = Pb for some doubly stochastic matrix P, which means that, with both lists sorted in decreasing order, each partial sum a₁ + ⋯ + aₖ is at most b₁ + ⋯ + bₖ and the full sums are equal.
nodes.by: Named after Robert Franklin Muirhead
nodes.note: In that case [a] = [b] only when a = b or all xᵢ are equal. The inequality generalizes the inequality of arithmetic and geometric means.

nodes.name: Inverse function theorem
nodes.statement: If a real function f has a continuous derivative on an open interval, then around any point where the derivative is not zero, f has an inverse function, which is also continuously differentiable and has derivative 1/f′(x) at the point f(x). More generally, if f is a continuously differentiable map from an open subset of ℝⁿ into ℝⁿ whose Jacobian determinant at a point a is nonzero, then f maps some open neighborhood of a one-to-one onto an open neighborhood of f(a), and this local inverse is continuously differentiable with derivative at f(a) equal to the inverse of the Jacobian matrix of f at a.
nodes.by: First established by Picard and Goursat using an iterative scheme
nodes.note: The continuity of the derivative cannot be dropped: f(x) = x + 2x² sin(1/x) with f(0) = 0 has f′(0) = 1 but is not one-to-one on any interval containing 0. Versions exist for holomorphic functions, maps between manifolds and maps between Banach spaces.

nodes.name: Bertrand–Diguet–Puiseux theorem
nodes.statement: Let p be a point on a smooth surface M, and let C(r) and A(r) be the circumference and the area of the geodesic circle and disc of radius r centered at p. Then the Gaussian curvature K(p) equals the limit as r → 0⁺ of 3(2πr − C(r))/(πr³), and also the limit as r → 0⁺ of 12(πr² − A(r))/(πr⁴).
nodes.by: Named after Joseph Bertrand, Victor Puiseux, and Charles François Diguet
nodes.note: The theorem is closely related to the Gauss–Bonnet theorem.

nodes.name: Riemann–Lebesgue lemma
nodes.statement: If f is a Lebesgue integrable function on ℝⁿ, that is, a measurable function with finite integral of |f|, then its Fourier transform tends to 0 as |ξ| → ∞. Together with the continuity of the Fourier transform, this means the Fourier transform maps L¹(ℝⁿ) into the continuous functions vanishing at infinity.
nodes.by: Named after Bernhard Riemann and Henri Lebesgue

nodes.name: Schwarz–Ahlfors–Pick theorem
nodes.statement: Let U be the unit disk with the Poincaré metric ρ, let S be a Riemann surface with a Hermitian metric σ whose Gaussian curvature is ≤ −1, and let f: U → S be a holomorphic function. Then σ(f(z₁), f(z₂)) ≤ ρ(z₁, z₂) for all z₁, z₂ in U.
nodes.by: Lars Ahlfors, 1938
nodes.note: It extends the Schwarz–Pick lemma, which says holomorphic self-maps of the unit disk do not increase Poincaré distance. Shing-Tung Yau proved a generalization in 1973.

nodes.name: Pokhozhaev's identity
nodes.statement: Let g be a continuous real-valued function with g(0) = 0, and let G(s) be the integral of g from 0 to s. Suppose that u is locally bounded on ℝⁿ, ∇u is in L²(ℝⁿ), G(u) is in L¹(ℝⁿ), and u solves −∇²u = g(u) in the sense of distributions. Then ((n−2)/2)·∫|∇u|² dx = n·∫G(u) dx, with both integrals taken over ℝⁿ.
nodes.by: Obtained by S.I. Pokhozhaev; the general form stated here is due to H. Berestycki and P.-L. Lions
nodes.note: It is similar to the virial theorem and is also known as G.H. Derrick's theorem.

nodes.name: Hardy's inequality
nodes.statement: If a₁, a₂, a₃, … are non-negative real numbers and p > 1, then ∑ₙ₌₁^∞ ((a₁ + a₂ + … + aₙ)/n)^p ≤ (p/(p−1))^p · ∑ₙ₌₁^∞ aₙ^p. When the right-hand side is finite, equality holds if and only if every aₙ = 0.
nodes.by: G. H. Hardy, 1920
nodes.note: An integral version says that for p > 1 and a non-negative measurable function f, the integral from 0 to ∞ of ((1/x)∫₀ˣ f(t) dt)^p is at most (p/(p−1))^p times the integral from 0 to ∞ of f^p. Hardy's 1920 note proved at least the discrete version with a worse constant, and his original formulation was an integral form slightly different from these.

nodes.name: Parseval's identity
nodes.statement: Let f be a square-integrable function on [−π, π] with Fourier coefficients f̂(n) = (1/2π)∫ f(x)e^(−inx) dx, the integral taken over [−π, π]. Then the sum of |f̂(n)|² over all integers n equals (1/2π) times the integral of |f(x)|² over [−π, π].
nodes.by: Named after Marc-Antoine Parseval
nodes.note: It is a generalized Pythagorean theorem: in a Hilbert space with an orthonormal basis, the squared length of a vector equals the sum of the squares of its components. The Plancherel theorem is the analogous result for the Fourier transform.

nodes.name: Open mapping theorem (functional analysis)
nodes.statement: If a bounded (continuous) linear operator between Banach spaces is surjective, then it is an open map. In particular, a bijective bounded linear operator from one Banach space to another has a bounded inverse.
nodes.by: Named after Stefan Banach and Juliusz Schauder
nodes.note: Completeness of both spaces is essential: the statement fails if either is only a normed vector space.

nodes.name: Reynolds transport theorem
nodes.statement: Let Ω(t) be a time-dependent region with boundary ∂Ω(t), and let f be a scalar-, vector- or tensor-valued function. Then d/dt of the integral of f over Ω(t) equals the integral of ∂f/∂t over Ω(t) plus the integral over ∂Ω(t) of (v·n) f, where n is the outward unit normal and v is the velocity of the boundary surface element (not the flow velocity).
nodes.by: Named after Osborne Reynolds (1842–1912)
nodes.note: It is a three-dimensional generalization of the Leibniz integral rule and is useful in formulating the basic equations of continuum mechanics.

nodes.name: Borel graph theorem
nodes.statement: Let X and Y be Hausdorff locally convex spaces and let u : X → Y be linear. If X is the inductive limit of an arbitrary family of Banach spaces, Y is a Souslin space, and the graph of u is a Borel set in X × Y, then u is continuous.
nodes.by: L. Schwartz
nodes.note: It generalizes the closed graph theorem and shows that the closed graph theorem holds for linear maps between most spaces encountered in analysis.

nodes.name: Dixmier–Ng theorem
nodes.statement: Let X be a normed space. Then the following are equivalent: (1) there is a Hausdorff locally convex topology on X for which the closed unit ball of X is compact; (2) there is a Banach space Y such that X is isometrically isomorphic to the dual of Y.
nodes.by: Kung-fu Ng, who called it a variant of a theorem proven earlier by Jacques Dixmier
nodes.note: The direction from 2 to 1 follows from the Banach–Alaoglu theorem and the direction from 1 to 2 follows from the Bipolar theorem.

nodes.name: Haar's Tauberian theorem
nodes.statement: Let f(t) be non-negative and continuous for t ≥ 0, with finite Laplace transform F(s) = ∫₀^∞ e^(−st) f(t) dt for s > 0, so that F(x+iy) is defined for all x > 0. Suppose that: (1) for y ≠ 0, F(x+iy) has continuous boundary values F(iy) as x → +0, and on the imaginary axis F(iy) = C/(iy) + ψ(iy), where ψ(iy) has finite derivatives up to order r and the r-th derivative is bounded on every finite interval; (2) ∫₀^∞ e^(ity) F(x+iy) dy converges uniformly in t ≥ T for fixed x > 0 and T > 0; (3) F(x+iy) → 0 as y → ±∞, uniformly in x ≥ 0; (4) F′(iy), …, F^(r)(iy) tend to 0 as y → ±∞; (5) the integrals of e^(ity) F^(r)(iy) over (−∞, y₁] and over [y₂, ∞) converge uniformly in t ≥ T for fixed y₁ < 0, y₂ > 0 and T > 0. Then t^r (f(t) − C) → 0 as t → ∞.
nodes.by: Named after Alfréd Haar; this simplified form is given by William Feller
nodes.note: It relates the asymptotic behaviour of a continuous function to properties of its Laplace transform and is related to the integral formulation of the Hardy–Littlewood Tauberian theorem. A more detailed version allows several singular terms on a boundary line Re s = a.

nodes.name: Kan–Thurston theorem
nodes.statement: Every path-connected topological space X is homology-equivalent to the classifying space K(G,1) of some discrete group G: there is a map K(G,1) → X that induces an isomorphism on homology.
nodes.by: Daniel Kan and William Thurston, 1976
nodes.note: The group cohomology of G is the same as the cohomology of X, so the theorem is sometimes read as saying that homotopy theory can be viewed as part of group theory.

nodes.name: Weinstein conjecture
nodes.statement: On a compact contact manifold, the Reeb vector field of every contact form has at least one periodic orbit.
nodes.by: Alan Weinstein, 1978
nodes.note: It was proved for contact hypersurfaces in ℝ²ⁿ in 1986, later for cotangent bundles and wider classes of aspherical manifolds. Clifford Taubes proved it for all closed 3-dimensional manifolds.

nodes.name: Cramér–Wold theorem
nodes.statement: A Borel probability measure on ℝ^k is uniquely determined by all of its one-dimensional projections. In the form used for convergence: random vectors Xₙ of dimension k converge in distribution to a random vector X if and only if, for every (t₁, …, t_k) in ℝ^k, the sum t₁Xₙ₁ + … + t_kXₙₖ converges in distribution to t₁X₁ + … + t_kX_k.
nodes.by: Harald Cramér and Herman Ole Andreas Wold, 1936
nodes.note: It is used as a method for proving joint convergence results. If the Xₙ take values in ℝ₊^k, it suffices to take (t₁, …, t_k) in ℝ₊^k.

nodes.name: Open mapping theorem (complex analysis)
nodes.statement: If U is a domain of the complex plane ℂ and f : U → ℂ is a non-constant holomorphic function, then f is an open map: it sends open subsets of U to open subsets of ℂ.
nodes.note: It shows a sharp difference between holomorphy and real-differentiability. For example, a non-constant holomorphic function cannot map an open disk onto a portion of a line.

nodes.name: F. Riesz's theorem
nodes.statement: A Hausdorff topological vector space is finite-dimensional if and only if it is locally compact.
nodes.by: Named after Frigyes Riesz
nodes.note: The theorem and its consequences are used throughout functional analysis, often without being mentioned.

nodes.name: Radó's theorem on harmonic functions
nodes.statement: Let Ω be an open, connected and convex subset of the plane ℝ² with smooth boundary, and let D be the unit disk. Then for any homeomorphism μ from the boundary of D to the boundary of Ω, there is a unique harmonic function u : D → Ω that equals μ on the boundary of D, and u is a diffeomorphism.
nodes.by: Named after Tibor Radó

nodes.name: Hille–Yosida theorem
nodes.statement: Let A be a linear operator defined on a linear subspace D(A) of a Banach space X, let ω be a real number and M > 0. Then A generates a strongly continuous semigroup T with ‖T(t)‖ ≤ M·e^(ωt) if and only if A is closed, D(A) is dense in X, and every real λ > ω belongs to the resolvent set of A with ‖(λI − A)⁻ⁿ‖ ≤ M/(λ − ω)ⁿ for all positive integers n.
nodes.by: Einar Hille and Kōsaku Yosida, independently, around 1948
nodes.note: For contraction semigroups (M = 1, ω = 0) only the case n = 1 has to be checked; this case is widely used in the theory of Markov processes. When the name is reserved for contraction semigroups, the general case is called the Feller–Miyadera–Phillips theorem.

nodes.name: Dugundji extension theorem
nodes.statement: Let X be a metrizable space, A a closed subset of X, and L a locally convex topological vector space. Then every continuous map f : A → L has a continuous extension F : X → L whose image F(X) lies in the convex hull of f(A).
nodes.by: James Dugundji
nodes.note: It is in a sense a generalization of the Tietze–Urysohn extension theorem, replacing the real line as target by an arbitrary locally convex space.

nodes.name: Four vertex theorem
nodes.statement: The curvature along a simple, closed, smooth plane curve (smooth enough, for example C², that its curvature varies continuously) has at least four local extrema: at least two local maxima and at least two local minima. If the curvature is constant along an arc, every point of that arc counts as such an extremum.
nodes.by: First proved for convex curves by Syamadas Mukhopadhyaya, 1909; proved for more general curves by Adolf Kneser, 1912
nodes.note: A local extremum of the curvature is called a vertex, and an ellipse has exactly four. The vertices correspond to the cusps of the curve's evolute, so the evolute of such a curve has at least four cusps.
